items.title: Russian glide bomb attack on Zaporizhzhia kills at least 15 people including three children
paragraphs: Russia has attacked the Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia with five glide bombs, killing at least 15 people including three children, President Volodymyr Zelensky and emergency services have said.

The glide bombs hit residential buildings in the south-eastern city. At least 16 other people were injured in the attack, with more still missing and believed to be under the rubble after the strike on Saturday morning.
Zelensky said 13 other regions had also been hit overnight, adding: "Our responses to [these] Russian strikes will come".
The Russian attacks happened just hours after President Donald Trump announced a deal to import Russian diesel into the US.
Photos and videos from the site of one of the strikes show an apartment block mostly destroyed.
"The ground floor was hit, and the floors above just collapsed," acting Mayor Regina Kharchenko told Ukrainian television, speaking from the scene.
She said more than 80 workers were involved in ongoing search and rescue operations which are expected to continue throughout the day.
The rescuers regularly stop to listen for any noises made by survivors who could be under the rubble.
Kharchenko said Russia had struck at "our very heart" and "our littlest ones" were among those killed, adding that their deaths were "awful grief for their families. For the city."
Zelensky has heavily criticised Trump's diesel deal with Russia, calling it a gift to President Vladimir Putin that amounts to "an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged".
More recently, in his response to the overnight strikes, he said "Russia interprets any easing of pressure as a signal that it can supposedly continue the war.
"Russia must understand that the war needs to be stopped, and for that, it must feel its losses," he wrote on X, external.
Both Russia and Ukraine have stepped up attacks on infrastructure in recent months, as the war between the two countries drags on.
Zaporizhzhia is a major regional centre with more than 700,000 residents. It is located less than 10 miles (16 km) from the front line and is frequently attacked by Russian drones and missiles.
The latest strikes on the city comes amid a sharp increase in the number of Russian attacks that are causing higher numbers of civilian casualties.
On Thursday, at least 33 people were killed in another Russian glide bomb attack on two civilian buses in Kramatorsk, in the eastern Donetsk region.
The day before, 22 people including five children died as a Russian missile hit an apartment block in the town of Pryluky, east of Kyiv.
According to the UN, the number of civilian casualties in Ukraine jumped by 55%, external in the first eight months of this year.
Russia has also targeted Ukrainian energy infrastructure, ramping up attacks every winter since Putin launched a full-scale invasion in 2022.
For its part, Ukraine has attacked Russia's infrastructure - with the latest being strikes on data centres owned by tech giant Yandex.

items.title: Green Party MP wants to make sure it is 'not vulnerable to extremists'
paragraphs: A Green Party MP has said her party needs to make sure it is not "vulnerable to capture by extremists and racists" after members voted for a motion that claimed Zionism was racism.

The motion put forward by activists, which became formal policy after it was approved at the Green's conference earlier this month, has divided senior party figures and been criticised by Jewish groups.
Westminster leader Ellie Chowns told the BBC it was a "significant and damaging policy" and she would work to reform the Green Party.
It comes after ex-leader Caroline Lucas said it was not being protected from entryism - where people sign up to a party to try to change it.

Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today Programme on Saturday, Chowns said: "I don't know if there are extremists and racists in my party. But I want to make sure that my party isn't vulnerable to capture by extremists and racists."
The MP described Zionism as a "contested concept" and said the motion did not represent the views of the large majority of Green Party members, "nor of people in the country".
Chowns said the motion would be a "distraction from the very important work" the party has been doing campaigning for Palestinian rights.

She added: "I think it is clear that if we have policy, such significant and damaging policy, made by a vote of just 0.4% of our members, that something isn't working in our structures and our policy-making process."
Members of the Green Party of England and Wales endorsed the policy motion by 1,022 votes to 813.
There are 230,000 members of the Green party overall and not everyone attended the conference.
The policy also backs a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine", which includes modern-day Israel.
It defines Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state".

The Board of Deputies of British Jews and the Jewish Leadership Council, which criticised the motion, said: "Zionism is anti-racism, creating a refuge for Jews in their ancient homeland after millennia of persecution outside it."
Appearing on BBC Radio 4 programme Any Questions on Friday, Lucas said she was not putting any blame on the party's current leader, Zack Polanski, who she said had done "great things" for the party.
"Our constitution was written decades ago, well before we had MPs, before we had mayors, before we had anything like the number of that we have today," the ex-leader said.
Lucas, who was for years the face of the Greens as its first and sole MP until 2024, added the party needed to be made "a welcoming place for Jewish people."

A Green Party spokesperson said: "Green Party membership has increased since Zack Polanksi announced his leadership bid in May 2025. Unlike other political parties, our members can bring and set policy.

"This is one motion alongside dozens of others that was discussed at our biggest-ever party conference. Every motion submitted to conference undergoes debate and no single interest group drives policy. "
Polanski, who is Jewish, previously told the BBC he would not have voted for the motion and instead would have voted for an amended version.
However, he said the "substantial part of the motion", that "the displacement and genocide of the Palestinian people is clearly underpinned by a racist ideology" was "obvious".
Israel has repeatedly denied its actions in Gaza amount to genocide.
Ashok Kumar, a Green Party member and part of the Greens for Palestine group, voted for the motion and told the BBC last week it was about "Palestinian liberation."
He said he didn't feel the vote was harming the image of the Green Party, and that a growing number of people see this as a core issue.
"They see the violence that's (been) occurring over the last three years," he told BBC Politics Live., external "So, I think the Zionist position is actually the marginal position.

items.title: Dozens injured and buildings damaged as tornadoes hit Sicily
paragraphs: Two tornadoes have struck the coastal town of Marsala in western Sicily, injuring dozens of people, damaging buildings including a school, and overturning cars.
A series of videos began to circulate on Friday morning showing two waterspouts approaching the Sicilian town from the sea as people braced for their arrival.

Dozens of people were reported injured, with at least 11 taken to hospital after being struck by flying debris and shattered glass. Among the most seriously injured was a 70-year-old man admitted to Mazara del Vallo hospital in a critical condition with several fractures.

A school was also hit by the powerful winds, leaving six children with minor cuts and abrasions. At the time the tornado struck, 273 pupils were inside the building, all of whom were safely evacuated. Drone footage showing the aftermath revealed extensive damage to the school, with windows shattered and desks and chairs overturned.

In recent years, people in southern Italy have been bracing for the arrival of a “medicane” – a rare Mediterranean storm with hurricane-like characteristics, capable of producing winds exceeding 60 miles an hour and waves reaching five metres in height.

The weather system developed amid intense heat over north Africa and unusually warm Mediterranean waters. Scientists have warned that rising sea temperatures, driven by the climate emergency, can provide additional energy for powerful storms in the region.

According to experts, record temperatures in the Mediterranean contributed to the freak storm that sank the Bayesian, a super yacht off the coast of Sicily, in August 2024, killing seven people including the tech tycoon Mike Lynch and his teenage daughter.

items.title: Ongoing lawsuits allege GLP-1s can cause serious harm. But we don't know how often
paragraphs: Shelley and Todd Engel. The Engel family hide caption
Todd Engel had operated heavy machinery, like forklifts and rubber-tire loaders, around warehouses and highways in suburban Maryland for four decades.

In early 2023, Engel's doctor put him on Ozempic, a GLP-1, for diabetes. That winter, on New Year's Eve, Engel woke up feeling as if a patch covered his right eye: "I couldn't see anything. It was all dark. It was black."

The doctor told Engel and his wife Shelley it was a form of optic neuropathy — NAION, for short – an inoperable condition caused by tiny strokes that cut off blood flow to his eye. When the doctor listed all known causes, Shelley Engel specifically asked about Ozempic. "'We have heard nothing about that,'" she recalls the doctor telling her.

Seven months later, the journal JAMA Ophthalmology did publish research showing higher rates of NAION among diabetic patients taking Ozempic, or semaglutide, as the active ingredient name is known. But neither Engel nor his doctor were aware, so Engel kept taking weekly shots until his left eye went black, just as the other had done the year prior.

More than one in 10 Americans are taking a GLP-1 drug for weight loss, according to a recent Gallup analysis, and one in seven has taken them at some point. The drugs are prescribed for a growing number of conditions and come with a range of side effects.
Engel has filed a lawsuit alleging the maker of Ozempic, Novo Nordisk, failed to warn patients and doctors about the risk of NAION.
His suit is part of two main ongoing consolidated lawsuits alleging life-threatening or life-altering harm from GLP-1 drugs.
In a statement to NPR, spokespeople for Novo Nordisk pointed to subsequent research casting doubt on whether their GLP-1 drug causes NAION, for example, and said the cases are without merit.
Want the latest stories on the science of healthy living? Subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.

The legal question before the courts hinges in part on whether the GLP-1 drugs caused the harm. Observational data can show correlation — that people taking GLP-1s were perhaps more likely to have this eye complication occur — but not causation. For that, more detailed investigation is needed.

When the JAMA Ophthalmology study came out showing the correlation between NAION and diabetic patients on Ozempic or semaglutide, two medical groups critiqued it. The American Academy of Ophthalmology and the North American Neuro-Ophthalmology Society issued their own consumer clarification saying, in part: "This is not the type of study that can show the treatment caused NAION." The groups did acknowledge there is a potential link, but further research would be necessary to determine that. For now, they don't recommend that patients stop taking their GLP-1s.

The Food and Drug Administration keeps a database tracking adverse events. It's one of the only mechanisms for doctors, patients and drug companies to submit reports of complications possibly linked to pharmaceuticals. Reporting is mostly voluntary and the agency does not verify the reports, but it is a crucial first step to prompt regulators to do further research and eventually decide, for example, if labels need updating.

In this database, NPR found more than 1,000 reports of optic neuropathy linked to GLP-1s since 2024. That's out of nearly 190,000 reports made about the drug over that period, most of which included minor gastrointestinal issues, dosing errors or injection site redness.

Spokespeople for Novo Nordisk — maker of Ozempic and Wegovy — say NAION and other serious conditions are exceedingly rare in clinical trials. The company continues to collect and share data with the FDA about the side effects reported with the drug since going to market, but the agency has not requested warning-label changes. The FDA said in an email to NPR it has undertaken its own study to assess NAION risks, and is assessing claims and will "determine the need for regulatory action" once its assessment is complete.

That is not sufficient for patients today, says attorney Jonathan Orent, a lead court-appointed attorney on the two major multi-district litigation lawsuits alleging harms from GLP-1 drugs. He says drug makers ought to update warnings to doctors and patients — as they have in Europe — even if the conditions are rare.

It's necessary, Orent says, because "you're never going to have the population size to detect rarer events in a clinical trial; you're also never going to have the diversity of your real world population."

Orent's cases include 247 plaintiffs with NAION, and more than 4,000 with other serious digestive conditions like pancreatitis or gall stones. "These warnings would have made a difference in the lives of real people," he argues. In an emailed statement, Eli Lilly, whose GLP-1 drug brands Mounjaro and Zepbound contain the active ingredient tirzepatide said it will "vigorously defend against these claims."
NPR's analysis of the FDA's adverse events data show 1,928 reports of pancreatitis since 2024. (Other forms of pancreatitis are also listed, including 135 cases of necrotizing pancreatitis.)

Engel says he would've stopped taking Ozempic had he known that it might have put him at risk for blindness. Now, he mourns all he's lost, including the ability to work or walk the beach unaided. "Being able to play ball … with my grandchildren, I can't do these things anymore," he says. "I will never, never be able to see my wife's beautiful face every day."

Obesity and diabetes are complex metabolic diseases that affect many organs, and increase risks for other ailments. That's part of what makes it hard to pinpoint whether problems that patients encounter on GLP-1 drugs are caused by the drugs themselves.

That's part of why Emory University diabetes specialist Mohammed Ali, for example, did not report any of the three patients he's treated who developed serious problems, like pancreatitis or gallstones, while taking GLP-1s, to the FDA's adverse events database.
He says he wasn't certain those problems were caused by the drugs themselves, even if the timing was suspicious.
"They may have had subclinical disease," Ali says. "In other words, we didn't know they had preexisting pancreatitis or preexisting gallstones."
The boom in online sales, where GLP-1s are heavily marketed, also adds to the challenge, says pharmacist Robert Miller at the West Texas Poison Control Center.

Buying drugs on Instagram? "That's definitely a new thing," Miller says, and many sites offer little to no medical supervision of patients. That's why, he says, more calls are coming into poison-control centers like his, with patients reporting vomiting or other GLP-1 side effects.
"So is there even a physician who's motivated to report side effects or someone the patient feels they can report those side effects to?" he says.
These questions are playing out now in court, where plaintiffs like the Engels are seeking damages from drugmakers.
But Shelley Engel also wants more side-effect warnings, which she says might've helped her husband avoid blindness. She says her husband's outgoing, vivacious personality has changed
"This could have been prevented, if we only knew," she says.
NPR correspondent Sydney Lupkin contributed to this report.

items.title: The Telo MT1 is a big truck trapped in a tiny truck’s body
paragraphs: I’m bouncing down the road in San Carlos, California, zipping past behemoth tech companies like EA and Oracle, in America’s smallest electric truck.
The Telo MT1 (which stands for “mini truck”) unquestionably turns heads because it looks so remarkably different from everything else on the market right now.

It has a nearly cab-over design, meaning that front-seat passengers sit almost directly over the front axle. It looks a lot like a Japanese kei truck, with a super-short nose and four doors. People stop to stare as we sit at stoplights or roll silently past.

The interior is surprisingly spacious, and while the seats are firm, they’re not uncomfortable, at least for short jaunts on the bumpy roads around Telo’s HQ. Telo Trucks cofounder and CEO Jason Marks drove us to the company’s offices ahead of my short one-block test drive, and from the passenger seat, the ride was firm but stable, thanks to a low center of gravity provided by the battery pack beneath the floor.

Behind the wheel, the MT1 feels like a lighter, more nimble pickup truck with a stiff, slightly bouncy ride without any payload in the bed, combined with all the low-end power, torque, and acceleration of an EV. Once we circle back around to the road in front of Telo’s offices, Marks has me come to a full stop and stomp on the accelerator to get a feel for just how much power the little truck puts down, remarking that this was the same road where Tesla used to do its customer test drives of the Roadster many years ago.
People stop to stare as we sit at stoplights

Marks says that the production version of the Telo will accelerate 0–60mph in an estimated four seconds. The truck easily rockets from a standstill, just like any other electric vehicle on the market today, a feat for a small startup with just 30 employees.

Despite its diminutive appearance, the tiny Telo truck can go toe-to-toe with the giant SUVs and Teslas that populate this area. The Telo is, as Marks likes to point out, actually the same size as a two-door Mini Cooper, but far more practical with a tow rating of 8,000lbs, a full-size bed (96 inches), and a bevy of neat hidden features that Telo hopes will offer a viable, if somewhat pricey, alternative to the giant pickup trucks that dominate the American market.

“I hope that our truck shows how amazing and fun and useful — especially useful — a small pickup truck can be, because the current big trucks are literally killing us,” Forrest North, Telo’s cofounder and CTO, said during our interview at Telo’s headquarters. “I mean, they’re fun to be up super high and look out and feel like you’re dominating the world, but they’re killing an extra, roughly, 5,000 people per year, so do we want to just give them a pass for that?”

Marks and North both live and work in the San Francisco Bay Area with their families, and both own pickup trucks: Marks because he has a 150lb three-legged dog he shuttles back and forth to the office every day, and North because he has a passion for the outdoors. Large pickup trucks can be useful, but they’re far from suitable for city life. That disconnect, as well as the founders’ passion for urban transportation, is what brought the two, along with Yves Behar, together to start Telo in 2022.

Marks previously worked on automotive safety and validation at National Instruments, while North is a former battery engineer at Tesla, founder of Mission Motors (one of the first electric motorcycle companies to break the land speed record for an electric motorcycle), and cofounder of Recargo, which developed EV charging app PlugShare. Behar is the founder of fuseproject, an industrial design and brand development firm. Marks and North met through a mutual friend in the startup space and discovered they’d gone to the same high school in Washington, where they both pole-vaulted. It was a “kindred spirit moment,” according to Marks.
“I hope that our truck shows how amazing and fun and useful — especially useful — a small pickup truck can be, because the current big trucks are literally killing us.”

Originally, their idea wasn’t about trucks at all — it was about electric motorcycles. Their initial pitch to an unnamed Silicon Valley VC firm included a slide deck comparing three concepts: an electric motorcycle, a small car, and a tiny truck. Everyone they talked to kept gravitating toward the tiny pickup. Sensing the enthusiasm, North pushed Marks to consider pivoting to building a truck, even though the motorcycle they’d planned was nearly complete. They even went so far as to poll about 200 people on the street and found that nearly 90 percent would rather have the truck. The next week, they pivoted from motorcycle to truck.

“It’s clear to me that the trucks have just kind of jumped the shark,” North said. “The only thing they can do now is be big.” Telo aims to change the conversation about what electric transportation in urban centers can look like.

For a small truck, the Telo MT1 packs a lot of range. At launch, the truck will come with a 77kWh battery pack, or a larger 106kWh pack that the company estimates will deliver up to 350 miles of range. The MT1 has a unique battery layout: a split pack with both 800V and 400V architecture. The 400V setup makes the Telo chargeable on Tesla’s V3 Supercharger infrastructure, while the 800V will let customers take advantage of new, higher-powered stations coming to market in areas like San Francisco.

Telo currently builds its battery packs in-house. Each cell is individually fused so that a single failure won’t trigger a cascade across the pack. According to Marks, in-house manufacturing allows them to maximize energy density and longevity — a feat that hinges on thermal management. The passive thermal management system operates while the vehicle is parked, maintaining cooler temperatures even in direct sunlight, while active liquid cooling engages only when the vehicle is running. Additionally, North noted that Telo’s latest cells deliver roughly 20 percent more energy than those they sourced just a year ago.
For a small truck, the Telo MT1 packs a lot of range

I drove one of two prototypes that Telo has been using for road testing. From the outside, the Telo looks smaller than its 152 inches of length suggest. With the lower rear section of the passenger seats (called the midgate) laid flat, you get a full-size, 96-inch truck bed.

To make up for the lack of a frunk, which most EVs have, Telo also developed a “monster” tunnel (named because, like in a kids’ story, it’s a “monster under the bed”), which passes door to door beneath the front of the truck bed. It’s accessible from either side and is large enough for a pair of roll-aboard carry-on suitcases to slide in endwise. Marks said that while they knew the front of the MT1 would be difficult to engineer, adding the monster tunnel created a tough engineering challenge because it sits exactly where the battery pack connects.

The interior is still being finalized, but Marks said that it will get two 13-inch digital displays that will support both Android Auto and Apple CarPlay. The steering wheel also has small scroll wheels, but most features will be controlled through the screen interface.

Japanese kei vehicles became a White House talking point late last year when President Donald Trump invited the tiny trucks to be built in the US. But making that actually happen is far more complicated because kei vehicles don’t meet US crash safety regulations.

Marks claimed that Telo has solved this problem with a completely new front end and an innovative front hinge pillar that took nearly four years to develop and hundreds of thousands of hours of simulated crashes to verify. In the Telo, the redesigned hinge pillar does the structural job of a conventional one while also carrying the strut mount, the cross-car beam, and the dash — consolidating several separate parts into one. This allowed the company to cut the front-end part count roughly in half, Marks said.

“We pretty much threw all [the conventional crash architecture] away and had to start from scratch,” Marks said. The company’s team includes Tesla’s former head of crash safety, brought on to help tackle the new front end and completely reengineer it.

“We have effectively six crash [paths], two bumper beams and two shock structures, a completely different architecture of a hinge pillar, a completely different architecture of a torque box to distribute the energy appropriately to the various parts of the car and save that occupant compartment as much as possible,” he said, comparing the crash innovations to those in a Smartcar. “Would any other automaker say we’re going to bet the world on being able to rethink crash?”
The company’s team includes Tesla’s former head of crash safety

AI tools have made the virtual crash-testing process much more affordable for startups, and Telo recently locked in its body in white, the sheet metal shell made up of the major structural pieces of the truck (think of it like a skeleton of a vehicle). It’s currently being built by US supplier Schwab Industries in Michigan.

Marks said Telo uses AI to run virtual crash tests around the clock, averaging roughly one test per hour. The next phase of crash testing will include cutting the body in white apart for what Marks called a “quasi-static validation,” and full crash testing (slamming the vehicle and its various parts into a wall to validate the virtual testing the company has done) will start next year before Telo starts customer deliveries.

“I think it’s one of the most exciting times to start a hardware company,” North said. “It’s always been like, hardware is hard. That’s always been the cliché, and I wouldn’t say hardware is easy, but I would say it’s gotten so much easier because of software and AI.”

The Telo MT1 will come in single-motor (rear-wheel drive) and dual-motor (all-wheel drive) layouts and offer add-ons like a solar-capable tonneau cover or camping shell. Reservations are open now for a refundable $152, and the base vehicle starts at $41,520. Marks said the company isn’t really worried about larger competitors like Ford’s upcoming midsized electric truck or Slate’s bare-bones EV because he sees their market entry as proof that a viable market exists for small electric pickup trucks.

North argued that Telo is also in a better position than either Slate or Ford right now because the company has fewer parts moving in and out of the country; it’s assembling its own battery packs and building the body in white stateside, making it largely exempt from the Trump administration’s tariffs. “The pack is the most expensive part of the vehicle build and the heart and soul of the vehicle,” Marks said, “so we had to keep it in-house.”

Marks said he’s been surprised by the volume of reservations: just over 14,000, with 70 percent of reservation-holders configuring AWD versions with the longer-range battery pack. He also noted that around 20 percent are first-time car buyers.

Telo is aiming for profitability at around 5,000 vehicles within roughly 24 months of deliveries. The company plans to get vehicles into customers’ hands sometime in 2027, depending on the validation timelines, but the MT1 still has to go through EPA and California air quality certification. Most reservations have come from places like LA, New York, the Bay Area, Seattle, Dallas, Washington, DC, Miami, and Denver, with almost everyone opting for the larger battery pack, regardless of drive configuration.

Marks pointed to Tesla as the trailblazer of EVs’ first real wave, proving electric cars could be fast, fun, and sporty. However, he believes the industry ultimately missed the chance to fully exploit their potential. Telo is tackling the problem by rethinking vehicle architecture from the ground up, returning to a “one-box” design made possible by eliminating wasted space.
Ultimately, Telo’s focus comes down to purpose, according to Marks: “What does electric enable for the experience of the user, and what value does that bring?”

While history has shown that the market isn’t kind to EV startups, in a world where giant American trucks increasingly barely fit in an average parking spot, the Telo MT1 and its creators are aiming to offer a capable electric pickup built for today’s cramped cities in the hope that Americans can get behind smaller and more capable electric vehicles.

items.title: The director of Fjord takes the ‘risky position’ of moderator
paragraphs: Cristian Mungiu’s sixth feature, Fjord, concerns a family on trial. They seem like good people, God-fearing. They’ve just moved from Romania to a small hamlet nestled in the fjords of rural Norway. There is Mamma (Renate Reinsve), Tata (a bald and bespectacled Sebastian Stan), and their passel of children. They are an openly religious and proselytizing family. The parents, unfashionably, believe in punitive consequences to actions. They would never be accused of gentle parenting. All ought to be well, only Norway in 2026 is extravagantly suspicious of the devout — their famous tolerance reserved for the secular.

Fjord starts quietly and builds subtly. We are with the family as they are introduced to their places of learning, employment, and worship. A second, Norwegian, family serves as their foil. Sort of. Questions arise, about what counts as discipline, what as punishment. To those wanting answers, objective analysis, which is to say a kind of measured purity, Mungiu says, come down to the mud with us! In the morally complex world of the movie, nothing is spared — a piano chord, a passing remark, hems of clothes — all are cast in a different light. We are all the more enriched for it.

The Verge spoke with Mungiu, who is himself Romanian, about how his early tenure in journalism informs his writing, what it was like living under Nicolae Ceaușescu’s dictatorial reign, Marxist literary theory, and the challenges and pleasures of thinking for oneself.
This interview has been condensed and edited for clarity.
I’d like to start with you at Cannes, where you said the question that Fjord raises is: Are there good minorities and bad minorities? I wonder if this question has changed for you since.

Not so much. I think that as much as we need to understand that there are good values in society, like tolerance for all the other minorities and inclusion of those who are different than us, we should always focus on this idea that sometimes even if there are minorities with whom we don’t share the same values, we need to be tolerant to those as well. If not, what makes us believe that we have a more liberal, progressive view on the world?
Of course, there is a limit. We all need to condemn violence, and we all need to be on the same side of helping people out.

But whenever we talk about, for example, religious beliefs, even if we are people who don’t share such beliefs, it’s good to be tolerant with them, if they want to share different views. You need to let them be.
“Even if there are minorities with whom we don’t share the same values, we need to be tolerant to those as well.”

There are so many people next to us who share a lot of irrational beliefs, from reading the horoscope to believing in alternative medicine. We let them be. Why would we condemn people for being religious? It’s good to try to convince them that actually it’s good to see that your beliefs are based on something rational, because eventually, we all influence the lives of others, and it’s good to make choices based on rational things. But you need to advance little by little, step by step. I don’t believe in this way of imposing views on others and making rules for others to change what they think. If you do that, you will only radicalize people.
You said you kept chancing upon articles about immigrant families in Nordic countries. Is reading the news part of your practice? Otherwise, where have your ideas come from?

I read a lot of news every day, and I keep a lot of these articles in special folders under different themes. And it took years before I decided to make a film based on the ideas in these articles, because in the beginning they are very spectacular. They are just informing us about something spectacular that has happened. While for me, the film should be something deeper, more profound, in the sense that I’m trying to figure out why those things have happened and what do they tell us about the world around us?

I try to avoid the sensational part of it and to try to dig down, and to understand what is it that it could tell you about your own life, and this is what I did for the original story as well. I needed some eight years from the moment when I read about it to the moment when I decided to make a film out of it.

Tell me more about your excavation process. Can you walk us through what is actually happening in those eight years? And specifically, can you tell us about the moment in the process when you go from research to fiction? What does that leap look like, or maybe it’s seamless?

It’s fair to say that I haven’t used all these 10 years to investigate. But I was aware all the time that this exists. For example, I decided to talk to this family who was involved in the most prominent case, in the most spoken-about case, from three years ago. I talked to them. I talked to their children. I went to Norway. I met their relatives. I went to see the house where everything happened. I took advantage in that moment to investigate more, and I met everybody that I could who was involved in that case. And people who were willing to talk to me. I talked to lawyers. I talked to all the press that covered the case. I talked to the translator they were having when talking to the police. I talked to the Barnevernet [Norwegian child welfare agency]. I talked to the NGOs who were involved a lot in such cases. Later on, I was a witness to the trials they were having on children issues. So I did my best to find all the points of view of people involved, not only in that case but in other cases.

And finally, I crafted the screenplay based a lot on the arguments that I was recording. I didn’t have to invent much. I just needed to organize the material, but I didn’t need to build a lot on what are the arguments of each of these two sides.

The fictional part of the film comes a lot from this second family, which is fully fictional, and that gave me the possibility of following the film from the point of view of the adults. I needed to be with the family, but I wanted to balance this point of view of the family with the point of view of another family with children and sharing the values of the society in which they live, a family with whom they need to communicate with because they are secluded in this fjord at the end of the world, and it was important for me to see how these values collide, and what changes in this process of being forced to communicate with others.
Tell us about your time as a reporter, early in your career. How did you decide to turn to film?

I started working in the press in 1987, and also this was a part of me getting closer to what I wanted to do. I wished that I could become a storyteller, and I wished already at that age — I was 19 — that I could become a filmmaker. Back then, becoming a student at the film school during communist times wasn’t really a fair process, so it wasn’t for me. So I was starting to get closer to becoming a writer. This is what I thought I could do. I started writing. And then I got to this newspaper, and I started practicing my writing and taking pictures. Two activities which were as close as I could to becoming a filmmaker without being able to become one on the spot. A lot of my style of writing screenplays today is still based on that period in which I learned how to write a piece of news.

But happily, you know, the wall fell. Communism collapsed. It was very passionate to be in the press for a while because people were hungry for what they were calling “truth” after such a long period in which we didn’t have a free press.

My style of writing was shaped in that period. I am not bringing, when I describe things, my own point of view. I’m describing an external situation, the way in which these things manifest, but I don’t draw the conclusion. I depict a situation, and I encourage you to use your critical spirit to understand the way it manifests. I am encouraging you also to take on this responsibility as a spectator, in which I’m not guiding you through the story. You have your freedom of interpreting based on facts, and making sure you analyze the facts. If you’re just analyzing what the characters say, you might be very easily manipulated. Manipulated, because, as you know, in cinema, characters lie, and are as manipulative as people are in real lives.
So it’s not that you wanted to be a filmmaker as such, but that you wanted to be a storyteller, and you found film?
I wanted to be a storyteller, and I thought that I’m going to be a writer. Then I was undergoing this period in my life in which I was watching a lot of films, very popular films.

Also being influenced by the Romanian films that I could watch in the period, which were very strange. Maybe it was, in part, the censorship, but probably it was also that the people that were encouraged to make films were not very talented. But they seemed to be made with people looking like us, and apparently using the same language as us, but actually nothing like that ever happened in reality. They were psychologically so unbelievable, and the dialogue was also a message that somebody wrote in the right order grammatically, and it was pure propaganda.
So, we started developing this idea that it shouldn’t be this complicated to make films. You just need to co-opt reality.
I want to tell you something funny about the message that I got today. Following a lot of these cases in the Nordic countries and talking to so many people, I became some sort of an expert.

I got a message this morning from a half-German, half-Norwegian family saying, Help. Help us. Nothing has changed. I’m trying to bring this forward. This is a topic about which we all need to have an opinion. But I’m not this superhero that can solve the situation.

It’s important to make this clear that the film is not just about Romania and Norway and the Barnevernet. The film is about what happens in the States too, for example. I think that this polarization of people needs to have an answer because we can’t continue living in these bubbles. This degree of hatred and aggression, which might end up badly, and very violent.
What do you do when people call you for help?

I started this promotional tour in Norway, and I met a lot of people from both sides talking to me. We ran across this very difficult confession of a spectator, this lady who was crying, telling us that she was experiencing these cases with such emotion that finally she decided, for fear of having her children taken away by the authorities, she decided to rather have an abortion.

We also met people telling us that they are 100 percent behind the point of view of the protection in the film, because if they were in the situation of having their children taken in a conservative society, nobody would care for them. I think this shows that people rather tend to imagine that the wrong and radical way of seeing the society can be compensated by another wrong and radical way, and this shouldn’t be the answer. The answer should be more attempts at integration, trying to be more empathic and more open to dialogue, if we wish to give a good example to the part of the society who think they can’t escape this idea that they already know the truth and there’s no way out.

In the court scene, Sebastian Stan’s character gestures at the ways in which liberal societies privilege physical harm over emotional or verbal harm. There is, of course, no such thing as a view from nowhere. I know you said your opinion doesn’t matter, but I would still like to know how you relate or do not relate to this argument.
Of course, we need to make this clear. As soon as there is proven violence in a family, we all need to act as soon as we can and save them. Be it children or women. Of course, we need to act.

But the film talks about the fact that in most cases, you are supposed to make a choice, not knowing what happened in the family. You are just having assumptions in most of these cases, and this is why Fjord is crafted as such.

After investigating for two years and talking to all the parties involved, I can’t tell if this real family, which was involved in the real case, was violent or not. I don’t know. I’m not saying that they were not. I don’t know, because even if I talk to them and to their children... But I noticed that when people are making choices in Norway, for example, or us in society in general, we tend to be biased by our own stereotypes about the situation, and it’s very difficult to position yourself in an objective point of view. This doesn’t really exist.
“I was curious enough to see what happens in liberal, progressive societies when the conservatives all of a sudden become a minority. ”

So you need to be aware that you’re biased, that you are seeing the situation from your perspective, and when you’re mentioning that you’re doing whatever is best for the benefit of the children, actually you tend to believe that your solution is for the best, while the others will believe the same if they act on their opinions.
And of course, you know, we need to make sure that there is enough freedom accepted by everybody into our societies, so that minorities have the right to be who they want to be.

But after making a film that was speaking a lot about how minorities are being discriminated in conservative society, I was curious enough to see what happens in liberal, progressive societies when the conservatives all of a sudden become a minority. Wouldn’t you expect that they are treated with more empathy for not sharing the same values with the majority? Well, actually, they are not. The fact that you belong to the majority tends to be more important to you than the values that belong to your ideology.
Literary theorist Terry Eagleton has a quote that goes, “Ideology is like bad breath. We only recognize it in other people.”

I understand precise choreography is part of your process. You have talked about how you also try your best to avoid cutting because that is an interpretation. Does that mean the point of art is verisimilitude, capturing reality? And if not that, what are movies for? Why do you make movies?

I believe in diversity in filmmaking, and I think that making entertainment is also a valid way of making films, but it shouldn’t be the only way. The films that I try to make are films that try to make people think a little bit more, and to make them aware of the world which exists next to theirs. I’m using this as a tool to make you aware that you should be very careful of what happens next to you.

There isn’t anything like an objective point of view, but the best I could do is not to be manipulative with my style. I’m not making a film biased by one of these points of view. I’m taking this risky position of a moderator, bringing two sets of values in front of you so that you can double check your values and to remember when was the last time when you doubted that you are on the good side of things? Everybody else is so convinced that they are as right as you, but you know the first step into entering some sort of a dialogue is listening to others.
Fjord was released in select US theaters October 9th, with a wide release on October 23rd.

items.title: Rogue Anthropic AI agent gave US police fake tip in unsolved murder case
paragraphs: An artificial intelligence (AI) agent, developed by Anthropic, went rogue and sent US police a fake tip about an unsolved murder earlier this year, authorities have revealed.

The Philadelphia Police Department said the tip, sent on 18 July, was "flagged as spam" and not passed on for investigation, but it criticised the tech company for taking more than two months to detect and report the breach.

In a statement police said that the bogus tip came through a public website where people can share information on unsolved murders, and that the AI agent had written that it may have information on a case, and claimed to have seen "someone matching the description".

It is believed to be the first time an AI agent has sent fabricated information to authorities, but is the latest in a series of incidents involving rogue AI activity, including hacking systems or taking control of platforms.
Citing Anthropic, the police department said the AI agent had been running a test that involved interactions with randomly selected websites, when it sent the fake tip.
Anthropic discovered the breach on 28 September, more than two months after the message had been sent, and shut down the automatic testing process that was behind it, police said.
But authorities were not notified for another nine days - on 7 October.
"The company must strengthen its safeguards to prevent similar incidents from impacting city systems without the city's knowledge," Philadelphia police said in a statement to local media, external.
"The two-month delay in detecting and reporting the incident to the city is unacceptable."
The police department added that there were no signs of breaches to any departmental systems, and that its safeguarding processes stopped the fake tip from getting past its spam folder.
But the safeguards "do not diminish the seriousness of an AI system presenting fabricated information as though it came from a person with knowledge of a homicide," the police statement said.
Anthropic this week published a report, external detailing multiple types of "unintended" actions its agents have taken.
Organisations that have been impacted also included several US government agencies including the White House, it said.
The US State Department said the AI agent had filed 20 visa applications using a form on its website, but that they were incomplete and not processed, according to reports.
President Donald Trump recently announced an AI taskforce, which he said will coordinate engagement between the government and all parties, including AI companies, consumers, and religious groups.
Earlier this year, a rogue agent by rival tech company, Open AI, hacked an Australian government website and accessed private data on the country's universal healthcare scheme, Medicare.
In another instance, more than 1,200 OpenAI agents went rogue and started unexpectedly communicating, leading to a large group banding together to hack into AI platform Hugging Face.

items.title: UK must not be beholden to foreign AI, says head of Alan Turing Institute
paragraphs: The UK must not become dependent on foreign AI systems that can be switched off at short notice and must develop its own versions of the technology, according to the head of the Alan Turing Institute.
The country needs a stronger domestic position in AI in response to the US and China’s runaway leadership in the field, with “national resilience” a key focus for ATI said George Williamson.
The institute is the UK’s leading AI research body and is under new leadership after the government, its main source of funding, demanded a strategic shift.

“As AI becomes more embedded in critical services, in domains like defence, national security, critical infrastructure and healthcare we shouldn’t depend solely on systems we can’t inspect or control, or that could be restricted or even switched off,” said Williamson.

In June Washington temporarily blocked the release outside the US of Anthropic’s latest models, and has reportedly asked leading AI labs to withhold their models from being tested by the UK’s AI Security Institute until they have been examined by AISI’s US counterpart.
“We’ve seen now that both political and commercial pressures mean we may not have access [to AI] in all the circumstances when we want it. That is not a place where a nation wants to be,” he said.
Williamson added: “There’s a set of circumstances where it would be a good idea for us to have something that we don’t have to ask other people’s permission to use.”
He said national resilience would be a focus of ATI’s work amid concern about the geopolitical situation and the risk posed by increasingly powerful AI systems.

Those concerns were highlighted last month by the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, announcing a new national centre to tackle state-backed disinformation, and Anthropic predicting the technology had a greater than 10% chance of wiping out humanity by 2030.
“It’s a moment when national resilience is definitely what the country needs and it’s definitely a thing I think the Turing institute can help with,” he said.

“We are facing a more adversarial world, more frequent shocks to our critical infrastructure and now powerful AI amplifying these threats. To strengthen national resilience, the Turing will focus on securing critical systems against disruption, countering threats from AI itself and helping to shape the right strategic AI capability for the UK.”

Williamson said the institute could assist in building such resilience by helping produce uses for AI “for the public good”, working on areas from weather forecasting to farming, as well as helping spot disinformation. Referring to state-led disinformation campaigns, he said: “It’s very dangerous for the state of democracy and it’s an area that we can monitor.”

Williamson is the former head of His Majesty’s Government Communications Centre, a secretive government body that makes gadgets for UK spy agencies and counts Alan Turing – the second world war codebreaker and AI pioneer after which ATI is named – among its former staff.

Williamson said it had become clear in recent months that the UK needed “more agency on access to technology” and a stronger sovereign position in AI. “It feels pretty uncomfortable if you don’t have some control or ability to use technologies when you want them, and also harder to imagine how you build an economy on the top of stuff that can disappear,” he said.

In recent weeks Christine Lagarde, the president of the European Central Bank, and Ursula von der Leyen, the president of the European Commission, have urged Europe to be more self-sufficient in AI, with Lagarde speaking about the threat of being “cut off” from US and Chinese technology.

Williamson cited China as another reason for boosting domestic AI, amid concerns that Chinese-made systems might not “coincide with our values”. He said: “Try asking some of these models about some events in the recent past in China and you’re not going to get an answer that’s particularly helpful if you’re doing GCSE history.”

“This is the defining technology of our time. We want to be able to shape that technology … in a way that accords with who we are and our values,” he said, adding that while ATI and the UK probably could not match the financial resources of major AI labs, they could still produce “nationally owned IP” or smaller models that could be made available to startups.
“We can be ambitious here without trying to copy what frontier labs are doing,” he said.

Williamson said ATI, a registered charity, could be an “objective and helpful” arbiter of concerns about AI, including existential threat. “A national institute should be an active partner to government and the public more generally in helping to navigate some of this stuff.”

He said there was a “a lot of stuff being tossed around” on the existential threat risk that “is not always well grounded in science”. Referring to the penchant among some in the sector for expressing the risk of AI-triggered extinction in percentage terms, he said: “I’m not sure it’s helpful trying to assign particular percentages to it because I have not seen anyone show me a convincing evidence of how they’ve arrived at the number they then start throwing around.”

Williamson indicated that the focus on national resilience would enable ATI to keep doing work on the environment that Keir Starmer’s government had wanted to sideline. In 2025 the then technology secretary, Peter Kyle, wrote to ATI’s chair demanding the institute switch its main focus to defence and security. Williamson’s predecessor Jean Innes resigned soon afterwards.
“For me climate is as much a national security issue as defence. For me, it [national resilience] is a frame that enables us to cover the range of threats and opportunities to the UK,” he said.

items.title: ‘They looked like two curtain-twitchers, though not very subtle ones’: Peter Crome’s best phone picture
paragraphs: Walking home after dropping his little girl at school, Peter Crome sensed he was being watched. A former professional ballet dancer now living in London, he had supplemented his income with photography work for 20 years. “But since having my daughter, my Nikon gear has sat idly by,” he says. “I got so used to lugging my heavy equipment around with me, it’s been quite refreshing to go somewhere just with a phone and still come back with wonderful pictures. My iPhone has also been a blessing for keeping in touch with family back home in Sydney,” Crome adds.

The cause of his disquiet that day was, to his happy surprise, these two dogs. “It was such a comical moment,” he says. “They looked like two curtain-twitchers, though not very subtle ones. I liked how they were perfectly framed with the different layers of window frames, and the brickwork and hedge provided some pleasing textures, but it was the disapproving expression on their faces that made the photo for me.”

Crome waited for a while as the dogs watched other passersby, turning their heads in unison. He crossed the road to draw their attention, then took a single photo on his iPhone 14 Pro. “This is the sort of picture I would have sent my mum before she passed away a couple of years ago. I think this one would have really tickled her,” Crome says.

items.title: New Balance’s Steve Jobs homage is so subtle you might have missed it
paragraphs: It's been 15 years since the world lost tech visionary Steve Jobs. While Apple has continued to evolve since his passing, the spirit of his innovative work and motivational thinking has continued to inspire countless big brands, including the more unexpected.

In a subtle yet touching homage, shoe brand New Balance has recreated one of Jobs' most iconic looks, honouring his legacy as a creative inspiration. Quiet and authentic, New Balance proves that honouring the past can be done with small yet thoughtful actions.

Appearing among promo shots for the grey 992s, New Balance subtly recreated Steve Jobs' iconic pose from the original iPad presentation in 2010. A key part of Jobs' 'uniform', the quiet homage is a tasteful Easter egg that honours the icon without grand gestures and loud design. Minimalist, just as Steve Jobs would want it.
"Proof that the best branding doesn’t need to shout. If you know, you know. Brilliant little detail," one X user praised. "The kind of details I adore," another added.
For more creative inspiration, take a look at how Apple became the world's most valuable brand or check out the best Apple ads of the last 50 years.

Natalie Fear is Creative Bloq's staff writer. With an eye for trending topics and a passion for internet culture, she brings you the latest in art and design news. Natalie also runs Creative Bloq’s 5 Questions series, spotlighting diverse talent across the creative industries. Outside of work, she loves all things literature and music (although she’s partial to a spot of TikTok brain rot).

items.title: How drones are hunting fires hidden beneath the Cairngorms
paragraphs: It is 06:00 and I'm meeting drone pilot Pete Short for a dawn patrol in the Cairngorms National Park.
It is a job he has been doing for almost three months, since a huge wildfire tore through this landscape in July.
The flames which swept across the hillsides are gone. From where we are standing, there is little to suggest there is still a fire here at all.
But that is exactly what we have come to find.
After a bumpy drive into the woodland, Pete launches a thermal drone into the early morning sky.
I am given a job too: keeping the aircraft in sight while he studies the images being sent back to his screen.
"Every week I hope that I find none," he tells me. "On the last thermal flight I did we found eight."
"We might have something here," Pete says, as a white glow appears on the thermal image beneath a tree.
"Some of that will be incredibly quick, some of it will take years, decades, or even beyond our lifetime," she says.
"It will recover, but we just don't know what that's going to look like yet."
And the drones that helped during the fire - and are still searching for what remains of it - are being given another job.
Pete is programming them to repeatedly fly exactly the same routes over the damaged landscape.

Using predetermined waypoints, photographs and video can be taken from the same positions month after month and year after year, allowing conservationists to build up a picture of how the landscape changes.
"This standard drone route will have exactly the same route flown month by month, year by year and visually it's going to give us some amazing information about how it's recovering," Sarah says.
There could be another role for the tech too - spotting future fires before they have a chance to spread.
Pete believes getting a view above the tree canopy quickly could prove critical.
"It's those moments before a wildfire gets out of control that could be critical to stopping it before it gets out of hand," he says.
Back on the ground, our patrol has found another hot spot.
Again, there is almost nothing visible from a distance. But guided by the drone, we find the precise spot.
Beneath a thin layer of earth, it is hot and the smoke becomes obvious after we stoke the soil.
Another location to report. Another fire for the ground teams to extinguish.
Above us, the forest is already showing its first signs of life but below our feet, the last of the fire is still burning.

items.title: Head of Met's volunteer force fired after AI tool found deleted intimate images on work phone
paragraphs: The Metropolitan Police has fired the head of its Special Constabulary after Palantir's AI monitoring uncovered that he had used his work phone to copy intimate images of a woman.
Special chief officer James Deller, who led the force's volunteer officers, was dismissed following a misconduct hearing on Friday.
The Met said investigators used lawful business monitoring and Palantir's Foundry system, which uses artificial intelligence (AI), to find the misconduct by Deller.
Cdr Pete Stevens said: "SCO Deller failed to meet that bar. His actions were an abuse of the trust put in him and it is right that he is no longer able to serve in policing."
Investigators found that in July and August 2025, Deller used his police-issued phone to take photos of two intimate images that had been sent to his personal phone.
The pictures had been sent using WhatsApp's "view once" feature, which makes them disappear after they are opened.
He then sent the copied images back to his personal device before deleting them from his work phone.
The misconduct was discovered during a week-long operation called Project Galatasaray, which used the AI technology in a bid to identify corruption and professional misconduct within the Met.
Deller will be added to the College of Policing's barred list, meaning he will not be able to serve in policing again.

Stevens added: "The vast majority of Met officers and staff serve London with dedication and integrity, and they rightly expect robust action against the small minority who abuse their position and undermine public trust.
"That is particularly true of those who serve in the Special Constabulary. They are volunteers who selflessly give up their time to keep London safe.
"They deserve to be led by people who demonstrate the highest standards in all parts of their lives."

In April, the Metropolitan Police Federation, which represents rank-and-file officers, urged officers to be "extremely cautious" about carrying Met-issued devices while off duty after the force upgraded its Lawful Business Monitoring software.

The federation's general secretary, Matt Cane, said staff had not been told the upgrade included the introduction of Palantir's artificial intelligence technology, appearing to mark its first deployment to monitor Met systems.

In May, Metropolitan Police Deputy Commissioner Matt Jukes told the London Assembly's Police and Crime Committee that officers were not under any "additional surveillance in the workplace" after the force began using AI in a bid to root out bad behaviour.
He said the Met had considered the reputational risks of using the "divisive" technology, but added that it helped identify "unacceptable, dishonest, corrosive behaviours" among officers.
The London Mayor's Office for Policing and Crime (Mopac) blocked the Met from signing a two-year contract with Palantir to provide artificial intelligence technology for criminal investigations.
Mopac said the force had failed to set out its procurement strategy, describing this as a "clear and serious breach" of procedure.
Palantir is now suing Mopac, alleging it unlawfully blocked the deal after taking the company's "values and ethics" into account, which it said was an "irrelevant consideration.
Palantir, founded by controversial tech billionaire Peter Thiel, holds contracts with a number of UK public bodies, including the NHS and the Ministry of Defence.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham is currently facing growing pressure from Labour MPs and trade unions to end government contracts with Palantir.
Former Labour deputy leader Tom Watson, who recently joined the company, warned against "mob rule" in government procurement.

Lord Watson told BBC Radio 4's Political Thinking With Nick Robinson: "One of the things I'd say to my former colleagues is, 'Do you want to let the rule of law lead procurement practice, or do you want to let mob rule lead procurement practices?'
"Because you get yourself in a lot of trouble if you go down on the latter one."

items.title: Public executions in the US stopped nearly a century ago, why are they resuming now?
paragraphs: An estimated crowd of 20,000 gathered in Kentucky in 1936 for the public hanging of Rainey Bethea
They came in their thousands from near and far. Men, women and children lined up on a Kentucky riverfront for the public hanging of a black man convicted of raping and killing an elderly white widow.

It was 14 August 1936 in Owensboro, Kentucky, a sweltering Friday in the middle of a legendary heatwave. Some slept overnight near the gallows to preserve their spots. Others held "necktie" parties the previous evening, arriving hungover as teenagers sold popcorn and soda to the spectators.
By the execution time of 5am, the crowd had swelled to an estimated 20,000.
That's when Rainey Bethea, an orphan in his 20s, stepped up to the gallows - sentenced to death after allegedly confessing to robbing, raping and killing Lischia Edwards, 70.
The previous afternoon, he'd eaten a last meal of fried chicken, pork chops, mashed potatoes, pickled cucumbers, cornbread, lemon pie and ice cream.

Many of those gathered - including press from as far away as Chicago and New York - came to see the rumoured "Lady Executioner;" the local sheriff had died four months earlier, and his widow became the unlikely female replacement. She declined to pull the trip lever herself, however, and it was hired hangmen who instead sent Bethea to his death.
That moment marked the last high-profile public hanging in America. The circus surrounding Bethea's death embarrassed many in Kentucky, and the governor outlawed public executions 18 months later.

By then, most states had abolished capital punishment in view of the masses as societal attitudes sought more humane and private methods. Another hanging was attended by a few hundred in Missouri in 1937, but that was lesser known and marked America's final public execution - until now.
Men, women and children attended the hanging, which marked the last high-profile public execution in the US

A little more than 90 years after Bethea's killing, US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth announced that the military would publicly execute Nidal Hasan, who killed 13 unarmed fellow soldiers in 2009 at the Fort Hood military base in Texas.
The Pentagon followed up by saying the execution by firing squad in December would be live-streamed.
"People need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things," Hegseth said.
University of Colorado professor emeritus Michael Radelet, a long-time scholar of capital punishment, was shocked.
"I never imagined [another] public execution," he told the BBC.
He noted how public support for the death penalty in general has been steadily declining; it was 80% in 1994, for example, but now stands at 52%.
"It's gone down precipitously, especially when you give the alternative of life without parole," he said.
It's too soon to know what the American public thinks of the idea of livestreaming an execution. But it's likely that millions or more will tune in.
With Hegseth's announcement, Radelet said, "the justification for the death penalty becomes entertainment … bring your popcorn, invite your friends".
Americans discuss their views on the death penalty after the botched execution in Tennessee of convicted murderer Christa Pike
Sonya Lea, who just last year published a book about Bethea's execution, "felt absolute horror for our descendants" when she heard of the announced firing squad livestream.

"What they called it in 1936 was a carnival of sadism," she said. "That we now have the technology that can make it go wider than the 20,000 people who showed up … to witness in Owensboro, Kentucky, it just makes it even more horrific."

Lea's grandparents were teenage newlyweds among that 1936 crowd. She only found out after her grandmother's 2002 death, when she read an account her late grandma had given detailing how they were close enough to hear Bethea's neck snap.
The author's subsequent years of research taught her that many Kentuckians were "haunted" by that execution.

"I really thought, with all my heart, that we had put this in the rearview mirror, this level of grotesquery that only a few countries in the world engage in - Iran, North Korea, Afghanistan," she said. "Are we now, as the United States of America, considering ourselves to be part of that kind of government? It's just horrific."
But the polarisation and rhetoric in American politics may have set the stage for such an announcement, said Kurt Gray, a social psychology professor at Ohio State University.

"Some Americans might thirst for blood, but I think a lot of Americans don't, and, if anything, I think a lot of other Americans are just kind of maybe desensitised," he said. "So it's not like they're cheering a public execution; they're just like, 'Oh, yeah, I guess that's where we're at now.'"
Can the Fort Hood shooter’s execution be livestreamed?
Other research indicates that Hegseth and the administration may be reading the country wrong.
Garen Wintemute, director of the Violence Prevention Research Program at the University of California, Berkeley, said survey data points to a declining appetite for violence in the US.
"This morning, the chair of the US Conference of Catholic Bishops labelled this [livestream execution announcement] as barbaric," he said. "And I think he speaks for a lot of people."
"I think it's this: A public execution is not who we are," he added. "It's not who we aspire to be as a country."
The debate over Hegseth's surprise announcement appeared to be playing out within the White House on Friday.

Vice-President JD Vance expressed uncertainty to reporters about whether the public execution would go ahead as planned, saying: "I don't know that that's actually going to happen." He added that "if it's through livestream, I'm not going to be watching it".
Hours later, President Donald Trump said he "absolutely" approved of the livestream plan but said the Pentagon was still "making a determination" on it.
The president did not answer the question of whether he'd watch Hasan's execution.
"I really don't care how he goes as long as he goes," Trump said. "And I think that the death penalty is a very worthy way of going for him."

items.title: ‘We’re not asking for luxury’: school protesters in Paris suburb feel abandoned by French state
paragraphs: On a normal school day, Mohammed, 17, wakes at 6am, cares for his younger siblings to help his single mother who works as a security guard, then takes two crowded buses and a local train to get to his high school in Sevran, a low-income banlieue town in the suburbs north-east of Paris.

“There aren’t enough chairs or desks to go round, so some students have to stand up,” Mohammed said. “Classes can be so packed you can’t interact with the teacher. In this year’s heatwaves, it felt like 40 degrees in overcrowded classrooms with no shade or curtains. It was so hot my brain couldn’t function.”

The 17-year-old in his last year of high school wants to study management and digital communication at a Paris university. But he said conditions were so poor, he felt all odds were stacked against him and his classmates.

“Some of us have to go months without teachers when absent staff aren’t replaced,” he said. “One class had no French teacher for several months just before the French baccalaureate, so they couldn’t even study all the set texts for their exam. Recently we needed a teacher for a subject taught through English, but when that teacher arrived they didn’t speak English.”

The biggest youth protest movement in the country in decades brought hundreds of thousands on to the streets across France this week demonstrating against inequality in the French education system, decrepit schools, a lack of teachers and large class sizes. Hundreds of schools were blockaded, thousands of teenagers were arrested, and rights groups warned of alleged police brutality, with one child losing the use of eye and another losing a hand.

Mohammed and his classmates, often supported by their parents and teachers, have been at the frontline, barricading their school, the Lycée Blaise-Cendrars, which is in one of mainland France’s poorest départements, Seine-Saint-Denis. They have voted to continue their protests next week, taking their grievances to the local mayor, elected officials and education representatives. Many local politicians have supported their demands. Even the French prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, conceded that teenagers had “legitimate” concerns.

Photos on the Sevran students’ phones showed broken classroom chairs, holes in walls, holes in ceilings, mould, buckets to catch leaks, faulty lights. They said basic needs weren’t met, with some toilets broken, others with no doors and often no toilet paper or soap. Video projectors and science equipment were lacking.

“We’re not asking for luxury, just the basics to learn in decent conditions,” Mohammed said. “And yet police on horseback charged us when we were gathered to protest outside our school, firing teargas at us and making arrests. It’s so dangerous to be charged by a horse, it could kill you. I just ran, I was trying to help my classmates.”

The high schools of Seine-Saint-Denis, a suburban area nudging against northern Paris, have been a driving force in the protests. The area has the youngest population in mainland France, one of the highest birthrates and the among the lowest average income. Local high schools have a high turnover of young teachers.

Despite co-hosting the 2024 Paris Olympics, and numerous government plans to try to combat long-running problems of inequality and poverty, the area north-east of Paris is still disadvantaged compared with the capital.

In 2005, Seine-Saint-Denis was the starting point for weeks of unrest on housing estates across France, leading to a state of national emergency being declared, after the death of two young boys hiding from police in an electricity substation. This week’s protests have shown that inequality and discrimination has not been addressed in the Paris suburbs and the mistrust between young people and police persists.

Sevran’s Lycée Blaise-Cendrars, with more than 1,000 pupils, has been at the heart of protests about school conditions before. In 2024, students and teachers made a viral video about the state of classrooms, toilets and equipment. The local Île de France region said it had put in place a major refurbishment project for high school buildings. But the teenagers said key issues had not been addressed.

“We’re starting at an unfair advantage because our parents aren’t as rich as others, they can’t buy us books, they can’t take us to films,” said Ilian, 17, whose family has Moroccan roots and whose father is a traffic warden. “We’re missing school during these protests, we risk falling behind in an exam year, we’re desperate to get back into class to study, but the conditions we’re facing are so bad we can’t stop until the government promises action.”

The education ministry this week promised 3,000 teachers to urgently fill gaps, but teachers’ unions expressed doubts and said longer-term plans and more funding was needed, even if the government argues there is little spare cash.

Children’s mental health is also an issue in Seine-Saint-Denis. Ilian has been waiting to see a child psychiatrist for months. At the high school, there was no school nurse and a lack of support staff for children with disabilities, he said.

“The police look down on us as if we’re animals”, Ilian said. “They talk to us with such cruelty.” He told local politicians that some teenagers alleged police had made racial insults against them during protests.

Stéphane Troussel, the Socialist head of the Seine-Saint-Denis département council who met the pupils this week, said: “It’s intolerable that policing is causing part of the difficulties.” He called for the police to stop using a type of rubber-bullet launcher, after they suspended use of stun grenades following injuries. The French interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, has defended policing tactics.

Stéphane Blanchet, the mayor of Sevran, said he supported the school protesters’ demands. He said many in his town of 52,000 people, with a higher than average poverty rate, felt “relegated” and forgotten by the state.

Sarah, 17, who wanted to study at an elite Paris engineering faculty, and whose warehouse worker father was proud she was protesting and meeting the mayor, said teenagers in the banlieue “really feel abandoned”.

She said: “We’ve been surprised and so appreciative of other teenagers in better-off places in France marching in the streets to support us this week. We know we’re disadvantaged and that we have to work 10 times as hard as others to escape discrimination against our postcode. But we can’t learn properly in these conditions when we’re not even guaranteed a chair to sit on in school.”
