items.title: After losing ground with Latino voters, Democrats are turning to influencers for help
paragraphs: Democrats are trying to rebuild trust among Latino voters, and turning to content creators for help. Above, Spanish language voting stickers which read "He Votado Hoy" ("I Voted Today") at a Philadelphia polling place in 2019. Matt Rourke/AP hide caption
Democrats lost the 2024 elections in part because of their eroding support among Latino voters, a constituency that was once a reliable segment of their base.
That November, Kamala Harris won the Latino vote by three points, according to the Pew Research Center. In 2020, Joe Biden carried them by 25 points.
This year, swing districts with large Hispanic populations could help decide which party controls the House. And Democrats are scrambling for ways to win those voters back.

One new effort comes from the campaign arm of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus, also known as BOLD PAC. In February, they launched a program to personally connect social media influencers with voters.

"We're turning to trusted voices in local communities that have followings giving them information and then allowing them to create content in a way that is organic and authentic," said Rep. Linda Sánchez, D-Calif., who chairs BOLD PAC.

That includes Latina content creator Alexa Flores, who not long ago mostly posted about beauty tips and fashion. But the Arizona resident shifted to politics in response to the Trump administration's immigration policies.
She says she wants Latino voters to understand their impact if they vote.
"My job is to get people to understand that so that they can go and move that needle," said Flores, who has nearly 500,000 followers across her platforms.

Her job now includes "get-out-the-vote" events with BOLD PAC in swing districts around the country. Flores, for her part, will appear at a wine tasting event in Las Cruces, N.M. – where Democratic Rep. Gabe Vasquez is locked in a close race against Republican Greg Cunningham. She'll also appear at a Día de los Muertos event with lowriders and voters in Tucson, Ariz., where Marine veteran JoAnna Mendoza is trying to unseat GOP incumbent Juan Ciscomani.
BOLD PAC says it is not paying content creators for posts. Instead, they're providing stipends of $1,500 for flights, hotels and other travel costs for each event.

Sánchez says content creators could help bridge a gap for her party. Thirty percent of Latinos regularly get their news from influencers on social media, according to Pew Research Center. That's more than any other demographic.
"So whether that's ... Instagram or YouTube or TikTok, that's how they're getting their information," she said. "So we need to be in those spaces."

Rep. Linda Sánchez, D-Calif., chairs BOLD PAC. She says content creators can help bridge a gap for her party. Above, Sanchez speaks on immigration at the U.S. Capitol on May 10, 2023. Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images hide caption

Democratic strategist Stephanie Valencia says Democratic efforts to win back long term support from Latino voters is going to be an uphill battle. Valencia is co-founder of Equis Research, which estimates that roughly a third of Latinos are considered independent voters.
Of those, more than 40% think neither party cares about people like them.
"One election cycle is not going to solve the problem that Democrats have had and a frayed trust with Latino voters that has developed over the last several election cycles," Valencia said.

In 2024, Latinos shifted right in response to what they saw as liberal immigration policies and a focus on foreign intervention over domestic policy under former President Biden. That year, President Trump grew his party's share of Latino votes by double digits to 48%, leaving Democrats with a slim majority, according to Pew Research Center.
It's those kinds of swings that can cost a party a close election.
This year, leaders at BOLD PAC sense an opportunity, as they've watched a growing number of Latinos say they feel betrayed by President Trump's immigration and economic policies.

Still, Valencia warns that some Democratic campaigns continue to underestimate how "swingy" a good chunk of the Latino electorate is. That is, they show up with too little, too late when it comes to campaign spending and messaging.
"Latinos are just a more persuadable universe and can't just be treated as a base turnout universe for Democrats," she said.

Solangie Hernandez Hollowell, a Texas influencer who is also working with BOLD PAC, agrees. Like others, her posts often don't even mention specific candidates, but they do focus on issues that Democrats are campaigning on this cycle – issues like taxes and immigration.
So she wants to help Latinos connect with candidates in a way that goes beyond the transactional.
"Latinos feel like politicians show up just right before the election. I don't feel like we feel very heard," she said.
So she's translating what this political moment can mean for them.
"My main goal right now is making sure that everything that's happening around the world reaches my family and my community in a way that they can understand it," she said.
Flores, the Arizona influencer, says she hopes for more awareness that Latinos are having a growing impact on major pieces of American life.
"The wave of Latinos growing in this country is becoming a bigger voice for a lot of things," she said.

items.title: 16 cozy activities to add to your fall bucket list
paragraphs: One clever way to celebrate the season? Put a rest day on your calendar. As the days shorten, you may feel lower energy when the sun sets at 5 p.m. instead of 8. So create the space in your life to recharge. Hannah Churn for NPR hide caption
Never miss a story or episode from Life Kit. Sign up for our weekly newsletter to get our journalism delivered directly to your inbox.
Many of us do the same things every year to celebrate the fall. We bust out the autumn wreath. Light the pumpkin spice candle. Pull those fuzzy sweaters out from the back of the closet.

But there are so many other fun ways to make these coming months feel cozy. Here are 16 satisfying activities and rituals to add to your fall bucket list. As the days darken and plants prepare for winter dormancy, they embody the best of what the season has to offer: an opportunity for warmth, introspection and rest.

Add this secret ingredient to your soup. Sohla El-Waylly, chef and author of Start Here: Instructions for Becoming A Better Cook, shares her secret superhero ingredient for making good soup: a pinch of MSG. It adds "a little bit of savory depth that makes you want to keep eating more."

Switch from a cold breakfast to a hot one. It's tiny changes like this one that "reorient my attention from the negative things about the cold, dark and wet to the things I enjoy when the temperature drops," says Kari Leibowitz, a health psychologist and the author of How to Winter: Harness Your Mindset to Thrive on Cold, Dark, or Difficult Days.

Cook this one-pan cheesy baked pasta dish. Food writer Melissa Clark loves cooking easy meals for her family with just one pan. This tactic, she says, can help reduce the time we spend cooking and cleaning — and leave us with more time for lounging. Try her recipe for this comforting baked pasta with tomato, sausage and ricotta.

Write a gratitude letter. Got a quiet evening to spare? Think of someone in your life who you have not had the chance to thank, says psychologist Christina Costa. "Why are you grateful for that person? Think of a specific instance when they helped you. Then send them a letter, an email, or even better, deliver the letter in person and read it to them."
If you're stuck, she says, "think of a K-12 teacher. That's going to give you a big boost." Expressed meaningfully, gratitude can have positive effects on our mental and physical health.

Take stock of your holiday traditions. Before the holidays get into full swing, take a moment to reflect on your traditions so they feel more intentional, says clinical psychologist Andrea Bonior. What do you want a particular holiday or event to mean?

"Is it about giving back to others? Gratitude? Finding the light in the darkness?" she says. If you're holding on to traditions out of obligation, or if they no longer feel meaningful, maybe it's time for a change. (This story has great advice on how to make new holiday traditions.)

Decorate for all five senses. If you want your home to feel like a fall celebration, infuse the vibe more deeply throughout your home through sight, sound, scent, touch and taste, says interior designer Elaine Griffin.

That might mean throwing a velvety blanket over the couch; getting a candle with a loud, crackling wick; hanging up a cinnamon broom; displaying decorative gourds; and keeping a tin of chocolate chip cookies in the kitchen.

Rotate your cherished mementos. Make your home feel comforting and inspiring by swapping out the items you display in your house, says Sally Augustin, a psychologist who focuses on environment and design.

Think of these items as a visiting exhibit that you can swap out every month. "It continually refreshes your familiar environment and gives you a feeling of control," she says. Replace a photo of you and your mom with a more recent one. Or swap the knick-knack you brought home from a vacation with a painting that a friend made you.

Spend the morning reading in bed. Lynn Neary has been covering books for NPR for over a decade. In our episode on how to get into a reading habit, she told us: "I love to lie in bed and read — particularly on weekend mornings." It's a good way to start your day and you're less likely to fall asleep while reading, she adds.

Refresh yourself before bed with an evening walk. Yes, even if it's dark and cold out. It makes you feel "awake but calm and ready for bed," says Leibowitz, who has studied how people survive in places with extreme winter. Don't let the weather discourage you. In Norway, she says, they have a saying: "There's no such thing as bad weather, only bad clothing."
Create a home theater. Devika Girish, co-deputy editor of Film Comment Magazine, explains what you'll need to mimic the immersive experience of a movie theater at home.

Watch the film on the biggest screen available to you (if you can, get a projector). Get some blankets. And fix yourself some snacks. Girish particularly loves munching on crisped chickpeas and popcorn and sipping a hot cup of cider while watching movies.
Put a rest day on your calendar. As the days shorten, you may feel lower energy when the sun sets at 5 p.m. instead of 8. So create the space in your life to recharge.

Tricia Hersey, author of the book Rest is Resistance: A Manifesto, likes to block off a rest day on her calendar each week. "I don't look at my email. I don't respond to anything work-related. I lay around the house."

If you can't take a full rest day, take sensory breaks, says Dr. Saundra Dalton-Smith, author of Sacred Rest: Recover Your Life, Renew Your Energy, Restore Your Sanity. If you've been in virtual meetings all day, take five or 10 minutes to shut the screen and close your eyes.

"It's similar to the reboot we do on our computers when it gets frozen and won't respond to us anymore. We do a hard reset, and everything's back to normal," she says. Alternatively, you can look out a window at a faraway object. That helps reduce eye strain.
Let go of that feeling of FOMO. When you find yourself thinking the grass is greener on the other side, remind yourself why you're watering yours.

"Maybe [you chose to stay in] because you had a long week and you need to recharge with some alone time. Or maybe you have an early start the next day. Whatever the reason might be, it's important to remember that as humans, we live by making a series of trade-offs," says clinical psychologist Aarti Gupta.
Put one group activity you've been wanting to do on your calendar. If you are craving more community and connection this time of year, go ahead and make the first move.

Try hosting something, anything. It doesn't even have to be at your home. "Start with something you feel sounds fun," says Priya Parker, author of The Art of Gathering. Invite three friends to visit a new bookshop across town. Go apple picking. Organize a horror movie-watching marathon.
Create an ancestral altar. Create a place in your home to honor beloved family members and friends who have passed away. Display family heirlooms or tchotchkes that represent each ancestor.

These things "carry an energetic signature that connects with our sense of history and our imagination, which will give us the parts of [our] history that may have been lost," says Camara Meri Rajabari, a psychotherapist who helps Black, Indigenous and people of color explore their ancestral roots.

Make a powerful spiritual connection on your next nature walk. Lucretia VanDyke, author of African American Herbalism: A Practical Guide To Healing Plants And Folk Traditions, shares an exercise to help you create a profound connection to the flora and fauna around you.

Think about how trees communicate with each other through their network of roots underground. Then interpret that connection as energy, VanDyke says. For example, if you are looking at a tree in Louisiana, and you miss your family in North Carolina, envision that network of trees and roots connecting you to them. You may start to imagine your "spirit being at home with them," she says.
Email us at lifekit@npr.org with your response and full name, and we may feature your story on NPR.
This digital story was edited by Meghan Keane. The visual editor is CJ Riculan.
We'd love to hear from you. Email us at LifeKit@npr.org. Listen to Life Kit on Apple Podcasts and Spotify, and sign up for our newsletter.

items.title: The Met puts a modern artist front and center (and there's some Jackson Pollock, too)
paragraphs: When Lee Krasner was asked in a 1978 interview what she was doing while her husband Jackson Pollock was becoming so famous, she said, "I was working all the time." Krasner is shown above, at work, in 1981. Ernst Haas/Getty Images hide caption

There's a new blockbuster show at New York's Metropolitan Museum of Art. Past Continuous features two artists: Jackson Pollock, with many of his instantly recognizable "drip" paintings, and Lee Krasner, an artist often overshadowed by Pollock, who was her husband. But in this major exhibition, Krasner is finally getting her due — and on her own terms.

This gargantuan show is replete with Pollock's greatest hits, the giant, frozen dances of paint splashed on canvas that have become iconic. But this exhibition of more than 120 works (74 from Krasner, and 48 from Pollock) reveals Krasner as an Abstract Expressionist titan, too.
One of the first works that catches your eye is a 1955 Krasner collage.

"Collage was very catalytic for her at these crucial moments in her life," said Brinda Kumar, one of the two Met curators who put together this exhibition. "She was literally sometimes tearing up older bodies of work to create a new chapter."

This work is 1955's Bald Eagle, a riotous mix of browns, blacks, fuchsia, and orange, with a claw-like slash of yellow. And right in the middle is a cutout whose shape evokes the head of a bald eagle — and that's the name that Krasner gave to this collage.
Lee Krasner, Bald Eagle, 1955, Oil, paper, and canvas collage on linen, ASOM Collection 2026 Pollock-Krasner Foundation/Artists Rights Society (ARS), New York hide caption
2026 Pollock-Krasner Foundation/Artists Rights Society (ARS), New York

Pollock's rejects were the source material for Bald Eagle, according to Kumar. "Krasner has very intentionally and deliberately cut up discarded Pollock works from this era in the 1950s, where you can see his distinctive drip still evident," she said.
When you put Krasner's collages next to Pollock's drip paintings, we see something new in the juxtaposition, said another Met curator, David Breslin.

"But that doesn't mean that the individual parts forgo their histories or their pasts," Breslin said. "We see that almost as a metaphor for couples in relationships as well. You form a unit, yet you also have all the things in your head, in your mind, in your heart that are your own, that don't change."

And sure enough, just past these collages, a visitor will see one of Pollock's classic drip paintings — 1952's Convergence, with neon orange and electric yellow so bright and bold that they foreshadow 1980s subway graffiti. The curators have put Convergence on a freestanding wall near windows, with daylight shining through — evoking the energy of a contemporary gallery.
Installation view of Krasner and Pollock: Past Continuous, on view at The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Oct. 4, 2026 – Jan. 31, 2027. Anna-Marie Kellen/The Met hide caption

The unspoken challenge of this show is to invite comparisons between wife-and-husband artists. In popular imagination, Pollock is often the troubled genius and hero, and Krasner is sidelined as a helpmate. She knew what people thought — but she didn't care.
In a 1978 interview on a television program called Inside New York's Art World, the interviewer asked Krasner what she was doing while Pollock was becoming so famous.

"I was working all the time," Krasner replied. "I doubt our relationship could have existed at all if I weren't working. In terms of what other people think, I can't do anything about that. You know, that's not my preoccupation anyway. As long as I was able to work, I went about my business."
That's true, but Krasner was also very savvy about her market value as a female artist, said curator Brinda Kumar.

Lee Krasner, Mosaic Table, 1947 Mosaic of mixed media (including broken glass, keys, coins, ceramic, and pebbles) in cement; iron wagon-wheel armature with steel Anna-Marie Kellen/The Met hide caption
"She was very cognizant of the gender dynamics and the gender politics. His career was the one that was more successful at the time."

To that end, she made certain calculations. They made their home in Springs, N.Y., a small fishing community on the far side of Long Island — a location Krasner chose specifically to get Pollock away from the business and booze of Manhattan. Pollock used a barn on the property to work on his enormous canvases, while Krasner painted first in the kitchen and then in a small, upstairs bedroom.

Lee Krasner was all about reinvention — both artistic and personal. Born Lena Krassner in Brooklyn, she was the child of Orthodox Jewish parents who came from a shtetl in what is now Ukraine. Nobody in her family knew anything about art.

She gave herself a series of new names: first Lenore, then Lee Krasner. She sculpted a new life as a young, bold artist. And she became a quintessential networker who knew everybody in New York's art scene.

Journalist Mary Gabriel has written extensively about Krasner, including in her 2018 book Ninth Street Women: Lee Krasner, Elaine de Kooning, Grace Hartigan, Joan Mitchell, and Helen Frankenthaler: Five Painters and the Movement that Changed Modern Art. Gabriel says that unlike her husband, Krasner kept reinventing her style.

"Krasner was so fascinating because she changed, not even by the decade. Every few years, she tries something new," Gabriel said. "She was always searching, which in a way is the most, I think, honest way to be an artist, because art is about discovery."

These include what Krasner called her "Little Images" — densely populated paintings from the late 1940s of nearly hieroglyphic looking symbols, all jostling for space on small canvases — as well as immense works she created, especially after Pollock died in a car crash in 1956. Pollock was plagued by alcoholism and depression, and he cheated on her; his girlfriend of the time was one of the passengers in the crash.

Krasner continued to be financially savvy as well. After Pollock's death, she more than tripled the price of one of his most famous works, Autumn Rhythm (Number 30), to sell it to the Met — a sum that not just set the pace for Pollock's market value, but for a tide of modern artists.
For this show, Autumn Rhythm was moved off its traditional museum wall to a freestanding display, Kumar noted.

"It is almost architectural in a way, because it's set against this slate grey color," she said. "The swirling blacks get animated in a whole new way, and the familiar teals and the familiar whites surge with a new energy."

Krasner seized upon her own new energy in the years after Pollock's death. She took over the barn studio that had been her husband's — and made giant, joyful work, brimming with life and lushness, as curator David Breslin noted.
Lee Krasner, The Seasons, 1957, Oil and house paint on canvas, Whitney Museum of American Art The Pollock-Krasner Foundation/Artists Rights Society (ARS), New York hide caption
The Pollock-Krasner Foundation/Artists Rights Society (ARS), New York

"You see this incredible painting that's almost 17 feet wide called The Seasons, that has these forms and bodies, eyes and body parts and these things that look like vegetation sprawling out of it," Breslin said. "So she makes, almost in a contradictory way, some of the brightest, most vibrant paintings the year after his death."
And in some way, this whole show is all about Lee Krasner finally being able to claim her own space. Krasner and Pollock: Past Continuous runs at the Met until Jan. 31.

items.title: A year of ceasefire in Gaza through the lens of NPR's reporter
paragraphs: A Palestinian mother mourns her son, who was killed in an Israeli airstrike just over a month into the ceasefire, at Al-Shifa Hospital, in Gaza City, on Nov. 20, 2025. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
Editor's note: This story contains graphic images of violence and death.

GAZA STRIP — President Donald Trump promised an end to Israel's war in Gaza after he pushed Israel to agree to a ceasefire and Hamas to release remaining Israeli hostages. The deal came into effect on Oct. 10, 2025.

A year later, however, there's still no international peacekeeping force in Gaza as promised and no reconstruction. Instead, Israel's military has expanded its control to roughly 70% of Gaza, squeezing more than 2 million Palestinians near the sea's edge.

Israel has also continued targeting Hamas throughout the ceasefire. Those attacks have killed more than 1,400 Palestinians this past year, nearly 500 of them women and children, according to Gaza's Health Ministry.
Although the bombings have not stopped, they have slowed down during the ceasefire.

That has given people in Gaza a chance to recover from what U.N.-backed experts declared was a famine in the north of the territory last year. More food is now entering, reversing starvation across Gaza.
NPR's reporter in Gaza, Anas Baba, has been capturing moments of respite and continuous grief over the past 12 months of the ceasefire. Below are a selection of his photos.
Palestinians returned to the ruins of Gaza City after Israeli forces withdrew and ended their ground operation on the first day of the ceasefire, on Oct. 10, 2025. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
In Khan Younis, families greet Palestinian prisoners who were freed in exchange for Israeli hostages on Oct. 13, 2025. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption

At Al-Shifa Hospital on Oct. 23, 2025, Joud Al-Angar, 12, and his younger cousin are covered in dime-sized scabs after they were wounded by a piece of shrapnel from an Israeli munition. They found it in the rubble and thought it was coal they could use to help their family cook dinner. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption

The bodies of multiple people, including children, are covered in shrouds at a morgue at Al-Shifa Hospital on Nov. 20, 2025, after Israeli airstrikes targeted homes and tents. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
People inspect the aftermath of a deadly Israeli airstrike that destroyed a home in Gaza City six weeks into the ceasefire on Nov. 20, 2025. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
A father and his son wade through flooded streets in Gaza City after picking up humanitarian aid on Nov. 25, 2025. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption

Children wear virtual reality headsets as part of a TechMed Gaza initiative that aims to help provide children with psychosocial support for trauma, in Al-Zuweida, Gaza, on Dec. 10, 2025. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption

Saqer Al-Ankah holds his dying 10-year-old granddaughter, Bayan, in his arms at Baptist Hospital in Gaza City on Dec. 10, 2025, after she was shot in her tent by Israeli troops who occupy northeast Gaza. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption

Makeshift tents like these in Gaza City on Dec. 11, 2025, offer little protection from the winter cold, but the U.N. says roughly 1.5 million people have only these for shelter after Israeli airstrikes destroyed nearly all the buildings in the war. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
Raed el-Ghazawi and his children stand in a tent in Gaza City on Dec. 11, 2025. The family of five says the tent is freezing cold and damp from winter rainstorms. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
On Dec. 17, 2025, Palestinian Christian children decorate a Christmas tree inside the Holy Family Church in Gaza City for the first time since the beginning of the war. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
Fresh produce returns to Gaza City's streets on Dec. 23, 2025, after U.N.-backed experts declared a famine there amid Israeli restrictions on aid during the war. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption

Patients sit in a clinic run by Doctors Without Borders in Gaza City on Dec. 31, 2025, a day before Israel banned more than 40 international aid organizations from bringing in staff or aid to Gaza. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
Palestinian female artists gather at the beach in Gaza City for the first time since the war began to paint as a form of therapy, on Feb. 12, 2026. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
Palestinian rescue workers begin the work of retrieving corpses from under the rubble of homes bombed by Israel during the war in Beit Lahia, Gaza, on Feb. 16, 2026. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption

The skeleton of Shawqi Abu Naser, 60, is retrieved from under the rubble on Feb. 16, 2026, more than a year after an Israeli airstrike killed 132 people from the same family in Beit Lahia. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
Palestinians gather in an open space in Gaza City for early morning prayers that mark the end of the Muslim holy month of Ramadan on March 20, 2026. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
A child smiles next to a man dressed as a clown on the first day of Eid al-Fitr, celebrations that mark the end of Ramadan fasting, in Gaza City on March 20, 2026. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
A Palestinian boy shakes hands with Hamas militants on the first day of Eid al-Fitr, following the end of the Muslim holy month of Ramadan, in Gaza City on March 20, 2026. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
Palestinians stand next to boxes of U.N. food aid in an area that aid groups need Israeli permission to enter in Jabalia, Gaza, on April 18, 2026. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption

A yellow block placed by Israeli forces marks the expanding territory controlled by the military in Bureij, Gaza, on May 7, 2026. Palestinians are barred from entering the area. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
Young Palestinian chess players gather at a coffee shop in Gaza City for the first tournament since the start of the war, on May 12, 2026. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption

A Palestinian child carries jugs of water as he passes by a mural of Spanish soccer star Lamine Yamal that is painted on the rubble of a home destroyed by Israeli airstrikes, in Al-Shati refugee camp, Gaza, on May 14, 2026. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption

A building burns after an Israeli airstrike killed Izz al-Din al-Haddad, the leader of the military wing of Hamas, his wife, his daughter and a neighbor in Gaza City on May 16, 2026. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption

Children jump on a trampoline during the Eid holidays on May 31, 2026, in Beit Lahia, which the Israeli military had deemed an "orange zone." Aid organizations are restricted from entering the area. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption

A child looks into a burned car that was targeted in an Israeli airstrike on a busy street in Gaza City on June 22, 2026. A teenage girl who was going to find internet access to take her final exams was killed in the strike. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
A plume of smoke rises after an Israeli airstrike targeted a home in Gaza City nine months into the ceasefire on July 12, 2026. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption

Thousands of displaced Palestinians gather under Egyptian flags amid the rubble in Gaza City for a public screening of Egypt's match against Argentina in the World Cup on July 7, 2026. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption

One-hundred corpses are wrapped in Palestinian flags in Gaza City on Aug. 4, 2026, after being retrieved from under the rubble of a building that was hit in an Israeli airstrike in October 2023. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
A Palestinian child whose brother was killed in an Israeli airstrike cries at the door of a morgue at Al-Shifa Hospital in Gaza City on Aug. 19, 2026. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption
Palestinian children form a chain for a global solidarity initiative called Swim With Gaza that raises money for swimming lessons in Khan Younis on Aug. 25, 2026. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption

A child's toys are stained with blood in Gaza City on Sept. 1, 2026, following an Israeli operation to kidnap a Hamas security officer. His family was killed in Israeli airstrikes. Anas Baba/NPR hide caption

items.title: Did a book from 1973 predict the logo designs of some of today's biggest companies?
paragraphs: The best graphic design books can be great sources of inspiration for designers, but the idea is not to directly copy from them, right? Some people are wondering whether a single publication from the 1970s could have directly influenced dozens of contemporary designs.

A classic graphic design reference book has resurfaced on social media, and it's getting attention for the familiarity of some of the symbols it depicts. Some of them look incredibly similar to identities belonging to modern-day companies, from AMD to Google.

The book is Trademarks & Symbols, Vol. 2: Symbolical Designs by the Japanese designer Yasaburo Kuwayama. While Volume 1 had focused on alphabetical and letter-form designs, the second tome centres on symbolical and pictorial designs. It's a directory of real symbols and logos organised according to their form, for example circles, squares, trees, eyes and human figures.

From a just a few pages shared on social media, people have spotted designs that resemble the logos of chip maker AMD, Google Drive, Chase Bank, Natwest, Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce, Portugal's state bank, Renault and more.

@Frozune actually, flipping through this book now after seeing this and it's basically every logo ever. Also found Perplexity, Antigravity, Snowflake, The London Underground and the Jedi Rebellion. https://t.co/KgjnFCpuxtOctober 8, 2026
@Frozune No like actually, holy crap https://t.co/j69fy6r9K3October 8, 2026
@Frozune Ancient designs are fascinating and far richer than imagined. This might be an App Store icon from thousands of years ago. https://t.co/PZnYaXyObH https://t.co/aBseqkZHJhOctober 8, 2026
@Frozune Raia Drogasil S.A. - a drugstore company in Brazil https://t.co/Dgg1VLX0fxOctober 8, 2026
@Frozune Eh pero si es el logo de cinepolis https://t.co/7DxydSlyx9October 8, 2026

Have the graphic designers behind modern big brand logos been picking and choosing old designs to recycle? Probably not. Geometric forms are relatively universal, and Yasaburo's book is so extensive that it's logical that modern brands could arrive at similar shapes on their own.
One observer has pointed out that in the book's appendix some designs are listed as being used by multiple companies. Even today, we see brands with similar logos.

When it comes to minimalist geometric symmetry, there are only so many options. Nevertheless, if you're looking for a logo design for your startup, some people reckon the book still has a few gems that could be available for the taking.
@Frozune unused gems hanging out here https://t.co/uFCZe8e4DzOctober 9, 2026

Trade Marks & Symbols was originally published in Tokyo by Kashiwa Shobo and Orion Press and internationally by Van Nostrand Reinhold Company. You might have to part with a lot of money to get a copy today. There's a hardcover copy selling on Amazon for over $2,000.
The nearest contemporary equivalent I can think of are Jens Müller's Taschen books Logo Beginnings and Logo Modernism, which I can highly recommend.

Joe is a regular freelance journalist and editor at Creative Bloq. He writes news, features and buying guides and keeps track of the best equipment and software for creatives, from video editing programs to monitors and accessories. A veteran news writer and photographer, he now works as a project manager at the London and Buenos Aires-based design, production and branding agency Hermana Creatives. There he manages a team of designers, photographers and video editors who specialise in producing visual content and design assets for the hospitality sector. He also dances Argentine tango.

items.title: India cracks down on youth protests as anger grows against Modi and election chief
paragraphs: An armored vehicle with a banner warning citizens against unlawful gathering stands near the venue of a youth protest demanding the resignation of the country's election chief Gyanesh Kumar, in New Delhi, India, Saturday, Oct. 10, 2026. (AP Photo/Manish Swarup) Manish Swarup/AP hide caption

Indian authorities deployed a sweeping security crackdown across New Delhi and detained thousands of protesters Saturday as India's youth "Cockroach" movement sought to intensify a nationwide campaign against a contentious voter list revision that has fueled anger at Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Hindu nationalist government and election authorities.

Police intercepted demonstrators before they could reach Jantar Mantar, the designated protest site in the heart of India's capital, chasing off some and detaining many others. Some were dragged away before being bundled into police vehicles and taken to temporary detention centers. Several "Cockroach" movement leaders were detained before arriving, effectively crippling the protest ahead of its start.
The crackdown extended beyond the protest venue, with police stopping buses, cars and other vehicles at checkpoints on routes into the capital and searching for demonstrators.

Jantar Mantar was barricaded, while anti-riot vehicles equipped with tear gas launchers were stationed along key routes. Restrictions on mobile internet and access to parts of the city added to the hurdles facing protesters.
Police said Friday they had denied permission for the protest because the request was submitted late.

The scale of the crackdown underscored the authorities' determination to disrupt a fast-growing protest campaign that has mobilized thousands of young people, drawn opposition support and intensified scrutiny of Modi. The protests also come at a politically sensitive time, months after demonstrations led by the "Cockroach" movement over exam paper leaks forced Modi's education minister to resign in July.
Police detain leaders and tighten grip around protest site

Leaders of the "Cockroach" movement Abhijeet Dipke, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, who were expected to be at the forefront of the protest, were detained after arriving at Delhi airport from Mumbai on Saturday. A video shared by the "Cockroach Janta Party" on X showed police boarding the aircraft and detaining the three men.
"The pre-planned interception by Delhi Police aims to cripple the leadership of today's peaceful demonstrations before they even reach the protest site," the movement said in a statement.

Loudspeakers around the protest site warned that gatherings of five or more people were banned in parts of New Delhi, as authorities imposed sweeping security restrictions rarely seen in the capital. Journalists also faced restrictions in some areas.
Some protesters nevertheless broke through police cordons, chanting slogans against Modi and election authorities before being detained.

"We are a democracy, yet peaceful protests are being crushed by force. Shouldn't we fight for our rights," said Tanya Negi, a college student who traveled from Mumbai with two friends and arrived early Saturday. "Why is Modi afraid of India's young people?"
The crackdown drew criticism from opposition leaders, who accused the government of curbing dissent.
"Is there a democracy in this country? A total siege over the city. Citizens are being driven out," opposition lawmaker John Brittas told The Associated Press.
India's voter list dispute raises election fairness concerns

The protests center on India's Election Commission's Special Intensive Revision, which the opposition says has disenfranchised millions of eligible voters. Protesters demand the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and an end to the change, which has removed more than 130 million names from voter lists so far.
The Election Commission and the government reject allegations of voter manipulation, saying the revision is intended to eliminate duplicate and ineligible entries.
The dispute has become a rallying point for opposition parties seeking to challenge Modi's Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party.

Saturday's planned demonstration follows days of protests in the Indian capital where opposition lawmakers also stepped up their campaign, with Congress party leader Rahul Gandhi being briefly detained by police.

Gandhi and other opposition leaders have accused the commission of conducting the voter revision in a way that benefits Modi's party. The opposition says voters more likely to support its parties have been disproportionately affected by the removals, while supporters of the BJP have been spared or added to the lists.
The commission and the government deny the allegations.
India's youth movement broadens campaign against Modi
For the "Cockroach" movement, the voter list dispute offers an opportunity to broaden its campaign.

The movement began online in May and gained prominence through demonstrations, sit-ins and hunger strikes over alleged exam paper leaks. Those protests culminated in the resignation of Modi's education minister in July, a rare political setback for a prime minister who has maintained a firm hold on national power for more than 12 years.

For Modi, the protests pose a challenge midway through his third term, though their political impact remains unclear. National elections are not due until 2029, but state elections next year in BJP-ruled Uttar Pradesh, India's most populous state, and Gujarat, Modi's home state, will test the party's standing.

items.title: The iPhone 18 Pro just ended my affair with the iPhone Air
paragraphs: It's not you, iPhone Air, it's me. Actually, no. It's you. I tried to love you. I defended you for over a year, stuck up for you in the face of ridicule from my Pro-wielding colleagues. But now that the iPhone 18 Pro is in my hand, I'm sorry to tell you, it's over. This is the end of the affair.

I really did think the iPhone Air was for me when Apple announced it last year. As an iPhone mini apologist, I've always favoured design over features, whilst lamenting the trend towards massive, heavy bricks. But all of those compromises that tech nerds have accused the Air of making in its pursuit of ultimate thinness? Yeah, they're valid.

I still love the design of the iPhone Air. From the ultra thin profile to the polished titanium edges, this is the most premium looking and feeling iPhone ever. It's the closest thing we've had to Steve Jobs' dream of a device that's genuinely all-display – the phone is so thin and light that it disappears into the background when looking at the 3,000 nit display.

But yes, it only has one camera lens. And despite Apple's claims that it's somehow worth two (still not sure how that checks out), the limitations are a pain in everyday use. Countless times I've tried to take a 0.5x photo, only to remember the feature doesn't exist on the Air. Same goes for zooming in on anything further than the near distance – the digital zoom just doesn't cut it.

The other major drawback, of course, is battery. Over the course of a year, my iPhone Air's battery health has degraded to 91%, which is much quicker than my iPhone 15 Pro degraded. The result is not-quite-all-day battery life, which has got me into trouble a few times when travelling.

And while I said I love the design of the iPhone Air, I do take issue with one aspect: the width. Why, oh why, is the so-called thinnest, lightest and therefore most portable iPhone too wide to use one-handed? It makes no sense to me that the iPhone Air is taller and wider than the iPhone 18 Pro.

Speaking of which, it's the 18 Pro that's finally turned me off the Air. I've been using the Pro for a week now, and realised just how much I've missed those basic features: a better camera, and better battery life. And despite the heft, I'm actually finding it easier to use one-handed, because it's less wide. It's almost a novelty that my thumb can reach the edge of the screen.
It may not be as 'pretty' as the iPhone Air, but the 18 Pro just feels more solid as a device that fits into my life. I'll miss looking at the Air, but it's time to admit: looks aren't everything.

Daniel John is Design Editor at Creative Bloq. He reports on the worlds of design, branding and lifestyle tech, and has covered several industry events including Milan Design Week, OFFF Barcelona and Adobe Max in Los Angeles. He has interviewed leaders and designers at brands including Apple, Microsoft and Adobe. Daniel's debut book of short stories and poems was published in 2018, and his comedy newsletter is a Substack Bestseller.

items.title: Why ‘boring’ AI is Hollywood’s best bet
paragraphs: A single box office bomb can lose studios tens, if not hundreds, of millions. Disney’s Strange World reportedly lost $200M, and The Flash set DC back by over $150M. Those are among the worst cases, but failing to turn a profit is a common occurrence in the filmmaking industry, with even conservative estimates suggesting 10% of major productions flop.

Given the high risk, the temptation to use generative AI in filmmaking is entirely understandable.​ It can bring entire projects to life in a fraction of the time and on a much smaller budget. But at what cost?

Egor Dubrovsky is the co-founder and CEO of Filmustage. Drawing on prior experience in film production and tech, he has helped over 30,000 filmmakers to save 3.5 million hours and $119 million by replacing inefficient, manual workflows with streamlined, automated processes. The platform was used on titles including Masters of the Air (Apple TV) and The Gentlemen (Netflix).

AI is capable of throwing together a semi-coherent script and generating visuals that pass the eye test without much scrutiny. Yet, we’re nowhere close to the point where AI can write scenes, organize productions, act naturally, and shoot movies without any human assistance.

The industry will continue to rely heavily on the creativity and vision of its writers, performers, directors, designers, and wider production teams for the foreseeable future, and they’ve already made it abundantly clear that they’re unwilling to share a set with AI if it’s given a starring role. Preventing AI from taking creative jobs in the field was one of the primary causes of the 2023 SAG-AFTRA strike, which caused losses in excess of $5 billion.

Audiences share that sentiment, regularly panning the use of generative AI for creative purposes. And not just heavily AI-generated projects, such as Misaligned, starring AI actress Tilly Norwood, but movies that used it sparingly, such as Young Washington.

While the technology is constantly improving, algorithms are infamous for producing inconsistent narratives, repetitive tropes, and uncanny imagery. With that in mind, something as simple as using generative AI in a promotional poster can, and has, caused backlash. The actual film might be perfectly watchable, but like a poor critic score, that label alone is bound to put plenty of people off buying a ticket.
There’s an important distinction, however. Netflix’s The Gentleman received positive reviews from critics and audiences – despite the use of AI.

The difference is, the technology was used exclusively behind the scenes to break down the series’ action-packed script, inform shooting decisions, and help the production run smoothly. Viewers weren’t presented with AI-generated visuals or a storyline shaped by algorithms. Many productions now use AI in this way, assigning it menial, repetitive pre-production tasks such as script breakdowns, shooting schedules, and budget planning that do not influence what ends up on the screen in any way.

That isn’t a change that’s going to result in another costly strike. I worked as a director’s assistant in Hollywood, and I can confidently say the vast majority of the industry’s workforce would be happy handing over these tasks. Film production is a gruelling, high-stress environment, where 12-hour days are the norm and 16-hour days aren’t uncommon. Nobody suffers through that because they love combing through call sheets for clashes or calculating expenses item by item. These tasks are all vitally important to a successful production, yet creatives would much rather spend their time on the creative side of the process.

AI, on the other hand, is perfectly happy taking on tedious pre-production processes. And, unlike the creative process, it’s far better at it than humans. It can process far greater amounts of information at far greater speeds, and it doesn’t make mistakes due to fatigue or boredom like humans often do.

Pre-production on a Hollywood film typically takes anywhere from three to seven months. A simple scene breakdown would take days. However, using AI, you can produce the same document in minutes, and the industry has already saved over 5.2M hours of manual work by automating these processes.

Automating ‘boring’ pre-production tasks might not save as much as replacing A-listers with AI stars or generating VFX instead of creating it. However, pre-production still accounts for 10-15% of the total budget on average. That alone would have shaved $80M off of Star Wars: The Force Awakens’ $537M production cost. It’s a huge saving for studios, without the risk of losing your audience.

For AI to pay off, however, the aim shouldn’t be to reduce budgets. Studios should view it as an opportunity to focus more money, time, and attention on the things that actually matter to audiences: refining scripts, improving special effects, perfecting performances. Essentially, creating better films. After all, the real issue with AI in Hollywood isn’t the technology itself – automation has been streamlining creative processes for decades, without complaint. The concern is what happens when all those cost cuts and shrinking teams ultimately compromise the quality of the final cut.

Natalie Fear is Creative Bloq's staff writer. With an eye for trending topics and a passion for internet culture, she brings you the latest in art and design news. Natalie also runs Creative Bloq’s 5 Questions series, spotlighting diverse talent across the creative industries. Outside of work, she loves all things literature and music (although she’s partial to a spot of TikTok brain rot).

items.title: Recruitment boss accused of being behind ‘doxxing’ campaign against RNLI and anti-racism activists
paragraphs: The owner of a recruitment firm has been accused of being at the centre of a so-called “doxxing” campaign against the Royal National Lifeboat Institution (RNLI), anti-racism activists and business executives who recruit black, Asian and minority ethnic workers.
Tom Watson, from Worcester, is alleged to be behind an X account calling itself “Big Time Charlie”, which was deactivated shortly after he was named by the campaign group Hope Not Hate.

The account had almost 50,000 followers and had become increasingly prominent in recent weeks as RNLI staff found themselves being harassed and attacked online as far-right activists targeted them over their involvement in rescuing people trying to cross the Channel in small boats.

The account, which has a history of racist comments, appears to have been using AI to scrape data from LinkedIn and other sites to build a so-called Traitorbase. The Big Time Charlie account was removed almost immediately after Hope Not Hate alleged that Watson was behind it, and after the Guardian approached him for comment.

Like the posts on Watson’s LinkedIn account, the X account has frequently praised the hard-right MP Rupert Lowe. It also claimed to have donated £2,500 to Lowe’s Restore Britain party and joined its “Cromwell Club” for those activists who pay a certain level of donation.
Targets of doxxing by the Big Time Charlie account told the Guardian of the impact.

They included Chantelle Lunt, a Green party councillor in Merseyside who has already been targeted by the far right, and who made a report to the police after details about her were published online by the account.

She said: “Someone told me that I had been doxxed and when I went to look I saw that details about me appeared to be on a spreadsheet which included reference to other people who were involved in Stand Up to Racism.

“The climate at the moment is horrendous and I’m no stranger to people targeting me and my family, but there’s a big concern when this information is actively put out there. You can see people engaging with it and actively encouraging each other.”

A spokesperson for a charity that was targeted told the Guardian: “This is another example of a cynical attempt to spread misinformation that has unfortunately gone unchecked on social media platforms.
“This is an attempt to sow discord and division among communities and prevent organisations trying to help the most vulnerable communities in this country from operating at their full potential.

“Time spent combating misinformation and bigotry is a distraction from these organisations’ programme work here at home, which actually makes a difference in the ordinary lives of people in the UK. Social media companies, the media and politicians have a responsibility to clamp down on misinformation and the division it causes.”
A number of businesses, big and small, were also doxxed on the account, which posted the photographs and names of executives who were said to have been involved in hiring minority ethnic staff.
A businessperson who was also targeted described their doxxing by the account as “bizarre”.

“Thankfully it doesn’t seem to have led to any problems, but it’s not something that you expect to have to contend with. It’s a pretty unpleasant thing to do, especially if it’s someone who is involved in their own business,” they added.

Watson divides his time between the UK and US and founded the recruitment firm Futura Energy Group, which describes itself as “a specialist recruitment and build-with talent partner for companies operating across AI”.
Archived online records show that the Big Time Charlie account originally bore the name Tom Watson, while a range of other evidence links him to it.
That included regular references by the account to being in Puerto Rico, where Futura is based according to its LinkedIn account, and references to working in recruitment for technical roles.

The Big Time Charlie account posted on 20 July that they were in Zurich and shared a photo taken in the grounds of the Vitznauerhof hotel. Two days later, Watson posted on his LinkedIn profile that he was in Switzerland and shared another image taken from the Vitznauerhof hotel.

items.title: My brief romance with an AI bird feeder
paragraphs: It started off promising enough. Dozens of tiny, colorful birds were drawn to my garden just a few weeks after I mounted a $350 $269 Kiwibit Bird Feeder 2 Pro. “Looks like Great Tit!” read the first AI-driven alert sent to my phone. “Looks like Eurasian Blue Tit!” read another. I chuckled, still waiting for adulthood to kick in.

This went on for days. Hundreds of miniature tits came to snack on expensive sunflower seeds already husked. They’d skulk about in nearby trees before flittering in to grab a single seed to be safely enjoyed in the canopy above.

I took great delight in my new house guests. I admired them in crisp 4K HDR video recordings. I looked for unique markings in the hope of naming my new feral pets. I clicked deeper into the Kiwibit app to read about my visitors’ migration habits, where they nest, and what they like to eat. It was all going swell until he arrived.

“Looks like Common Wood Pigeon!” came the alert. All I saw was a battleship-gray blob obscuring the live camera feed. The winged rat was so fat and imposing that he blocked the lens. Ugh, no, go back to the tourists!

In mild panic, I triggered the feeder’s Nuisance Animal Alarm, a feature typically reserved for squirrels and the like. The pigeon tensed, looked around, but wasn’t deterred by the audible siren that was surely annoying my neighbors. Soon it went back to gorging on the haute cuisine purchased for more refined guests. It ate and ate and ate. For 15 minutes, it ate until I walked outside and shooed it away.

Thereafter, that pigeon, or pigeons (who can tell) moved in. They’d perch for 30 minutes or more, slamming their faces into the seed pile with the clumsy enthusiasm of a tween bobbing for apples. Mice arrived below to feast on the spoils. Admitting defeat, I dismounted the expensive bird feeder and shoved it into a closet.
I’m not mad at Kiwibit. The “Bird Feeder 2 Pro 4K AI Camera with Solar Panel (Lifetime AI Included)” I tested was a joy to use, until it wasn’t. That’s not Kiwibit’s fault.

If you’ve been tempted to buy a smart bird feeder, I’d suggest starting with something simple, inexpensive, and without AI instead of going all in on day one — you can’t return a used feeder just because it attracts pests.

items.title: The Carrie remake is getting roasted over its changes to one of the most iconic scenes in horror
paragraphs: Based on Stephen King's debut novel, Brian De Palma's 1976 Carrie remains a timeless classic. I must have seen the film for the first time in the early nineties, at least 15 years after its release, and it didn't feel old or in need of a remake.

Yet since then, we've had a sequel, Carrie 2 in 1999, plus three remakes: a TV movie in 2002, Kimberly Peirce's 2013 movie, and now an eight-part series released on Amazon Prime Video this week. All of them felt a bit unnecessary, but none prompted as much debate as the latest interpretation.
Warning: this article may contain spoilers for those who have not watched Carrie on Amazon Prime.
Carrie – Official Trailer | Prime Video - YouTube
Developed by Mike Flanagan (The Life of Chuck), Amazon Prime's Carrie stars Summer H Howell as the eponymous teenage girl with telekinetic powers.

In contrast to the movies, it sticks closer to the documentary format of the novel. It also recognises the impact of the social changes that could make the story worth retelling: metal detectors in US schools, the additional harm of cyberbullying and online harassment via social media.
But it makes other changes that go far beyond merely updating the story to a different age. Carrie's personality has been changed dramatically, making her more optimistic and likeable.

For some, this reduces the concept of what defines Carrie to a series of setpiece scenes. Over on X, someone's provided a side-by-side comparison of one of the most famous: the prom scene, comparing the 1976 Carrie against Amazon's series. Opinions are not favourable to the latter.
I need people to see these two clips of Carrie (1976) and Carrie (2026) side by side to understand you are being fed slop and calling it a gourmet meal https://t.co/GRCxhSAnKoOctober 8, 2026
"The sound design. The cinematography. The lighting. The editing. The pacing. The score. The performances. How did we regress this badly?" one person asks on seeing the comparison above.
Some point to the inanity of a script that has fleeing characters redundantly explain that the doors are locked and that Carrie's coming for them. Yeah, I think we could gather that.

Others feel that the more sympathetic portrayal of Carrie lightens or even glamourises the scene, making her a heroine in a "crush the bullies" fantasy. The blood looks carefully painted, more like a Halloween costume than a revolting humiliation. Carrie looks like she's "aura farming", one person thinks.
"Carrie is not a 'girlboss moment', it's a mass killing," another person points out. "It ought to convey the horror of a school shooting, hundreds of people trapped in a burning building."

The ending is drastically different too, adding the kind of plot twist that's obligatory in any TV series that's aiming for a second season. I don't want to give too many spoilers away, but it seems to open the possibility of Carrie becoming a kind of X-men/Heroes/The Tomorrow People story.

Flanagan has said that he felt there was more of Carrie's story to tell and that he aims to bring in elements that reflect the larger world that King built through his later books like The Shining, Doctor Sleep and The Institute.
But is the series really telling more of Carrie's story of writing a completely different one that happens to have the same name?

Joe is a regular freelance journalist and editor at Creative Bloq. He writes news, features and buying guides and keeps track of the best equipment and software for creatives, from video editing programs to monitors and accessories. A veteran news writer and photographer, he now works as a project manager at the London and Buenos Aires-based design, production and branding agency Hermana Creatives. There he manages a team of designers, photographers and video editors who specialise in producing visual content and design assets for the hospitality sector. He also dances Argentine tango.

items.title: Hurricane Isaias downgraded after making landfall in Florida
paragraphs: Hurricane Isaias, the first of the 2026 Atlantic season, made landfall Friday night along the northern Gulf Coast of Florida, bringing with it heavy rains, powerful winds and the risk of life-threatening flash flooding and storm surges.
Isaias is continuing north across the Southeastern United States after being downgrade from a hurricane to a post-tropical cyclone, the BBC's US partner CBS News reports, external.
Florida, Alabama, and Georgia have each issued states of emergency amid warnings of life-threatening storm surge that could cause up to 9 feet (2.7m) of flooding in some areas.
Isaias is one of three storm systems affecting North America this weekend, with the two others hitting Mexico and Southern California in the El-Niño fuelled warm waters of the Pacific Ocean.
Both Florida and Alabama instituted mandatory evacuations to thousands of people due to the storm.

In Florida, those evacuations include coastal communities in direct aim of the powerful storm. Florida Senator Rick Scott encouraged residents in designated areas to evacuate as soon as possible, as he warned in a social media post: "DO NOT WAIT! Get out NOW!"
Governor of Alabama Kay Ivey issued a mandatory evacuation for all non-residents, tourists and visitors in key counties likely to be heavily affected by the storm.
Hurricane Isaias is the first hurricane in the Atlantic's hurricane season, which largely has been delayed due to El Niño conditions in the Pacific.
It marks the first time in more than 30 years that a hurricane did not form till October.
The storm is likely to bring "life-threatening storm surge" to the US Gulf Coast, the National Hurricane Center (NHC) warned.
After hitting Florida, the centre of Isaias is forecast to move across Alabama and into the Tennessee Valley on Saturday and Sunday, the National Weather Service said late on Friday.
As of Friday evening, hurricane-force winds extended outward up to 35 miles (55 km) from Isaias' centre, and tropical storm-force winds extended as far as 205 miles (335 km).

On Saturday morning, the NHC said all hurricane warnings had been discontinued, while a storm surge warning is in effect for parts of Florida. There is also a tropical storm warning in the state, as well as in east Alabama.

Even before the storm made landfall, hundreds of thousands were without power in the country's southeast - and Alabama, Florida and Georgia have issued states of emergency as they brace for heavy rains and flooding.
More than 430,000 were in the dark in Florida and nearly 300,000 in Alabama saw outages, according to PowerOutage.us on Saturday morning.
The hurricane's winds are expected to be felt further inland in Georgia, albeit at a lesser intensity, where already about 40,000 customers were without power.
People on the coast of the Florida panhandle have been told to seek immediate shelter under an "Extreme Wind Warning".
Some Florida officials have ordered residents to "Get out NOW!", urging people to follow evacuation orders.
John Guoth, a resident of Navarre, Florida, told the BBC that he and his wife will remain in their home despite the rest of his street having already left.
"It's a hurricane, we get them all the time... we kind of knew that when we moved here," he said.
"Pretty much everything that can fly and will fly is battened down, and everything that cannot fly is really, really secured," he said,
Guoth said he put his ducks and chickens in the bathroom and weighed down his boats and trailers so "nothing flips over".
A few households have remained in the area, describing them as "long-term locals" who are "going to protect our homes".
Pensacola resident Brandin Ruth told the BBC that they have been turning the gas off to the buildings, icing down product and trying to get team members home.
People in the Florida city have "seen bad storms before" but are "bunkering up", he said, adding: "You don't want to underestimate a storm like this".
Two other storms are also forecast to batter North America this weekend.

Hurricane Simon is bearing down on the Pacific coast of Mexico as a category one hurricane. It is set to pick up speed and become category four by Saturday, eventually making landfall near Puerto Vallarta on Sunday, according to Reuters.
Further north, Tropical Storm Rachel, a downgraded hurricane, is heading toward landfall around the US-Mexico border, along the Pacific.
While, Rachel is expected to reach the coast late on Saturday, the impact of the storm is already being felt due to high tides in southern California.
Video footage and photos show several streets under water in Newport Beach, California, through a combination of the tropical storm swells at sea and high tide.
Posting on its account on X, the City of Newport Beach advised people to "avoid the Balboa Peninsula due to street flooding caused by recent storm conditions and elevated tides".
It also urged people not to drive through flooded streets. Bulldozers have been shoring up the beach to try and prevent further flooding.
With additional reporting by Simon King and Hafsa Khalil

items.title: Asbestos mystery leaves beloved beach closed
paragraphs: Mount Batten Beach was fenced off in July
For more than six years, asbestos has been washing up with the tide, turning one of Plymouth's handful of swimming spots into the centre of a growing environmental mystery.
Mount Batten Beach has been fenced off since the summer, and access restricted to two other areas on the peninsula.
It comes after tests in April and July found asbestos fibres in sand samples at levels that could pose a risk to health if inhaled, Plymouth City Council said.
Inhaling the fibres can increase the risk of serious diseases - including lung cancer - decades after exposure.

The first discovery came in 2019 when 500kg (1,100lb) of material containing the toxic substance was removed from the shoreline, which sits on Plymouth Sound in one of the South West's most popular holiday destinations.
In total, more than 1.5 tonnes of material containing asbestos, external, including both white and the more dangerous blue varieties, has been cleared from the beach and nearby sites.

Residents and experts believe the material may be coming from roofing and construction waste linked to the former RAF Mount Batten base, where coastal erosion is thought to be exposing the buried material.
Grace Stickland said losing the beach had broken up a community

The closure has left swimmers, business owners and residents wondering when, or even if, the beach will reopen, and how it looks against the backdrop of Plymouth Sound being named the UK's first National Marine Park., external

City councillor Grace Stickland, who has been bathing at Mount Batten for several years, said dozens of people regularly gathered for swims throughout the year, with festive dips attracting as many as 80 participants.
"It was a really popular little beach and everybody loved it," she said.
"All the swimmers feel as though they've been evicted from their homes."

Stickland said older swimmers and people with mobility issues particularly valued Mount Batten because of its accessibility, adding that the closure was "breaking up" a community that had grown around the beach.
The National Marine Park in Plymouth Sound has faced a number of challenges in the past, including hundreds of old tyres being discovered on the seabed and sewage spills.
Yet the asbestos contamination problem has proved difficult to solve.
When asbestos was first discovered in 2019, the council temporarily closed the beach and expected the amount of material washing ashore to decrease over time but that has not been the case.
"Our beach collections have shown that the amount of material washing up on the beach hasn't shown any real decline," a council spokesperson said.
Earlier testing suggested the risk was low. Warning signs were installed and visitors were advised to avoid parts of the beach where asbestos fragments had been found.
But council officials described the latest results as a "new and worrying development".
Swimmers at Mount Batten before the beach was closed
Although two rounds of testing have found no evidence of airborne asbestos on the beach, the discovery of fibres in the sand was enough to trigger the closure.
Professor Steve Maddern, Plymouth's director of public health, said shutting the beach had been a last resort.
"We understand the disappointment this will cause but the latest sand samples are concerning and we must prioritise the safety of the public," he said in July.
While the beach remains closed, attention has turned to the question: Where is the asbestos coming from?
Residents have long suspected the source could be the former RAF Mount Batten site, which occupied the peninsula for much of the 20th Century before closing in 1992.
During its heyday it was one of Britain's most important flying boat bases, with Sunderland aircraft carrying out anti-submarine patrols and sea rescue missions during World War Two.
Today little remains beyond memorials and historic seaplane hangars.
Mallory Haas believes buried asbestos from the former RAF base is the cause of the contamination

Maritime archaeologist Mallory Haas, director of the Ships Project CIC in Plymouth, said she believed asbestos-containing roofing materials from the RAF base had been buried and were now being exposed through coastal erosion.
"If you look at what's on the beach, and if you also look at the deposits behind the staircases when you walk down to the beach, you can see it eroding out of the land there," she said.
She added: "It's Britain's Ocean City, the UK's first National Marine Park and it's an MPA [Marine Protected Area].
"It should be some of the most protected waters around."

The properties of asbestos made it an ideal material for use in a number of products, including insulation material for buildings, boilers and pipes; car brakes and floor tiles, insulating board to protect buildings and ships against fire; asbestos cement for roofing sheets and pipes.
Due to the risks to health following inhalation exposure to asbestos the importation of blue and brown asbestos has been banned in the UK since 1985.
This ban was extended to include white asbestos in 1999.
Asbestosis is a rare but serious lung condition that affects people exposed to asbestos. It cannot be cured but treatment may improve the symptoms.
in more advanced cases, swollen fingertips
It can take 20 to 30 years after being exposed to asbestos before symptoms appear.
The advice is to visit a GP if you have symptoms of asbestosis and think you have been exposed to asbestos.
Sources: UKHSA, external and NHS, external
Plymouth City Council said re-opening the beach was a high priority
Local MP Rebecca Smith has been pressing the council for answers; arguing the closure is having a significant impact on sea swimmers, watersports users, businesses and the wider community.
More than 140 people attended a public meeting about the issue, while a petition has been handed to Parliament calling for urgent action to reopen the beach.
The Conservative MP for South West Devon questioned why the problem had still not been resolved more than six years after asbestos was first discovered.
"You can't be the National Marine Park on one side of the peninsula and have a closed beach on the other side of the peninsula," she said.
"I will find it incredibly difficult to stand up in Parliament and talk about the National Marine Park if that beach remains closed."
Smith said the city council had a strong record of securing external funding for major projects and argued it should use those same skills to find the resources needed to resolve the beach closure.
"There's a will, there's a way," she said. "They need to be using that track record and that skill set to get whatever it takes to sort this beach out."
Nearby businesses are beginning to feel the strain as well.
The Bridge restaurant closed in September, citing the beach closure as a significant factor affecting trade.
For now, Mount Batten's future remains unclear.
Giant hangars and a slipway are all that remains of the RAF base

A council spokesperson said re-opening the beach was a "high priority" but a "complex task" due to the type and location of the contamination, the potential risks to public health and the need to definitively identify the source of the asbestos.
Further tests in other waterfront locations have been taking place to check whether the contamination is confined to the Mount Batten area.
A contractor, which would identify the source of the contamination and provide solutions to re-open the beach, has yet to be appointed.

"This critical work needs to be robust and comprehensive, but our aim is for it to be carried out as rapidly as possible as we fully understand – and share – the frustrations of those who want the beach to re-open as soon as possible," the spokesperson said.

items.title: Chemicals at former fuel depot 'have been removed'
paragraphs: Barrels of chemicals left at an approved development site have been removed and testing carried out, a developer has said.
The Islip Fuel Depot in Oxfordshire is a former RAF and Esso fuel storage and transfer facility and has had outline planning permission approved to build residential and affordable homes.

Concerns were raised after campaigners discovered about 40 barrels of firefighting foam liquid, which contains PFAS - a group of chemicals often dubbed forever chemicals, had been left at the site for decades.
Developer, Newcore, said it had already identified the potential contamination and that "this potential risk and any contamination identified will be cleaned up immediately."
The depot previously supplied fuel to the former RAF Upper Heyford, around five miles north, which is suspected to be the source of forever chemical, or PFAS, contamination from firefighting foam.

Images show the barrels to be manufactured by Angus Fire Armour, that settled a legal battle out of court with residents in Yorkshire, after claims they had been exposed to PFAS near the company's foam manufacturing plant.

CEO of Newcore, Hugo Llewelyn, who took over the site in 2012, said it plans to regenerate the site with 50% affordable housing and that it was made aware of the barrels "in recent weeks" and had them removed in a "responsible and professional manner".

"Whilst firefighting foam containers were present on site from the MOD's operation back in the 20th Century, we do not believe it was ever deployed; the containers were sealed; and successive surveys have confirmed that there is no "pathway" for it to cause pollution," he added.
Mr Llewelyn disputes the quality of the testing carried out by campaigners.

"A 'pressure group' has trespassed unlawfully to obtain a questionable sample from this site to demonstrate that in the secured area of the site that was purposefully designed to accommodate foam for firefighting purposes, which is likely to contain PFAS, does, according to their findings, contain PFAS.
"I'm not sure there is anything to be surprised about here," he said.

He added that a Phase 1 assessment of the site last year had already identified the potential for contamination and that, "the specification for the Phase 2 investigation has therefore been designed to specifically address this potential risk and any contamination identified will be cleaned up immediately".
The Environment Agency's Chemical Compliance team had contacted the site owners to ensure that the drums are properly managed.
