Miss Marple aka Hart wasn't going to let her off the hook that easily, however, noting how Fry's argument the previous night had contradicted that of the innocent but now sadly now departed Myha'la.

In a nice moment of levity in another tense debate, comedian Joe Lycett reminded the traitors - and pointedly, Hesmondhalgh - that he would "like to be recruited at some stage". He stressed: "I'm still very much available."
Hesmondhalgh laughed about how "going all dry mouthed" while defending herself was not helping her cause.
"It would be a cruel move taking the most trusted member of our group," noted Sheen.
Ranganathan offered: "The person that we nominated as our most trustworthy person, we have now completely flipped on."
Newfound Traitor Hannah Fry survived a stressful episode
The conclusion was to banish Hesmondhalgh, who, in her parting words, said it had been an "immense experience".
"Alas," she continued, confirming her fidelity as tears appeared in eyes around the table: "It may mean I am not a phenomenal actor."
Singer Blunt, who had led the charge against her, appears to have now put himself in the frame. He told the group: "I'm so sorry, that's my fault."
"He's been wrong about every theory he's came up with," said Rooney.
Hart declared that "everything is up in the air" now, following Hesmondhalgh's eviction, which King Kenny called the team's "biggest loss" so far.
First recruit, Acaster's strategy is to continue playing the game as if he is a faithful, he said. Jama is clearly loving life on the dark side while Fry, it's fair to say, is not.
"You two saved me," Fry told the other two of her stressful day, while back in the turret in their cloaks.
The episode ended not with a murder but a fresh twist - the promise of a deathly game of hide-and-seek for four chosen contestants.
Ross Kemp, Rob Beckett, Leigh-Anne Pinnock and Romesh Ranganathan looking delighted to have been chosen for a game of killer hide-and-seek
The traitors opted to stay out of the game themselves, before settling on Kemp, Ranganathan, his comic pal Rob Beckett and Little Mix and solo singer Leigh-Anne Pinnock.
"I think this is gonna mess with everybody's heads," said Fry.
Presenter Claudia Winkleman greeted the four of them outside the castle in the dead of night.
"If only it was that easy Romesh," replied the host, explaining how when they go down to the woods tonight they'll be in for a big surprise: one of them will be killed face-to-face.
Only Pinnock, it was decided, will be immune from murder in the game within a game, though the Traitors aren't to know that.
This much terror and mischief and it's not Halloween for weeks yet.
Celebrity Traitors continues on Thursday at 20:00 BST on BBC One and iPlayer.
Have you played a version of the Traitors or another social deduction game at home or socially? Share your experience.

items.title: Kalshi taps former FBI agent to fight against money laundering
paragraphs: Sean Fern, a former FBI agent, is joining the prediction market platform Kalshi to lead the company's efforts in fighting money laundering. Provided by Kalshi hide caption

Kalshi, a leading prediction market company, has hired a former FBI agent to run its first anti-money laundering team as prediction markets come under increasing legal scrutiny by state and federal regulators.

Sean Fern will work closely with law enforcement and regulators and senior staff at Kalshi to keep an eye on suspicious and potentially criminal activity on the platform, which has exploded in growth in the past year.
According to the firm TickerTracker, Kalshi has crossed $260 billion in bets so far this year, already triple the amount traded in all of 2025.

In an interview with NPR, Fern, who worked as a federal prosecutor in Brooklyn before his time at the FBI, said his aim is to build defenses against people trying to use the platform to commit financial crimes.

"I want to make sure it's a hard place to launder money or evade sanctions and commit fraud," Fern told NPR on Friday. "On a day-to-day basis, that involves knowing who our customers are, knowing where their money comes from, and making sure we aren't doing business with sanctioned entities or parties," he said. "And when something looks off or looks suspicious, we can catch it and make referrals to law enforcement."

The announcement echoes what cryptocurrency companies did during that sector's boom times in the early 2020s. The cryptocurrency exchange Binance, for instance, hired former federal prosecutors and FBI agents to beef up its compliance and anti-money laundering divisions. Several years later, Binance's founder Changpeng Zhao pleaded guilty to money laundering charges.
Avoiding its own money laundering scandal, Fern said, is the reason Kalshi tapped him.

At the FBI, Fern was a special agent in the bureau's international corruption squad, where he helped lead the investigation into the multibillion-dollar bribery scheme tied to Malaysia's sovereign wealth fund, a scandal that became known as 1MDB.
Kalshi hopes adding Fern will lend credibility to the surging platform as it faces mounting scrutiny over insider trading and market manipulation.

Prediction market bettors can place wagers on everything from sports to what politicians say at public events to the outcome of elections. Experts have warned that introducing betting into domains like voting and policy decisions encourages people to monetize insider information.

Federal regulators and law enforcement in Washington have launched criminal investigations into alleged abuse on prediction market platforms. Earlier this year, regulators settled with former U.S. Rep. George Santos over market manipulation. Federal prosecutors have also indicted a former U.S. Army soldier and a former Google employee for allegedly using non-public information to cash out on Polymarket, Kalshi's main rival. In August, President Trump's former teleprompter operator was fined by regulators for using advance notice of the president's speeches to profit on Kalshi's so-called "mention markets."

Elisabeth Diana, a Kalshi spokeswoman, said that as banks, hedge funds and other financial institutions use Kalshi, the need to shore up financial crime safeguards has become apparent. "We are growing up," Diana said.
The company, which PitchBook estimates to be worth around $40 billion, has 250 employees, and it plans to double its headcount over the next six months.

During his time in federal law enforcement, Fern was one of the lead prosecutors in the trial of OneTaste, an "orgasmic meditation" wellness company whose founders were sentenced to prison following convictions for forced labor conspiracy.

items.title: Controversial vaccine trial touted by RFK Jr gets go-ahead in Guinea-Bissau
paragraphs: A controversial research trial that will withhold hepatitis B vaccines from some African newborns was given approval to move forward this week.
It is a central part of the vaccine vision for Robert F Kennedy Jr, the secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and a longtime vaccine opponent.

At an anti-vaccine conference last month, Kennedy praised the Danish researchers behind the trial and touted US-supported research on hepatitis B in newborns as exemplifying the Trump administration’s agenda for vaccines, which has included slashing vaccine recommendations and casting doubt on the safety and effectiveness of shots.
Kennedy “wants to make it so we don’t use a birth dose here in this country,” said Paul Offit, an infectious disease physician at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia. “That’s the goal.”

Kennedy would never be able to do the trial in the US because of its significant ethical concerns, Offit added. “He’s taking advantage of a developing country … Is it because children in Africa are more expendable than children here?”

Danish researchers plan to enroll 14,000 infants in Guinea-Bissau in the trial, giving the hepatitis B vaccine to half of the babies at birth and withholding it from the others for the first six weeks of life.

An ethics committee at the researchers’ home institution of the University of Southern Denmark voted this week to proceed with the trial, and officials in Guinea-Bissau have also greenlit the project, which the health minister, Quinhin Nantote, initially said was suspended after international uproar earlier this year.

Stig Børsen Hansen, a founding member who was one of two reviewers who presented the study to the Danish committee, resigned from the group in protest on Friday, citing major ethical issues with the study.

“You are now enrolling newborns in a lottery to test a hypothesis,” Hansen said. The children who are randomly selected not to receive the birth dose of the vaccine, those who “lost the lottery”, face in their earliest days the risk of contracting hepatitis B, which can cause irreversible lifelong damage. “They contract hepatitis B in the context of being part of a research project,” Hansen said, which made their infection happen, in effect, “by design”.
Three other members of the committee have also resigned in protest.

The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has reportedly set aside $1.6m in this year’s budget for the project, and it will be matched with private funding from the Pershing Square Foundation, which was co-founded by the billionaire activist Bill Ackman, and the Bluebell Foundation.
The CDC, the Danish researchers, Pershing Square and Nantote have not responded to the Guardian’s questions about this trial.
The news that the trial was approved by the Denmark ethics committee was first reported on Thursday by CIDRAP News. This is the first time details of the updated protocol have been disclosed.

The Guinea-Bissau study protocol has changed since it was posted in January, according to details shared with the Guardian. The researchers will now test mothers for hepatitis B before they give birth. The babies of mothers who test positive will be given the vaccine and will not be included in the trial. But the babies of mothers whose tests are negative may be enrolled. The new protocol has not been shared publicly.

In previous research, half of children who contracted hepatitis B did so after birth, through community exposures. “This virus can be transmitted casually,” Offit said. It can live on surfaces for up to seven days, and it can be acquired by sharing washcloths, toothbrushes and fingernail clippers. In addition, the hepatitis B test has a 5% false negative rate, which could provide false assurance that a birthing parent does not have the virus.

Decades of research make it clear that the vaccine would be beneficial, which means it would be unfair to place some children in the vaccinated group and some children in the unvaccinated group, said Henrik Støvring, a professor of statistics and pharmacometrics at Aarhus University in Denmark.
According to the Helsinki declaration, international medical research must be approved by ethics committees in both the host and sponsor countries.

The Danish research ethics committee at the University of Southern Denmark had never considered medical studies before, but it changed the rules in order to vote on this one. While committee members with expertise argued against approving it, the majority ruled to move forward.

“It’s very unusual to bring this into a committee like that,” Støvring said. The national ethics committee in Denmark oversees medical research, but this study was outside of their purview because it won’t take place in Denmark.

Yet “I don’t see why you couldn’t do it in Denmark,” Støvring said of the trial. In fact, several conditions make it a better location. The hepatitis B vaccine is not usually given to newborns in Denmark unless the mother is positive for the virus, for which all pregnant people are tested in Denmark.

Guinea-Bissau has some of the highest rates of hepatitis B in the world, with about 18% of adults carrying the virus. While it may be transmitted from mother to child during birth, it could also be transmitted from another parent, relatives, siblings or caregivers. Children who are infected with hepatitis B in the first year of life are significantly more likely to develop severe outcomes, including chronic infection and liver cancer.

The Bandim Health Project, run by Danish researchers Peter Aaby and Christine Stabell Benn, has operated in Guinea-Bissau for decades and is closely enmeshed in the country’s health system. At least one top official, the current director of public health, held a dual appointment with Bandim as recently as December.

Kennedy praised the Danish researchers at a recent anti-vaccine conference, calling them “the deities of vaccine research”. Kennedy claimed that a prior study they conducted indicated that after vaccination, “you can have mass injuries, and catastrophic injuries, and they’re hiding in plain sight.” He did not mention that another follow-up study from the same researchers found no effects at all.

This study will focus on vaccination and mortality, as well as outcomes such as skin conditions and neurodevelopmental conditions. “The main problem of this trial is that you have some very well-known bad diseases that you can protect with this vaccine,” Støvring said. “And what they then want to study is something highly speculative – in a situation where WHO and others are saying that you should give this vaccine at birth, period.”

When asked about the study in a Thursday briefing, an official with the Africa CDC, which has opposed the trial, said there were “ongoing discussions” between the US and Guinea-Bissau and more details would be shared shortly. Guinea-Bissau planned to begin vaccinating all newborns against hepatitis B in 2027, but they pushed the campaign back to 2028.

Kennedy and the Danish researchers were “taking advantage of that delay in practicing standard care to put these children at risk unnecessarily”, Offit said. “What a terrible thing to do. What a horribly unethical and cruel thing to do.”

items.title: Three men found guilty of murders of Australian surfer brothers and US friend in Mexico
paragraphs: A Mexican judge has convicted three men of the 2024 murders of two Australian surfers and their American friend in a case that sparked international outrage.

Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, aged 30 and 33 respectively, and their friend Carter Rhoad, 30, were on a surfing trip to Mexico’s Pacific coast when they were shot dead in Baja California state in a suspected robbery.
The deaths of the trio sparked an outpouring of grief and condemnation in Australia and the United States.

Jesus Gerardo – known as “El Kekas” – was accused of leading the attack. His surname has not been disclosed for legal reasons. He and two other defendants, Irineo Francisco and Angel Jesus, were found guilty on Friday local time.
The judge ruled that the three Mexican defendants acted with premeditation.
Martin and Debra Robinson, the brothers’ parents, traveled from Australia to the port city of Ensenada for the trial, which began on 7 September.
“They took our sons from our lives forever,” said Debra Robinson, who testified on the final day of the trial. “What hurts us most is that, in their final hours, they were treated with such cruelty.”
She burst into tears when the guilty verdict was pronounced.
Addressing the court at the start of the trial, Martin Robinson described his sons’ murders as “hell”.
“It’s hard for a parent to lose a son, and we lost two sons,” he said.
Rhoad’s mother, Page, and his fiance, Natalie Weirtz, also participated in the hearing in a video call from the United States.
“The accused are guilty and must be punished so that no other family suffers the same pain,” Weirtz said. “Since Carter’s death, I feel paranoid and isolated.”
The prosecution requested 210 years’ imprisonment for each of the accused, though the maximum sentence in Baja California is 60 years.
The surfers were camping in a remote beachside area when they were attacked in April 2024. Their bodies were found in a clifftop shaft, with gunshot wounds to their heads.
In November 2025, Ary Gisell Silva, the then-girlfriend of the main defendant, was sentenced to two decades in prison after admitting that she instigated the robbery.

Baja California is one of Mexico’s most violent states, plagued by organised crime and drug trafficking, although cartel activity does not usually affect tourists. Other foreign visitors have, however, been targeted in criminal attacks on Mexico’s Pacific coast.
Two Australian surfers, Dean Lucas and Adam Coleman, were killed in 2015 while traveling through the north-western state of Sinaloa. Their bodies were later burned.

items.title: Fired OpenAI employees question the company's commitment to safety
paragraphs: Three employees recently fired by OpenAI allege the company punished them for being outspoken about safety. OpenAI disputes the claims and says they were dismissed for mishandling sensitive information. Andrej Ivanov/AFP via Getty Images hide caption

Three former OpenAI employees are raising concerns over the circumstances of their dismissals and the company's commitment to safety, amid intense public scrutiny of the artificial intelligence industry's ability to responsibly develop the technology.

The former employees, Mikita Balesni, Tomek Korbak and Jasmine Wang, alleged that OpenAI fired them last week over pretexts and punished them for either being outspoken about safety or working with outside researchers. They also expressed worries the company may walk back a recent safety commitment.
OpenAI has repeatedly denied the allegations. It said the employees were fired for mishandling sensitive information and said the company has not abandoned its safety commitment.

The dispute comes at a fraught time for the AI industry and OpenAI in particular. Over the summer, OpenAI's agents hacked into companies, communicated with each other without authorization and attempted to cover their tracks. Unlike chatbots, agents are AI systems that can carry out tasks autonomously for an extended period of time.

The most serious hack, of software company Hugging Face, contributed to the resignation of a researcher at rival Anthropic who issued dire warnings about the trajectory of the technology. The resignation captured the attention of figures outside of the AI field including lawmakers. Many, including some executives of the top AI companies, have called for various ways to avert disaster, including slowing down the development of the most advanced AI.
In the meanwhile, OpenAI has been reviewing its agents' activities in recent months and notifying organizations whose digital infrastructure has been affected.

As a response to the safety concerns, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said on Sep. 12 that the company will follow its rival Anthropic in expanding access to third-party evaluators, who assess the safety of AI systems and the practices of developers.

The three employees dismissed by OpenAI last week worked on teams that focus on AI safety and making the company's models follow human intentions and values. Two of them were involved in investigating the Hugging Face hack.

In a letter to OpenAI's safety leadership that the fired employees posted on X this week, they urged the company to stay committed to working with third-party researchers, to preserve human's ability to monitor model behavior and to "continue to support an open and transparent culture of dialogue" between in-house safety researchers and external ones. They also warned their firings were having a chilling effect on their former OpenAI colleagues.

In a statement OpenAI posted on X, the company said it is still committed to bringing in third-party evaluators and that it agreed with the fired employees's recommendations. The company said the three were fired last week because they "violated clear policies on handling sensitive information."
The former employees have disputed OpenAI's explanation of their firings. None of them responded to NPR's interview requests.

"In the exit call, I was told OpenAI no longer trusts me because I was speaking too much to third party safety organizations, implying I leaked company [intellectual property]. I never shared company IP," Balesni wrote on X on Thursday. He said he was involved in investigating the OpenAI agents' hack on Hugging Face.
"If OpenAI has specific concerns, I invite them to write to us directly. I expect they will not, because our firing was pretextual," Balesni continued.

He said he worried that OpenAI will use the firings as an excuse to cut off its relationship with Model Evaluation and Threat Research (METR), a nonprofit that focuses on evaluating risks of humans losing control of AI. OpenAI allowed researchers from METR and Redwood Research, another AI safety research organization, to examine internal records related to the Hugging Face hack.

A second fired OpenAI employee, Korbak, was the technical point of contact for the METR/Redwood Research investigation. "I was told verbally I was fired because of the way I communicated with METR. No details on what I said or did or when. No other reasons were given and nothing was put in writing," Korbak wrote on X, echoing Balesni's concerns.

The report produced by METR and Redwood Research in the wake of the Hugging Face hack shed light on the scale of the attack as well as the degree to which the agents acted in undesirable ways. The authors of the report called the investigation "brief" and many in the AI safety field have called for expanded access to independent evaluators at AI companies to make sure they investigate similar incidents or other safety concerns thoroughly.
In a statement to NPR, METR declined to comment on the OpenAI employees' firings.

Wang, the third OpenAI employee fired last week, coined the word "pacing," which describes a way of slowing down development of the most advanced AI systems so that safety can catch up, according to the letter she and her two colleagues sent to OpenAI's safety leadership. The term was invoked in an open letter calling for such a slowdown signed by over a thousand staff members from top AI companies in July, after the Hugging Face hack.

Wang wrote on X that she was fired over accessing an executive's email. But she said she had access to the inbox for work reasons in the past and wasn't able to get IT to remove the access once she no longer needed it.

"The reasons that we were provided for our terminations are simply not adding up. We're hearing people are now being told vague rumors internally to discredit us," Wang wrote. "The message to everyone still at OpenAI is clear: raise concerns or work closely with outside safety groups, and you could be next, without being told why."
OpenAI said in a statement to NPR that the three terminated employees violated policies more than once, and the mishandling of information went beyond their work with an outside evaluation group.
OpenAI also shared an internal memo from an unnamed research leader that it said was shared with the company on Wednesday, before the three ex-employees took to social media.
In the memo, the research leader said the company "strongly" agreed with the three ex-employees' recommendations. "We do not terminate employees for raising concerns," the leader wrote.
"OpenAI leadership is saying they strongly agree with our letter. Let's see how that pans out," Wang wrote on X.

items.title: US says Taliban failing to combat human trafficking in Afghanistan
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Dari article.
The United States says the Taliban government in Afghanistan does not ‘fully’ meet the minimum standards for combating human trafficking and is not making significant efforts to do so.
In the U.S. State Department’s 2026 Trafficking in Persons Report, released on Thursday, Taliban-ruled Afghanistan remained in Tier 3.

During the reporting period, from April 2025 to March 2026, “... there was a pattern of recruitment and use of child soldiers in combat and support roles and a pattern of sexual slavery (bacha bazi — a practice in which men exploit boys for social and sexual entertainment),” the report said.

Tier 3 refers to countries where government agencies and other public sector institutions do not fully comply with the minimum criteria for combating human trafficking and do not make significant efforts to improve the situation.
The report listed 20 countries, including Afghanistan, Iran, Russia, Cuba, Venezuela, Sudan and South Sudan, in Tier 3.
The State Department said the Taliban did not take any steps to address the problem of trafficking.
“The Taliban did not report any investigation, prosecutions, or convictions, nor did it identify or protect any trafficking victims," the report said.
In July, the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime and the International Organization for Migration called for coordination of efforts to prevent trafficking and assist victims.

“Victims continue to be pushed into unsafe work, forced labor, sexual exploitation, slavery-like conditions, or even have their organs removed against their will. Women, children, returnees, and indebted households remain at heightened risk,” said UNODC and IOM in a joint statement.
The U.S. State Department noted that referring to the Taliban in the report does not mean recognition of the Taliban as the Afghan government.
According to the report, the Taliban and other armed groups employ children illegally and use them in war and to perform support duties, the report said.

“The Taliban recruit children through coercion and fraud, including from schools in Afghanistan and Pakistan, enrolling them in jihadi madrassas that reportedly provide military training,” the report said.
In addition to the Taliban, groups such as the Islamic State Khorasan, also called ISIS-K, and the National Resistance Front, an anti-Taliban armed group, also use children in the fighting.

Although the Taliban have issued a decree banning human trafficking, the report noted that it “did not provide a clear definition of human trafficking or penalties that were sufficiently stringent. The new edict also included provisions that recognized aspects of slavery.”

items.title: Nashville honors 50 Years of Kurdish community in the United States
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Kurdi article.

The Metropolitan Council of Nashville and Davidson County in the southeastern U.S. state of Tennessee has officially recognized the 50th anniversary of the arrival of the first group of Kurdish families in the U.S., honoring their contributions to the city's cultural, social and economic development.

According to an official proclamation obtained by VOA, the first group of Kurdish families arrived in the United States on May 1, 1976. Many later settled in Nashville, Tennessee, while others established communities in cities and states across the country.

The proclamation highlights the Kurdish community's efforts to preserve its language, culture, and traditions over the past five decades, while playing an important role in Nashville's growth and development.

According to the document, Nashville is now home to more than 20,000 Kurds, making it one of the largest Kurdish communities in the United States. The city has become an important center for Kurdish cultural and community life.

The proclamation also recognizes the longstanding relationship between the United States and Kurdistan, highlighting cooperation between Kurdish Peshmerga forces, U.S. troops and their allies in the fight against terrorism.
Metropolitan Nashville Council member Mike Cortese, who represents District 4, led the official recognition of the anniversary in cooperation with other council members.
The proclamation was signed on October 6, 2026.

items.title: Human Rights Group: Repression Intensifies in Russia for Participation in ‘Undesirable Organizations’
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Russian article.

The number of politically motivated prosecutions in Russia involving restrictions on freedom of association increased by 50% in the first nine months of 2026, according to a new report by the Support for Political Prisoners Memorial Center.

The human rights group was part of the Memorial Human Rights Center that was liquidated by a Russian Court in 2022. Operating as the Support for Political Prisoners Memorial center, the group continues to work independently to help political prisoners in Russia.

According to the new report, the number of people charged in politically motivated criminal cases rose to 328 from 219. Those targeted are primarily supporters of late opposition leader Alexei Navalny, “USSR citizens,” Jehovah’s Witnesses, and members of organizations designated as “undesirable.”

Meanwhile, the number of prosecutions linked to Navalny’s organizations increased by 107% over the year, from 69 to 143 people. The number of people accused of financing an extremist organization rose by nearly 117%, from 77 to 167.
Human rights activist Anna Karetnikova points out that one of the main trends in recent months has been a change in the nature of political repression.

Whereas a significant proportion of criminal cases previously involved public statements, including those made online, she says law enforcement authorities now are increasingly targeting people for actions that the authorities interpret as support for or participation in “banned” organizations.

“The focus is shifting to people who do not openly protest but express their disagreement in various ways or support the side they believe is right in the conflict,” Karetnikova told VOA’s Russian service.
According to Karetnikova, such activities may include running chat groups, providing materials for publication, or financially supporting organizations.

The Support for Political Prisoners Memorial Center report said the number of cases involving money transfers to the Navalny-founded Anti-Corruption Foundation (FBK), which Russian authorities have designated an “extremist organization,” has risen particularly sharply.

At the same time, the overall number of cases related to persecution for public statements fell by 22% over the year. There was an increase in other types of cases, however, such as in the number of cases involving calls for extremism. Those rose by 26%, while cases brought under articles concerning crimes against state security increased by 13%.

According to Karetnikova, people who were not previously considered political activists are increasingly becoming targets of criminal prosecution. She attributes this to the fact that, as the best-known opponents of the Russian authorities are imprisoned or leave the country, the repressive apparatus begins to expand the pool of potential targets.
“This includes tractor drivers, teachers, rural doctors — anyone,” Karetnikova said.

The report’s authors also note a significant increase in the role of the Federal Security Service (FSB) in political prosecutions. In 67% of politically motivated criminal cases, at least one charge falls under the FSB’s investigative jurisdiction.

items.title: Iran and its allied militias continue attacks on Iraq's Kurdistan
paragraphs: Erbil & Sulaimaniyah, Kurdistan Region of Iraq —
Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Kurdish article.

Iran and Iran-backed Shiite militias in Iraq have intensified their surveillance and security activities in the Kurdistan Region, following the withdrawal of U.S. and coalition forces, Kurdish officials say, as a new drone attack targeted a camp housing Iranian Kurdish refugee near Erbil.

The Kurdistan Region's Counterterrorism Unit confirmed that two explosive-laden drones struck the camp in Kawrgosk, in Khabat district, about 35 kilometers from Erbil, the regional capital, late Thursday.
"Tonight, Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026, at 10:19 p.m., two explosive-laden drones targeted the camp of Iranian Kurdish refugees in Kawrgosk," the directorate said in a statement.

Kurdish officials suspect Iran was directly responsible for the attack, although many previous strikes have been attributed to Iran-backed Shiite militias operating under Iraq's Popular Mobilization Forces.

Afsana Rahimi, a member of the central committee of the Organization of Iranian Kurdistan Struggle, told VOA that the attack targeted a camp hosting the group’s families, causing a large explosion fire and spreading panic among residents.
Emergency crews brought the fire under control, but the extent of the damage has not been disclosed.
Mardin Zahedi, the organization's head of relations, told VOA on Friday from Erbil that the drones were believed to have been launched from Iranian territory.
"According to our information, last night's drone attack was carried out by Iran, and the two drones may have been launched from the Piranshahr area inside Iran," Zahedi said.

Zahedi said Iran had previously attacked the area seven times and that nearly 10 other attempted attacks had been thwarted. The area houses members of the Organization of Iranian Kurdistan Struggle and their families.

"Since the withdrawal of U.S. and coalition forces, surveillance by Iran and Iraqi militias has intensified," Zahedi said. "We have no means of defending ourselves, so we are exercising extreme caution, conducting our activities discreetly and avoiding group gatherings."

According to Kurdistan Regional Government figures, Iran has launched more than 1,000 drone and missile attacks against the Kurdistan Region since Feb. 28, when the United States launched Operation Epic Fury against Iran.
One of Iran's main concerns is the presence of thousands of Iranian Kurdish opposition members and their families who have lived in Iraq's Kurdistan Region since the 1990s.

Iranian officials have also accused the Kurdistan Region of serving as a safe haven for U.S. and Israeli activities. Kurdish authorities say they are closely allied with the U.S. but refuse allegations of relationship with Israel.

items.title: Powerful 7.6-magnitude earthquake hits Panama and triggers tsunami warnings
paragraphs: A powerful 7.6 magnitude earthquake has struck Panama and triggered tsunami warnings along the west coast of Central and South America, according to the US Geological Survey (USGS).

The quake hit along the southern coast of the country, the USGS said. It was centered near the southern tip of the Central American country, about 14km (9 miles) south-west of the remote community of Pitaloza Arriba, the USGS said.

The Institute of Geosciences of the University of Panama said the quake struck at just before 1pm local time near the southern town of Tonosí. The Panamanian institute said that a second 6.0 magnitude earthquake struck soon after, at 1.22pm.
By 1.3opm there had reportedly been 13 aftershocks.
The president, José Raúl Mulino, said he had asked a key minister to call for calm. “What happened should not be used to generate alarm and disorder,” Mulino wrote on X.
Local newspaper La Prensa said that across the Central American country, buildings, schools and homes were evacuated as a result of the “powerful movement of the earth”.

Footage published by La Prensa showed severe damage to several buildings in the city of Penonomé, including the St John Baptist Cathedral. Other photos showed a highway to the west of the capital that had been completely sheared in half by the earthquake.

Tremors were felt strongly ​in the ⁠capital of ⁠Panama ​City, ‌according ‌to ‌witnesses who spoke to Reuters. The Associated Press reported that buildings shook and visibly shaken residents gathered outside as they waited for news of the quake’s impact.

The USGS said hazardous waves were possible along the coasts of Costa Rica, Ecuador, Peru, Nicaragua, Guatemala, El Salvador and Mexico, although the tsunami warning for Chile was cancelled at 4.18pm local time.

items.title: France in technical talks with Taliban on deportation of Afghans
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Pashto article.

The French government has confirmed ‘technical’ talks with the Taliban to facilitate the deportation to Afghanistan of Afghan nationals residing without legal status or who are considered a national security threat in France.

This is “strictly technical to facilitate the removal of Afghan nationals, nationals who are illegally on the [French] national territory and who pose a national security risk,” a spokesperson for France’s Ministry for Europe and Foreign Affairs said Thursday in a press conference.

Agence France-Presse reported on the talks on Tuesday, citing unnamed French officials. These sources told AFP that the talks did not mean that France would recognize the Taliban’s government as the legitimate government of Afghanistan.
France suspended expulsion of Afghan nationals whose asylum applications had been rejected in 2021, when the Taliban took over Afghanistan.
France has not maintained diplomatic relations with the Taliban since they returned to power in August 2021, and its embassy in Kabul remains closed.
No country, except Russia, recognizes the Taliban, who seized power in 2021.

However, 20 European Union nations, including France, Germany, Belgium, and Sweden are in favor of establishing contacts with the Taliban to return Afghan nationals whose asylum cases have been rejected or who have been involved in crimes.

In June, a meeting in Brussels between European officials and Taliban representatives sparked criticism from human rights organizations. They condemned any engagement with a regime that, since returning to power, has imposed a strict interpretation of Islamic Sharia law and deprived women and girls of fundamental rights.
The spokesperson for France’s Ministry for Europe and Foreign Affairs noted that female asylum seekers would not be deported to Afghanistan.
Under the Taliban, Afghan women have been barred from working with government and non-government organizations, education beyond sixth grade, going to public baths, beauty salons and gyms.
According to UNESCO, approximately 2.4 million Afghan girls are currently excluded from secondary education.
Noshaba Ashna and Roshan Noorzai from VOA's Afghan service contributed to this report.

items.title: Tested: The Mac Studio M5 Max claims its crown as the best of all Apple computers
paragraphs: Astonishingly powerful, very compact, and perhaps not as expensive as you might think as long as you don’t go mad on the RAM, the 2026 version of the Mac Studio sports an M5 Max CPU that tears through creative work as well as things like running local AI models. It’s so good you’ll stop wondering where the Mac Pro has gone.
Why you can trust Creative Bloq Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

The latest Mac Studio uses the M5 Max chip, which we’ve already seen in the form of a MacBook Pro. There's an M5 Ultra too, which takes things to another level, but the price gets excessive enough to make the Max version look reasonable. Still, this should be enough computer for anyone, whether you’re chewing through 8K video or trying to break the record for the greatest number of layers and filters in a Photoshop document.

On the outside, it’s the same old Studio we’ve seen for generations, but Apple keeps piling on the improvements and innovations in its silicon, and that’s lead to a machine that’s pulling ahead at the top of many of Creative Bloq’s benchmarking charts, will be a great alternative to the best laptop for animation and is looking hard to catch.
4x Thunderbolt 5, 2x USB-A, 2x USB-C, 1x HDMI, 1x 10Gb Ethernet, 1x 3.5mm audio

Opening up any new Apple product is always an exciting experience as they’re just so well packaged. You pull tabs and tear strips away from the box, then follow arrows to fold down the sides and reveal, in the case of the Studio, the aluminium monolith inside.

The M5 Max version of the Studio looks little different to the way it has all the way back to 2022, with all the changes concentrated on the inside. This means you get something that looks like a Mac Mini under a magnifying glass, only without any of the slight annoyances that have crept into the little computer over the years. The power button is at the back but you can reach it without turning the Mac over, there are loads of USB ports including some Type-As, there's an actual light on the front to tell you if it’s on, and a port for everything so there's less need for a dock or adapter. If you’re lucky enough to own an Apple Studio Display, it will sit on the foot like it was designed to go there.

If you’ve bought the M5 Ultra version of the Mac Studio, it’s heavier than either M5 Max edition due to the presence of an enhanced cooling system for the hotter chip, but the M5 Max is barely heavier than many laptops, and for something that’s settled nicely into the Mac Pro’s niche at the top of the product stack, that’s remarkable.
• Thunderbolt 5 aplenty• Easy to reach ports

As Apple is reusing the same Studio chassis we’ve seen previously, and the M5 Max version even has the same IO as the M4 Max we reviewed previously, there's very little new here. The Wi-Fi has had a bump to version 7, the Bluetooth to version 6, but there's still plain Thunderbolt 5 (which is plenty fast enough) and a boring old HDMI port.

This machine doesn’t use the M6 - we haven’t seen that chip yet - but the M5 Max takes the already excellent M5 and just adds more to it. Apple is claiming 3.9x faster AI performance than the prior generation and 4.3x the peak AI compute performance of an M3 Ultra. You can spec it with up to 512GB of RAM, if you dare, and you’ll find that this has 50% more memory bandwidth. If that’s not enough, you can use Thunderbolt to connect multiple Mac Studios together to load the most demanding frontier-class open-weight models available. A cluster of four Mac Studios, so it’s claimed, can deliver up to 3x faster AI inference than a single system.

Apple is really pushing the AI capabilities, presumably getting in on the local model and agent action before the first crop of Nvidia RTX Spark machines arrives. But you know what else likes huge amounts of RAM and enormous bandwidth, not to mention loads of processing power? Creative work, that’s what. If you want hardware-accelerated H.264, HEVC, ProRes and AV1 decode, or to colour-grade uncompressed 8K footage while processing multiple concurrent video streams, this is the Mac to do it for you.

It’s also worth noting that Apple has moved its in-house creative apps to a subscription model, called Creator Studio. You get Final Cut Pro, Logic Pro, Pixelmator Pro and a bit more for a monthly fee rather than a large up-front cost, something that will hopefully rekindle interest in these underappreciated apps.
We test every one of our laptops using the same benchmarking software suite to give you a thorough overview of its suitability for creatives of all disciplines and levels. This includes:

• Geekbench: Tests the CPU for single-core and multi-core power, and the GPU for the system's potential for gaming, image processing, or video editing. Geekbench AI tests the CPU and GPU on a variety of AI-powered and AI-boosted tasks.• Cinebench: Tests the CPU and GPU's ability to run Cinema 4D and Redshift.• UL Procyon: Uses UL Solutions' Procyon software suite to test the system's ability for AI image generation in Stable Diffusion, its Microsoft Office performance and its battery life in a looping video test.• Topaz Video AI: We use Topaz Video AI to test the system's ability to upscale video and convert video to slow-motion.• PugetBench for Creators: We use the PugetBench for Creators benchmarking suite to test the system's ability to run several key tasks in Photoshop and Adobe Premiere Pro, as well as its performance when encoding/transcoding video.• ON1 Resize AI: Tests the system's ability to resize 5 photos to 200% in a batch process. We take the total time taken to resize the images and divide by 5.
• Good at everything• Even the fan isn't too loud

The M5 Max Studio we’ve got here is the top model, with six Super cores, 12 Performance cores (for a total of 18) and a 40-core GPU. It sits one level below the M5 Ultra, which is two M5 Max chips stuck together and can have up to 36 cores, split between 12 Super and 24 Performance, but which costs a lot more. You don’t get Efficient cores on this level of Mac, and it’s essentially the same chip we saw in the M5 Max version of the MacBook Pro, just given slightly more room to breathe in the Studio chassis. It’s backed up in the model sent to Creative Bloq by 128GB of RAM and a 4TB SSD, which contributes to the cost as well as appealing to the new crop of AI types who want to run their models locally.

And so we see it head to the top of our benchmark charts. In Geekbench 6 it takes the top spot in both the single- and multi-core tests, butting even more of a gap between the M5 and its closest rival, the Snapdragon X2 Elite. In Geekbench 2026 it leads the Core Ultra 9 290HX+ in the Razer Blade 18 by almost 3000 points in multi-core rendering, and it’s the first CPU to break the 200-point barrier in Cinebench 2024’s single-core test, in which we used to say that 100 was a good score.

The GPU does well too, sitting 4.2% behind the GeForce RTX 5070Ti in the latest HP Omen 35L - a full-size desktop card - in Cinebench 2026. It beats the popular 24-core Intel Core Ultra 9 275HX laptop CPU in multi-core rendering, and almost doubles the score of the Omen 35L’s CPU, the AMD Ryzen 7 9800X3D beloved of gamers, in the same test.

Speaking of games, if you were thinking of dropping this much money on a Mac and want to use it out of hours, it can get 60FPS out of Cyberpunk 2077 at 4K resolution using the ray-tracing ultra preset, as long as you turn on MetalFX upscaling and AMD FSR frame generation. Drop the res down to 1440p and you can go as high as 89FPS.

In single-precision AI workloads the M5 Max sits between gaming laptops with GeForce chips in our charts, still behind the big desktop PCs. It drops in the Quantized test, however, sitting behind the likes of the Geekom A9 Max, but still ahead of the vanilla M5.

It shines in creative apps though, taking a long lead at the top of the Premiere Pro benchmark chart, beating its portable sibling and the HP Omen 35L. It’s the same in Photoshop, where its results are 6% better than the MacBook Pro with the same CPU.

In the spec we’ve reviewed here, the Mac Studio costs £6,899/$6,899, but with a lesser spec (M5 Max 16-core, 36GB RAM, 512GB storage) it starts at a more reasonable £2,499/$2,499. That’s still a big chunk of change, even if you are getting a lot of power in a small chassis, and you should definitely look at what a (much larger and noisier) PC with an Nvidia card can do for you in the same price bracket. There's not much else like the Mac Studio, however, and if it has the capabilities you need in a form factor you covet, you’re going to have to open your wallet.

Apple is going big on AI, but has also made a Mac that should be able to do the heavy lifting for many different creative disciplines. It will be overkill for many, as the basic M5 and the M6 that’s on the cusp of arriving are good enough for a lot of tasks. But if you find that you could do with a speed boost in your work, then it’s well worth looking at.
Looks the same as every other Mac Studio. And that's OK.
Thunderbolt 5, and lots of other ports too.
An expensive computer, but one with a lot to offer.
With this laptop, Apple has squeezed the kind of power you’d expect from a desktop Mac Pro in a tower case into a 14-inch chassis, and backed it up with plenty of RAM.

The choice of the 9800X3D CPU and GeForce 5070Ti GPU mean this compact-ish desktop has the capability to push pixels around at great speed. Whether it’s video editing, AI applications or the latest games.
With the G1a, HP has created a potent rival to the Mac Studio, equipping it with its Wolf security software, to make a PC that will appeal to FX pros and AI developers alike.

Ian Evenden has been a journalist for over 20 years, starting in the days of QuarkXpress 4 and Photoshop 5. He now mainly works in Creative Cloud and Google Docs, but can always find a use for a powerful laptop or two. When not sweating over page layout or photo editing, you can find him peering at the stars or growing vegetables.

items.title: 'People don't think recycling at work is part of their job description'
paragraphs: There was still "lots of room for improvement" when it comes to how much we recycle at work compared with our habits at home, according to an expert.
Figures suggest only 61% of people in Wales recycle often at their workplace, with one in five saying they do not recall seeing the appropriate facilities to do so.
Providing more bins or clearer labelling are some of the ways in which businesses could make a difference, said waste reduction charity Wrap.
But one business had already seen a "significant improvement" at their offices after removing staff's personal bins, a move that was initially met with resistance.
When recruitment firm Acorn by Synergie first moved into their offices on the outskirts of Newport in 2003, they were producing six large wheelie bins' worth of rubbish a week.

It now has just one weekly collection thanks to increased recycling, including food waste, which was their biggest adaptation, following the introduction of the Welsh government's Workplace Recycling Law in 2024.
"I don't recycle as much when I am out and about, I just bin it," admits Gerwyn Pugh, 56, from Barry.
"It's routine [at home], but out and about every bin takes a bit more time to work out."
James Jenkins, 30, said he often took rubbish home with him given the limited options where he works.
"We only recycle cardboard because that's our only waste.
"The more industrialised businesses need to do more, because they'll have more of an impact than smaller businesses."
Natalie James, 47, said she recycled "probably about the same" at work and at home.
"Because I work at a hospital we've got the recycling categories everywhere, so we have to."
Although businesses in Wales are now required to sort their waste into six categories, collection arrangements can vary from area to area.
In the Vale of Glamorgan, businesses use a mix of council and private services, and the local authority said the change has resulted in a "higher quality of recycling".
Carys Stephens, the council's waste project officer, said there had been a "fantastic response from businesses."
"There's obviously going to be some that are critical of the idea, and they're worried about extra costs and effort that goes into segregated recycling.
"But we've been doing segregated recycling for a couple of years now, and most people just take it in their stride."
Although Wales' workplace recycling rates are "reasonably high", said consultant Rebecca Colley-Jones, "there's lots of room for improvement".
"It is a new system, so there's always a period of settling down."
She said that she was sure "we would see that 61% rise".
"Often they can be tourism or hospitality businesses, so they're having to educate their customers what to do."
Colley-Jones said individuals also needed to personally take more care.
"Our home is our castle, we're responsible for the waste and people are under a little bit of pressure, perhaps from their neighbours to look like they're recycling.
"Whereas you don't have that in the workplace.
"When people come to work, they come to work, they don't necessarily thing recycling is part of their job description.

She added: "It's trying to get people to understand that they also need to be buying into the culture of an organisation, and also the culture of Wales as a country. We are the second-best recycler in the world."
She added that the changes had inevitably led to some costs for businesses, and varying collection arrangements can sometimes be "confusing".

items.title: Hollywood actor Luke Evans on 'joyous' four months filming in rainy Wales
paragraphs: In The Party, Evans, 47, stars as Martin Gilmour, a journalist shaped by his lifelong friendship with a wealthy and charismatic politician played by Aberystwyth-born Tom Cullen.
Speaking on BBC's The One Show, he said that he had "shot in Wales" previously - when filming The Pembrokeshire Murders - but "never that close" to his family.
"Pembrokeshire is miles away from where my family are in the valleys," he said.
"They were only 25 minutes from me up the road [this time]."
He joked: "They were there all the time."
His parents Yvonne and David Evans still live in the same "narrow" terrace house he grew up in IN Aberbargoed in the Rhymney Valley.
He added: "We were having dinners on the weekend, walking the dog, enjoyed a rainy three, four months in Wales over the winter period.
Some family members even managed to get a short cameo in the final episode of the upcoming drama.
Evans said: "[My cousins] were like 'can we be in the show?'
"They are, they're in it. My cousin and his wife and their kids are in the final episode."
After filming wrapped up, Evans headed back to New York where he starred as Dr Frank-N-Furter in the Broadway revival of The Rocky Horror Show.
"I did the show for seven months and I was coming to the end of the run - I had such an incredible experience doing the show," he said.
"It was just the most wonderful, inclusive, joyous two hours of my day. It was wonderful. The audience were just loving it."

Evans said that actor Tim Curry had been a part of his "whole journey", and that he would have people on the stage door and messages "comparing me" to him, and "how proud he would be of the performance."
Curry, who died in August, aged 80, first played the role on stage before the film version, which was released in 1975 and has remained a cult favourite.
Evans added: "So I had to send him a letter, even if he'll never read it.
"I just felt like I had to say thank you because I really believe that if it wasn't for Tim's performances as Frank-N-Furter, I don't think that film would still be around.
"He really kept that show, and the messages throughout the show are so prevalent and strong and important today as they were 53 years ago."
He received a response from Curry's team three weeks before his final performance, saying that he was "very appreciative" of that letter and thanked him for sending it.
"Sadly he passed the day after I finished," Evans said.

items.title: US 7th Air Force seeks 'combat-verified' anti-drone capabilities on Korean Peninsula
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Korean article.
The U.S. 7th Air Force is seeking combat-proven drone countermeasure capabilities to modernize joint base defense in the Korean Peninsula operational theater.

The U.S. 7th Air Force began searching for companies with drone defense technology to be applied to the 'Project Iron Sentry' project through a Request for Information (RFI) released on the U.S. federal government procurement site on the 5th.

The U.S. 7th Air Force is headquartered at Osan Air Base, and the U.S. Pacific Air Force describes the 7th Air Force's mission as "to deter, protect, and defend the Republic of Korea from attacks by North Korea."
This information request comes amid growing concerns between the U.S. and South Korea regarding North Korea's drone capabilities.
According to the announcement, the official name of the program is 'Project Iron Sentry, Korean Peninsula Theater of Operations (KTO) Joint Base Defense Modernization'.
The 7th Air Force stated that the purpose of this information request is market research, not a bid for an actual contract.
At the same time, they stated that they are seeking “field-verified, theater-wide Small Unmanned Aerial System (C-sUAS) and Unmanned Aerial System (C-UAS) capabilities.”

Countering Small Unmanned Aerial Systems (C-sUAS) is a system for responding to small drones, and it refers to a series of capabilities that involve locating and tracking drones using radar, electro-optical equipment, etc., and then neutralizing them through jamming, electronic warfare, or interception means.

The 7th Air Force specifically requested capabilities that could be eligible for support from the U.S. Department of Defense's 'Advanced Procurement and Deployment of Innovative Technologies (APFIT)' program.
APFIT is a program designed to rapidly advance the procurement and actual deployment of innovative technologies required by Defense Department organizations, such as combat commands.
The 7th Air Force requested that qualified companies submit confirmation letters, quad charts, proposal briefing materials, etc.

This announcement did not specify which bases or facilities the drone countermeasure system will be deployed to, what types of drone threats are being anticipated, or whether changes in North Korea's drone capabilities influenced the implementation of this project.

North Korea announced that it conducted a joint firepower strike drill on the 12th of last month, mobilizing four types of weapon systems, including cruise missiles, ballistic missiles, large-caliber multiple rocket launchers, and attack drones.

items.title: Prize-winning image which sparked backlash was AI-generated, Nikon rules
paragraphs: The winner of a prestigious scientific photography competition has been disqualified following concerns raised by other scientists that it was fake.
Nikon said the use of generative AI in the composition of the video broke the rules of its Small World In Motion contest, which accepts photos and video taken using powerful microscopes.
The firm said the video "did not comply with the competition rules regarding generative AI", but added it was not a judgement of the entrant's professional reputation or scientific contributions.
It said it would now look at the rules and procedures of the annual contest, which has been running for 15 years and is specifically for microscopic images.
Nikon said it came to the decision "after thoroughly re-evaluating the video and supporting materials and consulting with members of our judging panel".

The winning entry came from Dr Ning Xu, from Tsinghua University in China, who submitted a short video showing tiny, hair-like structures called cilia moving in the airway of a child with the respiratory condition PCD.
A number of scientists, including former competition judges, complained to Nikon on its LinkedIn page that the video did not appear to be real.
Xu had acknowledged using AI, but said he believed he had acted within the rules, and had cooperated with Nikon's investigation.
University of Leicester scientist Dr Robert Hirst, who was among the first experts to voice concerns, said he was "not surprised" and he "knew immediately that the video was fabricated".
"I have been diagnosing PCD for 20 years by examining their cilia waveform, length, cell size and shape," he said.
Hirst, who is lead scientist for the NHS centre for PCD diagnosis at the university, said the cells and cilia "look nothing like those from PCD patients".
"This controversy has impacted a lot of patients, scientists, doctors and PCD support networks around the world," he said.

items.title: Wait, the best multicolour 3D printer for beginners is now even cheaper than it was in Amazon's Prime Day sale earlier this week!
paragraphs: Earlier this week, I highlighted what was a pretty great 3D printer deal running as part of Amazon's Prime Big Deal Days. The AnyCubic Kobra X, a machine we rate as one of the best FDM 3D printers for beginners who think they're going to stick with the hobby, was reduced by $130 to $329. This is a rare case where a Prime Day deal has got even better after the sale finished: there's now another $30 off for a record-low price of $299.

If you're not sure which type of machine is best for you, see our guide to the best 3D printers based on our own reviews, but we rate this mid-range FDM printer very highly, and particularly for beginners who want to avoid buying a printer that they might outgrow too quickly. It provides native multicolour printing and larger print sizes than cheaper options, providing more flexibility to develop your craft.

The Kobra X isn't the cheapest 3D printer for beginners, but we think it could be a better long-term investment for newcomers who think they're going to want to stick with the craft and possibly even develop professionally. It's simple enough for a newcomer to get started with it but also versatile enough that most users won't outgrow it quickly.

Auto levelling, app control and AI monitoring make it easy to use, while the native 4-colour printing – expandable to 19 – mixed-material capabilities and large build volume mean you can grow into the hobby without having to upgrade your machine a year or so down the line.
If it's your first time looking for a 3D printer, be aware that there are two main families of device: resin and FDM printers.

For most beginners, and for 3D printer users in general, FDM is the way to go. It's easier and safer to handle, has lower running costs, less clean up, and you can get larger print sizes for your money. The exception would be if you really need the extra detail that resin 3D printing can provide for small things like tabletop gaming miniatures or small, detailed jewellery (for that, I'd recommend the Anycubic Photon Mono M7 Pro, currently reduced from $669 to $449 at Amazon).

items.title: Two Renoir paintings stolen from French museum are recovered
paragraphs: Two paintings by Auguste Renoir stolen a month ago from a museum in the south of France have been recovered, the local town hall has said.
The two works were seized on 8 September when thieves cut through a fence and smashed a window at the Renoir Museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer, where the French impressionist had lived during his final years.
The local mayor praised authorities for recovering the paintings and said the news gave immense joy and profound relief.
Six suspects have also been arrested in relation with the heist at Renoir Museum, the town hall confirmed in a statement.
The theft was the latest in a series of high-profile art heists in Europe.
The two missing paintings were the Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano (1910) and Jeune fille au puits (1886).
The thieves had used an electric saw to cut through the frame mountings inside the museum and had initially made off with four paintings, but dropped two of them in the museum's garden as they fled

"These two paintings are far more than works of art. They are part of our city's history, our cultural heritage and the legacy Auguste Renoir left to Cagnes-sur-Mer," said Mayor Bryan Masson, who is part of France's National Rally.
The town hall said initially that it would provide further details of the recovery on Friday, but cancelled a planned press conference.
The Renoir Museum is home to 12 of the famous painter's artworks.
Opened in 1960, it houses a variety of objects that once belonged to him, including his easel and wheelchair, as well as photographs and personal letters.

Earlier this year paintings by Renoir, Paul Cézanne and Henri Matisse were stolen from a museum near the Italian city of Parma, in a raid that lasted just three minutes. They were recovered in August.
France saw its biggest art robbery in years last October, when crown jewels were stolen in broad daylight from the Louvre in Paris.
Disguised as construction workers, the thieves broke into the Louvre's first-floor Apollo Gallery during the museum's opening hours.
They used an angle-grinder to open display cases and made off with €88m (£78m) of jewels that once belonged to France's 19th-Century queens and empresses.
The Louvre was subsequently criticised for under-investing in security.

items.title: French students protest – level 2
paragraphs: Thousands of students and teachers are protesting across France because public high schools are in terrible condition.
Classrooms are overcrowded, buildings are falling apart with leaks and rats, and there are not enough substitute teachers when staff are sick.

The protests began near Paris and spread to many cities. Unfortunately, some protests became very violent. Protesters set fire to bins and damaged school buildings, while riot police used tear gas and grenades to clear the streets. Police arrested thousands of people.

The French Prime Minister said that violence will not fix the school system. With an important presidential election coming in six months, these angry protests show that the country is divided over public education and government spending.

Difficult words: substitute teacher (a teacher who takes over a class when the regular teacher is sick or away), violent (when someone uses force to hurt people or break things), divided (split into different groups with different ideas).
You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: French students protest – level 3
paragraphs: Tens of thousands of students and teachers have taken to the streets across France to protest severe under-investment in public high schools.
Protesters are demanding immediate action over overcrowded classrooms, decaying 1970s buildings with leaking roofs and rats, and long-term teacher shortages caused by years of budget cuts.

The movement, which started in deprived Parisian suburbs, has quickly turned into a nationwide crisis. However, the protests have grown increasingly violent over the past three weeks, and resulted in thousands of arrests, damaged schools, and injuries on both sides, including a 15-year-old student who lost his hand to a police grenade.

Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu strongly condemned the rioting and insisted that destroying schools doesn’t solve funding problems. While police have used tear gas to disperse crowds, demonstrators accuse authorities of using heavy-handed tactics. With a presidential election just six months away, these widespread demonstrations highlight deep social political divisions across the country.

Difficult words: under-investment (providing less money or funding than is necessary for something to work properly), deprived (suffering from a lack of necessary resources, money, and good living conditions), heavy-handed (using too much force or authority to control a situation).
You can watch the video news lower on this page.

items.title: French students protest – level 1
paragraphs: Thousands of students and teachers in France are protesting today. They are angry because high school buildings are old, dirty, and broken. Many classes are full, and there are not enough teachers.

The protests start near Paris and are now everywhere in the country. Sadly, some protests become violent. People burn bins and break school doors. Police must stop them. Thousands of people go to prison, and some people get hurt.
Leaders say that these protests will not help schools. France is voting for a new president in six months. It is a big problem for many people. They are worried about their schools.
Difficult words: dirty (not clean), violent (when someone uses force to hurt people or break things), vote (when people choose a new leader or someone for an important job).
