items.title: New spate of stabbings, overdoses and fires at Australian immigration detention centres run by ICE-linked US prison firm
paragraphs: A new spate of stabbings, overdoses and drug use in Australia’s immigration detention centres has put the Australian government in likely breach of laws designed to protect staff and detainees, internal documents show.

Earlier this year, Guardian Australia revealed catastrophic security failings across Australia’s onshore immigration network since Management and Training Corporation – a US private prison company used by Donald Trump to hold ICE detainees – won the $2.3bn detention contract in late 2024.

The federal government has repeatedly attempted to take a stick to MTC and its local subsidiary Secure Journeys to improve its performance, including through financial penalties and a fiery meeting last year between the home affairs minister, Tony Burke, and the company’s global president.

But new documents seen by the Guardian show serious security lapses have continued since, including through a spate of eight fire-related incidents at Villawood immigration detention centre and violence and drug use at Melbourne immigration detention centre (MIDC). Those failings have again put the department itself in the crosshairs of Comcare, the federal work safety regulator.

The documents reveal a string of incidents at MIDC involving violence, aggression, illicit substances and improvised weaponry since August. That includes a violent altercation on 18 August between two groups that led to six detainees being hospitalised for “slashing and stabbing injuries made using improvised weapons”.
On 10 September, a detainee was found overdosed in his room, requiring staff to administer Naloxone, a drug that reverses opioid overdose effects.

The incidents at MIDC prompted Comcare to warn the government that it was failing to control the rising number of “incidents of this type at MIDC and across the broader immigration detention network”. That failure meant it was likely to be in breach of the law, the document said.

“I have formed the reasonable belief that the department is contravening section 19 of the WHS Act by failing to ensure, so far as is reasonably practicable, the health and safety of workers and other persons,” Comcare said in its notice. “In particular, the risks associated with violence, aggression, and the presence of illicit substances and improvised weaponry are not being adequately managed.

“While the department has advised that a range of actions have been undertaken to address these risks, it has not sufficiently demonstrated that the control measures currently in place are effective in eliminating or minimising the risks, so far as is reasonably practicable.”
Comcare said the information available indicates these hazards pose an ongoing risk of serious harm to workers and others in the centres.
A separate Comcare document revealed that a series of eight fire-related incidents had taken place at Villawood immigration detention centre between February and May.

That’s despite prior warnings to government to intervene after previous fires lit inside Villawood exposed serious gaps in MTC’s preparedness. That includes one fire on 23 September 2025, when MTC staff rushed into a detainee’s room to save him from a fire without proper safety equipment, causing two workers to be hospitalised.

The regulator found the department had not conducted its own systematic review of “all fire and smoke control measures falling within its influence or control”, a likely breach of work health and safety regulations.

“The occurrence of multiple notifiable fire incidents over a period of approximately four months, particularly after previous regulatory intervention concerning substantially the same risk, provided repeated and compelling circumstances requiring the department to review the effectiveness of relevant control measures,” the Comcare document said.

The Guardian previously revealed a series of incidents across the centres since Secure Journey took over, including escapes, staff injuries and sick detainees missing medical appointments due to a lack of staff to escort them.

Lyndal Ryan, national president of the United Workers Union, which represents workers in the centres, said the notices from Comcare show “the continuing dangerous situations facing workers and detainees inside detention centres, and Secure Journeys’ inability or unwillingness to address those issues”.
The union has continually raised concerns about understaffing in the centres, and Ryan said Comcare has made it clear that the department has the responsibility to pull Secure Journeys into line.
“The list of eight fires at Villawood over a four-month period are signs of the instability and chaos our members are witnessing almost every day,” she said.
A spokesperson for MTC’s local subsidiary, Secure Journeys, said:
“In response to your questions, I can confirm that Secure Journeys’ commitment to maintaining safe and secure operations, as well as both staff and detainee welfare remains our top priority.”
The Australian Border Force was contacted for comment.

items.title: The Filter is two! 31 things we loved this year, from cloud-like duvets to the perfect running shoe
paragraphs: The Filter is turning two! To celebrate, we asked our contributors for their favourite products from the past year, and rounded up the team’s picks too.
From handbag-sized umbrellas and stylish yet practical wellies to reading lights and luxurious duvets, these are the products that stood out.

One of the best tools I’ve tested this year is Revamp’s Straight & Go cordless for my review of the best hot brushes. It’s compact, so easily fits into hand luggage, a work backpack or even a decent-size handbag. It’s my hot brush of choice when I’m away from home (and at home: it’s cordless so I can use it in the bathroom without trailing cables all over the hallway). Lise Smith
Illiyoon ceramide ato concentrate cream, 75ml

The best product I’ve bought on another writer’s recommendation is the Illiyoon ceramide ato concentrate cream, which Sarah Matthews wrote about in her best facial moisturisers roundup. It’s rich but gentle and leaves my rather dry skin soft, smooth and plump. LS

I wrote about Brick, a device that helps reduce screen time, for my phone addiction piece. I didn’t view myself as having a problem, but after finding that Brick really improved my wellbeing, I became the first person in history for whom admitting you have a problem is the last step on the road to recovery. Alan Martin

I’m continuing to cook with the Gozney Arc Lite, which I reviewed for our guide to the best pizza ovens, and starting to relax more and enjoy it. Slowly, my hand-stretched bases are getting better, though I think I would still be laughed out of any self-respecting pizzeria: “Don’t quit the day job.” Rachel Ogden

I trust all beauty recommendations from my beloved colleague Sali Hughes implicitly, so after reading her guide to makeup brushes, I thought it was perhaps time I stopped slapping foundation on by hand and invested in this Saie brush. It makes foundation sit more lightly on your skin and makes blending at the neck and hairline foolproof. Jess Cartner-Morley

For my rundown of items that make camping with kids easier, I tested a pair of square flexi-tubs during a trip with my six-year-old. They were a godsend then – helping keep everything organised and tidy – but they’ve since found a place in home life as indispensable declutterers. Kids’ toys everywhere? Throw them in the flexi-tub. Doing some DIY? Tools in the tub! Too many tubs? Stack them! You get the picture. Matt Collins

In the past I’ve opted for more fashion-led wellies, but these days I use them more for dog walking than festivals. So I took Danielle Wilkins’ recommendation in her roundup of the best wellies and bought her top pick of Barbour boots. With a classic look and excellent grip (even across muddy fields), I get to balance style and practicality. Sabine Wiesel

When I needed an umbrella this year, I turned to Pete Wise’s umbrella test. I’m terrible for not carrying a brolly and getting caught out by rain, so I wanted something small I could leave in my handbag. I picked the Davek Mini. It has saved my veggie bacon many times already and its lifetime guarantee is reassuring. Caramel Quin

Having tested lots of walking pads and under-desk treadmills for the Filter, I have become quite attached to the Urevo SpaceWalk 5L model (a review for which is on the way). I walk on it most days in an attempt to rack up at least 10,000 steps. It’s an easy way to burn extra calories when I’d otherwise be glued to my desktop, and I’ve found this model exceptionally quiet, while the automatic incline is great for varying the terrain without lifting a finger. Leon Poultney

I tested the Primus Lite Plus for our guide to best camping stoves. I recently took it on a three-day trek in the Lake District and found it simple to use and clean, and great for boiling water. Sian Lewis
Jess Cartner-Morley also inspired me to buy a jazzy cashmere bandana from Rise&Fall. SL

My Panda duvet from my test of the best duvets has been a real bedding upgrade. When you go from a cheap polyester duvet (which was perfectly fine, I thought) to this cloud-like breathable bamboo hug, there’s no going back. I always look forward to wrapping myself in it at night. I now have two versions – the winter 10.5-tog one I tested for best duvets, and the 4.5-tog summer version. Jane Hoskyn
Beauty of Joseon relief sun rice + Probiotics SPF50+, 50ml

I bought a double pack of Beauty of Joseon’s Relief Sun Rice + Probiotics SPF50+, which not only took the top spot in Sarah Matthews’ best face SPF guide but was also raved about by Sali Hughes in her hero skincare 2025 roundup. I’ve got fair skin, so I need a good daily SPF, ideally one I can slap on without looking like I’ve fallen face-first into my cereal, but my skin is also greasy and spotty, so the light texture of this is such a lovely relief after the thick sun creams I’ve been used to. JH

I’ve been tempted to buy an air fryer for ages but didn’t think I had the counter space. So, when Rachel Ogden highlighted the Ninja Double Stack as the best compact air fryer (with a smaller footprint than most) in her roundup, I decided to go for it. As someone who mainly cooks for one, I’ve found it makes mealtimes far more convenient (and saves energy because I no longer need to heat up a whole oven for just me). It also produces the crispest, most delicious jacket potato skin I’ve ever had. Lily Smith, researcher

The Stihl SHA 56 leaf blower and garden vacuum, which I tested for our guide to the best leaf blowers and vacuums, has been an absolute hit in my garden this year, not just for collecting leaves but for doing any of the work I’d normally use a broom for. Its added superpower of collecting whatever it’s been blowing about at the end of the job is the icing on the cake. Andy Shaw

I’ve taken up pottery this year, and my hands have paid the price. There’s nothing like handling wet clay to extract all the moisture from your skin. So, as soon as I’m done wiping down my station and labelling my wonky creations, I’m in need of urgent relief. I opted for the E45 repairing hand cream from Sarah Matthews’ best hand cream guide for two reasons: it’s cheap enough to share around the studio, and (as promised) it has a thick, nourishing texture. Sarah described it as a “refreshing drink of water for the hands”, and I couldn’t agree more – my mitts absolutely slurp the stuff up. Millie Fender, commissioning editor

The best thing I’ve tested is this set of July packing cubes, which came out on top in my roundup. For a disorganised person like me, packing cubes are a revelation. The July set did a particularly good job of preserving the crispness of shirts and trousers during a chaotic cross-country journey this summer. Pete Wise
CeraVe skin renewing vitamin C serum, 30ml

I bought the CeraVe vitamin C serum on Danielle Wilkins’ recommendation. I was astounded when, after a week of using it, people started commenting on how “glowy” my face looked. I’m hoping it keeps me looking alive all the way through the grey winter months! Zoë Phillimore

We were switching my son’s and daughter’s rooms over and we needed extra incentive for him (Iggy) to accept the deal – he was moving into the smaller bedroom – and this chair from our best gaming chairs guide swung it. Iggy now has his own “gaming nook” (doubling up as my workspace), and the chair is saving my working-from-home slouching. Alex Jones, picture editor
Saucony Endorphin Azura running shoes Men’s

I’ve logged thousands of miles this year searching for the best running shoes. One of the standout all-rounders that can cope with almost anything is the Saucony Endorphin Azura. Go fast, go slow. No trouble. The perfect suitcase shoe at a pretty competitive price. Kieran Alger
Nobody’s Child floral starlight midi dress

This isn’t so much something I’ve bought as something I’ve bought into. The vast majority of the clothing I’ve bought this year has been secondhand, thanks to Jane Hoskyn’s money-saving tips. My favourite find is a long cream dress (with pockets!) from Nobody’s Child, which I snagged for £15, down from a usual £85. Sarah Matthews
VonHaus Smart dehumidifier with laundry mode

After reading Caramel Quin’s roundup of the best dehumidifiers, I was convinced the budget VonHaus Smart dehumidifier was exactly what our damp house was crying out for. Not only is it incredibly satisfying to see so much water sucked out of the air, but it’s also become my new favourite (and fastest) way to dry laundry. Ella Jinadu, audience editor

My partner and I each have a clip-on reading light, recommended in our guide to the everyday items that could improve your life, and can fully vouch for how the disturbance-free glow has transformed our reading routines – both at bedtime and in the dark early mornings. They also came in handy on a recent camping trip when the wind made it impossible to sleep. EJ
GreenPan Frost ice-cream maker and slushie machine

I love a kitchen gadget and became obsessed with the GreenPan soft-serve and slushie maker while I was testing it for best ice-cream makers. While I enjoyed the ice-cream, I loved making frozen cocktails even more – it was a real crowd-pleaser at parties too. Danielle Amato

When I am tasked with testing a specific category, it ends up reigniting my love and interest in it. So, since testing vodka, I’m still fully into mixing myself ice-cold martinis (dry, with a twist, please) and variations on the theme. The top vodkas I’m still reaching for are the Jo Vodka and the Chopin, though I also made a fab lychee martini recently using Sapling raspberry. Joanne Gould

I’m also a new customer of Scilly Flowers after reading Zoë Phillimore’s piece on the best flower delivery services. I like that it tends to do arrangements of just one type of flower, which I find elegant, and it has varieties you don’t usually find with online florists; plus it can be amazing value. I sent someone 40 narcissus, which looked stunning, and sent my friend a sweet arrangement of scented pinks for a post-op cheer-up. JG

Testing white T-shirts was my highlight, particularly Merz b Schwanen’s – the one Carmy wears in The Bear. After all, who doesn’t want to channel Jeremy Allen White sweating it out in a hot kitchen? At the risk of sounding like a true fashion nerd, there’s something fascinating about trying a dozen pieces that look identical but wear completely differently – and then deciding which takes the top spot. My partner now gets to hear all about 150gsm versus 220gsm and why Supima is the gold standard. Riveting stuff, I’m told. Peter Bevan

Niwaki’s hori hori tool has quite a cult following among professional gardeners (in tools pros can’t live without), but I could never see why I’d have much need for a knife in the garden. Now I realise it’s more of a sharp trowel – a very nifty garden tool – which has quickly replaced the old butter knife I previously used for all the same jobs. Kate Jacobs
Poon’s premium first extract soy sauce, 250ml

I’ve tasted so many good things this year, but it’s the simplest one-ingredient products that have stood out for their incredible quality. The best thing I tried was Poon’s premium first-extract soy sauce (best overall from my soy sauce taste test). It’s wildly complex and fruity, made from non-GMO soya beans grown in Kaohsiung, southern Taiwan, pressed only once and naturally fermented in earthenware jars. Tom Hunt

There are times when I wish the steady flow of big, brown boxes entering my home would slow to a drip, but KitchenAid’s recent deliveries have earned their keep. The standouts were from its new trio of slightly – just slightly, mind you – more affordable coffee machines.

The range-topping £899 KF4 (featured in our guide to the best coffee machines) is a delight, but it’s the fully automatic £749 KF3 that I think is the best value of the bunch. The coffee quality is superb, the milk froth is a delightfully dense, creamy microfoam, and given the performance, the price is fair. The slimline build is perfect for cramped kitchen worktops, too. A full review is on the way. Sasha Muller

One of the most original and unexpectedly fun products I’ve tested this year was for my sexy gifts for Valentine’s Day guide. Twinkle Tongue is an all-natural, sour cherry-flavoured liquid that instantly provokes your salivary glands.

What’s the point of a product that makes you slaver and slobber? If you suffer from dry mouth caused by smoking, menopause, or as a side-effect of certain medications, then Twinkle Tongue can help make all sorts of intimate oral activities easier and more comfortable.

items.title: Adidas sues White Fox in battle of the stripes
paragraphs: Over the years, Adidas has become one of the most iconic athletic brands, so it's understandable that it would want to protect that status. Now it's taking on Australian clothing boutique White Fox in a heated legal dispute over who gets to own their stripes.

While Adidas uses several iconic logo designs, its three-stripes have become synonymous with the brand. The athletics company claims that White Fox's four-stripe design is "deceptively similar" to its own, calling for a legal resolution.

White Fox's four-stripe clothing designs have appeared throughout its advertising, which Adidas claims shows an "intention to trade off our reputation". Adidas has trademarked the iconic three stripes in Australia since 1957, and the athletic giant alleges White Fox's designs are "substantially identical with or otherwise deceptively similar."

White Fox's legal team has defended the move, claiming that other Australian brands like Cotton On and Sportscraft sell items with "similar decorative stripes". But Adidas has countered the defence, claiming that White Fox's advertisements feature "genuine" Adidas items, which could form "an association in the minds of consumers."

Adidas is seeking legal damages for the alleged infringement, including profits earned from the products, along with interest and legal costs. For more design disputes, take a look at why New Balance sued this rival athletics brand over a shoe logo or check out the latest Washington Commanders logo controversy.

items.title: 'Tropical jungle' of wallabies, porcupines and parrots must move after neighbours complain
paragraphs: A man who lives in a log cabin and keeps wallabies, mongooses, porcupines, parrots and other rare birds has been told to move.
James Wale relocated to the rural Carmarthenshire site two years ago, having previously run a rare bird business in Pembrokeshire.
Neighbours said the site sounded like a "tropical jungle", especially at night.
Carmarthenshire Council issued Wale with an enforcement notice alleging he had broken planning rules, but he has been given more time to relocate the animals.

Planning agents representing the bird enthusiast said he wanted to create a "major tourism venture", and that his former business in the grounds of Picton Castle ended because the lease was not renewed.

Wale moved to the 17-acre woodland near Llannon and had hoped to set up an owl garden centre, but scaled back his plans to create a private bird welfare home along with some forestry and farming activities.
As well as the exotic animals, Wale also kept horses, goats, chickens and ducks, according to the enforcement appeal.
Documents said the abandoned venture planned to include "reptile, mongoose and several animal enclosures".
A planning application was then prepared for a smaller-scale venture including about 30 bird and animal enclosures, with Wale not intending to live onsite.
Llannon councillor Llinos Mai Davies claimed the site adversely affected neighbouring properties and had a negative impact on the character of the area.
Photos of the land were submitted showing the boggy conditions and the woodland access track off the A476.
A planning inspector appointed by Welsh ministers has now dismissed the appeal after seeing the cabin during a visit to the land.

"The appellant keeps a few chickens, ducks and horses on site along with a variety of more unusual animals including eagles, falcons, parrots, hornbills, mongooses, skunks, porcupine and wallaby," they said.
The inspector said there was a minor element of forestry and agricultural activity taking place, but that the main operation was of a "fundamentally different character" and unauthorised.
Wale should be given 12 rather than six months to stop using the land to keep non-agricultural animals, remove the enclosures and restore the site to its original condition, the inspector concluded.
"Given the unusual type and mix of the animals, it may well take more time to find a suitable alternative location," they added.
Wale also has 12 months to stop living on the land, remove the cabin and its associated foul drainage.
His agents told the Local Democracy Reporting Service that a planning application would be drawn up in a bid to keep the birds on site.

items.title: ‘This is not an anti-tech town’: backlash to datacenter in city once home to IBM
paragraphs: For decades, East Fishkill helped build New York’s tech industry.
The hamlet, located 70 miles north of New York City, was home to a 460-acre campus where IBM researched and manufactured semiconductor chips for nearly fifty years.

So when the news broke in early 2026 that a real estate developer, Treetop Companies, was exploring plans for what could become one of the largest artificial intelligence (AI) datacenters in the country, a roughly 1-gigawatt campus spanning more than 1m sq ft across about 143 acres, it seemed the town would welcome a new phase in its technological evolution.

Instead, a furious backlash erupted before even a single permit application was filed with the municipal government. Residents began attending town board meetings, organizing rallies and advocating for a temporary ban.

Even before any plans for the facility were drawn up, East Fishkill’s existing zoning laws did not allow for the construction of large data centers. The town issued a three-year moratorium on them anyway, a sign of the extreme ire against datacenters.

The temporary ban, adopted unanimously in late June, forbids the town from considering new datacenters larger than 20 megawatts until July of 2029, while officials study their potential impacts on water resources and local ecosystems. The development company at the center of the controversy has appealed the measure.

“I just think that we’re at this moment where things are happening very quickly, we need to get our ducks in a row and think about the various ways in which datacenters and new energy usage will affect our long-term community cohesiveness, environmental quality, and character,” said East Fishkill resident and professor Tanya Radford.

The fight unfolding in East Fishkill is a single piece of a growing divide. Both rural towns and communities that once eagerly welcomed high-tech development are increasingly questioning whether AI infrastructure adds enough local benefit to justify its enormous appetite for electricity, water and land.
“This is not an anti-tech town,” said Radford. “I’m an educator. I use technology.”

The saga began after Treetop Development purchased property in East Fishkill, initially pursuing approvals for a warehouse development. Residents later discovered that the company, through local property owner Donovan Drive Holdings, had entered the queue to have a project approved that would use approximately 1,000 megawatts of electrical service, an amount more consistent with a large-scale AI datacenter than a warehouse.

This request for approval was not submitted to the town of East Fishkill. Rather, it was submitted to New York Independent System Operator (NYISO)‘s interconnection queue. NYISO is an independent organization responsible for managing New York’s high-voltage power grid, meaning whenever a company wants to build a massive new project, it must formally ask NYISO for permission to connect to the grid.
For those that call East Fishkill home, the NYISO filing quickly raised concerns.
The proposed datacenter would consume more electricity than the entire town of Buffalo, which has about 275,000 people. East Fishkill is home to just 30,000.

“Residents have been speaking out against it to stop any application from coming into the town for the datacenter,” said Melissa Hoffmann, an East Fishkill resident and organizer with a local chapter of Food & Water Watch, an environmental advocacy nonprofit.
But because no formal application had been filed with East Fishkill, town officials repeatedly stressed that there was nothing before the planning board to review or reject.

“There is no application before the Town. There has never been an application for a datacenter,” East Fishkill supervisor Nick D’Alessandro wrote on Facebook in June. D’Alessandro later took down the post. His office did not respond to the Guardian’s request for comment.

He stressed that standalone datacenters were “not even listed as a permissible use” under the town’s zoning laws. Nonetheless, in June the board banned their construction for three years “to give our community certainty and allow time for further study and discussion”.
Hoffmann said months of public pressure ultimately convinced the town board to extend what had initially been discussed as a seven-month pause into a three-year moratorium.
East Fishkill has often been described as an “innovation hub”, making opposition to the datacenter proposal remarkable precisely because the town has not been hostile towards new technology.

International Business Machines Corporation, better known as IBM, transformed the town during the latter half of the 20th century into one of the nation’s leading semiconductor manufacturing centers, employing thousands of workers and laying the foundation for what is now iPark 84, home to mixed-use commercial and residential facilities.

Former IBM facilities remain a defining part of the local economy, and iPark continues to house technology companies. One tenant is currently seeking to expand an existing datacenter by approximately 150 megawatts, far smaller than the facility proposed by Treetop.
Residents have insisted that their opposition is not meant to hinder forward-looking tech, but is directed at the unprecedented scale of emerging AI infrastructure.

“The pushback is really to the size,” resident Fran Caracappa, a candidate for county legislature, said. “The Treetop center would be 1,000 megawatts. People do not want to pay higher electricity rates because of a larger datacenter coming in and putting pressure on the grid.”
Residents have also questioned whether the supposed economic benefits justify the costs.
Hoffmann worried that the data center would “provide very few jobs”. Caracappa similarly expressed doubt that temporary construction jobs would lead to lasting employment for locals.
“It’s not going to provide work to keep people here like the previous tech businesses did,” Caracappa said. “So what’s the benefit to the town?”
The town’s skepticism toward a massive industrial project is also informed by the consequences of its past.

IBM’s manufacturing operations helped establish the region’s tech-industrial identity, but groundwater contamination associated with semiconductor production left lasting scars. Several polluted Superfund sites remain in the area.
In addition to groundwater protection, residents have raised concerns about noise, diesel backup generators, property values, wetlands and the area’s rural character.
Radford, whose home sits near the Appalachian trail, said that the serene, woodsy landscape that currently surrounds the proposed site is one of the reasons she moved there.
“My neighbors and I agree that additional development in the area could only negatively impact the quality of life here,” she said.

Barely two weeks after the East Fishkill moratorium passed, New York became the first US state to enact a moratorium on new datacenters when governor Kathy Hochul signed an executive order mandating a one-year statewide pause on so-called hyperscale datacenters.

Donald Trump, an ally to tech billionaires and AI investors, responded with rage. He called the move “a terrible decision” on his Truth Social platform and accused Hochul of implementing the ban for purely political reasons.

“One of the biggest Driving Forces in the Future for Jobs, are Data Centers. They are big, strong, bold, and Money Machines for the State in which they are built,” Trump wrote. Later in the summer, he called towns rejecting datacenters “backwards and poor”.

Like Trump, Treetop did not take kindly to East Fishkill’s three-year ban. In a 17-page objection letter submitted to the town board and reviewed by the Guardian, attorneys for the company argued the three-year moratorium unlawfully targets the company’s property and effectively amounts to a permanent prohibition rather than a “legitimate temporary planning measure”.

In the letter, the company said it spent years and significant resources advancing development plans for the site, including environmental reviews, wetlands investigations, traffic studies, and utility coordination.

Town officials have maintained that no datacenter application has ever been submitted and that the moratorium provides time to evaluate whether existing zoning properly addresses an entirely new class of industrial development.
East Fishkill residents are claiming victory.
“People are winning,” Hoffmann said. “Communities that fight these datacenters are winning.”

items.title: Anthropic bans users from being 'cruel' to its AI systems
paragraphs: Anthropic has raised eyebrows by announcing it will ban users from "sustained and needless" abusive behaviour towards its AI.
The Claude-maker said on Thursday it was updating its usage policy to let its tools end interactions where people are "cruel" - something it said it had done in "rare" cases prior.
It will now be included on a list of forbidden conduct which also contains bullying others, promoting self-harm and creating non-consensual intimate imagery.
While Anthropic said the policy would only apply in "extreme cases" of repeated abuse, it has reignited debate over how we should communicate with AI tools.

The company said it would not apply to "common versions of user frustration, pushback, dark creative themes, or model testing and research" - suggesting it would only apply in clearly deliberate instances.
But what Anthropic would consider "abusive or cruel behaviour" towards its models remains unclear.
Screenshots of the new policy have been widely shared and commented on across social media - with some praising it as advancing good manners or "model welfare".
But others criticised the plan, with one person calling it "deeply wrong, external" and another suggesting it might undermine abuse directed at humans and animals.
"You can't be cruel to numbers and maths," wrote Dr Barry Scannell, technology partner at Irish law firm William Fry, on LinkedIn, external.
"This level of anthropomorphisation of AI is harmful. It leads people to believe that it's something it's not."
Microsoft AI director Mustafa Suleyman, who in September criticised rival firm Anthropic for treating AI like it is human, reacted to Anthropic's update with a melting face emoji.
The changes, first reported by tech outlet The Verge, came following an annual review of the usage policy at the firm.

It was also updated to address new or emerging risks in other areas, including by forbidding use of Claude for "deceptive campaigns" or clarifying that, as US midterm elections loom, it cannot be used to "deceive voters or disrupt elections".
Anthropic also said on Thursday its usage policy previously prevented its tools being used to develop weapons.
But none of the updates have attracted as much attention or scrutiny as its move to forbid users abusing its chatbots.
It has also tapped into the much-debated question of whether we should be curt or polite when using generative AI tools.

Some experts say writing or saying "please" or "thank you" to tools like ChatGPT is unnecessary and wastes tokens - used by the large language models powering generative AI tools to process and reply to you.
Others argue politeness can lead to higher quality answers or responses.

When a X user last year asked about electricity costs incurred by ChatGPT replying to users' "please" and "thank you" messages, OpenAI boss Sam Altman said it was, external "tens of millions of dollars well spent - you never know".
The Collins Dictionary meanwhile last November highlighted the re-emergence of the term "clanker" for disparagingly referring to AI tools.

Used to describe robots in Star Wars games and movies since the mid 2000s, the term made its shortlist of words reflecting the mood of 2025 after last July saw many take to TikTok to share their frustrations with AI-powered machines.
Some experts have also posited that being rude to AI chatbots could adversely impact human communication, by seeping into how we talk to and treat others.

items.title: Candlelit theatre in Havana – in pictures
paragraphs: Widespread blackouts have become increasingly common in Cuba since the US imposed energy sanctions in January. Outages frequently surpass 24 hours as the ageing grid fails. The Impulso theatre group has had to adapt as power cuts pose severe challenges for the performing arts Continue reading...

items.title: Cop31 host urges wealthy countries to spend ‘much more’ on climate than defence
paragraphs: Wealthy countries should spend far more on dealing with the climate crisis than the 5% of GDP promised by Nato members for defence because “the climate issue is the security issue”, the host of the next UN summit has said.

But, in comments that are likely to prove contentious, the Cop31 president-designate, Murat Kurum, hedged on whether countries should try to repeat a previous agreement to “transition away from fossil fuels” – the primary cause of the climate crisis – when they meet in Turkey next month.
Kurum, the Turkish climate change minister, told the Guardian the world was “already in a transition” and suggested fossil fuel use could be addressed indirectly through other steps.

Kurum was among national leaders and ministers, officials and civil society members in Fiji this week to prepare for Cop31, which will take place in the Turkish city of Antalya in November. Australia, which has the new role of “president of negotiations” at Cop31, had pushed to hold the pre-Cop meeting in the Pacific to bring attention to island nations.

Geopolitical turmoil from war, a historic energy crisis and an unpredictable and climate-denying US administration – combined with the knowledge that many would be attending the main climate summit in a few weeks – meant only 13 national leaders joined Australia’s prime minister, Anthony Albanese, in the Fijian city of Nadi, and most were from the Pacific.

But there were also about 30 ministers, including from India and European nations, representatives from the big emitters China and Saudi Arabia, the heads of global agencies and about 4,000 other attenders.

On Tuesday, a delegation flew north to see Tuvalu, a low-lying atoll country of about 10,000 people that is among the most at risk from the climate crisis. They were shown a 20-hectare (49-acre) land reclamation project and heard stories of life in a country that is mostly only about 2 metres above sea level, and where rising waters, storm surges and intensifying extreme weather pose an accelerating threat to survival.

In a powerful speech, Melelusi Sokotia, 13, told the visitors her friends’ dreams to be “teachers, doctors, builders” were being subsumed by the question of whether they could “grow safely here in Tuvalu”.

Back in Nadi, Fiji’s climate minister, Lynda Tabuya, was moved to tears and received a standing ovation during her closing address. She urged delegates to “remember the people you met” and “carry something of the Pacific with you”.
Tabuya said: “This pre-Cop draws to a close tonight. Our responsibility does not.”

The governments of about 190 countries will head to Antalya with clear evidence that responsibility is not being met. A recent report by the UN environment programme warned that under the most optimistic future, global heating would reach at least 1.8C, well beyond the 1.5C ceiling of the Paris climate agreement. It called for immediate and sustained emissions cuts and said every fraction of a degree of heating avoided would save lives and reduce economic losses.

Throughout the pre-Cop, Pacific leaders repeated their demands: that countries must act to “keep 1.5C alive”, that climate finance must be easily accessible for poor and vulnerable communities who have not caused the problem but are most at risk, and that the health of oceans must be prioritised.

Australia’s climate change minister, Chris Bowen, said only 0.2% of global climate finance was spent helping small island developing countries adapt, and that the countries that needed it the most, such as Tuvalu, “get it the least”. “That has got to change,” he said. “It’s a key priority of Cop31.”

Kurum said Nato countries should be much more focused on climate spending. He said they had promised to increase their defence budgets to 5% of GDP by 2035 as a result of “concerns for their own safety and security”, but had committed much less to addressing the climate crisis despite expressing concerns and it posing an even greater risk.
Asked if he thought as much should be spent on climate as defence, he said: “Much more.”

“The climate issue is the security issue itself,” Kurum told the Guardian through an interpreter. “If you don’t spend one unit of money prior to the disasters, then you are left in a position where you have to spend 10 units of money after the disaster. It’s cheaper pre-disaster.”

Kurum and Bowen reiterated they would focus in Antalya on winning support for a global goal of 35% of the energy needed to run homes, businesses, factories and vehicles coming from electricity by 2035. Now it is about 21%.
But the question of what direct action the global community should agree to take to phase out fossil fuels remains far more vexed.

Both host countries backed a multi-country statement in Fiji that supported a global “transition away from fossil fuels”, echoing language adopted by the global community at Cop28 in Dubai three years ago. But both faced criticism, and accusations of hypocrisy, for continuing to back new coal and gas developments and being largely silent before the pre-Cop on the need to phase out fossil fuels.
Bowen said the way to stop using fossil fuels was not to cut supply of the dirty fuel but to build enough renewable energy so there would be no need for fossil fuel power plants.

Kurum said the world was “already in a transition” and suggested the focus at climate talks on wording about transitioning away from fossil fuels might not be productive as he did not think further progress could be made. Delegates from some countries, including Saudi Arabia, Russia and other oil-producing states, strongly opposed naming fossil fuels at Cop30 in Brazil.

Dozens of countries frustrated with what they see as a UN stalemate on the issue met separately in Colombia this year to discuss a path away from fossil fuels. They are due to meet again next July in Tuvalu, and want the issue to be in an agreement in Antalya.
Tzeporah Berman, the chair of the Fossil Fuel Non-Proliferation Treaty Initiative, said Pacific leaders had been clear in Nadi that there should be an urgent fossil fuel phaseout.
“This means no new projects,” she said. “You can’t phase something out by building more of it.”

items.title: ICJ judge Navi Pillay wins Nobel peace prize for promoting international law
paragraphs: The Nobel peace prize has been awarded to Navi Pillay, the South African former UN human rights chief who chaired the UN commission that concluded Israel was guilty of genocide in Gaza.
The Norwegian Nobel committee said Pillay, who is serving as a judge at the international court of justice (ICJ), has “shown that legal measures can help prevent acts of war and violence”.

“Navi Pillay’s commitment to universal legal principles and her firm moral compass are constants in a long career,” the committee said, mentioning her early work defending Nelson Mandela under South Africa’s apartheid regime, serving on international criminal tribunal, and then as the UN high commissioner for human rights, as well as chairing the UN independent international commission of inquiry on the occupied Palestinian territory.

That commission concluded last year that the state of Israel was guilty of genocidal acts in Gaza “with the specific intent to destroy Palestinians in Gaza”, and said the country’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, its president, Isaac Herzog, and its former defence minister Yoav Gallant had “incited the commission of genocide”.

“It is clear that there is an intent to destroy the Palestinians in Gaza through acts that meet the criteria set forth in the genocide convention,” Pillay said on the publication of the commission’s findings in September last year.
Israel refused to cooperate with the commission, arguing it was biased, and rejected its report as “scandalous”. The Israeli foreign ministry reacted furiously to news of Pillay’s award on Friday.

“If there were an award for lies, hatred, and blood libels, Navi Pillay wouldn’t just be a contender. She’d be a frontrunner,” the ministry said on X, adding: “Awarding Pillay the Nobel Peace Prize isn’t a recognition of justice. It’s the grotesque weaponization of an award to legitimize anti-Israel hatred and prejudice.
“Now that the Nobel commission has rewarded the biggest lie of the 21st century, Joseph Goebbels is certainly applauding from hell.”
In its statement, the Nobel committee said Pillay, 85, had “contributed to strengthen the institutions of international law”.
“Her independence, expertise and steadfastness have made her one of the most respected international jurists of our time,” the committee said.

“In awarding this year’s Nobel peace prize, the Norwegian Nobel committee wants to remind the world that the rule of law – national and international – underpins the system we have set up to ensure peace and resolve conflicts non-violently,” its statement said.

The committee said it had not been able to locate Pillay before its announcement on Friday morning. She was attending a meeting of human rights lawyers and jurists in Nuremberg, Germany, at the site of postwar war crimes trials of Nazi leaders, and heard the news from colleagues. She responded with disbelief.
“I don’t know about it so much. The question is: is it true? Being a lawyer and a judge, I still want to verify it,” she said.

“The last thing I did was the report on Gaza naming what’s happening there as genocide,” Pillay added. “One of the main reactions to that report was people [complimented] me for my courage. You can imagine how surprised I was. Why would you need courage to speak the truth. You interpret the law. You look at all the facts, so it’s an impartial decision.”
Pillay is currently overseeing a genocide case against Myanmar at the ICJ.

Hours after the announcement, the Trump administration unveiled broad new sanctions against the International Criminal Court (ICC), on which Pillay also once served. The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said the measures were to ensure the court would never prosecute Americans.

The ICC has not charged any US nationals, and has previously pointed out that it is a court of last resort, unnecessary in the case of countries with effective legal systems. Last year, Donald Trump, who has long coveted the Nobel peace prize, imposed personal sanctions against ICC officials deemed to be involved in investigations of Americans or Israelis. The new sanctions target the court as an institution, blocking any ICC assets in the US and giving US companies and individuals six months to wind down any business with the court.
The ICC said the sanctions were “an attempt to obstruct the course of justice and to prevent the court from doing what it was created to do”.

“It is an assault on the rule of law and on the very foundations of the international legal order which strikes at the simple principle that no one stands above the law,” the court said in a statement.

Pillay’s award was welcomed by human rights activists and hailed in South Africa, home to four previous laureates. The country’s president, Cyril Ramaphosa, said: “Justice Pillay’s crowning as winner of the Nobel prize allows us to celebrate the progressive contributions she has made to strengthen peace, uphold human dignity and bring hope in South Africa and to peoples globally.”

Edwin Cameron, a retired South African constitutional court justice, said: “The award of the prize to Navi Pillay re-emphasises that the prize embodies an international aspiration to peace, and to respect and understanding across borders – and that leaders of great stature in our country – [Desmond] Tutu, Mandela, now Pillay – are recognised outside it, on the international stage.
“This may help reset our national debate on South Africa’s position in the region, and in Africa,” he said.

Yasmin Sooka, a human rights lawyer and commissioner on both South Africa and Sierra Leone’s truth and reconciliation commissions, said Pillay “follows in the footsteps of Chief Albert Luthuli and Archbishop Desmond Tutu, carrying forward South Africa’s proud tradition of linking peace with justice and human dignity”.

“From defending apartheid’s most vulnerable to her pioneering role in the Akayesu judgment, she has transformed international justice. That judgment helped establish rape and sexual violence as weapons of war – a historic breakthrough that placed survivors’ experiences at the heart of international justice,” Sooka said.
In 1998, the international criminal tribunal for Rwanda found Jean-Paul Akayesu, a former mayor of Taba, guilty of genocide and crimes against humanity.

“At the ICC, as UN high commissioner for human rights, and leading the inquiry that found Israel responsible for genocide in Gaza, she has brought unwavering integrity and courage to holding power accountable,” Sooka added.

Last year’s award of the peace prize to the Venezuelan opposition leader, María Corina Machado, drew widespread criticism because of her calls for US military intervention in her country. Machado heightened the controversy in January by handing her winner’s medal to Trump. The prize committee insisted that the honour of being a Nobel laureate could not be transferred.
On Friday, Pillay joked that she could do the same: “If you clap a little bit more, I’m going to share this prize with Trump.”

items.title: The new Darth Vader: how tech execs became the film villains of our age
paragraphs: When The Social Network came out, Mark Zuckerberg organised a staff viewing of a film he described as “fun”.
A group corporate outing to the sequel is unlikely.

The Social Network hardly portrayed the Facebook founder and his company in a hagiographical light (Zuckerberg later described the film as “hurtful”), but there was at least an element of the plucky upstart to the rise of Zuckerberg as he takes Facebook to 500 million users and a valuation of $25bn (ridiculously small numbers now – Meta has 3.6 billion users and is worth $1.8tn).

By the end of that film, though, a steely CEO is emerging and his company is on the brink of global hegemony. The Social Reckoning picks up from there, with a clear perspective that both the founder and his company – as well as the industry they represent – are corporate villains now.

This is set to be underlined by the release of the OpenAI drama, Artificial, where its CEO, Sam Altman, is reportedly given a deeply unflattering portrayal. Elon Musk completes the villainous trilogy by appearing as himself – aside from the odd deployment of an AI avatar – in Alex Gibney’s four-hour documentary, Musk, about the world’s first trillionaire.

Tech is the obvious thread joining these films, but another is the scathing portrayal of the company leaders in them. Film villains used to be hoodlums, ex-deep state operatives, people with posh British accents. Tech execs are the new Darth Vader.

This is underlined by the casting of Jeremy Strong, who looks a touch on the old side to be playing 2019-2021 era Zuckerberg (the Meta CEO was in his mid-30s at the time of the film’s events whereas Strong is 47), but is embedded in our minds as the tortured Roy family scion Kendall in Succession.

Strong also brings a straitjacketed simmer to the role here, one that breaks slightly at the end as he backtracks on being a “free speech absolutist” under intolerable pressure. It is the most human Zuckerberg moment in the entire film.

Peter Bradshaw describes Strong’s performance as a “very interesting Zuckerberg impersonation, standing and sitting like a Thunderbird puppet”. It is much less sympathetic than Jesse Eisenberg’s in The Social Network and is a sort of corporeal representation of Meta as the monolithic, corporate bad guy.

Elements of the portrayal chime with some former Meta employees, including a whistleblower, Arturo Béjar, who describes it as “accurate”. Another former employee tells the Guardian that Zuckerberg was “unemotional” in meetings (perhaps what you’d expect from a $1.8tn company CEO, admittedly). Well, Strong’s performance certainly is that.

There had already been a turning point in public perception of Facebook before the Haugen leaks, with the Cambridge Analytica scandal, which raised questions about the privacy of account holders’ data and how it is used.

Haugen’s revelations in 2021 compounded this disquiet. By the time of the 2022 inquest for British teenager Molly Russell, who took her own life after watching harmful content on Instagram, regulation of social media around the world was inevitable.

The tone of The Social Reckoning and Strong’s performance reflect this shift. In the UK, screenings of the film are carrying an advert for the online safety charity established by Molly’s family, in which her father says: “‘Instagram helped kill my daughter”.
Responding to Russell, Meta says it has worked to improve the safety of its platforms.
The regulatory, legal and political backlash against social media – as well as the release of The Social Reckoning – reflects a lack of trust in such statements.
Strong’s Zuckerberg says in the film that “the debate is over”. If it is, The Social Reckoning portrays a world where Meta is on the wrong side of it.

items.title: Tate sounds eerie, Frieze returns and Cindy Sherman takes surreal selfies – the week in art
paragraphs: Tarek AtouiSound art inspired by everyday objects and the eerie harmonies of history provides the latest artistic intervention in Tate Modern’s biggest space. Read more here. Turbine Hall, Tate Modern, London, from 13 October to 11 April

Shopfront, scaffolding, throbbing car bodies … 37 artists take the temperature of the nation in a show which demonstrates the breadth and eccentricity of British identity. Read more about British Art Show 10: A Chorus of Strangers.
Tate Britain missed the mark with breathlessly superficial exhibition of 90s art and fashion
Why children have always adored taking pictures – and what their images can tell us
Whether your brain can handle a show that only has white paintings
The Greek goddess Aphrodite was thrown on the rubbish heap in Oxford
Australia’s historic theatres and cinemas are the stuff of ritzy glamour
A £110m gallery can still run the risk of looking like a fashion mag
Tories could be in hot water after using Stanley Chow’s cartoon portrait of Andy ‘Bottler’ Burnham without consent
An Angel in Red With a Lute by Giovanni Ambrogio de Predis, c1495–1499

Leonardo da Vinci is said to have been sent to the court of Milan by Lorenzo de’ Medici to play on a bizarre stringed instrument of his own invention. His drawings do include inventions for novel musical devices. This painting is closely influenced by Leonardo: not only does it imitate his shadowed, dreamy style but it was originally part of the same altarpiece in Milan as his National Gallery masterpiece The Virgin of the Rocks. Leonardo, De Predis and every other Renaissance artist associated music with the mathematics of Pythagoras and the harmony of the universe: the angel here is playing, could we but hear it, such heavenly music. But it is the lute that suggests a very direct influence by Leonardo. The precise and detailed, entrancing way that De Predis depicts its nine strings and the angel’s highly realistic fingering echo Leonardo’s fascination with machinery and technology – in this case the sweet machinery of music. Painted under the hypnotic sway of the Tuscan polymath who was Milan’s court artist, this painting holds you charmed and soothed by the sound of silence. National Gallery, London

items.title: Cricut Joy 2 vs Cricut Joy: which compact cutting machine should you buy?
paragraphs: The original Cricut Joy was nice and neat; it's still one of the best Cricut machines, and I've had one for years. But I always thought of it as the machine for fun projects, not for my main work as a quilter. The Joy 2 is different. It's more powerful, quicker and more agile, and it now slots into my workflow when my Cricut Maker 5 is busy or just too big for the job.

It's also still a joy, if you'll forgive me. Everyone I know now gets a card I make personally, which is handy when you forget a birthday and can't get to the shop in time (that's happened more than once).

Below, I test and compare the older Joy and the new Joy 2 to see if the updated model is better, especially as right now the original cutter is on sale. I'll start with a basic comparison and then dig a little deeper into how they are to use.

The original Cricut Joy is small, simple, and good for cards, labels, and decals, with Smart Materials and foil transfer on board. No Print Then Cut, no scoring, and you have to open the front section every time you use it.

By comparison, the new Joy 2 follows the same small, compact craft-machine idea, but in a lighter, flatter body that's ready to go straight out of the box. Print Then Cut means full-colour stickers, and the bundle includes a scoring tool. This newbie is fully automatic, too, making it incredibly easy to use.
The original Joy is compact, simple, and great for cards, labels, and decals, but it lacks Print Then Cut and scoring and is bulkier overall. But it's always on sale now.
The new Joy 2 is lighter, flatter, and quicker to set up, and it includes Print Then Cut and a scoring tool, though its cutting area is small and it requires an inkjet printer.

The Joy 2 starts at $99 / £99.99; for comparison, the original Joy started at $179, so the new model already looks like a bargain. That's for the machine alone, and most people will end up buying a bundle. The Essentials Bundle includes a fine point blade, a scoring tool, a dual-tip pen, a LightGrip mat, a card mat, a portable trimmer, a weeding tool, a scraper and a spatula, so there's plenty to get started with, and you don't need to buy extras before your first project.

These days, the original Joy is much cheaper and often on sale as Cricut promotes its new machine, so expect to pay closer to £50-£69 for this older model. If you are buying a Joy 2, look for bundle deals on the Cricut store for a good deal.

When the older Joy is in use, you have to open the front section, and it measures 23cm deep. The Joy 2 is 15cm deep and ready to go because nothing folds out. It's slightly wider at 24cm vs 22cm, but much flatter at about 7cm tall vs about 11cm, and it weighs around 1kg vs the original's 1.7kg. It's noticeably easier to pick up.

I used to store my Joy in the cupboard because it was taking up space on my desk. The Joy 2 can just stay out, or you can slide it into a desk drawer. The plug also comes with adaptors for each country, and they're easy to swap, so it travels well (and I've seen people unpack this at airport security, so it's a gadget some crafters can't live without).

Print Then Cut is the big addition. You print your images on an inkjet printer, upload them to Cricut Design Space, and the Joy 2 cuts them out with high accuracy. The original Joy couldn't do this, so stickers and other full-colour printable projects are new territory.

Scoring is the other one. The Joy 2 comes with a scoring tool, which opens up a lot more projects, especially folded cards. It also comes with a card-making mat, and I've found it ideal for cards. I use it for labels too, cut from card or vinyl.

For quilting, it's been great. I cut cardboard templates on the Joy 2, then use them to cut quilt patterns, and it's a quick, easy way to fit it into a job without bringing out the larger Cricut Maker 5, which I always save for larger projects because of its size.

It's also easier to use than the original Joy. Everything with Cricut is easy, but at first I found it odd to leave the little cutter to decide what to cut and how. It's sensor-driven, so you set up the project in the Cricut app, press your material against the rollers, and the Joy 2 does the rest. If you use the mat, you put it in at the "load and go" stage, and it gets on with it. If you're new to digital crafting, this machine gets you cutting quickly with no hassle.

Cricut says it works with 75+ materials, up from 50+ on the original, and you can use Smart Materials without a mat. Design Space now includes AI tools that make it easier to create highly personalised cards and projects.

Both machines are compact and beginner-friendly, work with Smart Materials and foil transfer, and have the same cutting width: 4.5 inches (11.4cm). That's why neither suits big projects. With Smart Materials, you can cut lengths of up to 48 inches (about 122cm) without a mat, which suits long banners and decals.
The software is the same, but when you log in to Design Space, select the Joy 2 from the drop-down menu so you only see compatible projects.

If it's your first compact Cricut, buy the Joy 2. It's well-priced for the tech and use cases, takes up much less room, is easier to use, and adds Print Then Cut and scoring. With all this on offer, I wouldn't buy the original new.

If you already own a Joy, it depends on what you make. For simple cards and vinyl labels, the original is still a really good machine (and if that's all you need, it's on sale so at a reasonable price).

But overall, it's hard not to opt for the new Joy 2. If you want stickers, are short on desk space, or are a crafter like me who wants a small machine to support the big one, the Joy 2 is worth the upgrade.

Julie Dean is a former doctor and occupational therapist by profession, which inspired her to start sewing and quilting as a therapeutic activity. She is passionate about her craft and has been quilting and using Cricut for over five years. As well as selling her own designs and products on Etsy, Julie has taken commissions for interior design agencies to create bespoke quilts, including Beata Heuman. Julie's work has appeared in Architectural Digest.

items.title: Crazy Rich Asians to return as TV show with original film's stars
paragraphs: Four of the stars of 2018's Crazy Rich Asians film are reprising their roles for a TV show of the same name.

The series will pick up events after the end of the hit film, with Constance Wu and Henry Golding playing their lead roles of Rachel and Nick, while Ronny Chieng is back as Eddie and Oscar winner Michelle Yeoh will have a recurring role as Nick's mother Eleanor.

"It's a 'Crazy Rich' family reunion!" said Adele Lim, who co-wrote the film, calling it the sequel we've been waiting for". It will "delve into the characters and worlds of Kevin Kwan's brilliant books" over eight episodes, she said.
The show will be made by HBO, and the news was announced days after HBO's parent company Warner Bros announced its £110bn (£82.8bn) merger with Paramount Skydance.
Adapted from Kwan's bestseller books, written between 2013 and 2017, the film topped the US box office and was nominated for two Golden Globes.
It featured an all-Asian cast and told the story of an Asian-American woman who gets a culture shock meeting her boyfriend's ultra-wealthy family in Singapore.
Lim is showrunner for the new TV series and will be one of the executive producers, as will the the film's director Jon M Chu.

items.title: Alison Hammond: 'I thought I was having heart attack on air'
paragraphs: Hammond returned to This Morning one week after her dramatic early exit
Alison Hammond has said she feared she was having a heart attack on air when she had to rush off ITV's This Morning midway through the programme last week.
The presenter appeared to clutch her chest as she left the show last Friday, and was taken to hospital to have a heart check-up.
She turned out to have suffered a panic attack, and said the experience was "probably one of the most scariest things I've ever been through".

Returning for her weekly slot on Friday, she told viewers: "I couldn't catch my breath and I genuinely thought I was having a heart attack. I'm so glad I'm here. I feel so grateful. I feel so thankful to God, to everything in life."
She added: "It felt like a heart attack. It was very real."
Hammond was alongside Dermot O'Leary as usual on This Morning on Friday
Alongside co-host Dermot O'Leary, Hammond introduced the programme by thanking him for holding the fort after her dramatic early exit, and also thanking everyone who sent good wishes.
She added: "It was the first time I've ever experienced anything like that. Secondly it was live on TV so I thought, oh my gosh, my son might be watching.
"So I just ran. I ran off TV. I would never do that normally but I just couldn't catch my breath."
The panic attack came on very quickly, she explained.
"It just was like a wave, something which I've now found out is adrenaline. That came into my body. I couldn't catch my breath and I genuinely thought I was having a heart attack."
The experience has given her a new perspective on life, she continued.
"I'm so happy that I'm here, and I'm so happy to see you," she said, putting both hands on Dermot's cheeks before hugging him.
"You were absolutely wonderful. And I'm so glad we're alive, and if anything it's made me look at life so much differently. Taking stock, look after my health. I'm drinking a lot of water."
The 51-year-old compared the feeling of the panic attack to crossing into a "surreal" place like the otherworldly Upside Down in TV show Stranger Things.
"I felt like I went into the other world - what's that show that I loved? Stranger Things. You know when you go into the Upside Down world? I felt like I went into the Upside Down world.
"I couldn't grasp my breath, and it was a panic attack."
Hammond and O'Leary also spoke further about panic attacks with former BBC Breakfast host and psychologist Dr Sian Williams, who has written a book about anxiety.
Hammond said she had been unsure about returning to This Morning - but felt that if she didn't come back this week, she may never do so.

"I'll be honest with you, I was anxious about coming back. But I thought, if I don't come back today, I probably wouldn't come back... because then I would have made a thing that it's This Morning that's causing the panic.
"But it can happen anywhere. It comes in ebbs and flows."

She and Williams also discussed the pressure of presenting live TV. "I do live TV all the time, I didn't realise it was having - I don't know if it was having an impact - the fact that you have to be 'on' in order to do it. I don't know," Hammond said.
She concluded the segment by telling viewers: "I'm back, babes. Keep rolling."

Earlier, looking ahead to the programme on ITV's Lorraine, Hammond had appeared to parody former This Morning presenter Holly Willoughby's 2023 monologue, which she famously began by asking viewers "are you OK?" in the wake of co-host Phillip Schofield's departure.
Hammond said on Lorraine: "I'm going to tell you everything, guys. Are you OK? I hope you are."
That line was met with laughter by Lorraine Kelly, who declared it "genius".
Hammond can also currently be seen on Channel 4's The Great British Bake Off

Hammond was taken to hospital after her departure from last Friday's episode of This Morning. She posted a video saying she was "getting my old ticker checked out" after what she described as "a little bit of a palpitation", which she hoped "was just a little panic attack".
She missed the Attitude Awards on Wednesday, where she won the The Honorary Gay Award.
The Birmingham-born presenter also hosts TV shows including The Great British Bake Off and For the Love of Dogs.
Also known as anxiety attacks, panic attacks can affect anyone, regardless of age, background or whether they have a history of anxiety.
Speaking on This Morning, Dr Williams described panic attacks as "anxiety on overdrive, when you can't find the reason".

They affect more women than men and can last between five and 20 minutes, she said. People experiencing one can "ground yourself" by focusing on the moment and the safety of their surroundings, and by steadying their breathing, she added.
"A heart attack and a panic attack are different, but they can feel the same because there are similar symptoms - choking or tingling or pain in the chest.
"If it's a heart attack it tends to radiate, so if might go down your arm or into your jaw. A heart attack doesn't subside with breathing or grounding in the same way."
According to the MIND mental health charity, panic attacks are an extreme anxiety response. They can develop quickly, and come with very intense symptoms.
These are both physical and mental and the NHS's extensive list of symptoms, external includes:

items.title: Video game Cyberpunk 2077 to get live-action movie adaptation
paragraphs: A live-action movie version of smash hit video game Cyberpunk 2077 is being developed by Paramount Pictures.
The Hollywood studio is working with producer Lorenzo di Bonaventura, known for his work on the Transformers films, and CD Projekt Red (CDPR), the developer of the sci-fi role-playing game.

CDPR's joint-chief executive Michał Nowakowski said in a statement, external the company was "excited about Paramount as a future partner who shares our creative ambitions for the Cyberpunk franchise".
Details of the film's story, potential release date and casting information are yet to be revealed.
Despite a troubled launch in 2020, the Cyberpunk 2077 video game, which stars Keanu Reeves, has sold more than 40 million copies worldwide.
The John Wick star plays rockstar Johnny Silverhand, a terrorist whose consciousness is stored on a chip inside the body of main character V.
Set in Night City, a fictional metropolis in a dystopian version of California, players work to uncover a conspiracy involving the shady Arasaka megacorporation.
An expansion, Phantom Liberty, starring Idris Elba was released in 2023 and has sold more than 15 million copies, according to CDPR.
Cyberpunk has already been successfully adapted into a popular animated series - Edgerunners - with a second season due to premiere on Netflix later this month.
The streamer also produced The Witcher, an adaptation of CDPR's massively popular fantasy role-playing series.
It originally starred former Superman actor Henry Cavill, but he was replaced by Liam Hemsworth in the show's fourth season.

items.title: Isaias strengthens to become first Atlantic hurricane of 2026 season
paragraphs: Isaias has become the first Atlantic hurricane of the 2026 season, with wind speeds of 80mph and a minimum pressure of 975mb. It is expected to strengthen to a category 2 hurricane as it approaches the US’s northern Gulf coast on Friday, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).

As a result of the strong El Niño, it has been a notably quiet Atlantic hurricane season. The first hurricane of the season has not formed this late since 8 October 1905, which pre-dates the satellite era (1960s) for tracking hurricanes that has allowed for more non-landfall hurricanes to be discovered.

Isaias is expected to make landfall on Friday evening local time, bringing an estimated 75-150mm (2.9-5.9in) of rainfall across the Gulf coast. There may be up to 250mm in places, with a possibility of flash flooding and isolated river flooding.

The NOAA also said there was increasing likelihood of life-threatening storm surge along portions of the northern Gulf coast and damaging hurricane-force winds over portions of the Florida panhandle, southern Alabama and Mississippi. A hurricane warning has been issued and people have been told to prepare for long power outages and to obey any evacuation orders issued.
In Zimbabwe, a state of disaster was declared in the south-east Masvingo province on Tuesday after a severe hailstorm caused widespread damage to homes and critical infrastructure.
Preliminary assessments found the roofs had been torn off 8,500 homes. A further 15,300 people reported shattered windows, leaving many exposed to the elements as the rainy season begins.
The country’s power infrastructure was badly affected, disrupting drainage and sewerage systems, raising concerns about public health.

In Australia, a rare tornado hit the town of Ulladulla, about 140 miles (230km) south of Sydney, on 3 October. Tornadoes are relatively rare in Australia, where there are about 50 each year. This Ulladulla tornado damaged properties and felled trees.
