items.title: Anthropic bans users from ‘needless abusive or cruel behavior’ towards Claude
paragraphs: Anthropic has barred users from exhibiting “sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior” toward its models, as the company’s leaders continue to ponder machine consciousness.
The Verge first reported the change in policy.
A spokesperson for Anthropic, which is behind AI chatbot Claude, did not immediately respond to an inquiry about what could be considered “abusive or cruel”.
In an online user policy, the San Francisco-based company noted that its ban would not apply to common user frustrations, model testing or “dark creative themes”.
Anthropic’s usage policy previously contained restrictions on abusive conduct.

The company’s large language models have the ability to end a conversation if a user is being persistently harmful. When that feature rolled out last August, the company framed it as a safeguard for AI’s welfare.

“We remain highly uncertain about the potential moral status of Claude and other LLMs, now or in the future. However, we take the issue seriously, and alongside our research program we’re working to identify and implement low-cost interventions to mitigate risks to model welfare, in case such welfare is possible. Allowing models to end or exit potentially distressing interactions is one such intervention,” according to its website.
The notion of AI systems being conscious has been highly polarizing in and outside the tech world.
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has said he cannot rule out the possibility.
Meanwhile, Sam Altman, CEO of rival OpenAI, has appeared averse to the idea.

“I am very uncomfortable about people trying to ascribe religious force or a surrender of human judgment to AI models, and think it is a real safety issue,” he wrote in an X post, days after the New York Times reported on Anthropic leaders’ extensive conversations with religious scholars.

items.title: Phantom Blade Zero's dark wuxia world feels like a playable kung fu movie
paragraphs: It's no surprise that the big AAA games emerging from China have also taken inspiration from the country's previous successful cultural exports, from mythology to martial arts. In Phantom Blade Zero's case, it's not just about leaning into martial arts through its combat but as a philosophy and aesthetic, so much so that the developer S-Game is coining its action RPG as 'kungfupunk'.

It's something that's apparent from the moment I press the button that begins my demo, where even the tutorial feels so flashy and cinematic that you could easily imagine being a QTE in one of Sony's first-party blockbusters, except the difference is you're still in control of these actions yourself.
Phantom Blade Zero — Pre-Order Trailer - YouTube

While I'm not able to go into the details of the opening sequences and how they relate to the story of your protagonist Soul, a skilled assassin who has just 66 days to live, while also framed for the murder of his master, I came away feeling like I had experienced a playable kung fu movie, reliving the iconic martial arts duels of classic wuxia films like Once Upon A Time In China or Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon, but where instead of just hitting a button prompt, I was in fluid control of my actions.

Mechanically, Phantom Blade Zero may share similarities with other action RPGs or Soulslikes, including colour-coded attacks to indicate whether you should dodge or parry, but what really sells the martial arts fantasy is just how fluid and dynamic the combat animations feel.

It's something you can tell when just holding L1 to block, which in another game would just be quite rigid as your character holds their weapon or shield to guard, but here it looks like Soul is attacking by clashing his blade against his opponent's, precisely how it looks in a wuxia fight.

That authenticity is down to how S-Game has not only mocapped the game's action with real martial artists but even employs wires just like those used in wuxia films that allow actors to perform larger-than-life acrobatics. Even Hong Kong action film veterans including action choreographer and film director Kenji Tanigaki and martial arts legend Donnie Yen are involved, though even in this considerably chunky hands-on time I didn't manage to run into the latter's in-game character.

Yet while these very cinematic animations and visuals realised in Unreal Engine 5 is the main draw, S-Game also elegantly incorporates hand-drawn aesthetics into other parts of the game, perhaps in reference to the original 2D Rainblood: Town of Death, which Phantom Blade Zero is technically a AAA reimagining of.

There's the game map for the Wulin, which is presented in the style of a Chinese ink painting, with more elements added the more of its semi-open world that you explore. While this style means it's actually more of an artistic representation than a more no-frills top-down map, it actually still felt very accurate as I was able to make out spaces and landmarks of areas I had already been to, from its treacherous rocky mountain paths to an outpost held by another faction calling themselves The Mandate.

While this outpost also happens to be located in a bamboo forest that's become a common trope amongst wuxia films, Phantom Blade Zero doesn't just stick to tradition, its kungfupunk aesthetic being a way to differentiate itself with taking subversive influences from more contemporary or even Western ideas, from cyberpunk to modern pop and rock music.

One such example is when I reach a tower where the architecture outside looks quite traditional yet inside also contains a furnace with steel pipes, while it also has another unusual design where it's decorated with red threads, symbolic in Chinese for fate, or marriage, though in this case it's meant to serve a more ominous connotation.

The most kungfupunk example however surely belongs to a fight I got to attempt at a later point in the game, a lion dance grandmaster that's even soundtracked to real percussions, except the lion's head is also designed with metal spikes while it's also able to breathe fire. But while it all looks spectacular, it's definitely not a game that's just dazzling you with cinematic set pieces that require simple QTE prompts.

After all, when I finally reach the Hunter of the Order at a great waterfall for a showdown that the whole chapter had been building up before, it would have been too anticlimactic if I had just wiped the floor with him on the first try.

To some extent, I felt that it might have been tougher than I expected, though it does a very generous thing of at least checkpointing between the phases of a boss fight (difficulty options to make things a little easier, or indeed tougher, are also available). But if Phantom Blade Zero manages to achieve the fine balance of making you look and play like a kung fu master in the same way that Onimusha: Way of the Sword makes you look and play like a samurai master, this could end up being very special.
Phantom Blade Zero is coming to PS5 and PC on 29 October.

Alan Wen is a freelance journalist writing about video games in the form of features, interview, previews, reviews and op-eds. Work has appeared in print including Edge, Official Playstation Magazine, GamesMaster, Games TM, Wireframe, Stuff, and online including Kotaku UK, TechRadar, FANDOM, Rock Paper Shotgun, Digital Spy, The Guardian, and The Telegraph.

items.title: OpenAI caught Russians and Iranians using ChatGPT for influence campaigns
paragraphs: OpenAI says Russian operatives used its AI chatbot to update their bosses, shedding light on influence campaigns previously not attributed to Russia. Jeff Chiu/AP hide caption

OpenAI said in a blog post on Thursday that it banned Russian and Iranian accounts that were using the company's artificial intelligence tools to help with influence operations in multiple countries. The operatives said they managed to get their false narratives picked up by news outlets, and in once case, prompted a response from a member of the European Parliament, according to internal reports the operations produced using OpenAI's chatbot, ChatGPT.

OpenAI investigated the impact of the different campaigns the accounts mentioned and found that those focused on placing false narratives in established media outlets appeared to have reached a wider audience than campaigns that focused on using fake social media accounts to spread their message.

The Russian operations targeted countries in Latin America and appeared aimed at undermining support for Ukraine and influencing local politics, OpenAI said. The accounts appeared to be mostly using ChatGPT to write reports detailing their work to unspecified higher ups, OpenAI said. The company said one of these reports appeared to describe the widest-reaching influence operation OpenAI has come across so far, because it led to public response from a political figure.

In this campaign, the Russian operatives said they impersonated a regional educational authority in Peru and tricked some schools into organizing activities about Ukraine that featured Stepan Bandera. Bandera is a controversial figure, admired by nationalists for leading a drive for Ukrainian independence before and during World War II. He is reviled by others, including in Poland, because his movement sided with the Nazis and killed Poles and Jews. Peruvian outlet Extra reported that one such event did take place at a Peruvian school.
A Polish news report about the school event prompted a far-right Polish member of the European Parliament to suggest banning the entry of people who professed support for Bandera.
"The Russian fake thus both fed on, and fed into, historical tensions between Ukrainians and Poles," OpenAI wrote in its report.

"Russians are constantly engaging in these sorts of active measures," said Darren Linvill, a co-director of Clemson University's Watt Family Innovation Center Media Forensics Hub who studies online influence operations. "Trying to engage in narrative laundering, creating fake stories, fake persona to either create or spread propaganda that aligns with Russia's worldview and Russia's political agenda."

The Russian internal memos created with ChatGPT also claimed that the operatives ran a fake think tank in Latin America and recruited unwitting researchers to interview experts and compose reports. OpenAI said that effort was similar to a 2020 Russian operation posing as an independent news outlet linked to the late oligarch Yevgeny Prigozhin's Internet Research Agency, which was involved in efforts to influence the 2016 U.S. election.

In other instances, OpenAI said, the Russian operatives took credit for events they were not responsible for. The Russians did use AI to generate fake material, OpenAI said, but it was a minority of the workload.
"These Russian underlings were trying to use AI to create a shortcut and do less work in the same way that a lot of us use AI, but in this case it helped get them caught," Linvill said.

While the Russian operatives primarily used AI to update their superiors, Iranian operatives used AI to help them push out content in Persian and English. The campaign mainly focused on the U.S.-Iran war and, to a lesser degree, American politics. OpenAI said the operation's activity "appeared consistent with a commercial actor running a for-hire influence campaign" but that it was unable to identify who that was.
According to OpenAI, Iranian accounts made up seven fake authors to pitch and polish long articles to small media outlets around the world. They published almost 100 articles in this way.

The fake authors published articles in outlets including the progressive U.S. news site Daily Kos and the U.K.-based Middle East Monitor. According to NBC News, the Middle East Monitor published at least 21 articles by four fake authors. The outlet, which didn't respond to a request for comment, has since taken down the author pages.

The Daily Kos wrote in response to NPR's request for comment that its community section, where one of the fake personas posted, is separate from staff reports. Anyone can sign up to post in the community section and posts are "not subject to review by Daily Kos staff prior to publication," according to a disclaimer on the site. The community section does have rules for posting, including prohibiting "Pretending to be someone you're not." The posts by the persona are still up.

"AI was valuable to them above and beyond just being a shortcut," Linvill said. "It helped them create language that ... looked and felt and read authentic to the point where it was being published by legitimate outlets. And I think that is something that a few years ago, an Iranian operation like this would have struggled a lot more with."

items.title: Plans for Sydney’s controversial new public square in doubt after NSW government intervention
paragraphs: Plans for a grand new public square in centre of Sydney are in doubt after the New South Wales planning minister declared the project “state significant”, wresting the approval process away from the City of Sydney.

The lord mayor, Clover Moore, released renders in August for the plaza opposite Sydney’s town hall. The design for the space, which the council had expected to be completed by 2031, include a semi-circular clearing projecting eastwards towards Hyde park, with a fountain and a grove of native trees.

The plans have been the source of a battle between Moore and the NSW premier, Chris Minns, who has said he does not support the project, describing it as “too expensive, majorly disruptive for Sydney”, and said it would close down businesses in the area. It had also become a flashpoint in a culture war, ridiculed in the Sydney tabloid The Daily Telegraph, which published AI-generated images of the new square heaving with protesters.

The council began finalising discussions with the owners of the last of seven buildings needed to be acquired and bulldozed for the project in recent months. The demolition and construction was expected to cost $150m.

But on Friday, the planning minister, Paul Scully announced he had declared the project a state significant development (SSD), after seeking advice from the NSW Independent Planning Commission, taking the decision for approval away from the council.

“This process will allow for a rigorous whole-of-government assessment by the department and provide an opportunity for individuals, the community, and other stakeholders to have their say on any development application,” he said.
They have also been opposed by Woolworths, whose town hall location occupies one of the buildings that would be demolished under the plans.

Scully said the IPC would make the determination on any proposal submitted by the City of Sydney. Under the SSD pathway, the planning minister himself is the consent authority, unless the IPC is delegated to take on that role.
In a surprise statement on Friday, Moore welcomed the decision to declare the project state significant, saying, “I could not agree more”.
“Regardless of who assesses it, we remain confident in the merits of the proposal and see no planning reason why it should not ultimately be supported.”

“The City owns the buildings, has responsibly saved the money over a 40 year period to deliver the project debt-free, and has had some of the world’s leading designers and architects work on the plans.”

“This has, however, been an unusual intervention. The government generally takes planning decisions away from councils to speed up development, not slow it down, and in this case it stepped in before a development application even existed.”

items.title: Why are more roofs not made of solar tiles?
paragraphs: Some people in the US "still hate the look of solar", Kate Collardson acknowledges.

She would know. Collardson handles operations for the Solar Service of Colorado, a solar maintenance and inspection company. She's also held just about every other job in the industry, from installer to instructor.
For those that hate the look of solar panels, an alternative is a solar roof, where the tiles (or shingles) house solar cells, but look much the same as regular tiles.
This is especially important for historic buildings, where heritage rules limit changes to their appearance.

For many people, the first time they'd heard of this product category was in August, when Tesla's website stopped offering solar roofs, external. This followed disappointing sales and a lawsuit over sudden price hikes, external.
Other companies have also pulled out, but Tesla's decision in particular sent shockwaves through the solar roof industry.
Some see it as a death knell for solar tiles; others, as an opportunity.
For instance, the small Swiss company Freesuns is considering expanding to the US.
Deborah Learoyd, Freesuns' CEO and managing director, estimates that the company's sales have grown 20–30% since it was established in 2019.
In general, solar roof components continue to be manufactured in smaller batches. This limits the economies of scale and standardisation, though flexible manufacturing could help somewhat.

Learoyd says that while the unit costs for Freesuns' products are slowly decreasing, "a lot of the cost is actually the fact that every roof is a little bit different. And so it has to be engineered a little bit differently, installed a little bit differently".
Solar roofs typically require collaboration among roofers, solar installers and electricians. And building regulations tend to be more complex than for solar panels.

The additional time and paperwork can take a toll on a roofing business, Collardson explains. "You try to put a roofer into the equation and they're going, 'This is taking forever. I'm losing money. I could have sold 10 roofing jobs in the time that it takes me to sell this one'."
Collardson has to charge more for repair of solar shingles, compared to a standard photovoltaic (PV) setup.

She explains, "With traditional solar, we generally have electronics on the panel and a map that shows us exactly how much each panel is producing." So when something goes wrong, it's easy to spot where.
"With solar shingles, we don't really have the benefit of that mapping; there's no room underneath the shingle for the electronics." Thermal cameras can identify the trouble spots, however.

But then there's the matter of accessing them. "You can remove the one in the middle of the array, but you have to walk on the others, and you really shouldn't walk on them because you're going to create micro-fractures and that's going to cause issues down the road."
Before repair costs are factored in, a solar roof might cost twice as much as a system of solar panels mounted on a roof.
Solar roofs are also less efficient - one reason is that the tiles are just smaller.
Another factor is the energy lost as heat. Since the tiles sit close to the roof, there's less airflow than with standard solar panels mounted on a roof. Heat impairs solar performance.

Coloured tiles are even less efficient, comments Ben Graves, co-founder of UK solar company Sunsave. "The reason why all solar cells are black, and increasingly the whole panel is now black, is because black is the best absorbing colour."
Overall, much more space would need to be devoted to solar roof tiles to produce the same amount of energy.
Sunsave does not offer solar roofs. "Most people in the UK just don't have enough money to pay for it," Graves believes.
While appearance was a bigger factor five years ago, now "the vast majority of consumers are most interested in how much they can save".
But supporters of solar roofs argue that they should not be pitted against standard solar modules on roofs.

"Let's not compare PV roof tiles to a standard PV system, but look at PV roof tiles as generating additional electricity from our roofs instead of just having the roof sit there," urges Martin Heinrich who leads a research group at the Fraunhofer Institute for Solar Energy Systems in Germany.
While standard solar panels have gone from strength to strength, solar roofs have not advanced to the same extent.
One advancement that could especially help solar roofs is matrix shingling technology.

This is a different way of connecting solar cells. The solar cells are cut into narrow strips, layered like overlapping shingles, and connected to each other using electrically conductive adhesive, rather than metal wires.

This means that the electrical current can flow around shaded areas, unlike with standard modules. "If you get like a bird pooping on a part of the cell, the current can go around it," Learoyd explains.
In addition to increasing energy output, this improves the appearance as the silver wires aren't visible.
Another advantage, Heinrich says, is that "since we cut the cells into smaller areas, we can fill out special sizes more easily. You don't have to adhere to the regular pattern size."
Freesuns is an early adopter of matrix shingling technology in building-integrated PV. "We see it as a big opportunity for the future in terms of how we would make our tiles," Learoyd says.
What would also help the company is better software for automated design. This would speed up the design process, since each roofing job is unique.
Learoyd believes this would lower costs and give "the whole construction industry much more confidence in using the product".
Ten years after her own solar roof was installed, and despite the sector's setbacks, Learoyd remains optimistic.
She believes that for people with the means, it will eventually become standard to install a new roof with some sort of embedded solar. "It's just a no-brainer."

items.title: Olivia Colman on viral Wicker memes: 'This has never happened to me before'
paragraphs: Olivia Colman stars alongside Alexander Skarsgård in new film Wicker
Culture correspondent at London Film Festival
It has already been described as 2026's weirdest rom-com, external.
And new film Wicker has sparked a deluge of viral memes and steamy jokes that have flooded social media ahead of its release.
Speaking to the BBC at its London Film Festival premiere, lead star Olivia Colman said she never expected such a big reaction.
"No, literally this has never happened for anything I've done before," she said.
"But you put Alexander Skarsgård in an interesting outfit, and everyone is looking."
The film tells the tale of a lonely, ostracised fisherwoman (Colman) living in a medieval village.
Tired of constantly being mocked for being single, she hires a basketmaker to mould her a new partner made entirely out of wicker.
Enter Skarsgård - but not as you've ever seen him before.
As the "wicker husband", he emerges as a strapping, dashing life-size piece of furniture.
And he proves to be a devoted partner, and passionate lover, sparking jealousy among the other village women.
The film has an A-list cast, with other stars including Peter Dinklage as the basket weaver, Elizabeth Debicki as the tailor's wife, and Richard E Grant as the village doctor.

Since the release of the trailer, there's been a huge buzz online around the film - from BookTok and FilmTok fans swooning over Skarsgård’s character, to questions being asked over splinter risks during the film's erotic scenes.
Swedish giant Ikea even got involved, posting photos of its rattan furniture on Instagram in a nod to the film, with the caption “husband material”.
When asked why she thinks people are so fascinated and so thirsty for the wicker husband, Colman answered: "We all love a little bit of escapism. That's what film is beautiful for.
"And it's magical, and a bit of fantasy, and people love that, especially currently. What's not to love about a little bit of escapism and fantasy?"
She also said it was the film's originality that drew her to it.
"You get a lot of scripts through the post, and you feel like you've seen a bit before. And this, I really hadn't seen this before, so I was excited," she said.
Like Colman, Debicki agrees that Skarsgård is the main reason the film has lit up the internet.
"I think it was a lot to do with Alex in a wicker man costume, really," she told the BBC. "I think that's something that apparently everybody would like to see."
But Skarsgård himself gives all the credit to the designers of the outfit. "All I had to do was get stuck into it," he says.
He also said the sex scenes were "super fun" to shoot.
"We wanted those moments when the bed crashes and breaks, and the way they comment on that in the scene is quite comedic," he said.
"But [the characters] also have tender moments and sexy moments, it was great."
The steamy new rom-com has been causing a stir at film festivals
The film is based on the short story The Wicker Husband by Ursula Wills-Jones.

After its premiere at Sundance film festival earlier this year, The Guardian awarded it, external two stars, praising the "eye-catching premise" but cautioning that there was "too much wood but not enough fire".
But The Hollywood Reporter, external was more positive, calling it "a warming, sometimes poignant pleasure".
Away from the social media buzz, the film's stars say it also taps into deeper themes, from gender roles to breaking societal rules.
"It's very funny and strange and wonderful, but I find it very moving. And it's a good one to discover beyond the Ikea memes," said Debicki.
"It touches on a lot of stuff. Hierarchy, social structure," said Skarsgård. "But it's done with such a light touch."
"It's about love, and it is funny, but it's also a romance, and it very gently laughs at the sort of traditions we have in marriage and community," said Colman.
"I think it's something that you will come out and discuss a lot."
Wicker is released in UK cinemas on October 30.

items.title: Emotions run high at the round table as Celebrity Traitors banish two players
paragraphs: Actress Sharon Rooney was visibly shocked to find which players returned to breakfast during Thursday's episode
Spoiler warning: This article reveals details from the third episode of The Celebrity Traitors, series two.
We normally expect raised voices, conflicting theories and a dramatic showdown from the Celebrity Traitors. But as this year's first round table got under way, the writing was on the castle wall.
Viewers who often get frustrated with the faithful and root for them to uncover a traitor had their wish firmly Richard E Grant-ed on Thursday, as the actor was banished in a landslide vote.

His questionable strategy of revealing he was a traitor to the other celebrities in the bar led to the first time in the UK version of the show that a traitor has been identified at the opening round table.
"Thank you for giving me an almost bingo full-house of votes," Grant told his fellow players. "I have always wanted to be a traitor, and sometimes in life your dreams do come true."

There was jubilation from the other celebrities as Grant confirmed his identity, waving his hands in the air. Ross Kemp was so happy it came out as borderline anger, with a vein-popping "get in there!"
Other players seemed genuinely shocked. "This is me with men all the time," joked comedian Joanne McNally, who hadn't voted for Grant. "I completely believed him!"

But although the faithful had successfully found a traitor, and even managed to spell his name correctly on their slates, the first round table saw some other players behave in ways that immediately aroused suspicion.
Myha'la winked at Richard E Grant before voting for him - which was picked up by some other players
Ross Kemp, meanwhile, was a scary level of delighted to have rumbled Grant

Julie Hesmondhalgh noticed Myha'la ostentatiously winking at Grant before she voted for him, which later prompted the former Coronation Street actress to make one of the most impassioned - but mistaken - speeches of the night.
"It was traitor-on-traitor," she declared (it wasn't). "I don't know if anybody else saw it," (we did). "I am so excited because I truly believe we can get two in a row," (don't count on it).
Where is the Traitors castle, and can you visit it?
Traitors commit first murder as Grant tries to save his skin
Celebrity Traitors cast: Who are this year's 'big dogs' and dark horses?

The remaining traitors, Maya Jama and James Acaster, met in the turret later with the choice of murdering previously shortlisted players Jerry Hall and Hannah Fry, or seducing a third traitor to replace Grant.
The pair ultimately decided to recruit mathematician Fry, who had the most wonderful and meme-able reaction when she found out that, not only was she not being murdered, she was being seduced.
Accepting the offer, Fry joined Jama and Acaster in the turret, exclaiming as she learned their identities: "I had both of you down as faithful!"
The new trio discussed how they would approach breakfast the next morning, before Acaster delivered the line of the episode.
"It's changing a lot, this Traitors," he observed of the fluid line-up. "It's like the Sugababes."
"I managed to checkmate myself," said Grant, "which as far as I'm aware, has never been done"
Mathematician Hannah Fry was shocked to find she was being recruited instead of murdered
The next morning, there were shocked faces when the players realised everybody had made it to breakfast unscathed, with the celebrities concluding that one player must have been recruited.

"It was fascinating seeing Jerry and Hannah come back," said Miranda Hart. "Hannah seemed different, as if something new has happened to her." Oh yes? "I definitely clocked a nervousness in her, which is very interesting."
We could have a first-rate traitor hunter on our hands here. But would any of Hart's fellow players feel the same way? "Poor Hannah," said McNally, "she's been recruited." Uh-oh.

As the theories continued to float around across various sub-meetings, with Hesmondhalgh, Bella Ramsey and several others setting their sights on Myha'la, the celebrities headed out to the next mission.

Presenter Claudia Winkleman explained the latest task would see them use a battering ram to break down the doors of four crypts, where they could find money to add to the prize pot - and also potentially bag some shields.
James Blunt immediately took control, assigning players various roles. "He was full army officer," Hart observed. "I found it mildly erotic."
"I don't think I've ever used a battering ram," Joe Lycett reflected. "I would use a battering ram to get into [Wicked star] Jonathan Bailey's house, but that's it."
Miranda Hart joked that she found James Blunt's command of the latest task "mildly erotic"

Myha'la and Fry entered one crypt, found a shield and debated who should keep it. They agreed on Myha'la, partly because she had grabbed it first, although she sweetly suggested that the pair could keep it secret from the other players to protect both of them.
Jama and Sharon Rooney, meanwhile, scored two further shields, but the players then found that some shields would have to be given up anyway in order to unlock the final chest of prize money.

Rooney and Myha'la surrendered theirs, but traitor Jama quietly held on to hers. The other players didn't know she had one, and the TV presenter asked Rooney to keep it secret. That decision could come back to bite her in later episodes.
In the cars on the way back, the players continued to debate various hunches, with one particularly awkward journey where Myha'la and Hesmondhalgh admitted they were suspicious of each other.
"I feel like you've been a little bit vague," said Hesmondhalgh. "That's only because I've thought it's been you from day one," Myha'la replied.
We've certainly come a long way from the pair's first exchange just two episodes ago. "It's lovely to meet you Myha'la, I'm such a big fan!" - "Oh my God, thank you!"
Back in the castle, Rob Beckett had adopted a new policy. "When someone comes up to talk to me, I just agree with them, whatever they say," he laughed in the castle's diary room.
James Acaster joked that he wanted to murder James Blunt to avoid confusion over them sharing a name
As the players gathered for the second banishment of the episode, discussion inevitably turned to prime suspect Myha'la.
"I've heard my name a whole bunch today," she acknowledged, as the others struggled to square her behaviour during the mission.
The actress became visibly emotional as she recounted the events of the crypt and attempted to justify grabbing the shield before offering it to Fry.
"I was going to give it to her," Myha'la said tearfully. "I was worried about my protection, but I thought maybe [Fry] had more heat."
Sensing that the tide was turning against Myha'la, Fry stuck the knife in. "Why would you scrabble for the shield, and then be keen to give it away?" she asked.
Watch on iPlayer with new episodes every Thursday and Friday
The latest banished and murdered celebs have their say in Uncloaked

Despite a sprinkling of votes for other players, Myha'la became the second casualty of the episode. "I have loved getting to know you all," she said as she confirmed her faithful status to the other players.

Hart became even more suspicious of Fry, however, after realising the mathematician had orchestrated events to make Myha'la's behaviour at the crypt look less innocent. "Miss Marple is so on," Hart said with a smile.
Later, the traitors met in the turret and debated who their next victim should be, settling on a shortlist of Blunt, Ramsey and Sebastian Croft.
Acaster had a characteristically unique reason for suggesting James Blunt.
"It would make my life easier," he said, "because every time someone says 'James', I'm turning around, and half the time, it's for him."
Celebrity Traitors continues on Friday at 20:00 BST on BBC One and iPlayer.

items.title: Will El Niño and the polar vortex bring snow to the UK this winter?
paragraphs: El Niño - the naturally-occurring climate phenomenon in the Pacific Ocean - is continuing to grow and by some measures is already the strongest on record.
The heat released from the warm Pacific Ocean into the atmosphere impacts weather patterns around the globe.
In autumn it increases the chance of wet and stormy weather in the UK - something that is reflected in the forecasts for this season.
In late winter, the waves of energy released by El Niño can move upwards through the atmosphere making it more likely that the polar vortex becomes disrupted, increasing the chance of ice and snow.
However, the links are unclear and the evidence is mixed.
The so-called Big Freeze of 2009/2010 was, at the time, the coldest winter in three decades - and coincided with an El Niño.
However, 2006/2007 was also an El Niño winter and was unseasonably warm.
The so-called Beast from the East in 2018 actually occurred during a La Niña year, effectively the opposite of El Niño.
So while El Niño is already having big impacts on global weather, and may influence the polar vortex later in winter, snow and ice in the UK is far from guaranteed.
Current forecasts suggest no significant cold or snow is likely in the near future.
You can read the latest outlook for the next month here.

items.title: Firmus pulls biggest ASX float since Telstra amid investor doubt about datacentre company
paragraphs: Firmus Technologies has scrapped what was set to be Australia’s biggest company listing in decades after investor demand for its much-hyped AI datacentre business failed to materialise.
A Firmus spokesperson said the board decided that proceeding with the offer was no longer in the best interests of the company and its shareholders.
“Firmus will now pursue capital from the private markets and consider alternative public and private market options,” the spokesperson said on Friday morning.
“We will provide additional information to shareholders as those options progress.”
Firmus, with an anticipated $44bn valuation, was expected to be the biggest ASX listing since Telstra in 1997.
But it faced mounting scepticism over its huge valuation, and forecast earnings, for a company in its startup phase with just two, small operational sites.

Backed by chip maker Nvidia and Wall Street firms Blackstone, Jane Street and Coatue, Firmus’s backers believed they could raise billions of dollars by selling shares in a public float with the help of five brokers.
The lack of demand means Firmus will need to raise money from private investors to fund its plans to build liquid-cooled “AI factories” in Australia and across Asia.

The polished Firmus pitch started to unravel midweek after it became clear the company’s bankers had vastly overestimated demand in their bid to raise $7bn from investors ahead of listing on the ASX on 23 October.
This prompted discussions about a heavy reduction in the company’s proposed $11-a-share initial public offering, according to one investment manager briefed on the matter.
The company ultimately decided to withdraw its application to list on the ASX altogether.

Guardian Australia previously reported growing concern that early Firmus investors were going to use retail investors buying into the float as their “exit strategy”, leaving small investors exposed if the excitement dissipated.
The datacentre company’s troubles have already rattled other parts of the market, with shares in Firmus investor Maas Group plunging more than 20% on Thursday.

The anticipated financial worth of the founders – Oliver Curtis, who has spent time in prison for insider trading, his cousin Tim Rosenfield, and Curtis’s former brother-in-law Jonathan Levee – will also be greatly reduced.

items.title: Trump hosts awards party for tech billionaires, almost as if he doesn’t care about ordinary Americans
paragraphs: He stands accused of being out of touch, enriching himself and his family, building a lavish White House ballroom and, with elections looming, neglecting the hardships of the voters who brought him to power.
Time for Donald Trump to show he still has the common touch? Nope.

On Thursday, the US president went to a building he named after himself, dished out awards to the world’s richest person – his old frenemy Elon Musk – and other tech billionaires and even received an award that belonged to his late uncle.

Given Trump’s gold fetish, the event was naturally entitled the Golden Age of American Innovation summit, which will be news to the many agencies and academies suffering billions of dollars in cuts to scientific research on his watch.

“We have an extremely high-IQ audience for a change,” the president told about 300 invited guests at the Donald J Trump Institute of Peace in Washington, a compliment he never pays to the crowds who line up for hours to attend his campaign rallies.

Standing on a podium with a white backdrop and series of US flags, the president gave a perfunctory speech, sticking unusually close to his teleprompter. He made references to artificial super intelligence but steered clear of the datacentres these tech overlords are erecting all over the country and, in the process, achieving the unique feat of getting Democrats and Republicans to agree on how much they hate them.

Michael Kratsios, director of the White House office of science and technology policy, then treated Trump to a video about his uncle, Dr John Trump, an electrical engineer and professor at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology who received the National Medal of Science in 1983.

The short film’s claims that John Trump’s research produced X-ray generators “used for the first radiation treatments for cancer” and that “his radars jammed German defences” on D-day in 1944 owe something to his nephew’s fondness for “truthful hyperbole”.

Six years ago, the president, who believes in “good genes” and “racehorse theory”, suggested that his uncle’s legacy would help him fight the Covid-19 pandemic: “He was a great super genius. Dr John Trump. I like this stuff. I really get it. People are surprised that I understand it. Every one of these doctors said: ‘How do you know so much about this?’ Maybe I have a natural ability. Maybe I should have done that instead of running for president.”

Kratsios had a surprise for the boss. He presented Trump with his uncle’s National Medal of Science in a handsome frame as the audience clapped. He looked happy enough, though it was clear this won’t displace the gaudy Fifa peace prize from his trophy cabinet.
Among the six tech leaders who came up on stage to receive an award for scientific and technological achievement, five were immigrants.

The “America first” president gave the National Medal of Science to SpaceX chief executive Musk (born in South Africa); Google co-founder Sergey Brin (Russia); Jensen Huang (Taiwan), whose AI chip maker Nvidia is the world’s most valuable company; and Lisa Su (Taiwan), head of the semiconductor company Advanced Micro Devices.

Trump also handed the National Medal of Technology and Innovation to Microsoft supremo Satya Nadella (India) and Dell Technologies chief executive Michael Dell (Texas). Hours earlier, JD Vance had announced Microsoft’s suspension from a programme allowing companies to sponsor foreign workers for green cards.

The trillionaire Musk was wearing a dark suit, white shirt and white tie. Trump gave him a pat on the back, handed him the medal and gave him another pat, then showed him a certificate and patted him once more. In earlier remarks, the president called Musk an “industrial titan”, “brilliant engineer”, “national treasure” and “modern-day Thomas Edison”. He observed: “It all works out well for Elon, right?”

These guys’ relationship is more complicated than Rhett Butler and Scarlett O’Hara. Musk helped buy the 2024 election for Trump and found Doge a useful vehicle to gut the federal agencies investigating his companies. The president considered Musk’s Grok chatbot ingenious after it accurately predicted that ordinary Venezuelans would celebrate the removal of leader Nicolás Maduro, according to Time magazine.

Then came their explosive falling out, with Musk tweeting on his own X platform: “Time to drop the really big bomb: [Trump] is in the Epstein files. That is the real reason they have not been made public.” It turned out both men were in the files.

Vance reportedly brokered a truce between the two titanic egos. The bromance has never been fully rekindled, but Thursday was proof that power and wealth can’t live without each other – especially with elections less than a month away and Trump’s approval rating in the doldrums.

When the ceremony was over, however, it was AI king Huang who remained on stage alongside Trump as the familiar strains of the Village People’s YMCA blasted from loudspeakers (“Young man, when you’re short on your dough,” did not resonate with this crowd). The pair were pointing and directing people, presumably for a photo op, and looking pleased with themselves. It was a fitting closing image of two men who rule the world and may yet find a artificial super intelligent way to destroy it.

items.title: Backlash as American tech giants look to build data centers in Australia
paragraphs: Facing legal challenges and public backlash at home, American tech giants are looking abroad for new opportunities in Australia. But the reception down under may not be quite as warm as they hope.

items.title: Oscar-winning Russian filmmaker says parents quietly support his work
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Russian article.

Pavel Talankin, the Russian documentary filmmaker and the creator of the Oscar-winning film “Mr. Nobody vs. Putin” told VOA’s Russian Service that parents and teachers have privately thanked him for exposing how the Kremlin brings propaganda into classrooms.

The film, which won the 2026 Academy Award for Best Documentary Feature, shows a cameraman working at school in Karabash, a small Russian town, tasked with capturing school life. In the process, Talankin manages to document how Russia is using schools and teachers to spread its patriotic propaganda following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Talankin said when he started working with David Borenstein, the American filmmaker and co-director of “Mr. Nobody vs. Putin,” he did not expect the scale of the response to it.

“I suspected that the material wouldn't leave people indifferent. I guessed there would be differing viewpoints on it. And that’s exactly what happened. But the Oscar - no, of course; I never imagined that. And to be honest, when I was filming these lessons, for some reason I even forgot that such an award existed.”

He decided to start filming because he realized the uniqueness of the material – the footage from inside the school. Before this, according to Talankin, there had been many interviews with teachers who refused to be part of the propaganda and quit their jobs.

His project was different: “Here, the camera captures the very things they were talking about: ‘Conversations about What Matters,’ the grenade - throwing drills, the assembling and disassembling of Kalashnikov rifles, and so on,” he said. “So, my initial goal was to preserve as much of it as possible, to film as much as I could and save it all. Because documenting this is important.”
Following the release of the documentary, Russian authorities pretended to know nothing about it.
But Talankin says the FSB paid a visit to the school.

“After the premiere at the Sundance Film Festival, they gathered the principals of all educational institutions and said, ‘Remember this yourselves and pass it on to your colleagues: this person never existed and doesn't exist now. The film never existed and doesn't exist now,’” he said.
And right up until the Oscars, the federal media pretended the film didn't exist,” Talankin said.
His colleagues and parents of schoolchildren still found a way to reach him indirectly.

"We knew that the 'Conversations about What Matters' sessions had started... But we had absolutely no idea what the actual content of those lessons was. Thank you so much for shedding light on this," one parent told him, according to Talankin.
Talankin said another parent disclosed that he planned to use the film to talk to his children about propaganda in schools.
“I couldn't think of a better approach than simply putting on your film for them to watch,” the parent told him.
His former colleagues also found a way to reach out and congratulate him indirectly.
As part of ongoing persecution of opponents, the Russian government declares as a “foreign agent” any person that they believe to be receiving support from a foreign person or organization.

In Talankin’s case, he was issued two administrative citations: one is for failing to submit a report to the Ministry of Justice regarding the activities of a so-called "foreign agent." The second is for cooperating with “an undesirable organization.”
Talankin says he has no interest in following up with the Russian government about the citations.

“To be honest, I don’t understand exactly which undesirable organization they are talking about, because I haven’t read the official order. As for the reports - I haven’t filed them, and I don’t intend to. Nothing will change. I have never accepted this "foreign agent" status,” says Talankin.
Following the Oscars, Talankin started receiving multiple offers to participate in or collaborate on various projects.
“We travel with the films, screening them and holding Q&A sessions and interviews,” he said.

items.title: Margaret Hamilton, whose software sent humans to the moon, dies at 90
paragraphs: Margaret Hamilton sits in mock-up of Apollo the command module on display at MIT in 1969. File/AP hide caption
Margaret Hamilton, the computing pioneer whose software put the first NASA astronauts on the moon, has died at age 90.
Hamilton's death — of unspecified causes, on Sept. 30 — was announced Wednesday by the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, where she worked from 1959 until the mid-1970s.

"To say Margaret Hamilton was a pioneer — to say she was ahead of her time — would be a dramatic understatement," said Olivier de Weck, interim head of the MIT Department of Aeronautics and Astronautics, in a statement. "She not only developed advanced code herself but also led a team in using that nascent technology to develop one of the most complex systems humanity had ever achieved."

Hamilton, who grew up in Indiana, earned a BA in mathematics with a minor in philosophy from Earlham College in 1958. She moved to Boston the following year — so her husband could pursue his law degree — and took a job in the meteorology department at MIT, working with the professor who discovered chaos theory.

It was her first foray into software engineering. Hamilton then got a programming job in another lab, working on the Semi-Automatic Ground Environment (SAGE) project, the United States' first air defense system.

"She had so much foresight in thinking through the ways that humans would use computers, and to create reliable systems that could be used even in the highest-risk, life and death kind of environments," said Teasel Muir-Harmony, curator of the Apollo Collection at the Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum.

In 1961, MIT's Instrumentation Lab won the NASA contract to develop software for the Apollo project. Hamilton saw a newspaper advertisement seeking people to develop the software to "send man to the moon," and applied. She was the first female programmer hired for the Apollo missions, starting with uncrewed flights and moving to onboard software.

By 1968, she had worked her way up to assistant director in charge of the Command and Service Module team, leading a crew of over 100 engineers. Hamilton was in her early 30s, as were many of her colleagues in the nascent field of software engineering — a term she herself is credited with coining.
Margaret Hamilton founded two software companies after leaving MIT. She's seen here in her Cambridge, Mass., home and office, in 1986. Carol Francavilla/AP hide caption

"In this period where she was working, this is a brand new field, and she really helped to define it," Muir-Harmony said. "Margaret Hamilton, like many of the people who worked on the Apollo program, helped really develop computing as we know it today."
Hamilton made an impression with her problem-solving and leadership skills. She often brought her daughter, Lauren, then 4, to the lab — resulting in an infamous "Lauren error."

"Her daughter overloaded a system during some kind of a test. And she thought, 'Oh my gosh, this is something that could actually happen in outer space. So I better account for this,'" said Dean Robbins, an author who published a book about Hamilton in 2017. "So her daughter actually played a part in her technical achievements."
Hamilton was known for her focus on "defensive" programming, building software that could anticipate and solve errors on its own.
"Her goal wasn't simply to build a system that worked when everything went right," Muir-Harmony said. "It was to build a system that could continue working when things went wrong."

Perhaps the most famous example of that is the Apollo 11 mission in 1969. Just three minutes before the first humans were supposed to touch down on the moon, alarms went off on board, signifying computer overload. Fortunately, Hamilton's team had built a system that could shut down unnecessary background tasks at that moment.

"Mission Control was able to recognize what was happening, able to trust the computer … to prioritize tasks, to know that the astronauts could continue … with the first lunar landing," Muir-Harmony said.

After leaving MIT, Hamilton founded two software engineering companies. She received the Presidential Medal of Freedom from Barack Obama in 2016, and the following year was immortalized in miniature as part of a "women of NASA" Lego set.

Hamilton is also the subject of a black-and-white photo from 1969 that often makes the rounds on social media, showing a young woman with long hair and glasses, smiling as she stands beside a towering stack of notebooks — filled with the code that sent humans to the moon.
President Barack Obama presents the Presidential Medal of Freedom to mathematician and computer scientist Margaret Hamilton in November 2016. Andrew Harnik/AP hide caption

But despite public recognition in her later years, Robbins said Hamilton was "not one to toot her own horn." In fact, she initially shied away from the idea of a biography and only agreed because she thought it would be fun to read with her great-grandchildren. (She is survived by four great-grandchildren, two grandsons, her daughter and son-in-law and three siblings.)

"She really warmed up to explaining what she had done, developing the software," he recalled. "She got very excited about telling me all about the technical aspects of developing this. And she was sending me photos and actual code that she had written, and pictures of the primitive machinery that they'd had to use back in the 1960s."

The entire process was painstaking. Muir-Harmony explained that programs were stored on the Apollo guidance computer by hand-weaving copper wire through magnetized cores ("which basically looked like little donuts"). As the overseer of that process, Hamilton earned the nickname "rope mother" in the lab.
Robbins struggled to simplify all of that for his grade-school audience, until he realized: Hamilton's story was all about problem-solving. And she broke barriers for women in the process.

"There was no playbook for how to use computers to get astronauts to the moon," he said. "She had to come up with it on the fly and under tremendous pressure. And I think she was proud of that in her own modest way."
Hamilton told MIT News in 2009 that from her perspective, the software experience was "at least as exciting as the events surrounding the mission."
"Looking back, we were the luckiest people in the world," she said. "There was no choice but to be pioneers."

items.title: White House blocks Microsoft from foreign worker hiring program
paragraphs: Microsoft and several other technology firms have been barred by the White House from hiring skilled international workers on a permanent basis through a widely used visa program.

Vice President JD Vance on Thursday accused Microsoft alongside other firms of committing fraud through the use of the H1b visa programme and a related process for workers from abroad to become permanent US residents.
Vance claimed that Microsoft, one of the most valuable companies in the US, has been effectively replacing American workers with "foreign indentured servants."
Microsoft said most of the H1b visas filed over the last financial year were for existing workers, who are paid the same as local staff.
"No company in the US has abused this system more than Microsoft," Vance said.
He also made similar accusations about Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL and Capgemini.

The US government will not process any new or pending Permanent Labor Certification Program (PERM) applications from Microsoft or the seven other companies, Secretary of Labor Keith Sonderling said during the same conference.
Sonderling said companies like Microsoft, as well as US universities, have turned into "visa mills" that were "flooding" the US with foreign workers.
The BBC has contacted all of the companies for comment.
The total number of H1b visas, a precursor to anyone seeking to go through the PERM process, is capped, external at 85,000 per year.
A spokeswoman for Microsoft noted to the BBC that "the vast majority of Microsoft employees in the United States are Americans." The company employs more than 200,000 people worldwide.

Vance put forward on Thursday that Microsoft had laid off about 6,000 workers and filed 6,800 H1b visa applications over the same period of time. He claimed this was evidence of the company using foreign workers to replace domestic workers and "undercut" their wages.
The Microsoft spokeswoman said that 80% of the H1b visa filings the company has submitted over the last fiscal year were related to employees already working at Microsoft, not new hires.
She added that the international workers that Microsoft does hire through the H1b visa program are paid the same level of compensation that a worker from the US would receive.
According to Ellis, a company which aids many tech companies with the process of hiring skilled workers from abroad, the median salary, external for an H1b worker at Microsoft is $155,000.
"We look forward to providing the Administration with additional information," the Microsoft spokeswoman said.
Satya Nadella, Microsoft's long-time chief executive, was at the White House on Thursday to receive a novel medal for technology innovation from President Donald Trump.
Introducing Nadella during the event, Trump said the White House was "honoured" to be awarding the medal to him and that it was "so well-deserved".
Other tech industry figures to receive medals from Trump were Elon Musk, Jensen Huang, Lisa Su, Sergey Brin, and Michael Dell.
Nadella and most of the other medal recipients were also present at other recent White House events, including a lunch on artificial intelligence and a state dinner for China's President Xi Jinping.
Yet, Microsoft was the focus of Vance's criticism on Thursday.

"Our message to Microsoft is quite simple: You're a great American company, you've got to hire great American workers. You cannot lay off American workers and then replace them with foreign indentured servants," Vance said.

He explained that his reference to workers from abroad in such a way was due to the fact that, should they be fired or laid off from the company that sponsored their visa, they "have to leave" the US.
Typically, such a worker has a 60-day grace period in that circumstance. Last month, the US government proposed eliminating, external that grace period altogether.
Every major tech firm in the US hires international workers through the H1b visa program, and has done so for many years, including Amazon, Google, Meta, Apple, Nvidia, and more.
None of those companies were included in Vance's Thursday comments.
The program has been aimed at highly skilled or specialized workers that a company needs, but is unable to find or hire domestically, for decades.
The PERM program is a pathway for such workers to become permanent US residents, often leading to a Green Card that would allow them to remain and work in the US indefinitely.
During the last fiscal year, the US Department of Labor certified, external more than 130,000 PERM applications accross ten business categories.

items.title: Chinese military facility in Laos raises questions about Beijing’s Indo-Pacific reach
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Mandarin article.

New satellite imagery shows Chinese-made light attack aircraft and military vehicles deployed at a newly opened Chinese-supported air facility in Laos, fueling debate among security analysts over whether the site could eventually expand Beijing’s military reach and intelligence-gathering capabilities in mainland Southeast Asia.

The Ban Keun Airport, about 50 kilometers northwest of the Lao capital Vientiane, was officially inaugurated by China and Laos as the “China-Laos Ban Keun Airport Joint Support and Training Center” and the China-Laos Friendship Aviation Academy.

Satellite imagery taken September 30 showed eight aircraft and more than 20 military vehicles at the site, according to a Reuters report. Analysts identified the aircraft as Chinese-made Hongdu JL-8 jet trainers, also known as K-8 light attack aircraft.

The facility currently has a roughly 2,000-meter paved runway, alongside aircraft parking areas, a control tower and newly constructed buildings. China’s Defense Ministry says the center is intended to help Laos strengthen the training of air force pilots and is “not directed against any third party.”
Some analysts say its longer-term significance, however, could go beyond pilot training.

Su Tzu-yun, director of the Division of Defense Strategy and Resources at Taiwan’s Institute for National Defense and Security Research, told VOA that if the runway is eventually extended to about 3,000 meters, it could accommodate larger Chinese bombers, transport aircraft and aerial refueling planes.
Deployment of longer-range combat aircraft theoretically could extend Chinese air power toward the Strait of Malacca and, with aerial refueling, farther into the Indian Ocean, he said.

Su said the location has limitations because landlocked Laos is surrounded by countries whose airspace could constrain Chinese operations. He sees Ban Keun as part of a broader effort by Beijing, though, to develop strategic access across mainland Southeast Asia.

“This is one of the main reasons China promoted the Belt and Road Initiative after Xi Jinping took office,” Su told VOA. “Through economic incentives, it invests in ports and airports in other developing countries, but behind that are strategic and military purposes.”

China has invested heavily in regional infrastructure, including the China-Laos railway, while expanding its military presence elsewhere, most notably at its base in Djibouti and through its involvement at Cambodia’s Ream Naval Base.

Su said the combination of transportation infrastructure, ports and potential military access could give China alternative routes connecting the Pacific and Indian oceans and reduce its vulnerability if maritime supply lines through the Strait of Malacca were disrupted.
But other analysts caution against overstating Ban Keun’s immediate military importance.

Collin Koh, a maritime security specialist at the S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies in Singapore, told VOA by email that Ban Keun currently has “more political-symbolic significance than actual operational significance.”
Nonetheless, he said the facility could support China’s growing defense diplomacy in Southeast Asia, including serving as a logistical stop during joint military exercises.

It also may have value for intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance, Koh said. “Ban Keun could also serve as a base for intelligence and surveillance missions, mainly monitoring Thailand’s Isaan region,” he said. “Various multinational military exercises are routinely held in this area, such as Cope Tiger involving Thailand, the United States and Singapore.”

Koh said China’s relationship with neighboring Myanmar does not necessarily mean Beijing will gain military access there. Myanmar is seeking to rebuild relations with other regional countries, he said, including India, which is particularly sensitive to potential Chinese military expansion toward the Indian Ocean.
Additionally, the emerging Chinese presence in Laos is drawing attention because of its proximity to Vietnam.

Alexander Vuving, a Vietnam specialist at the Daniel K. Inouye Asia-Pacific Center for Security Studies in Hawaii, was cited by Taiwan’s Central News Agency as saying Chinese access at Ban Keun, combined with its presence at Cambodia’s Ream Naval Base, could increase strategic pressure on Vietnam from its west and southwest.
Chinese military commentator Song Zhongping rejected suggestions that Beijing is establishing a network of bases aimed at neighboring countries.

He told VOA that China’s activities at Ban Keun and Ream should not be characterized as traditional military bases and stated that the limited deployments are designed to protect Chinese interests and support missions, such as counterterrorism, anti-piracy, and humanitarian assistance.

“China now has three aircraft carrier battle groups, and we already possess a basic capability to project military power overseas,” Song said. “We do not necessarily need to establish so-called military bases in other countries.”

For now, analysts interviewed by VOA generally agree the facility is unlikely to significantly alter the regional military balance, though its development is being closely watched as China expands its economic, diplomatic and security footprint across Southeast Asia.

items.title: Katie Price 'angry' when told of ex's rape claim
paragraphs: The mother of a teenage girl allegedly raped by Katie Price's then-husband said she felt the former glamour model was "angry" about the allegation and "didn't care" about her daughter, a court has heard.

Price's ex-husband Kieran Hayler is on trial at Lewes Crown Court accused of three counts of rape and one of sexual assault against the then 13-year-old girl in West Sussex in 2016, all of which he denies.

Giving evidence in court on Thursday, the complainant's mother said when she told Price about the allegations, "she was quite angry and I didn't feel she was particularly upset for [the complainant]".
She added: "I didn't feel she cared about my daughter."
The court heard the teenager told her mother a year after the alleged rapes that Hayler had "done everything to her" to which she was "shocked".
The jury was told she tried to ask her daughter to explain but she said: "I can't tell you any more."
Asked if she questioned her further, she replied: "I didn't because she was so distressed."
The mother told the court she told Price about the allegations because she felt like she "had to".
Asked how Price reacted, she said: "She was shocked and probably swore.
"I feel she was just angry and feeling revengeful towards Kieran."
But the alleged victim's mother said her daughter did not "want anyone to know" and they had to "respect her wishes".
In court she said she and her daughter had fallen out after she told Price.
Asked if this was because she felt she betrayed her trust, the mother replied: "Yes, she probably didn't want anyone to ever know and yes it did cause arguments."
The mother said she noticed changes in her daughter's behaviour including her becoming more "withdrawn".
"My main concern was her washing, she would shower about four times a day and scrub her skin and it really worried me," she said.
She told the court she asked her daughter why she was washing so often to which she replied: "I just feel dirty all the time."
The complainant contacted the NSPCC in 2021 about the allegations which referred her to the police, prompting the investigation.
Her mother told the court about the day her daughter informed her she had reported it to the police, adding: "She still hadn't told me exactly what had happened."
The court heard after it was reported the two discussed the matter.
The mum said: "She said it made her feel sick and dirty thinking about it whenever she thought about what had happened.
"At the time she thought it was normal but looking back on it she realised it wasn't because of her age and then she just felt dirty."
Hayler has suggested his ex-wife had "launched a campaign" against him when their marriage ended, and the allegations formed part of this, the court heard.
He was married to Price at the time of the allegations, before the couple's relationship broke down in 2018 and they divorced in 2021.
The alleged victim is not part of Hayler or Price's extended families.

items.title: Scientists discover 180,000 giant tortoises on one Seychelles island
paragraphs: A survey of the world’s largest free-roaming giant tortoise population has discovered that the once endangered species is thriving.
A population of Aldabra giant tortoises lives on an island in Seychelles called Aldabra Atoll.

The most recent survey, led by Seychelles Islands Foundation (SIF) and the University of Exeter, revealed there were approximately 180,000 tortoises living on the island. This is the highest figure ever recorded for the species and far exceeds the human population of Seychelles.
The new figure was obtained by a team who analysed five years of tortoise counts between 2018 and 2022. It is the first update since a widely cited figure of 100,000 tortoises from the late 1990s.
Aldabra Atoll is one of only two places in the world where giant tortoises are found in the wild, with a much smaller population living in the Galápagos.

Dr Frauke Fleischer-Dogley, the CEO of SIF, said: “More than 180,000 giant tortoises roaming freely on our atoll is proof of what long-term commitment to conservation can achieve. This is wonderful news for Seychelles, for the world, and for everyone who has worked to protect Aldabra.”

The study, published in the scientific journal Ecology and Evolution, found that the population was relatively stable for this period, with a best estimate of almost 183,000 adult and sub-adult tortoises.

In the 19th century, exploitation of the animals meant there were fewer than 1,000 Aldabra tortoises left on the island, but a recovery programme led to it becoming a strict nature reserve in 1981 and a Unesco site in 1982.

Researchers are now saying it is one of the greatest conservation success stories of the Indian Ocean, with the new study confirming it. “Aldabra’s giant tortoise monitoring programme is one of the longest running in the region, but the atoll’s dense vegetation makes counting tortoises genuinely difficult in places,” said Dr Nancy Bunbury, one of the study’s co-authors.

“By modelling what we didn’t see, as well as what we did, we’ve produced the most reliable baseline yet for this iconic Seychelles species, establishing a benchmark we can use to track the population for decades to come.”

Despite the good news, the study’s authors say that vigilance is essential. Aldabra’s climate is changing, with longer and more frequent droughts predicted to reduce the shade and food available to tortoises, while rising sea levels threaten low-lying parts of the atoll.

The study authors say invasive mammals remain a threat including feral cats and black rats that prey on tortoise eggs and hatchlings. The planned eradication of these remaining invasive mammals, the authors say, could lift the last barriers to further growth of the population and help it withstand future climate pressures.

“These results are great news for the tortoises and testament to the fantastic work done in the field,” said Dr Dave Hudson, a postdoctoral research associate at the University of Exeter’s Cornwall campus.
“But it’s important to remember that the numbers provide a baseline – not an endpoint.

“Hopefully we have provided the conservation managers the evidence they need to track future change and act early as the tortoises face increasing pressures from climate change, drought and invasive species.”

items.title: South Korea recalls its ambassador to Ukraine over North Korea
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Ukrainian article.

South Korea said on Thursday it was recalling its ambassador to Ukraine following a dispute over the transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war which Seoul says violated a confidentiality agreement reached with Kyiv.

Foreign Minister Cho Hyun during testimony before the parliament on Thursday said that Ukraine has apologized for disclosing information about the transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war to Seoul, but insisted the gesture did not meet the appropriate level.
He said the apology was expressed in a communication from Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha.
"Messages that I received (from Sybiha) included an apology. But there is a difference from the level we expect, so we intend to take firm measures," he said.

The diplomatic tension between the two countries emerged after Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy disclosed the transfer of the two North Korean prisoners to South Korea during his address to the U.N. General Assembly on September 23.

Ukrainian Armed Forces captured the two North Korean soldiers during an operation in Russia’s Kursk region in January 2025, the first North Korean troops to be captured alive. North Korea has sent an estimated 14,000 troops, millions of artillery shells and other armaments, aiding Russia in its war against Ukraine.

Seoul said the two sides had agreed to keep the matter confidential because of security and humanitarian concerns, including fears for the safety of the prisoners’ families in North Korea, and called for Ukrainian authorities to apologize. Kyiv has denied that there was a clear agreement to this effect.

During a briefing at Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry in Kyiv on October 7, Foreign Ministry spokesman Heorhii Tykhyi said that in his communication with Cho Hyun, Sybiha expressed regret that the situation had reached the stage of an exchange of critical public comments.

“I think you can see the difference between what the Korean side said and what was actually said,” Tykhyi said, adding that Ukrainian officials attribute the exchange of critical statements to a “difference in the interpretation of agreements concerning confidentiality arrangements.”
Tykhyi told the press that diplomatic efforts were underway to resolve the issue.

In addition to the dispute over the transfer of North Korean prisoners, bilateral relations between Seoul and Kyiv have also been strained by the alleged shipment of fuel supplies from South Korea to Russia.

The British newspaper The Guardian published the results of an investigation which found that 176,000 tons of fuel were shipped from South Korean ports to Russia in July and August this year, with some of the cargo transported allegedly by tankers under the European and British sanctions. Ukraine’s sanctions commissioner Vladyslav Vlasiuk said on October 6 that the supplies helped ease Russia’s fuel crisis.

The South Korean presidential office rejected Vlasiuk’s statement on October 7, calling it “inappropriate.” Responding to The Guardian report, South Korea’s Foreign Ministry said the government strictly complies with export controls on Russia and “supports and actively participates in global efforts to end the war in Ukraine and achieve peaceful recovery".

The Pentagon in 2024 warned that if North Korean troops enter the conflict, they could become legitimate targets for the Ukrainian soldiers. Also, the transport of South Korea fuel by sanctioned tankers could be a concern at a time when the alliance between Russia and North Korea deepens, as well as their growing ties with Iran and China.

U.S. experts expressed hope that the diplomatic tensions between South Korea and Ukraine would not harm bilateral cooperation as well as the broader trilateral cooperation between South Korea, Ukraine and the United States.

Since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion, South Korea has provided Ukraine with more than $730 million in non-military assistance, according to the Kiel Institute tracker. At the latest NATO summit in July, the South Korean government pledged an additional $100 million in aid.
Ukraine, for its part, is a valuable source of information for Seoul about North Korea’s military capabilities and tactics, as well as other characteristics of modern warfare.

“All three countries [Ukraine, South Korea and U.S.] have a major stake in understanding what the North Koreans are up to, what the Russians are up to, where this ongoing cooperation, which has been very significant, is going in the future,” says Evans Revere, a former principal deputy assistant secretary for East Asian and Pacific Affairs at the State Department.
“It has obvious frontline implications for Ukraine and its own security and safety.”

Sydney Seiler, Senior Adviser at the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) emphasized that Korea should continue providing non-lethal assistance to Ukraine because the reasons behind that decision have not disappeared.

“It would be unfortunate if somehow in some punitive type of way, aid and assistance were curtailed,” says Seiler, a former national intelligence officer. “This is so crucial when you consider the current situation on the ground, the hardships the Ukrainian people, Ukrainian military are undergoing because of this protracted war.”
Eunjung Cho, VOA Korean, contributed to this report.

items.title: Microsoft suspended from applying for green cards for H-1B workers, JD Vance says
paragraphs: Microsoft is suspended from applying for permanent residency for workers employed through a US visa program for high-skilled workers, JD Vance announced on Thursday.
The US vice-president accused the tech company of abusing the H-1B system, which allows those on the visa to work while they apply for and are in the process of obtaining a green card.

“Our message to Microsoft is, you’re a great American company, but you’ve got to hire great American workers,” Vance said at a press conference announcing the suspension. “You cannot lay off American workers and then replace them with foreign indentured servants.”

Microsoft said the vast majority of its workers were American and 80% of the H-1B applications it filed in the last year were for extensions or status changes for people who already worked for the company.

“Microsoft only files H-1B petitions for those who meet the rigorous standards of this visa category,” the company wrote in a statement. “We pay our employees some of the highest compensation in the tech sector, and our wages are among the highest of all H-1B filings. We pay our H-1B employees the same as any other employees doing comparable work.”
The US labor department also said Adobe had been similarly suspended.
“We will not accept any new or process any pending permanent labor certification applications involving these companies,” said Keith Sonderling, the US labor secretary, in a statement.

Microsoft applied for H-1B visas for nearly 3,700 workers in 2026, making it the fifth largest employer of workers on the visa. Tech companies are the biggest employers of H-1B workers across the industry. Amazon topped the list with more than 9,300 petitions this year. Sonderling said since 2009, Microsoft and Adobe had received about 230,000 approvals for H-1B visas and 100,000 “permanent labor certifications”, a step towards an employment-based green card.
“If you do the math, for every worker that Microsoft laid off, they replaced that worker with one and a half foreign indentured servants,” Vance said.

The Trump administration has set its sights on the H-1B program for some time, arguing that it is rife with abuse. Vance said that, on average, workers hired through the H-1B program were making $20,000 less than US workers in the same position.

“So I’m sure that everybody here understands the game that is being played,” Vance said. “You bring in indentured servants from outside the country, you lay off American workers and, if you’re a corporation, you make a ton of money by undercutting the wages of American workers, replacing them with people who, frankly, shouldn’t be in the United States of America to begin with.”

Immigration advocacy groups have long called for reforms for the H-1B program, though for different reasons. Those in the program are often beholden to their employer because their visas are tied to the company that applied for them, making it difficult to switch jobs if things aren’t going well or if they want to find a job with a higher salary.
These groups, like the National Immigration Forum, largely disagree with Vance. They argue that competing for specialized talent from around the world benefits the US economy.

“The United States has long benefited from its ability to attract talent from around the world, particularly in STEM, higher education, research, and innovation,” the National Immigration Forum wrote in a September 2026 blogpost discussing proposed changes to the H-1B program. “As countries increasingly compete for highly skilled workers, policies that make the United States less attractive could strengthen global competitors.”
