items.title: Black and African cinema hub opens in London
paragraphs: EbonyLife Place aims to platform black and African cinema
A new black and African cinema and hub has officially opened in south-west London.
EbonyLife Place, based near Nine Elms, was unveiled with a ceremony attended by the Mayor of London Lord Khan, and its founder Mo Abudu.
Abudu, a Nigerian media mogul who was born in London, explained that the project was born from a desire to showcase and celebrate stories that she felt previously lacked a home.
"I do think there is a younger audience of young people now that just want to see great storytelling," Abudu said.
She added: "We make great films, and I think we need to create experiences where people can come and they can see the great work that we do in black cinema, in African cinema.
"We don't have enough spaces to serve black cinema in the United Kingdom... representation is so important to us."
The 160-seat auditorium will have a full programme of black and African cinema
At the heart of the cultural centre is a 160-seat auditorium featuring a year-round film programme.
The screenings will primarily focus on Nollywood cinema from Nigeria alongside other movies connecting to the black experience.
In addition to film screenings, the venue will host masterclasses, industry panels, and live performances by established and emerging talent.

Beyond its cinema space, the multi-storey venue features a bar, a lounge called "Fàhinti" (a Yoruba word meaning to lean back and rest), a Nigerian restaurant, a boutique showcasing African and diaspora designers, and walls lined with African diaspora artwork.
Mo Abudu founded a media empire based in Nigeria and which is popular across Africa
The project, financed almost entirely by Abudu's media group, mirrors the upscale lifestyle complex she launched in Nigeria's biggest city, Lagos, in 2019.

Speaking at Thursday's launch, Lord Khan said: "London is the number one place in Europe to film," adding that the capital sits just behind Los Angeles and ahead of New York in the global film production footprint.
"As long as I'm mayor, we'll invest in culture," he said.
The opening coincides with the London Film Festival.

items.title: KeyShot 2026 review: fast, easy 3D rendering and with AI tools you might actually use
paragraphs: KeyShot 2026 represents another significant milestone of development for the popular product visualisation tool. They continue to embrace AI to improve rendered output and simplify workflows. This doesn't take away from the user's ability to harness their creativity to produce some truly impressive rendered results. The software is easier to use than ever, and it's faster too.
Why you can trust Creative Bloq Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

Having used the best rendering software for over two decades, one of my favourites is KeyShot Studio. Despite not being my go-to choice for rendering most architectural scenes, if I'm ever rendering smaller scenes or individual products, then I know there's hardly anything better on the market.

Now at version 2026, KeyShot is stronger than ever with a slew of new features to improve the user experience and elevate its capabilities. These include more realistic AI output through AI Shots with the ability to now edit and upscale, an upgraded Move Tool + Custom Pivot, and an all-new gallery feature.

It wouldn't be a software upgrade without some mention of AI, would it? In fact, KeyShot has been using AI for many years, specifically to deliver progressive denoising. But as for AI features, the primary one is AI Shots, which was introduced partway through the 2025 software cycle. KeyShot has determined this is the way to go, devoting a significant amount of development time to improving it.

If you're looking for help on where to start, then you could follow my KeyShot and Photoshop advice for perfect renders every time as well as find out how to create cinematic cameras in KeyShot. To complement KeyShot, you will also need one of the best 3D software packages.
• KeyShot Professional for $108.25 per month (billed annually)⁣ • KeyShot Business provides seat management features

Most Creative Bloq readers will need a KeyShot Professional subscription. This provides the complete 3D visualisation toolkit for individual designers, freelancers, and small studios. This costs $108.25 per month, although it's billed annually at $1,299.

If you do happen to be a larger team requiring centralised seat management, then you'll have to upgrade to KeyShot Business. For the privilege, this costs $133.25 per month, which equates to $1,599 billed annually.
• AI Shots brings generative AI into the heart of the rendering workflow• A new Gallery window makes it easier to find and organise renderings

The single biggest feature improvement in 2026 is AI Shots. This is KeyShot's generative AI workflow, and it was introduced in KeyShot 2025.2. With it you can either generate images from a CAD model or edit an existing image. Either way, it means artists can utilise generative AI in a dedicated 3D rendering tool rather than relying on alternative tools that were not designed with 3D in mind.

The AI Shots tool is particularly useful for artists wanting to create multiple images with small variations. They can do that easily using the generate multiple images feature when entering the prompt. KeyShot has also improved the overall AI model so it now works with much shorter prompts compared to version 2025.

One of the best improvements of AI Shots is the upscaling feature that enables artists to double or quadruple the resolution of both traditional 3D renderings and AI Shots in a "fraction of the time". This proves more effective than generating an AI shot at a lower resolution and then upscaling.

Beyond AI shots, KeyShot includes a more powerful Custom Pivot + Move Tool. With it users can "give parts or groups multiple custom pivots in addition to origin and centre. These custom pivots can be named for organisational purposes and are stored in your scene."

The move tool gizmo has now also been synchronised between realtime and geometry views, which makes it much more straight forward to work in both views at the same time. It was previously a little confusing, and even though this is only a user experience improvement, it's still a meaningful one.

The final feature to mention is called Gallery, and I love it. It's a new window, and it lets you quickly and easily find your render output once your renderings are complete. It's much more than just a viewer, though. With it you can search, sort, and organise all your rendered output.
• Creating product visualisations in KeyShot is an absolute breeze• The new AI shots feature provides a generative tool for customising the results

KeyShot is a wonderful piece of visualisation software that takes hardly any time at all to get your head around. Materials, lighting, camera, and environment tools are clearly laid out and easily accessible through various panels and menus. I had no issues finding settings quickly, and with results instantly displayed in the real-time view, it's easy to tweak settings until you get a result you're happy with.

I love how easy it is to cycle through lighting setups and see immediately whether your model catches the reflections nicely or not. With plenty of lighting and material options in the local and cloud libraries artists can quickly translate their 3D model into a beautiful photorealistic visual. Beyond setting up the scene it's also effortless to add post-effects including denoising, sharpening, and bloom, amongst many others.

AI Shots offers a basic interface for adjusting your output using a short prompt. Before doing so, though, you'll have to download near 20GB of AI data, so make sure you've got the necessary storage space before deciding whether KeyShot along with its AI tool is the right visualisation product for you.

I tested AI Shots on my MacBook Pro with 16GB RAM. This is less than the recommended 32GB RAM, but with RAM prices showing no signs of slowing down, I think my laptop is a fair representation of what a lot of users will have access to.

During my tests I found that all elements of the tool, including image generation, upscaling, and element replacement, worked without a hitch. It never crashed, and the progress bar kept moving in the right direction. My only issue with it is that it is quite slow, with some prompts taking upwards of five minutes to process. I found it to be a helpful tool, but it was subject to misinterpreting some of my prompts and couldn't therefore be relied upon for perfect recreation of prompts.
• KeyShot is designed almost exclusively for product visualisation

KeyShot was built with product visualisation in mind. It offers a simple workflow for 3D artists who regularly find themselves visualising products or product designers who want an in-house solution for creating their own images. KeyShot will work for other types of scenes, but if you're working in film, games, or architecture, then you'll need a dedicated rendering engine such as V-Ray or Cycles (Blender).
A significant outlay for freelancers and small scale product designers.
Significant improvements with every release, including more realistic AI output in version 2026.
Simple and straight forward to use, although you'll feel it creak if you push it beyond product visualisation.

Paul is a digital expert. In the 20 years since he graduated with a first-class honours degree in Computer Science, Paul has been actively involved in a variety of different tech and creative industries that make him the go-to guy for reviews, opinion pieces, and featured articles. With a particular love of all things visual, including photography, videography, and 3D visualisation Paul is never far from a camera or other piece of tech that gets his creative juices going. You'll also find his writing in other places, including Creative Bloq, Digital Camera World, and 3D World Magazine.

items.title: Someone just rebuilt Adobe Creative Cloud with AI – then gave it away for free
paragraphs: The world of Photoshop alternatives has become a lot more interesting in the last few years, and not just because of the plethora of worthy candidates that have emerged. The likes of Canva and Affinity continue to give Adobe a run for its money, but Adobe itself has also pushed some users away, thanks to its AI terms and cancellation policies.

And it's the latter that apparently inspired a solo developer to recreate several of Adobe's most popular tools, including Photoshop, Premiere and Illustrator. These were rebuilt using Claude and Rust.
Writing on Hacker News, software developer Brandon Thomas said he was inspired to create the clones after he "got bit by the dark pattern "cancellation fee" one too many times."

"I'm not just some casual vibe coder. I'm a 15-year industry veteran who has written everything from six-nines payment rails that move billions of dollars of transaction volume a day to advanced robotics and optics automation," Thomas announced on Reddit. "I've used Rust extensively for about a decade, and I know how to build and maintain large-scale Rust projects."
"Software is over," he added in a comment on Hacker News.

Is it? Really? It looks to me like Thomas used software to create a clone of some software. And while copying Adobe might sound exciting in a stick-it-to-the-man sort of way, I'm not sure it's a positive omen for the future of software or creativity. Is using AI to create a carbon copy of something as exciting as, say, creating something new?
And it's hard to imagine professional creatives feeling confident enough to place their files, and their livelihoods, in the hands of AI-generated software.

As one Redditor puts it, "There is a pretty fricking huge difference between an unproven software that vaguely looks like Photoshop and probably can do some of the things that Photoshop can do and a dependable, robust productivity software that you can count on working right and being maintained long-term."

Daniel John is Design Editor at Creative Bloq. He reports on the worlds of design, branding and lifestyle tech, and has covered several industry events including Milan Design Week, OFFF Barcelona and Adobe Max in Los Angeles. He has interviewed leaders and designers at brands including Apple, Microsoft and Adobe. Daniel's debut book of short stories and poems was published in 2018, and his comedy newsletter is a Substack Bestseller.

items.title: Willem de Kooning review – the artist’s lifelong rebellion against himself is thrilling to watch
paragraphs: Willem de Kooning was the last great artist who really knew how to draw. More precisely, if less provocatively, he was the last truly transformative painter to have been schooled in the academic tradition that produces what is still recognised, by most people, as “good drawing”. Accurate in the sense of a photograph but, like a filter on your cameraphone, also subtly tidying up the world to meet the ideals of classical proportion. “Draw what you see and not what you think,” the young De Kooning was told. Raw personal emotion had no place – a far cry from what this master of abstract expressionism was to become.

The intense labour required to build a connection between eye, brain and hand so quick as to be instinctive is illustrated by the charcoal still life Dish With Jugs. Made when De Kooning was in his mid-teens, and so minutely rendered that you might mistake it for a sepia photograph, the catalogue estimates that it took 600 hours at the Rotterdam academy to complete. The aim of this exercise was not to produce a single picture so much as to ingrain a way of seeing and reconstructing the world to the point that it becomes inescapable.

This brilliantly researched exhibition makes a compelling case for the success of that training. Setting a handful of standout paintings among a wider selection of drawings illustrates the artist’s lifelong rebellion against rules so thoroughly internalised that he could push fiercely at their limits without entirely breaking them. The battle is thrilling to watch.

De Kooning’s formative training is apparent in an early drawing of the dancer Juliet Browner and a marvellously deft portrait of the artist’s wife, Elaine. The influence of Ingres – the Pelé of academic drawing – on these works has often been remarked upon, not least by rival New York painters for whom De Kooning’s superior draughtsmanship was a source of suspicion (too prissy, too European). And it seems that the immigrant artist placed himself under pressure to unstitch the aesthetic conventions of the old world and rework them into something more appropriate to the new: irreverent, free, immediate, expressive.

It is important to note that De Kooning’s education was not limited to the academy. A working-class kid, his evening classes had been subsidised by the design firm where he worked in the day; after stowing away to the US at 22, he scraped a living as a sign painter and commercial illustrator. These lessons made their way into his art, and the difficulty of synthesising them might explain the struggles of his early career (he didn’t have a solo show until he was nearly 44) and how revolutionary the breakthrough was when it did arrive.

Central to that achievement was that he made no distinction between drawing and painting (the tradition being, in simple terms, that you draw the outlines and paint the space between them). In Queen of Hearts, a harbinger of women to come, he drags charcoal sticks across wet paint to create soft edges, sanding down and painting over layers like a housepainter. The big bang arrives in the seminal work on paper completed in 1949, an arrangement of white sparks against a black ground that calls to mind comets dancing through the night sky. But De Kooning was no starry-eyed mystic: at the bottom edge, transforming those white sparks into liquid spurts, is a scrawled cock and balls.

Excavation, a knockout masterpiece, likewise appears at first as an abstract pattern of interlocking shapes only to reveal itself as a maelstrom of screaming faces and dismembered body parts. Completed in 1950, it conjures both Europe’s mass graves and an orgiastic ecstasy of bodies dissolving into each other. Sex and death, heaven and hell, the end of the old world and the birth of the new. In one of many intelligent arrangements, Excavation is paired with a drawing from four years earlier, the aptly titled Judgment Day.

It is a quirk of the exhibition that its most famous painting, Woman I, hangs in a separate gallery normally reserved for the museum’s treasures from the Dutch golden age. Not only does this icon hold its own against Vermeer and Rembrandt, but she is also unexpectedly at home. Scandalous when first exhibited, the accusation that this cartoonish, charismatic and wild figure defames all womankind by its “monstrosity” seems now to rely on some mid-century assumptions about how women should be represented. Whatever you think about Woman I, she could never be mistaken for a submissive sex object or a Stepford wife.

De Kooning’s relentless attacks on convention, which is to say on himself and everything else, took their toll. A series of black-and-white works, made in Rome in the late 1950s, mark the end of his imperial phase. While these vaguely calligraphic graphic signs illustrate a point about the convergence of painting and drawing, they feel to me slapdash and derivative of Franz Kline. From here, this exhibition does little to overturn the conventional wisdom that De Kooning struggled over the next two decades to scale the same heights. There are standouts – notably the irrepressible Clam Diggers, a woozy portrait of two women standing in shallow water rendered in ice-cream colours and buttery textures, and a gorgeously fleshy painting from the mid-70s that advertises the painter’s occasionally overlooked gift as a colourist. If the paintings are hit and miss, the drawings from this period reveal that, even hindered by alcoholism and a chaotic personal life, De Kooning could always rely on his line.

That line holds to the end. The show closes with an astonishing painting from 1985, during the period when De Kooning’s cognitive decline was increasingly apparent. Sinuous blue and black lines curve across a mottled white ground, weaving a pattern suggestive of bodies and yet emptied of desire. It is serene, strange and straightforwardly beautiful, as if everything that the artist had struggled to pack into his work had been boiled down to basic principles. He is back to fitting the world to a pleasing form. The difference is that it is no longer a boilerplate inherited from the classical tradition, but shaped by his experiences and entirely his own. He doesn’t need to think about it. The battle is over.

items.title: 'Bold and inventive' Canadian poet Anne Carson wins Nobel Literature Prize
paragraphs: Canadian poet, essayist and translator Anne Carson has been awarded this year's Nobel Prize in Literature.
Carson, 76, is celebrated for works that often cross the boundaries between poetry, fiction and scholarship.
The Nobel Prize committee said they had selected her "for her bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature".

Carson responded by joking that the judges were "crazy" for honouring her. "I think they're all crazy... Well, you know, it's crazy," she told public broadcaster RUV in Iceland, where she is currently staying.
The Nobel Prize is awarded for a lifetime's body of work and is regarded as the most prestigious award in global literature, with the winner receiving 12 million Swedish kronor (£900,000, $1.2m).
Ingrid Carlberg, permanent secretary of the Swedish Academy, said she had broken the news to Carson on the phone shortly before the public announcement.
"She had time to tell me was that she is, for the moment, in Iceland, where she is listening to the wind," Carlberg, said.
"She was taken by surprise but very happy. I could hear that in her voice."

paragraphs: Disney loves animals and wants to help them. They have a big hospital for animals.

Disney gives lots of money to protect animals. They use bees to keep elephants away from farms. They want to help butterflies by planting milkweed in gardens.

items.title: 'My donated Brummie accent gives me confidence'
paragraphs: A man who appealed for help to no longer sound like a "character from Star Wars" says he has found his calling.

Christian Wilson, from Bromsgrove, has verbal dyspraxia - a difficulty in placing muscles in the correct position to produce speech. He uses text-to-speech software in order to communicate, but said he wanted to sound "like a man from Birmingham".

The 24-year-old's dream was made possible in 2024 when he selected two voice donors that blended a Birmingham accent and a Warwickshire accent, which he hoped would help him sound more like his father.
Since May, Wilson has worked at Worcestershire County Council as a SEND Peer Advocate. He said his new dialect had given him "the confidence to voice [his] opinion".
Speaking to BBC Hereford & Worcester on Thursday, he told presenter Tammy Gooding: "There was a moment where I thought, this is really what I'm meant to do.
"I was really excited about it, because as long as I can remember I've always wanted to be an advocate, plus I have always been passionate about education."
He said: "The representatives said they would definitely feed back what I had said. My hopes for the future are that I continue to use my voice as an instrument to do good.
"I hope to continue to advocate for disabled children and young people by sharing my expertise and experience with whoever necessary to improve the lives of others in Worcestershire."
In 2024, he described feeling emotional when he listened through to the voice submissions with his family.
"As I was listening to them, I knew I was getting closer to my dream, something that I thought never would happen," he said.
"I hope to use my new voice to share my experiences with other people - that would be great."
Wilson's sister felt an instant connection to the Birmingham accent he selected for his new voice.
He said: "I liked the voice originally, but when my sister heard it she said 'that is you.'"
Wilson's Birmingham voice donor, Martin Brennan, said: "It's such an emotional journey and even sitting here, I'm welling up now.
"I just thought why not - it was a no brainer and it was a joy to get involved."
Fellow donor, Stephen Robotham, from Warwickshire, said: "Having a voice is so important and especially having your own voice, it's integral to your identity."

items.title: Clive Barker's Hellraiser: Revival review: visually inventive, risky and authentic, but has its limitations
paragraphs: Hellraiser: Revival doesn't reinvent the immersive sim template it borrows, but a visually arresting, Brutalist-inspired Labyrinth, a story that respects Clive Barker, and a gleeful run of one-off ideas make it an authentic, unapologetically extreme horror.
Why you can trust Creative Bloq Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.
Format PS5 (reviewed), Xbox Series X/S, Nintendo Switch 2, PC
Content warning: this article discusses graphic violence, disturbing imagery, and mature themes in an 18+ game.

I expected a game about pleasure and pain to lean towards the pain. Clive Barker's Hellraiser: Revival leans the other way, and not only because it gets under the skin of the themes and imagery of Clive Barker's The Hellbound Heart (and the first two films). It hides those very adult ideas inside something accessible and familiar, a bit BioShock in its core mechanics, and a bit Condemned in its brutal melee combat and love of leather-bound mannequins, so somewhere around the second hour I stopped noticing the dildos (everywhere) and body parts strewn across the scenery and started enjoying how the systems work.

It's a trick, and a clever one. By the time I realised what I'd been wading through, what I'd just seen as our hero's girlfriend was opened up, torn apart and remade vein by muscle in graphic detail, I was already hooked.

Revival's story is original but inspired by Barker's original book. Set 20 years after the first film in the town of Clairport, north of Detroit. Sunny opens the Genesis Configuration, summons the Cenobites and meets her sticky end. To paraphrase Patrick Stewart, her lover Aidan Lynch sees everything, because they were Netflix and chilling at the time. He makes a deal with the Hell Priest (Pinhead, to most of us), enters the Labyrinth to free her soul, and sets about rebuilding her body.

It's a neat and very games-y setup that challenges Aidan to gather the hearts of three people marked by the box: Charlotte Strauss, an ex-dominatrix known as the Sister of Mercy, and Colin Marlowe, leader of the Scarlet Church, a cult of Leviathan worshippers who want to make Cenobites on Earth. It's a love story of obsession and bad bargains, and feels right at home beside Barker's novella.

So yes, it's very Hellraiser: unapologetically sexual, risqué, bloody and grotesque. Machete swings dissect bodies; past torsos lie on tables, hang like ghoulish wall art, and a late-game ability lets you tear enemies apart with Hellchains that hook and lash in from every direction. It's horrific, often inventively so, the kind of spectacle that demands to be seen and then you kind of want to unsee it, and then look again. So, yep, very Clive Barker (the included digital art book reveals how it was made).

The game's 'real' world is bold, garish and caricatured, violent and more than a little perverse, but it never lets me forget I'm playing a video game. Then you step through a teasing, glowing crack in a wall into Leviathan's domain, and Unreal Engine 5 drops the cartoon for stark photorealism. That divergence never stopped jolting me and makes the Cenobites' world so much more terrifying: this is the space that looks real, and the real is the space that feels like a game.

The Labyrinth itself is the kind of pain and pleasure Clive Barker would be proud of: puzzling, disorienting and, when the Chatterer (fans know him as the Child) is on my heels, properly terrifying. I found racing down narrow Brutalist concrete canyons, dodging spinning spiked traps and ducking sprouting chains among the best horror I've played this year. Here Aidan is vulnerable and afraid. These escape-meets-walking-sim sections add texture, make you think, and, when you're being hunted, make you feel something genuine.

Outside and back in the sex club, cult mansion and cemetery, Revival dresses up as a light immersive sim, and combat flows freely. A shotgun blast ignites a barrel, fire leaps from one enemy to the next, another steps on a carefully placed bear trap, and the group is dealt with until only body parts remain. The Genesis Configuration piles on top of that. Banishing an enemy with a finisher sends their soul back to the Labyrinth and earns Suffering, a currency you spend on the box's powers. Telekinesis lets you grab sawblades and steel pins from the environment and hurl them at leather-clad cultists, and pyrokinesis lets you pull fire from lamps and shoot it. A revolver, pistol, SMG, assault rifle and a mix of breakable melee knives and bats fill out the earthly arsenal, with upgrades, plus ammo and health you craft from scavenged junk.

It's solid and often a lot of fun, but it stops well short of reinvention. This isn't BioShock, Dishonored or Prey, and it never pretends to be. The Genesis Configuration, for example, never goes as deep as BioShock's Plasmids, though it could really have been developed further and even layered on obsession and pain debuffs and buffs. But no, it's a two-power cube that can occasionally be manipulated as a puzzle to open narrative-dependent gates.

What saves Hellraiser Revival is its structure. The game weaves in and out of Aiden's real world and the Labyrinth, merging the two elegantly in later stages, and the hunt for the three Marked Ones means lots of exploration, Resident Evil-style puzzling and maps that double back on themselves. They're elegantly rendered too, with ornate but grim paintings, statues and reflective surfaces to dwell upon.

It isn't flawless. Combat is at its best when it stays in immersive-sim mode, because boss fights can drag, and controlling Aidan under pressure can feel stiff and unresponsive. When the game asks for subtlety, it fumbles.

What lifts Hellraiser Revival is its refusal to sit still. A boss is teased in a stealth section that had me scurrying around a collapsing nightclub while the wraithlike Sister of Mercy hunted me, and then it never happened again. One Labyrinth sequence has you pushing and pulling the environment itself to line up stairs and paths. There's an actual cabin in the woods full of zombies – a fraught survival challenge. And a moment where you have to keep columns erect to hide from Leviathan's Gaze, the beam that exposes people to the darkest parts of their own psyche, is perfectly, gloriously Hellraiser and just on-the-nose enough to be appreciated.
These ideas arrive, get used once, and the game moves on, and that generosity is why the Hellraiser Revival never feels like a retread, even when its bones are familiar.

But those bones are familiar. Scrape away the meaty, fleshy shock value and impressively stylised Labyrinth and underneath is a streamlined immersive sim with very little original in what you do, even if what you experience in its world is refreshingly horrific. And what a world it supports. The Labyrinth is brilliant design, and the Cenobites are horrific and oddly seductive – each scene they're in just feels right. The game embraces its source with total commitment and isn't afraid to get filthy about it, too.

items.title: The You Can See Everything poster will haunt my nightmares forever
paragraphs: The teaser trailer for Nathan Fielder's documentary You Can See Everything recently caused a stir for its strange depiction of notorious Silicon Valley founder Elizabeth Holmes. Now the unblinking eeriness has been distilled into a poster, and they've doubled down on the weird.

More in line with the best horror film posters, the new You Can See Everything poster has all the makings of a spine-chilling scare fest, with suffocating visuals and minimalist design. Bold and frighteningly captivating, I find it impossible to look away, despite how much I want to.

The poster stars the documentary's subject, Elizabeth Holmes, in a claustrophobia-inducing close-up. Spotlighting only half her face, the design forces our gaze to Holmes' almost inhumanly bright blue eye, which appears almost strained in its wideness. Her half-concealed smile only adds to the poster's quasi-uncanny feel, creating palpable discomfort.

In the background, the blurred image of a straight-faced Fielder adds extra tension, while minimalist sans serif font bears the film's title. Slightly cut off on the sides, the title reinforces the subtly suffocating effect, making for a wildly disconcerting design.

"The reflection in the eye is doing more acting than most lead performances this year," one X user wrote in response to the strange poster. "You could tell me this was a horror movie and I'd believe you," another added.
For more poster design, take a look at the new Clayface poster that gets creepier the more you look at it, or check out why horror movie poster design has a problem.

items.title: Cavern Club sold to new owners after 35 years
paragraphs: Managing director Bill Heckle trained to be a Beatles guide in 1982 before forming the Cavern City Tours in 1983.
Alongside Dave Jones they organised their first Beatles convention, which evolved into the annual Mathew Street Music Festival.
In 1991, they acquired the Magical Mystery Tour - bus tours of Liverpool - and the Cavern Club venue.
Heckle said the decision to sell was "not taken lightly" but it was "time for retirement".
"It is an emotional day, but a proud day, for the four Scouse owners," he said.
"It was never about putting Cavern City Tours up for sale to the highest bidder and it has taken over five years to find a suitable and like-minded custodian.
"However, we leave with the confidence that the new owners will continue to follow the path we have forged over the last 43 years."

In a statement, the new owners, 14 Collective, said: "We look forward to working alongside the existing management team, with a real appreciation for what makes the Cavern so special and excitement about what comes next."

items.title: Lourdes gets a Vegas glow-up at Dublin theatre festival, where canvases are slashed
paragraphs: In a Dublin theatre festival programme tackling heavy themes of racism, conflict and prejudice, Lourdes! The Musical (★★★★☆) promises something effervescent. Xnthony Ltd, the creators of Oliver Cromwell Is Really Very Sorry, have turned their lightly quizzical gaze to the French pilgrimage town – “a holy Blackpool, a divine Las Vegas” and a site of hope or desperation for five unlikely travelling companions.

Back in his home village in “Countryland”, in 2008, following a diagnosis of HIV that punctures his dreams of Los Angeles, singer-songwriter Matthew (Riain Cash) lends his star power to a parish drama group taking a musical about Saint Bernadette to Lourdes. Interweaving this show-within-a-show and the pilgrimage strands, Xnthony’s lyrics and Matthew Floyd Jones’s score blend pop, club beats and soulful ballads. Directed by Sarah Meadows, the supercharged ensemble joining Cash as, variously, a droll priest (Iestyn Arwel), a terminally ill mother and her transgender daughter (Nichola MacEvilly and Danielle James) and an eager tour manager (Molly Lynch) carry the music’s tonal shifts effortlessly.

Instructed by neon signs to “please wait for a miracle”, characters reveal what brings them to this Marian shrine with its bizarre mix of tackiness and piety. Each has a Catholic faith of sorts – something that might have been more complicated to portray if set in the present day. Rather than settling on an archly ironic approach, Xnthony’s sensitive, often lyrical writing allows fear of death, regret and above all, grief, to seep through.

An aura of reverence pervades the white cube gallery setting of Heroes of Tomorrow (★★★☆☆), the latest production from the restlessly inventive Brokentalkers. Co-directors Feidlim Cannon and Gary Keegan are joined here by British theatre artist Andy Smith to burrow into the relationship between art and activism. Pinging through centuries and continents, they make connections between historical instances of human invention and resultant exploitation, technological breakthroughs and protest, underlining the point that progress is not linear.

If this sounds abstract, it is; much of it is delivered in carefully flat, affectless narration by Alice Roots, Michael Tient and Malua Ní Chléirigh, as if making a presentation in the gallery, taking turns to outline the biography of a (fictional) Norwegian conceptual artist called Jan Hansen. His latest work, The End of It All, has been commissioned by three global tech companies, a testing moment of groupthink for an artist who has acquired cachet for financially supporting climate activists who fling paint over old masters in museums.

Amid questions about whether it is possible for art to remain pure, uncompromised by its corporate sources of funding, the audience is teased into imagining what Hansen’s new artwork will be. As the performers playfully poke their heads through slashed canvases and make black imprints of their hands on the pristine gallery wall, this performance is itself a form of conceptual art, played out in a highly coded space. The result is clever and knowing but, for Brokentalkers, surprisingly tentative.

Zinc (★★★★☆) from Dead Centre focuses on a forgotten mini-state, Neutral Moresnet, on the border of Germany, Belgium and the Netherlands. A political anomaly, designated a neutral zone to protect its prized zinc mines, it was passed between European powers, its inhabitants’ nationality changing as borders shifted. Adapted from a book by Belgian political philosopher David Van Reybrouck, the production brings multiple perspectives to bear on the experience of one man, Joseph Rixen, born in Neutral Moresnet in 1903.

Playing with the idea of neutrality, co-directors Ben Kidd and Bush Moukarzel and the superb international ensemble – Julie Mughunda, Timmy Creed, Fabio Godinho, Cathy Min Jung and Mila Moinzadeh – rewind, wittily, to the 1815 Congress of Vienna. Reflecting on colonisation, annexation and the accidents of history, each actor explores their personal experience of exile, displacement and lost native languages.

A co-production with Théâtre de Liège, this is one of Dead Centre’s most ambitious works to date: multilingual, integrating video mapping, projection, layered music and sound design, and, as always with their work, commenting on the art of theatre itself. Richly allusive, it connects a performer on an empty stage, before the act of imagination begins, to the perceived neutrality of a geographical place – until it can be exploited, no longer a country but “a business”.

Moving away from the cartography of loss, the performance seizes on the lost political project of Esperanto as a possible neutral language of hope – literally utopian, with its root meaning of “nowhere”.

items.title: Gaten Matarazzo on life after Stranger Things as he makes West End debut
paragraphs: Keeping your balance on a revolving stage probably sounds easy when you compare it with battling demogorgons, but Gaten Matarazzo points out one big difference.
You don't get the luxury of "thirty takes" to get it right in front of a live audience.
The former Stranger Things star's currently playing Mark in a modern revival of rock musical Rent on London's West End.
He tells BBC Newsbeat that having a proper schedule and remembering to stay hydrated makes a "refreshing change" from filming the Netflix smash-hit that made him famous.
Matarazzo shot to fame in 2016 as endearing super-geek Dustin Henderson - a role he calls "the greatest honour of his life".
The saga finally concluded last December after five seasons, and there's been interest in what the show's cast will do next.
"It's something you do inevitably step away from," says Matarazzo
"We finished filming in 2024 - there's no more show to film."
"I still love what I do very much, I want to keep on doing it."
Casting big names from TV and film in theatre shows is a growing trend, and one that sometimes provokes accusations of cashing in.
But Matarazzo has plenty of stage experience, having performed on Broadway when he was a child.
He says the time commitment involved meant it was impossible to "blend both worlds".
"My favourite part of theatre specifically is the schedule," he says.
"Going to bed at the same time and waking up at the same time.
"I've always thrived under a schedule and when I don't have one I feel insane."
In Rent, Matarazzo plays struggling film-maker Mark, who chronicles and narrates the lives of his friends.
It has been 30 years since the show first opened off-Broadway in New York, but the actor says there are "certain songs that weirdly resonate now".
"What You Own, which feels like a reflection on information overload, is incredibly relevant," he says.
"That's really fun to sing in context of today."
When it was first performed, Rent shone a light on young friends and artists living in late 1980s and early 1990s New York during the HIV/Aids crisis.
It was considered groundbreaking at the time for tackling social taboos and centering stories of LGBT people.
Writer Jonathan Larson died suddenly the night before its premiere.
Matarazzo's co-star, Travis Ross, who plays Roger, says the show's themes still "ring true" today.
The 25-year-old says having Rent tends to attract people who "care so deeply" about the show's message, resulting in a connection between actors and the audience.
He calls it a "really beautiful community-driven piece of art".
Both Ross and Matarazzo are keen to acknowledge their fellow cast members and point out Rent is "an ensemble" piece.
"In the same way we get our moments to tell the story there's also ten other people who get their moments to tell the story as well," says Ross.
Many of those in the audience will be there to watch Matarazzo, and he says he's determined to get the role right.
"I'm on stage for the majority of the show and singing the whole time," he says.
"It's not anything that's particularly high or out of my range, it's actually a part that I think fits nicely in my pocket.
"But it's just so much singing, and making sure I'm doing it correctly is essential," he says.
Matarazzo also plans to embrace his return to the stage.
"Once we're in the run it will be great," he says.
"I just always love the opportunity to start and finish a character arc and story in real time.
"You don't get an opportunity to do that when you're filming."
Speaking of which - if he ever got the call to go back to Hawkins and step into Dustin's shoes, would he take the chance?
"If that happens, that's great, and if not, that's completely fine.
"I've loved doing the show so much, it's literally the greatest honour of my life."
Rent is at The Tom Stoppard Theatre, London. Gaten Matarazzo is booked to perform until 10 January.

items.title: Asos hackers took more personal details than first revealed, BBC finds
paragraphs: Asos has told its customers that hackers are in possession of detailed profiles of potentially millions of the online store's users.

It issued the update after BBC News told the retailer it had been contacted by cyber criminals who said this week's breach went beyond the "basic contact details" Asos previously said might have been accessed.
Names, addresses, phone numbers, emails and customer numbers are now in the hands of cyber criminals.
So too are the searches customers have made on the website. Terms like "reclaimed vintage", "glamorous wide fit" and "Asos petite" are visible in the data.
With this information, scammers may be able to craft potent phishing attack emails or phone calls.
The risk to individuals is now higher and customers are being warned about potential impersonation scams.
In its email to customers, Asos confirmed data profiles were taken but said no bank details or passwords were accessed.
"Please remain cautious of unexpected messages or calls claiming to be from Asos," it said.
"We will never ask you to share passwords, security codes or payment details through an unsolicited message or call."
The company did not respond to questions about the scale of the breach.
The high profile hack made global headlines on Tuesday when cyber criminals used Asos's own app system to send a pop up notification to potentially millions of people.

Later that day the firm confirmed to shareholders via the London Stock Exchange that the pop up was sent by an "unauthorised third party" and "basic personal information including name and contact details may have been accessed."
The company then sent an email to customers with similar wording.
On Wednesday evening the cyber criminals responsible contacted the BBC sharing a sample of the stolen data which showed the true extent of the hack.
The BBC held off publishing this article to allow Asos to contact its customers first.
Asos said it is still investigating the data breach and it would "contact customers directly where we believe additional information, support or action may be required".
The UK fashion site explained to customers that hackers gained access to an Asos employee account by "impersonating a trusted contact to obtain log in credentials".
With that log in to an unnamed service, the hackers were able to download the customer data.
In the pop up notification send to customers by the hackers, they claimed they had "compromised the Snowflake instance".
Snowflake is a popular data storage and analysis company whose customers have been breached in the past due to unauthorised log ins.
The cyber criminals, calling themselves Xuanyewen, claimed to the BBC they used a platform which is built natively on top of Snowflake - called Simon AI - to gain access to the data.
Simon AI has been contacted for comment. Snowflake previously said its platform had not been breached.
Asos said customers are not being asked to take any action.
But cyber security experts have warned users to change passwords as a precaution and be on alert for suspicious activity.

"Passwords have not been stolen, so be highly suspicious of any unsolicited text or email asking you to change or share yours," said Trevor Dearing, Senior Director of Critical Infrastructure at Illumio.
"Expect scammers to mention the attack, use your personal details to seem genuine, and create urgency, such as threatening to lock your account within 24 hours."
Asos said its website and app are safe to use and "we know our customers trust us with their information".
"We take that responsibility seriously and have already taken additional steps to further strengthen security controls," it said.

items.title: Actor Simon Pegg reveals ADHD diagnosis: 'It's just who I am'
paragraphs: Although many people may feel like they have some similar symptoms, genetics play an important role in ADHD and a full diagnosis is given to those who are negatively affected on a daily basis.
Pegg said he had previously been putting his symptoms down to "just character fault".
The actor and writer also spoke about his mental health, including having clinical depression and struggling to control his drinking, which he said he initially thought had "caused" his diagnosis.
"I felt like it was something that had come on in later life because I wasn't a naughty child.
"I've had bouts of depression in my adult life since 18 and I thought maybe it had come on with that.
"Maybe over the years with therapy and medication - whatever - I've been treating the symptoms and not the cause of why I feel that way."
Pegg said: "I did feel different in a way I might not be able to put my finger on. Maybe everybody feels that way.
"I just assumed ADHD kids were kind of chaotic and difficult and didn't pay attention in school," he added.
"But there were other things that I did do as a kid – fidget or whatever – that made me think, 'Oh no, maybe I've had this longer than I thought'."
Pegg said his wife has been supportive and is "dealing with it as if I'd been diagnosed ages ago", adding: "It's just who I am, and it's just things that I do.
"She makes allowances for forgetfulness and and lack of concentration."

Other celebrities who have been diagnosed with ADHD in adulthood include comedian and actor Johnny Vegas, comic and presenter Sue Perkins, presenters Ant McPartlin and Richard Bacon, comedian Rory Bremner and model Erin O'Connor.
ADHD is described by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (Nice) as "a behavioural syndrome characterised by hyperactivity, impulsivity, and inattention".
The NHS estimates that about 2.5 million people in England have ADHD, including those without a formal diagnosis.
Diagnosis rates of ADHD and autism have soared, and waiting lists for assessments on the NHS in England are at record levels, with lists even closing in some areas due to the huge demand.
Research from University College London suggests nearly a 20-fold increase in the number of UK adults diagnosed with ADHD between 2000 and 2018.
Despite these rises in diagnosis and referrals, some studies suggest ADHD is actually underdiagnosed.

In June, the Lancet Regional Health Europe journal published research suggesting that while around 1.2% of adults in England had an ADHD diagnosis, international prevalence data estimates it affects 3-5% of people. The authors of the study said this indicates it could still be under-diagnosed, particularly in older age groups.

items.title: As crypto and prediction markets expand, their regulator shrinks
paragraphs: President Donald Trump shakes hands with Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) Chairman Michael Selig during a meeting with technology leaders in the Roosevelt Room of the White House, Wednesday, Aug. 19, 2026, in Washington. Jacquelyn Martin/Associated Press hide caption

Trump-era staff reductions have significantly hampered enforcement at the Commodity Futures Trading Commission and its ability to regulate burgeoning new prediction and cryptocurrency markets, where hundreds of billions are traded each week.

By the end of 2025, the CFTC had 21% fewer staff on its payroll when compared to the previous 10-year average, according to U.S. Office of Personnel Management data. Between January 2024 and January 2025 alone, staffing dropped 22%. And the number of CFTC enforcement actions dropped even further. The agency made nearly 80% fewer enforcement actions in 2025 when compared to the annual average for the previous decade, according to the agency's annual reports.

The CFTC started hemorrhaging staff soon after President Trump won the 2024 election. This was not a coincidence, according to Jeff Le Riche, who worked as a CFTC enforcement lawyer between 2005 and 2025.
"The Trump administration had run partially on a platform that it would be friendlier to the crypto industry," Le Riche said.

Leading up to the 2024 election, the CFTC under the Biden administration had leveled enforcement cases against cryptocurrency companies such as Gemini, Mirror Trading, Voyager, Celsius and FTX for fraud. It did the same against the crypto prediction market Polymarket.

After President Trump's inauguration, "in order to show results to that industry, some people were punished for bringing those cases," Le Riche continued. "The end result was that a lot of the people that worked on those cases either left or were forced out."
In a statement to NPR, the CFTC did not address that claim directly, but praised the work of current agency head Michael Selig.

"The CFTC remains committed to promoting integrity and responsible innovation in U.S. derivatives markets, and Chairman Selig is grateful to the dedicated staff who continue to support this mission each day," CFTC spokesman Zach Fulton wrote in part.
To Le Riche, the 21% drop in employees and the nearly 80% decline in enforcement action go hand in hand.

"It castrated the enforcement team," Le Riche said. "Many of the people who were targeted were high-performing attorneys who had brought some of the most consequential and complicated cases over the past few years."
Joe Konizeski, who worked as a CFTC enforcement lawyer for 26 years, was one of the dozens forced out in 2025.

"The acting chair [Caroline Pham] said, 'We're closing all our crypto [cases],'" Konizeski said. "And so, of course, everybody who had a crypto scam had to close it and any matter that was even marginally related to crypto ended up getting closed."

Pham left the CFTC in December of 2025 and is now the chief legal and administrative officer at MoonPay, a cryptocurrency company. She did not respond to NPR's request for comment about whether she gave preferential treatment to the crypto industry.

Since Trump took office, the CFTC has rolled back its enforcement actions against crypto firms Gemini, Celsius, and FTX. But crypto cases weren't the only ones impacted. Konizeski said decreased staffing caused the CFTC to dismiss others such as a foreign exchange fraud case against WorldWideMarkets Inc. The company was accused of defrauding millions from users.
Before the explosion of the crypto and prediction markets, the CFTC largely focused on more traditional derivative markets — such as grain and stock futures contracts.
"Fewer cops on the beat… creates a real incentive to start engaging in fraudulent and deceitful behavior," Konizeski said. "Enforcement is down and that means that there's going to be more fraud."
For Konizeski, chief examples of this are prediction market advertisements that target young men. He accused Polymarket and Kalshi of "using fraudulent means" to entice young men to its platforms.
"CFTC knows this and allows it to continue," Konizeski said.
Neither Polymarket nor Kalshi responded to NPR's requests for comment about whether their advertising targeted young men.
A former CFTC lawyer, who spoke on the condition of anonymity for fear of professional repercussions, said they left the agency voluntarily soon after Trump took office and Pham curbed enforcement.

"Enforcement was particularly closed in crypto and prediction market cases," this former CFTC staffer said. "A lot of people left because, once Pham took over, it became clear that enforcement was not a priority."

The Government Accountability Office, a congressional watchdog agency, is now investigating the CFTC for its workforce reduction, according to a letter obtained by NPR. This new GAO probe into the CFTC comes after Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., requested a federal investigation into the agency's staffing and fraud enforcement in July.

"It's supposed to be out there regulating the market, but it doesn't appear to be doing it and frankly, doesn't appear to have the people to do it," Warren told NPR in an interview. "I want to know whether or not the watchdog is actually out there doing a little barking, or has the watchdog been locked up somewhere back in the barn?"
The GAO is gathering staff and resources for its investigation into the CFTC and will "initiate" the probe in December.
The CFTC did not directly comment on the GAO investigation but did respond to NPR's questions about its staffing levels.

"[The CFTC] is on track to hire roughly 100 employees in mission critical areas by the end of 2026," wrote CFTC spokesman Fulton in a statement. "Like many federal agencies, a number of CFTC staff opted to step away from public service in recent years, and the CFTC will continue to ensure it attracts and retains talented staff dedicated to fulfilling our critical mission."
During 2026, the CFTC has seen a slight uptick in staffing.

While the GAO investigation is narrowly focused on staff reduction, Warren said Congress could use its "power to investigate" possible corruption citing potential Congressional subpoenas and its ability to control the agency's funding.
"But that only happens if Congress has the backbone and right now, led by the Republicans, Congress not only doesn't have a backbone, it doesn't even have any interest in doing it," Warren said.
When asked if a Democratic Congress would subpoena the heads of the CFTC, crypto companies and prediction markets, Warren said, "it is our job to use all those tools to investigate."
In August, the current chair of the CFTC, Michael Selig, celebrated his agency's slowdown in enforcement actions during a White House event featuring the crypto industry.

"The era of political lawfare, debanking and regulation by enforcement is over," Selig said while flanked by crypto CEOs in the Roosevelt Room. "Innovators, like the people in this room, are welcome to the White House — not railroaded to the big house."

Coinbase CEO and co-founder Brian Armstrong speaks as President Donald Trump meets with technology leaders in the Roosevelt Room of the White House, Wednesday, Aug. 19, 2026, in Washington. Jacquelyn Martin/Associated Press hide caption

He argued that the U.S. needs to "dominate" these new financial technologies — like crypto and prediction markets — and "write the rules that define the next generation of financial markets." Selig is the sole member of the normally five-member CFTC commission, giving him unchallenged power over the direction of the agency.

Before his time at the CFTC, Selig was a corporate lawyer for cryptocurrency firms and prediction markets. His latest financial disclosure report shows that Selig sold between $65,000 and $150,000 in Bitcoin before he became a commissioner.

While Selig wants increased agency rule making for prediction and crypto markets, that requires a massive amount of work and staffing, according to former CFTC director Brian Young, who said the reduction in headcount limits the agency's ability to write new rules.

"With the growth of prediction markets and digital asset trading, the [CFTC] really needs to augment staffing in order to meet these increased responsibilities," Young said. "At the end of the day, they need people to process these applications."
A former CFTC employee — who speaks regularly with current employees — told NPR that the CFTC is so understaffed that it is struggling to execute Trump's 2025 executive order on cryptocurrency.
"My friends that are there are dying," this former staffer told NPR on the condition of anonymity for fear of professional retaliation.
Earlier this year, CFTC Inspector General Christopher Skinner acknowledged the difficulty of short staffing in a recent annual report.
"The CFTC should consider human capital management as a top priority," Skinner wrote. "To ensure the agency has the appropriate talent and skill sets to meet an expanding regulatory landscape."
Meanwhile, the CFTC's work load keeps growing.

In 2025, the agency greenlit six prediction markets — three times the average annual rate over the last decade. This year, the agency has authorized another 6 prediction markets with 18 applications pending.
After the Senate failed to advance a major crypto and banking regulation bill this summer, the CFTC announced this week that it is moving ahead with making its own rules without congressional input.

"The American people deserve clarity, certainty, and consumer protections in the crypto asset markets and the agency is committed to delivering this by incorporating crypto asset transactions into its uniform national market regulatory framework," Selig said in a statement.
Still, as of July, the agency's workforce was 16% below its decade-average or 100 staffers short. The CFTC is currently hiring for seven full-time positions.

items.title: This indie game about AI doesn't use gen-AI but features a lot of content from real people and creators
paragraphs: It's becoming second-nature for people to interrogate whether a new game or even fan project is being made with AI, and when your game involves AI as its subject matter, it perhaps runs more risk of people, rightly or wrongly, jumping to conclusions.

It's partly why the indie devs behind Limerence, a branching narrative thriller about an AI partner decided to explicitly declare on their Steam page that no gen AI has been used in the game's development, including a big bright badge reminiscent of Nintendo's Seal of Quality.

"We found that through Polygon Treehouse, indie dev friends of ours, and they had started this campaign of putting that badge on," Salix Games CEO Jessica Saunders tells me. "We didn't have it originally, and then we were having people messaging me going, 'I just heard about your game, but this has generative AI, so I can't support it.' And I'm like, 'No, it doesn't.' So, we're having to make a big deal out of that."

Yet while AI is being primarily pushed by tech companies, including Epic, which already plans to incorporate Gemini and Claude into Unreal Engine 6, one can see the appeal to create things faster when there are less resources.

Salix Games in particular has felt the pinch of budgets, following its 2019 debut, Dance of Death: Du Lac & Fey, an adventure game with Arthurian characters in Victorian London, which hadn't been financially successful, while the industry post-COVID with layoffs and closures still a daily occurrence, means funding for larger projects has been next-to-non-existent.

But rather than opting for AI shortcuts, Saunders has taken a different approach when considering how to better adapt and survive the current turbulence: "It's like, what could we do for the minimum budget that maximises the skill sets that we have?"

Part of this involved partnering with another studio called Game in a Frame, run by Vincent Joyau, a former colleague of Saunders when she worked at Splash Damage. "He'd been building up his own set of tools for his game, so I asked if I could use them, and he goes, 'I'll do one better, I will use my tools with you and we'll work together to create this new game because we both need to start thinking smaller production-wise if we're going to survive in this industry.'"

Joyau's custom tools created in Unity hasn't just been important for handling Limerence's heavy branching dialogue but also for modelling the game's sole onscreen character, Kai, a 3D AI avatar, who also exists within a fake AI app that's been created with its own fully customisable character creator, outfits, and hairstyles.

This AI partner is only part of the bigger picture of Limerence, which explores how digital dependency can impact our real-world relationships, as the game explores how 30-something woman Claire's life and real-world relationships are impacted by her new-found obsession with a seemingly perfect partner.

This is all presented by the player essentially interacting with Claire's phone, with Saunders citing inspiration from indie games that have played with the premise of snooping on someone's phone, notably A Normal Lost Phone, which then naturally includes other apps that can be accessed, from social media posts, photos, or streamed music.

"It's interesting because these found phone games also use real actors, building up their own photo galleries, but our team lacked production experience, so we've had to pull in a lot of favours from a lot of people," Saunders explains. "We basically said, "Can we have access to your Tik Tok, your Instagram, your small business, and let us use your material, either as a donation or a small fee."

To her surprise, many people were happy to help. They include a friend who loves taking photos of lots of food from restaurants, and a couple of friends who are essentially 'playing' the lead couple in the game, with photos spanning years that show a consistent relationship history that the narrative is able to create a fictional life around.

"We expanded on that too," Saunders says. "We ended up hiring a couple of models through an agency and held a low-budget fake wedding shoot in London which was great fun just to get some of those extra background photos. Honestly, things like Adobe Stock and Unsplash have been great for filling in blanks. That's really allowed us to create a very voyeuristic experience of looking into a real person's phone and just opening up a gallery and seeing things you shouldn't really see."

With stretched resources, mostly going into recording the voice performances, with only Kai's lines being recorded in a sound booth so that the exceptionally clean audio adds to his artificiliaty, it would have been easy for the peripheral aspects of the game to be created with AI, be it arty social media posts or songs playing off a fake streaming app. But Limerence's approach to world-building shows you can make something more lived-in and authentic that also respects and credits artists - you just have to ask.

"The thing is I'm not actually very anti-AI, I think AI as a data tool is marvelous, and it can be very helpful for certain industries," Saunders concludes. "But when it comes to things like making video games, film, TV, and art, I don't see its purpose at the moment because it's just stealing."
Limerence is releasing on PC on 29 October, while Gen's Story, a free demo separate to the final game, is available now on Steam.
Inspired? See our guides to the best game development software and the best laptops for game development.

Alan Wen is a freelance journalist writing about video games in the form of features, interview, previews, reviews and op-eds. Work has appeared in print including Edge, Official Playstation Magazine, GamesMaster, Games TM, Wireframe, Stuff, and online including Kotaku UK, TechRadar, FANDOM, Rock Paper Shotgun, Digital Spy, The Guardian, and The Telegraph.

items.title: How 'Musk' director Alex Gibney became a critic
paragraphs: Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk gestures on stage at the Capital One Arena after President-elect Donald Trump is sworn in as the 47th President of the United States in Washington, DC on Monday, January 20, 2025. Ken Cedeno/UPI/Alamy Live News hide caption
Some time ago, Alex Gibney got curious about how Elon Musk accumulated impossibly vast amounts of wealth and power.

So the Oscar-winning documentarian did what he does best, spending four years of deep research into Musk's world to create a film that's nearly as many hours long, each minute kept riveting by a trove of dreadful facts, videos, legal documents and interviews with people close to the tech entrepreneur.
"I started out as — if not an admirer — at least somebody who is sort of interested in what he was doing and liked it," Gibney told Morning Edition host Steve Inskeep.
Gibney, who narrates the film, says he was a "proud" owner of a Tesla Powerwall energy storage system at his home and Tesla solar panels on his roof.
But Gibney's perspective shifted as he prepared his film, Musk, which opens in theaters Friday. It's due to stream on HBO in a few months.

"I became increasingly resentful and angry. When [Defense Secretary] Pete Hegseth basically said that they were now going to use xAI to be fully integrated into the Department of War, it was like an out-of-body experience," he said, referring to the artificial intelligence company founded by Musk that's behind the Grok AI assistant.
Alex Gibney spent four years making his nearly four-hour film Musk. Jigsaw Productions hide caption

The leadup to the film's release has seen some controversy after Musk used several insults to describe Gibney — "an idiot" was among the mildest ones — and threatened a defamation lawsuit over the film.

In a letter sent to Gibney's Jigsaw Productions company that emerged in September, Musk attorney Alex Spiro focused on an exchange between Gibney and Ashley St. Clair, a one-time MAGA influencer who had a child with the billionaire.

St. Clair describes in the film text messages Musk sent her before the November 2024 presidential election in which he said he was "feeling more optimistic" about Donald Trump winning because "tomorrow we unleash the anomaly in the matrix."
Musk further told St. Clair that he planned on tapping "'lasers' from space," adding that "I have over 10 thousand lasers in space right now."
In the film, Gibney asks St. Clair if she believes Musk's texts referred to satellites owned by his rocket company, SpaceX. She responds, "I don't know where else he has lasers."
NPR has obtained and authenticated the texts between Musk and St. Clair, which were sent on Oct. 6, 2024.

Spiro's letter, which NPR has also reviewed, says that Gibney made a "false" insinuation that SpaceX's Starlink satellites somehow uploaded votes for Trump in swing states, a debunked conspiracy theory.

"We don't claim that he changed votes in the 2024 election. All we do is to show that he was bragging to his lover that he had special access to understanding the outcome of the election in a way that other people didn't," Gibney told NPR. "Was he lying to her or was he just bragging or was he telling us something that we shouldn't know? I don't know. That's for the viewer to decide."

Gibney, who's previously investigated the likes of Enron and blood-testing startup executive Elizabeth Holmes in his films, said that when he trained his lens on Musk, he prepared for the possibility that the maverick CEO would try to sue him.

"We had a battery of lawyers reviewing everything that we did. I actually hired an independent fact checker to check our own fact checkers inside. So against the richest man, the truth is not always a defense, but I'm counting on his commitment to the principles of being a free speech absolutist."
Gibney also noted that a lawsuit would also trigger a discovery process by which he could subpoena Musk's internal documents.

As he took a closer look at SpaceX and Tesla, Gibney noticed that while the two companies "had achieved great things technologically... their stock price was way out of proportion to their actual economic value." The filmmaker says Musk achieved this by overselling his products.
SpaceX performed a vital service, ferrying equipment into space… developing rockets that could be reused cheaply.
But the film says Musk cast the company as an even grander venture, forever about to colonize Mars.
Tesla made popular electric cars, but the film says Musk oversold them as self-driving.
According to the film, they weren't made with enough sensors for that, which is why some have crashed. "That's a level of overpromising that leans into fraud," Gibney said.
NPR has reached out to Spiro, Musk's attorney, about the specific claims made in the film but has not heard back.
The broadcast version of this story was produced by Kaity Kline.

items.title: BBC to cut raft of Radio 4 programmes including You and Yours
paragraphs: Winifred Robinson has presented You and Yours since 2000
The BBC has announced it will be cutting a raft of Radio 4 programmes including the long-running consumer and social affairs show You and Yours.
The social sciences show Thinking Allowed will also be cut along with arts and ideas programme Free Thinking, as the corporation seeks £500m savings.
Other shows such The Artificial Human and Open Country will also go, it was announced on Thursday, while Radio 5 Live will also see a reduction in commissioning on its schedule and podcasts.
The BBC has committed to investing in a new consumer programme, though, and two new weekly shows exploring ideas shaping the world, and the impact of technology and AI.
Radio 4's flagship history, science and culture show, In Our Time, will expand in length, as will Start the Week and Farming Today.

Director of BBC Sounds Jonathan Wall said they were "reshaping BBC speech audio" in order to "build a strong future for trusted journalism, distinctive storytelling and programmes that bring people together".
"By commissioning fewer programmes overall, we can focus our investment and make our best shows work across broadcast, on demand and different formats," he said in a statement.

"That means accelerating growth on our own digital platforms and reaching more people beyond the BBC, while maintaining the strength of Radio 4 and 5 Live, the country's two biggest speech radio stations."
He added that the "difficult decisions" about cuts to shows and staff were "not based on cost alone", saying: "We need to make significant savings while investing for the future."

Last month, director general Matt Brittin said the BBC's financial situation and changing audience habits "may well mean" some channels and radio stations have to close so resources can be invested in on-demand services.
Brittin told BBC One's Sunday With Laura Kuenssberg that "we wouldn't guarantee any programme or any channel will exist forever".
In June, the BBC announced 550 job cuts in news, nations and TV and radio content as part of its first stage in its plan to save £500m across the corporation over the next two years.
Staff were told of proposals including ending Radio 4's The World Tonight, and reducing the number of permanent presenters on Today from five to four, with a single anchor on Saturdays.
It was revealed that BBC One's Breakfast would no longer be shown on Sunday mornings, and that the production teams making Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg and Newsnight would merge.
It followed April's announcement that the BBC would cut between 1,800 and 2,000 jobs - or almost one in 10 - in an attempt to tackle "significant financial pressures".
Last week, an influential group of MPs said the BBC licence fee should be extended to cover services other than TV, and that the corporation's charter review should be scrapped and made permanent.
In its recommendations, the DCMS committee also said that political appointments to the BBC board should end, to improve public trust.

items.title: Fanta's AI slop Halloween advert is a real horror show
paragraphs: We wrote recently about the terrifying practical effects in the Resident Evil movie. But it seems that some moviegoers who went to see Zach Cregger's adaptation of the iconic game were subjected to an even greater horror before the film began.
In the case of the Fanta Halloween ad, the fright was unwelcome and the practical effects conspicuously absent. Yep, the Coca-Cola Company is still trying to do AI ads.

Developed by AI studio GRAiL, Fanta’s Haunted Universe is intended to serve as a platform that will help the brand "claim Halloween". If Christmas belongs to Coke, Halloween should belong to Fanta, the company thinks.

The universe has several "original" character designs, including a cyborg Frankenstein and a werewolf DJ, while Ghostface from Scream makes a guest appearance in the ad above. The idea is to make this an annual occasion, with the universe and story to develop in future years.

That won't be what some readers wanted to hear. Many people strongly oppose the use of AI imagery on ethical grounds. On social media, the reactions to the video above are no less severe than they were with the AI Coca-Cola Christmas adverts. Almost all of the comments are negative, and there are many from people vowing to never buy Fanta again.

I was at the cinema this evening and during the ads before the film there was a Hallowe’en ad from Fanta. I couldn’t quite believe my eyes, but it was certified AI slop. I couldn’t record, of course, but I’ve found it online. I’m sure the Coca-Cola Company of all companies could afford a real ad. Down with AI slop.October 1, 2026

Interestingly Fanta is the “headline sponsor” of Thorpe Park Fright Nights, which I’m attending in a few weeks. That event has been marred by its use of AI slop, examples of which have gone viral. Why is this crap inescapable?October 1, 2026
"I went to check if people were talking about this as soon as I left the theatre. Crazy they don't see how bad it looks and how it cheapens their brand," one person writes on X.

"I was watching a Tubi movie when this ad popped up and I cannot express to you how much more effort, creativity, and overall watchability went into that Tubi movie than this ad," someone else thinks.
"Makes you think what are they putting in their food to lower the production cost?" another person writes.

People who are strongly opposed to AI might be a lot louder on social media than the many more people who don't really care either way. But now the AI Coke trucks have been joined by Fanta ones, it's starting to feel like Coca-Cola's goading its critics.

"Look, we can do trucks with the right number of wheels now," it seems to be boasting, while serving up a mess of badly edited jump cuts in which the product itself looks like a toxic swill that no human should put into their body. Unlike Marmite or the new Jaguar. Coke and Fanta have traditionally been branded as universal in their appeal. So why is the world's biggest soft drinks brand now so unworried about upsetting a large portion of its customer base?

items.title: The daleks in the new animated Doctor Who do kind of look of familiar...
paragraphs: The future of the main Doctor Who series remains up in the air amid a competitive tender to take over production following Russell T Davies’ exit. In the meantime, the BBC has ordered an animated Doctor Who series to fill the timey wimey void.

What took them so long? I hear you ask. Possibly a fear of the kind of comments the news has inevitably sparked on social media. Many Whovians aren't impressed by the first artwork from Doctor Who: TARDIS Crew. And there's one criticism that hard to unsee.

There have been animated Doctor Who shorts before, and the BBC has used animation to remake lost episodes' Doctor Who: TARDIS Crew is more ambitious. Announced by BBC Children's and Education and created for the kids' channel CBeebies, it will have an initial run of 52 eleven-minute episodes.

The series will follow a young blue-haired Doctor and his friends Hannah, Beastie and Toast-IE. Villains will include the daleks. Blue Zoo Animation Studio is producing and Dominic Minns, who directed CBeebies' Mojo Swoptops and Supertato, is series director.

"Bursting with imagination, humour and adventure, Doctor Who: TARDIS Crew brings the excitement of the Whoniverse to a new generation of fans. Through action-packed, preschool-friendly stories, the series celebrates curiosity, courage and kindness, encouraging young viewers to explore new ideas, solve problems and embrace the unexpected.," the BBC says.

The series is bound to take some liberties with Doctor Who lore (if there are any left to take). But as a lifetime Doctor Who fan myself, it makes me sad that a lot of the criticism of the animation on social media is a bit ridiculous, particularly since we have only a single piece of artwork to judge it on so far.

Most of the disparagement appears to come from middle-aged men who have mistaken themselves as the target audience for the pre-school friendly cartoon.Some are worried that the series might have a strong female character (shudder).

One perplexing comment on X even suggests the artwork above uses 'bisexual lighting', because cosmic-looking purple gradients are something new in science fiction (I always suspected that the Dumbbell Nebula swung both ways, to be honest).
@bbcdoctorwho why the Dalek have a minion eye😭😭 https://t.co/qroeXi9NzDOctober 6, 2026

There is one recurring observation that I can't argue with though. The daleks do look like one-eyed minions. Whether the resemblance is intentional or not, it was my first thought when I saw the art work.

The toddler-friendly daleks redesign is actually quite clever. It leans into the silliness of their existing design with their sink plunger arms and takes it further, adding more utensils to the mix. Giving them real eyes and making the grille more mouth-like is a logical step to make them appeal to smaller kids, but it's almost inevitable that they'll continually remind us of Gru's henchmen.
@bbcdoctorwho I wasn't aware that this would also be a Red Dwarf crossover. https://t.co/CQnWSgjc9SOctober 6, 2026
Another detail that's raised eyebrows is the character called Toast-IE. Could he be Talkie Toaster from Red Dwarf?

That's actually a crossover I would watch, but the reference is presumably unintended. That makes it feel like the character could have been suggested by AI as an appropriate comedy companion for a sci-fi series. Surely, K9 could have done the job?
In the meantime, check out how they made the animation for last year's Lux episode in the main Doctor Who series.
