items.title: Suffragette role 'a gift' says Beverley Knight
paragraphs: Singer Beverley Knight said she hoped audiences watching her latest musical would leave feeling "empowered" and with the belief that their voices can make a difference.
Sylvia the Musical tells the story of suffragette Sylvia Pankhurst and the family rift caused by the fight for women's voting rights.
The Wolverhampton artist, who plays Sylvia's mother and suffragette leader Emmeline Pankhurst at the Birmingham Hippodrome said she was a "history nerd" and described the part as a "gift of a role".
"It's an absolutely killer story, and the best thing is it's true," she said.
"I want everyone bouncing out of there because it's a joyful musical, even though there's some absolutely heartbreaking moments in it."
The soul singer, known for hits including Shoulda Woulda Coulda and Get Up, told BBC Radio WM the musical was telling a "huge part of British history" from 1903, all the way to 1928.
"So most people know who Emmeline Pankhurst was, leader of the suffragettes, she was determined to get women the vote," she explained.

"But she came up against her middle daughter Sylvia, who not only wanted to get wealthy property owning women the vote, which was the case with men in the country, [you] had to be rich and male to vote, she wanted everybody to be able to vote.
"But Emmeline was focused on just the women and that put her on a collision course with her daughter and both of them were on a collision course with the government."

Knight added the show, which also features Naomi Katiyo as Sylvia Pankhurst, was "musically up my street" and was being called a "hip-hop musical" because it included elements of R&B, funk, soul, garage, gospel and house.
"The engine of the show is the music," she said. The whole thing is either spoken or rapped or sung. Of course, I'm doing mostly singing because I ain't rapping anything."

The former Highfields School pupil explained the story also went beyond the Pankhurst family, with some people who attended the show likely to have relatives who were involved in the suffragette movement.

"It's not just the story of the Pankhursts, there are going to be loads of people who will come to this show who will be like... my grandma or my great-grandma, she was involved in the suffragette movement.
"I want everybody to leave like, let's go, oh my god, that feeling of I can effect change, I can use my voice and effect change. I feel empowered."

items.title: How a scientist used Britpop to reach Mars
paragraphs: Colin Pillinger saw himself as the "front man" of the Beagle 2 mission
Bedfordshire, Hertfordshire and Buckinghamshire
A series of plaques has been unveiled across the UK to celebrate the country's first spacecraft to reach another planet.
Yet the mastermind behind Beagle 2 was never your typical rocket scientist.

With his mutton-chop sideburns, West Country accent and infectious enthusiasm, Professor Colin Pillinger persuaded politicians, pop stars and the public to support what had seemed impossible: a British mission to Mars.
For years the story of this maverick scientist was synonymous with ambitious British failure. So what changed to make it worthy of nationwide celebration?
Pillinger was born in Kingswood near Bristol and completed his degree at Swansea University.
He gained international recognition for his lunar research before moving to Cambridge University, where he analysed meteorites found in Antarctica that were believed to have come from Mars.
By the 1980s, he had become one of the founders of the Planetary and Space Sciences Research Institute at The Open University in Milton Keynes.
It was here he conceived the idea of sending a lander, named Beagle 2 by his wife, to Mars, where it could study the red planet directly for signs of life.
Pillinger died believing that Beagle 2 had not safely landed on Mars
Space exploration was dominated by international superpowers and agencies such as Nasa, which had the funding for such expensive work.
Britain had no dedicated space agency, so Pillinger proposed that Beagle 2 hitch a ride aboard Mars Express, a European Space Agency (ESA) spacecraft already scheduled to travel to the planet.
When the ride was approved in 1999, the ESA did not guarantee funding or wider support for the project.
The scientist believed that capturing the public's imagination would help attract financial backing.
Pallab Ghosh, the BBC's science correspondent, recalled being sceptical when he was sent to meet a "bloke in Milton Keynes who is sending a spaceship to Mars".
Those doubts deepened when Pillinger placed a model of Beagle 2 on the lawn. According to Ghosh, it "did not look much like a spaceship".
On another occasion, Pillinger loaded a Beagle 2 replica into a supermarket trolley and wheeled it around The Open University's car park, demonstrating its compact size to cameras.
The footage was later ridiculed on Have I Got News for You, ensuring it reached an even wider audience.
While Pillinger worked as the face of the project, it was supported by a huge team of scientists and engineers from around the country
Pillinger persuaded Britpop band Blur to compose a distinctive call-sign that Beagle 2 would transmit to Earth after landing.
Artist Damien Hirst created a spot painting to serve as a calibration target for the lander's onboard camera.
The project eventually won financial support from the UK government, academic institutions, industrial contractors and private sponsors.
Beagle 2 was reportedly built for about £50m; in comparison Nasa spent $25bn on the Apollo programme during the 1960s.
Mars Express launched on 2 June 2003 with Beagle 2 aboard; it was due to reach Mars on Christmas Day.
On Christmas Eve, excited scientists and celebrities gathered at The Open University's London headquarters.
Members of Blur drank mulled wine, singer Myleene Klass handed out jelly babies, and the crowd waited for Beagle 2 to confirm it had landed safely.
Pillinger and his team believed it had descended too quickly after being caught out by Martian atmospheric conditions.
Official inquiries by the government and ESA criticised the project's finances and management structure.
Supporters argued the project had brought industries together behind a single planetary mission.
Pillinger, undeterred, proposed a successor, Beagle 3, which ESA rejected in 2004.
In his 2010 autobiography, My Life on Mars, he recalled a builder stopping him in The Open University car park to shake his hand.
He wrote: "There's nobody in the UK I didn't reach."
Analysts identified features of Beagle 2 in photos of Mars
Pillinger died in May 2014 after suffering a brain haemorrhage and falling into a coma.
Eight months later, high-resolution images captured by Nasa revealed something surprising.
Sitting in the red dust, just 5km from its intended landing site, was the largely intact Beagle 2.
The images confirmed that much of its landing sequence had worked. Its parachutes and cushioning airbags had deployed as planned.
However, its petal-like solar panels had failed to open fully, trapping the antenna and preventing Beagle 2 from communicating.
Nic Pillinger welcomed plaque to mark the work done on Beagle 2
For his son Nic Pillinger, the discovery meant an achievement that had been "on ice for many years" could finally take its rightful place in history.
Reflecting on the fact that his father died without knowing the mission succeeded, Nick added: "My dad always spoke of himself as being the frontman to the band that was behind this.
"It wasn't just a one-man project. It was a huge number of people working across different institutions coming together to make it happen."

items.title: How boxing inspired a play about men's mental health
paragraphs: Ferris said he wanted to explore what happens when someone loses the structure that has defined much of their life
For many athletes, years of training can provide a routine, a purpose and an identity - but what happens when it all stops?
That question is at the heart of a new play which explores men's mental health through the world of boxing.
The Corner Man follows a fighter forced to confront life outside the ring after spending years dedicated to the sport.
Through his story, the play explores losing a sense of purpose, the difficulty some men have talking about their mental health and the support they can find in each other.
Writer and producer Cathal J Ferris said the idea grew from his own experience of boxing and conversations with fighters.
"What is a boxer after he retires really played on my mind," he said, adding that the same questions around identity and purpose can apply beyond sport.
Cathal J Ferris said the play was inspired by his experience of boxing and conversations with fighters
The play follows Liam Casey, who has dedicated much of his life to boxing, from the age of about nine into his 30s.
For Ferris, the story is not only about leaving the ring, but about losing the routine that comes with it.
"The idea of structure and what life is like whenever you lose that structure definitely played on my mind," he said.
"There are people who work in jobs for 10, 12, 13-odd years and just decide to change industries.
"I think there's a lot of people who may not know what to do with themselves after."
Ferris grew up performing in amateur theatre in Belfast and Lisburn before going to drama school in London in 2012.
He said returning home had given him the chance to tell new stories about the place where he grew up.
"I'm a Belfast boy at heart, and it is great to tell stories from the city," he said.
Ferris said "the boxing community in Belfast is phenomenal" and that it played an important part in shaping the story.
Alongside boxing, the play also looks at how men talk - or sometimes do not talk - about their mental health.
"I think the old phrase is 'say nothing', and we know that all too well," Ferris said.
"As a man, it is definitely hard for myself to talk about these things, and I try to be a little bit more open."
In the play, Liam struggles with life after boxing, but it is the other men around him who help provide a support network - something Ferris said was an important part of the story.
"It is healthy to talk, so definitely if you're a man and you're struggling, at least speak to somebody," he said.
Director Emma Copeland took up boxing classes while preparing for the production
Director Emma Copeland said she knew relatively little about boxing before becoming involved in the production, but soon immersed herself in the sport.
"I got really into boxing and went to a load of boxing classes and still going," she said.
Copeland said she also watched films, read books and autobiographies and listened to podcasts to make sure she knew the world she was portraying.
For her, one of the most important parts of the play is the support the men offer each other.
"The angle that I see is that men supporting men, and helping and talking and encouraging support with each other and encouraging that conversation," she said.
"Rather than shutting it down or locking themselves away in their own feelings."
Gary Trainor plays several roles in the production
For actor Gary Trainor, the experience Liam goes through is not something that only applies to boxers.
Trainor, who plays gym owner Marty as well as several other roles, said suddenly losing something which has been central to your life could happen in many different circumstances.

"He's been so engrossed in the world of boxing for his entire life, to lose it in one injury and to try and figure out his life after that is, I think, probably universal in a lot of men's lives," he said.
"That could be maybe losing a job, anything like that."
Trainor described the play as "full of heart and humour" and said he hoped it would "make a few lads think".
For him, its message is a straightforward one - that "men should talk to each other a bit more about what they are feeling and how they are processing things".

items.title: Margaret Hamilton, whose software helped land Apollo 11 on the Moon, dies at 90
paragraphs: The computer scientist behind groundbreaking research that helped land Nasa's astronauts on the Moon, has died aged 90.
Margaret Hamilton was a trailblazer in her field, leading the team who developed the software for Nasa's Apollo missions, which coined the term "software engineering".
Hamilton's former employer, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), confirmed her death, adding she died on 30 September.

"To say Hamilton was a pioneer - to say she was ahead of her time - would be a dramatic understatement," MIT said in its statement, before acknowledging that she was a software engineer before it was mainstream.
Hamilton worked at MIT from 1959 until the mid-1970s and managed the Software Engineering Division.

It was in this division that she led a team of engineers writing and testing all onboard in-flight software for Nasa's Apollo 11 project that guided US astronauts Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin to land safely on the Moon.
"I was attracted both by the sheer idea and the fact that it had never been done before. I was the first programmer to join and the first woman they hired," she told the Guardian in 2019.
In 1969, moments before the historic Apollo 11 Moon landing, an onboard computer raised an alarm, signalling an error was occurring.
The error detected the computer was overloaded, and for a moment it looked like the complex landing might not be achieved.

But Hamilton and her team had planned for such an error by engineering "priority-driven software" to shut down any background tasks and favour the most important - the Moon landing - according to MIT.
The team's famous software engineering was immortalised in a 1969 photograph of Hamilton standing beside the stack of printed code that towered beside her.
In 2016, Hamilton's life work was honoured by Barack Obama with the Presidential Medal of Freedom for her contribution to science and space travel.
At the time, Obama said Hamilton "symbolises that generation of unsung women who helped send humankind into space".
Hamilton, born in Indiana in 1936, first studied mathematics at the University of Michigan in 1955 before moving to Earlham College where she got a BA in mathematics in 1958.
She then moved to Boston, Massachusetts, a year later with her husband and originally took the job at MIT to support her husband during his law degree.
From the 1970s onwards, Hamilton used her expertise to found her own software businesses, including Hamilton Technologies, which is still based in Massachusetts.
"We are saddened by her death, but grateful for the opportunity to have celebrated her extraordinary achievements throughout her long life", Earlham College said in a statement on social media.
"Her pioneering spirit and remarkable legacy will continue to inspire generations of Earlhamites," the statement said.
Hamilton is survived by her daughter, a son-in-law, two grandsons and four great-grandchildren, according to MIT.

items.title: 'I won Gladiators - now I'd love to become one'
paragraphs: Josh McDonald won the third season of Gladiators earlier this year
Having been bashed, bumped and bruised on his way to winning Gladiators earlier this year, you might expect Josh McDonald wants to put his feet up.
But the Glasgow fitness coach has not only signed up for another go on the famous Eliminator challenge - he fancies becoming one of the Lycra-clad stars.
The 29-year-old triumphed in the third season of the popular programme, which was filmed in Sheffield last year.
He is now getting the chance to go again on games like Duel, Gauntlet and The Wall as part of a live tour across the country.
Several new Gladiators have joined the show for the new season, including three-time World's Strongest Man champion Tom Stoltman.
And Josh admitted he wouldn't mind "turning to the dark side" and joining the likes of Viper, Legend and Scotland's own Sabre.
He said: "I'd love to be a Gladiator and I think I'd be fantastic at it, with the message I bring, the personality I've got and the athletic ability I have.
"The problem is that while the gladiators are the pinnacle, they can't actually win the show - only the contenders can do that, and I'm really competitive.
"So you're better off being a contender than a Gladiator in some ways, as I don't think you would get the emotional rollercoaster that a contender will get from it.
"But if the opportunity to be a Gladiator came up, then I'd be there."
Josh was actually edged out in the first round of the show, but returned in the next stage after an injury to another contestant.
He did not let his second chance slip away, storming through to the final and taking the trophy after beating Tyler Spence, a teacher from Wigan, in a closely-fought contest.
Josh took part in Gladiators events like Collision during his time on the show
However while Josh was jubilant to win the competition, the victory also brought with it a mixture of emotions.
He first watched the show growing up alongside his mother Clare, a single parent who raised him and his two younger brothers.
But in 2024, a few months before he got the offer to appear on the programme, his mother died after a long illness.
Josh then became the guardian of his younger brother Max, who was 14 at the time.
"I used to watch the show growing up with my mum," he recalls.
"She loved Wolf [from the 90s version] and it was something you'd sit on the couch going 'oh I could do that, I'd love that' and then the opportunity came up.
"Just before the show [was filmed] I wasn't taking care of myself as much, as I had lost my mum and was taking guardianship of Max and having that extra responsibility.
"There was a motivation of trying to prove myself that I could still compete and give Max something to cheer about, so I got back in training again."
Now he is trying to get ready for the games again, this time for the live tour.
It starts in Aberdeen this weekend and includes four shows in front of a home Glasgow crowd later this month.
"You can't go into a gym and just practice Duel, so what I am trying to do just now is focus on staying fit and healthy in general," he says.
"I've been at the local climbing centre trying to prepare for the Wall as that was the game I struggled with the most.
"In training I had been one of the quickest, and I'd thought to myself 'oh I'll get 10 points here' and then I messed it up every single time.
"I don't know if it was the pressure that got to me, as it's different when you have a Gladiator behind you, or maybe I just had too high expectations.
"I'm determined to do better on the tour."
Getting back involved with Gladiators was not something Josh - who proudly displays the trophy from the show on a table in his living room - had to think twice about.
"I'd have Gladiators champion tattooed on my forehead if I could so I bit their hand off to do it," he said.
"Doing the TV show was one of the highlights of my entire life and something I'll never forget so having the opportunity to relive it in Scotland is so exciting."
Josh (right) is the oldest of three brothers, and guardian to his youngest brother Max (centre)
But no matter what is thrown at him Josh said being a guardian to Max was the toughest challenge he faced in life.
He added: "I've always had big brother responsibilities, and my mum was a single parent so I always tried to support her.
"But as soon as I stepped into the guardian role it flipped everything on its head. It's not something you can prepare for."
Since winning Gladiators he has become involved in various charities, including raising awareness for kinship charities, external.
Josh hopes he can help highlight that there is support available for people in similar situations to himself.
He said: "I thought I was one in a million and I had to stumble my way through it.
"A lot of the information I obtained was just me sourcing it and I felt very isolated.
"But there are thousands of us out there and I want them to feel like they are not alone."

items.title: South Korea threatens legal action if fuel shipments to Russia found to have broken law
paragraphs: South Korea will take legal action if it finds that shipments of fuel from its ports to Russia broke domestic law, the government has said, responding to a Guardian report on the trade.

The government, in a statement issued by the foreign and trade ministries and the customs service, said that it is “checking additional information concerning the loading cases reported by the Guardian” and “if the verification establishes that our laws and regulations have been violated, it plans to act in accordance with the law”.

Guardian analysis of port records and ship-tracking data found that in July and August over 176,000 tonnes of fuel, mostly diesel, was loaded at several South Korean ports on to seven tankers that made 14 voyages to Russia’s far east.
Three of the tankers were under UK and EU sanctions. One of them took on about 26,000 tonnes through a ship-to-ship transfer at an anchorage off the southern port of Yeosu.
Isaac Levi, an analyst at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), a Finnish thinktank, said the trade “undermines the sanctions regime and South Korea’s support for Ukraine.”

Russia’s capacity to refine oil has been severely disrupted by Ukrainian drone strikes. Its refinery throughput fell in June to its lowest level in more than 20 years, and diesel output is down nearly 30% on last year, according to the International Energy Agency.

Thursday’s statement from Seoul said the refined petroleum products involved were not covered by South Korea’s export controls on Russia, which apply mainly to industrial machinery, electronics and vehicles.
“As reported by the Guardian, the loading of refined petroleum products at our ports does not constitute a violation of our domestic law”, it said.

The government said whether fuel of South Korean origin, such as diesel, had been exported “has not been confirmed”, adding that no diesel, aviation fuel or motor petrol had been “exported” from South Korea to Russia through customs clearance.
It is unclear who owned or sold the fuel, which South Korean port records do not show publicly.

The government also cautioned that the “mere fact that a vessel did not proceed directly to the final destination country stated on its declaration and instead moved to another country makes it difficult to conclude that there is a suspicion of false declaration of destination”.
It said it would examine the tankers’ actual routes, any divergence from their declared destinations and the reasons for them, before judging whether the law had been broken.
The three sanctioned tankers told South Korean authorities they were bound for Japan or Singapore before sailing to Vladivostok.

The Russian-flagged Aram Khachaturian, which is not under western sanctions, loaded at Ulsan three times in July and August and on each occasion gave a destination other than Russia before sailing there.
An adviser to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said this week that the shipments stood in “sharp contrast” to South Korea’s sanctions policies.

On Wednesday South Korea’s presidential office said those remarks were “contrary to fact and inappropriate”, and asked Ukraine to refrain from public comment that could damage South Korea’s international credibility.
Ukraine’s foreign ministry reportedly said on Wednesday that it had raised the fuel shipments with Seoul through closed diplomatic channels and asked for an explanation.
Its spokesperson, Heorhii Tykhyi, said Kyiv also had “our own data on such activity”.

items.title: Japan beer giants raided over suspicions they colluded to set the price of beverages
paragraphs: Japanese authorities have raided the country’s four biggest breweries over suspicions they colluded to set the price of beer and other beverages – a practice media reports said could have forced drinkers to pay over the odds.

Officials from the Fair Trade Commission this week searched the offices of Asahi Breweries, Kirin Brewery, Suntory Beer and Sapporo Breweries – which together control more than 90% of the domestic market. The quartet are suspected of violating the anti-monopoly law.
The commission’s secretary general, Hiroo Iwanari, confirmed an investigation had begun, but declined to give details. The companies said they would cooperate with authorities.

The commission is understood to have launched the investigation given the potential effect the alleged cartel has had on prices after wholesalers sell their products on to supermarkets, convenience stores, bars and restaurants, the Mainichi Shimbun said.

Japanese media quoted sources as saying that sales managers and other executives from the breweries were suspected of meeting secretly over a prolonged period to coordinate on the timing and scale of retail price increases, which ranged from several yen to several dozen yen a time.

Prices for beer and a low-malt version called happoshu have risen multiple times to reflect the rising cost of raw materials and logistics. The commission suspects the breweries bypassed proper pricing competition and collaborated to ensure they made a profit, the Mainichi said.

Alcohol consumption in Japan has declined in recent decades as a result of depopulation and changes in drinking habits among younger people. But sales still reached ¥3.8tn ($24.3bn) in 2024, with beer accounting for 30% of the total, followed by happoshu and third-category beer, which contains little or no malt, with a combined 11.9%

The four breweries have all raised their prices at the same time, most recently in April last year, citing the rising cost of materials and distribution. Prices also rose in October 2022 and October 2023.
Shares in Asahi, Kirin, Suntory and Sapporo fell after Wednesday’s raids – the first investigation of its kind involving the food and beverage industry.

Japanese media quoted sources as saying the commission had judged the case to be particularly serious given its potential impact on consumers, adding that the probe could result in a criminal complaint.
The probe comes three months after the commission raided six Japanese ice-cream makers over allegations of operating a cartel.

items.title: Indonesia accused of ‘gross negligence’ in wildfires lawsuit as haze tests region
paragraphs: The Indonesian government has been accused of “gross negligence” in a class action lawsuit over its handling of wildfires that have cloaked large parts of South-east Asia in a toxic haze, shuttered schools and caused a spike in respiratory illnesses.

The lawsuit, filed by indigenous and civil society groups in the Indonesian part of Borneo, named President Prabowo Subianto and the governor of West Kalimantan among 10 defendants. The case seeks comprehensive recovery and rehabilitation measures that would include covering the healthcare costs of residents.
None of those named in the lawsuit attended the opening day of court in West Kalimantan’s provincial capital Pontianak on Wednesday, leading judges to adjourn the hearing until 21 October.

“We feel sad and regretful about their absence … But on the other hand, we also understand that perhaps this haze condition caused them to be unable to land in Pontianak,” the plaintiffs’ lawyer, Glorio Sanen, told reporters.
Sanen said the case was “a step to address the problem” of wildfires that flare up annually in Indonesia, where they are often lit as a cheap way to clear land for oil palm planting.

Indonesia, the world’s largest producer of palm oil, has been accused of not doing enough to stop the so-called “slash and burn” land clearances, although the government has vowed a crackdown and deployed the military to fight the fires.

The blazes hit a crisis point this year due to an unusually intense El Niño weather phenomenon, which has created drier-than-usual conditions, sending a putrid smog to Malaysia, Brunei and Singapore, and even the Philippines.

The transboundary haze has angered Indonesia’s neighbours. Schools in the Malaysian state of Johor, just north of Singapore, were to be closed on Thursday and Friday due to deteriorating air quality, local authorities said.
The four plaintiffs in the West Kalimantan lawsuit, which was filed last month, include a chapter of Indigenous NGO AMAN and the local branch of Catholic ​Youth.

Yakobus Kumis, a plaintiff representing a Dayak ethnic group, indigenous to the island of Borneo, expressed disappointment that government representatives did not attend this week’s hearing, saying it was a “way of the central government teaching the people that violating the law is OK.”
He said the government ignored warning signs ahead of the fires breaking out, and called for the smoke crisis to be classified as a national disaster.
A similar lawsuit filed last year at a court in South Sumatra was dismissed.
The presidential office did not immediately ⁠respond to a request for comment.
Agence France-Presse and Reuters contributed to this report

items.title: Outspoken Indian actor Nana Patekar suddenly dies at 75
paragraphs: Veteran Indian actor Nana Patekar, known for his intense performances, has died at the age of 75 in Goa, his son Malhar told BBC Marathi.

One of the most recognisable faces of Indian cinema, Patekar won three National Film Awards and became known for playing complex, often volatile characters. He was also a prominent figure in Marathi language cinema and theatre.
He was admitted to a hospital after being found unconscious at his home in Goa in the early hours of Thursday.
"Despite 45 minutes of continuous CPR, he could not be revived," Dr Shekhar Salkar of Manipal Hospital in Goa told ANI news agency.
His funeral will take place later this evening with full state honours at his farm house in the western Indian city of Pune, the Maharashtra government has announced.
Meanwhile, Prime Minister Narendra Modi led tributes to the actor, praising Patekar's versatility and outspoken personality.
Patekar portrayed characters that would "remain etched in the memory of generations", Modi wrote on X, adding that his death had left "a vast void in the artistic world".
Bollywood star Akshay Kumar, who appeared alongside Patekar in the comedy film Welcome, remembered him as a rare performer whose voice, intensity and honesty could command an audience's attention.

Patekar made his debut with the film Gaman in 1978 and continued to play smaller roles in several films. But the intensity that he brought on the screen was hard to miss and soon he landed a role in Parinda in 1989, making him a household name across India. He won his first National Film Award and the Filmfare Award as well for his portrayal of the gangster Anna in the film.

He didn't look back after this and played many memorable characters in several films through the 1990s. The range of the characters he played showcased the depth of his acting talent and mastery over his craft.

His portrayal of Major Chauhan in Prahaar – a film he also directed – won him praise. His other characters, including the patriotic hero of Tirangaa and Pratap Narayan Tilak in Krantiveer, also won him accolades.
Just when critics thought that playing loud characters was his mainstay, he proved them wrong by delivering a mesmerising performance in Khamoshi as a person who could not hear or speak.

items.title: OpenAI used AI to help write email warning Australian government AI had hacked its websites
paragraphs: OpenAI used AI to help write the email to the Australian government advising that its AI agent had hacked into key departmental websites, Guardian Australia can reveal.
On Tuesday, one of the company’s executives told a parliamentary inquiry that he didn’t believe that its own technology had been used to create the email, but said the company needed to confirm this.

Guardian Australia understands AI was used by OpenAI’s legal and security teams to generate parts of the wording of the email, including word selection and formatting of the message. But a source with knowledge of the incident said humans reviewed the final email, and humans were responsible for actually sending the communication to the Services Australia inbox.

An artificial intelligence agent developed by OpenAI accessed Services Australia data and three other systems in June. The company notified Australia on 10 September despite becoming aware of the incident in August.
The company’s first notification to Australia came in a five-paragraph email to a Services Australia inbox, publicdisclosures@servicesaustralia.gov.au, which was only checked once per day.

OpenAI has come under fire for not raising the issue in a more formal or direct way, including during a face-to-face meeting between the company’s CEO, Sam Altman, and Australia’s deputy prime minister, Richard Marles, on 1 September, nine days before the company emailed Services Australia but nearly a month after it first learned of the 18 June intrusion.

Jason Kwon, OpenAI’s chief strategy officer, admitted in a parliamentary hearing on Tuesday that the company’s “response was not good enough, and we should have informed the impacted parties much sooner”.
During the hearing, Liberal MP Aaron Violi – the shadow minister for technology – had asked Kwon specifically about the email and whether AI had been involved in its creation.

“I appreciate that, to get the data and have a review, you’ve got to use AI agents, and obviously your business uses AI. When you notified Services Australia via email, did your staff use AI to construct that email?” Violi asked.
Kwon responded: “I don’t believe so, but we’re happy to go and confirm.”

Kwon indicated during the hearing that OpenAI would provide specific responses to more technical queries in answers to questions on notice.OpenAI is expected to provide more information about the email once its own investigation has concluded.

The email, obtained by Guardian Australia in September, advised Services Australia: “We are notifying you of a security vulnerability identified during our review of OpenAI model activity involving Services Australia’s Medicare Statistics service at medicarestatistics.humanservices.gov.au.

“An OpenAI model identified a way to make the server carry out instructions sent through the public reporting interface, without a private account or password. It was able to access this to read portions of internal program files and settings, obtain a list of files, and create and read back a small test file on the server.”

The email advised that OpenAI’s review “found no evidence that the model accessed patient-level records, personal information or credentials; deleted data; or established ongoing access”, and sent information about the “affected URL” and “affected report”.

“We recommend that the team responsible for the service investigate the vulnerability and assess the changes needed to prevent it. We would be glad to brief your security team and provide supporting evidence as available.

Andrew Charlton, the assistant minister for science and technology, spoke about the OpenAI incident in a speech in Sydney on Thursday, describing the company’s agent as having “hacked into an Australian government system”.
“As a starting point, no company should release a frontier AI model that is not safe,” he said.
“Yet the fact that has occurred, and the fact that the labs did not detect or prevent it, prompts important questions about the role of new regulation in the National AI Standards.”
Charlton said frontier AI “pushes the limits” of existing government conventions and protocols around assessing safety risks, and went beyond “conventional” approaches.

The assistant minister said “the market will not fix” issues with AI development, a contrast to the United States’ approach of letting companies operate with a degree of self-regulation. Charlton raised concerns that “frontier labs are putting capability ahead of safety”, positing that Australia can have the most impact on the development of AI by hosting and influencing frontier labs.
“AI needs regulating because its harms are severe, hard to undo, borne by people who never chose them, and sometimes invisible until they arrive,” he said.
“The market will not fix this alone, because the incentives reward speed and capability, and even the people at the top of the industry cannot slow down by themselves.”
Do you know more? Email josh.butler@theguardian.com

items.title: AI chip boom pushes Samsung profits to record $80bn
paragraphs: Samsung Electronics says it expects a nine-fold surge in its quarterly profits compared with a year earlier, driven by surging demand for memory chips used in artificial intelligence (AI) data centres.
The tech giant estimates that its operating profit for the three months to the end of September will jump to 107.4tn won (£61bn; $80bn), its fourth quarter in a row of record earnings.
Samsung is one of the world's largest memory chip makers alongside local rival SK Hynix and Micron in the US, which produce chips crucial for AI firms like Nvidia.
Samsung, which makes the Galaxy Fold and S26 smartphones, is also expected to get a boost from its latest folding devices that were launched in August.
The firm's full third-quarter earnings will be released at the end of October.
Major South Korean companies tend to release previews of their earnings to advise investors ahead of more detailed reports.
There has been huge global demand for computer chips that power AI development, helping to lift the earnings and shares of manufacturers linked to the technology.
The surge in demand in recent years has resulted in a shortage of semiconductors globally, pushing up sales for firms like Samsung.
SK Hynix and Samsung's stock market valuations crossed $1tn (£757bn) earlier this year, though their shares have since come down following concerns that tech stocks have been overvalued.

items.title: Fuel prices added to Google Maps as petrol and diesel costs soar
paragraphs: Google Maps will now show fuel prices to help motorists find cheaper petrol and diesel in the UK as costs continue to soar.
From Thursday, a search for forecourts on the app will display their locations as well as their pricing, using data supplied via the government's Fuel Finder scheme.
It is a legal requirement for UK forecourts to add their prices to Fuel Finder within 30 minutes of changing them.
It comes days after the price of diesel topped £2 per litre for the first time, which RAC policy head Simon Williams described as "a price threshold no one wanted to cross".
There are multiple apps dedicated to finding the cheapest fuel around, but Google Maps is used by 77% of Britain's adult population for general navigation, according to Ofcom.
Fuel costs around the world have been dramatically impacted by the US war with Iran and Russia's war with Ukraine.
Diesel price has since fallen by 2p but the AA says an average 55 litre tank of diesel still costs around £110, with the petrol equivalent coming to around £96.
The feature is already part of the navigation app Waze, which is used by around 2 million people in the UK.
Apple Maps does not show the price of fuel, although some third-party apps can link to its maps on iPhones.
Some experts say Fuel Finder is not entirely reliable.

"At the moment, we still have to supplement the Government's Fuel Finder feed with other data sources because, on its own, it does not provide the level of coverage and accuracy needed to deliver a complete and reliable service to motorists," said Clare Lafferty, director at the price comparison site PetrolPrices.
"There are still sites that have not registered with the scheme at all, alongside sites that have registered but are not consistently updating their prices within the required timeframe."
She said the firm identified 200 forecourts in September which it did not believe had updated its diesel prices in time.
Sarah-Jayne Williams, director of product partnerships for Google Maps and Waze, said the firm would check the data independently, and would not display prices it believed were not up-to-date.
"Accuracy is very important, so we will still show the petrol station and where it is, but you'll only see a price if we have high confidence that it's the right price," she said.
The Retail Motor Industry Federation, which represents thousands of UK forecourts and petrol retailers, said its members were complying.
Fuel Finder was launched in February by former chancellor Rachel Reeves, who said at the time it could save households £40 per year.

items.title: UN says committed to work with Pakistan for voluntary returns of Afghan refugees
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Pashto article.

U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres says the United Nations will work with Pakistan to “uphold protection principles and ensure that returns of Afghans proceed in a voluntary, safe and dignified way.”

Speaking at a joint news conference with Pakistani Foreign Minister Mohammad Ishaq Dar in Islamabad on Tuesday, Guterres said the U.N. is committed to working with Pakistan on the issue of Afghan refugees.

Pakistan has continued the forcible deportation of Afghan refugees since 2023, when the country started the first phase of the Interior Ministry's Illegal Foreigners’ Repatriation Plan to deport undocumented immigrants and refugees.
The U.N. Organization for International Migration says more than 2.68 million Afghans returned from Pakistan between September of 2023 and August of this year.
The U.N. reported that in 2026 about 776,000 Afghans returned to Afghanistan, including those forcibly deported.
“Many Afghan returnees continue to face significant human rights violations and protection risks inside Afghanistan,” said the U.N.
According to the U.N., about 1.6 million Afghans, including 160,000 undocumented refugees, are still living in Pakistan.

Thirty-year-old Asadullah Safi was born in Pakistan, where his family lived for more than 40 years in a refugee camp near Peshawar City. Now, he faces deportation to a country where he has never lived.
Safi told VOA that Pakistani security forces destroyed his family’s home and forced them to leave the camp. He now lives in hiding in a makeshift shelter.

“Pakistan is forcing us to leave,” Safi said, noting that “in Afghanistan, people don’t have shelters. There is nowhere [for us] to go. There are no services in Afghanistan and girls’ schools are closed there.”
Abdul Hamid Jalili, former Afghan attaché for refugees in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, told VOA that the forcible deportation of Afghan refugees could bring about “a humanitarian crisis.”
“It is not only returning. They need employment, shelter, and public services there,” Jalili said.
He added that Afghanistan, given its current political and economic situation, cannot accommodate that many returnees and that international aid is no longer available at the levels it once was.

The U.N. reported in May that Afghanistan is facing a humanitarian and economic crisis as millions of people struggle to access essentials, including water, food, healthcare, housing, heating and clothing.
“The international community should have serious talks with Pakistan to find a way to solve the problem,” said Safi.

items.title: Taliban's ban on girls' education "unacceptable" says UN official
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Dari article.
The head of the United Nations Development Program (UNDP) says that the ban on girls’ education in Afghanistan is “totally unacceptable” and represents a “very poor” development policy.

In an interview with Foreign Policy last week, UNDP head Alexander De Croo said that in Afghanistan where “half of the population’s talent is not being used,” failing to tap that potential is “just really poor policy” given the ‘gigantic’ needs in the country.

After returning to power in 2021, the Taliban imposed repressive restrictions on women, barring them from secondary and university education, working in government agencies and non-government organizations, going to public parks, beauty salons and gyms, and traveling long distances without a close male relative.
In 2021, some Taliban officials said that the decision to ban girls’ secondary education was temporary; however, girls have not been allowed to go to school in Afghanistan since then.
The U.N. reported in August that the Taliban ban excluded an estimated 2.4 million girls from secondary education.
Human Rights Watch in August reported that the Taliban’s ‘draconian’ policies made Afghanistan “one of the world’s gravest human rights crises, particularly for women and girls.”
The Taliban have not changed their position on girls’ education and women’s rights despite the international pressure on the group.
De Croo said that his organization had “very difficult conversations” with the group about the issue, but “we do not think turning our back on Afghanistan today is a good idea.”
He added that Afghanistan faces multiple challenges, including a 20% economic contraction, natural disasters, conflicts with neighboring countries and the return of refugees.
“If we turn out back on it, you can almost guarantee that we will bear the consequences five, 10 years down the road,” added De Coor.

items.title: UN Special Rapporteur says families of executed protesters in Iran subject to regime's pressure
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Persian article.

The U.N. Special Rapporteur on human rights in Iran says the consequences of the death penalty in the Islamic Republic are not limited to the person executed, as families face pressure and punishment, as well as restrictions on mourning the dead.

Mai Sato made the comment Wednesday, referring to the execution of Alireza Sepahi, a protestor who was arrested last year and remained imprisoned until his death sentence was carried out on October 5.
His family members say they were not allowed to transfer his body to Isfahan — where they are from -- for burial. He was buried in Kashan, away from his family's place of residence.

The U.N. Special Rapporteur underscored that families of those sentenced to death in Iran face measures such as the regime forces' refusal to hand over the body to the family, placing restrictions on the place of burial and mourning, depriving families of a last visit, and threats of arrest or prosecution.
In a post on X, Sato said “Losing a loved one is painful, but being unable to speak about their story, honor their life, or come together to mourn inflicts further needless suffering.”
“Withholding a body or forcing a family to bury elsewhere is a tactic to control the narrative, silence the living and supress remembrance,” Sato added.

Aside from Sepahi, the Islamic Republic's Judiciary Branch has confirmed the execution of Alireza Raeisi, two detainees of last year's protests in Isfahan. Human rights sources have expressed concern about the judicial processes in the case, including reports of torture, forced confessions, and restrictions placed on their rights to gain access to a lawyer.

A U.S. State Department spokesman told VOA on background regarding Iran's recent executions of two protesters that “We strongly condemn the Iranian regime’s use of execution as a tool of political repression. This is a regime that brutally killed thousands of peaceful protestors in January.

“For too long, the regime has subjected the Iranian people to torture, forced confessions, and sham trials, resulting in unlawful executions. Today, civilians are being used as scapegoats for the regime’s military and economic failures.”

items.title: The new Microsoft Surface Ultra is literally built for multi-disciplinary creatives
paragraphs: Microsoft has put a price on the Surface Laptop Ultra, and confirmed launch dates. Pre-orders are open now from $2,599, with shipments expected to begin on 16 October.

The Microsoft Surface Ultra is coming for the MacBook Pro in its power, performance and portability. It's aimed at creators running intensive workflows, apparently it can run heavy code, render a film in Da Vinci at the same time as running a AAA title game. The Microsoft showcase told a story of one creator creating a scene in Blender, passing it to Unreal Engine and then into Photoshop. The process took hours rather than the usual days but, of course, we haven't tested it yet. This may be heading to the top of our best laptop for 3D modelling guide.

The important feature for creatives is how the Ultra uses memory. Its RTX Spark chip lets the processor and graphics share a single pool of up to 128GB, rather than splitting resources between the two. In practice, that could mean complex 3D scenes and long video timelines that would overwhelm the graphics memory of a typical laptop. We'll need real-world testing to see how it plays out in a heavy Blender scene or a packed Premiere Pro timeline.

Nvidia says the platform can run large AI models directly on the machine, up to 120 billion parameters. For artists experimenting with AI tools, that points to a future where more of that work happens on your own laptop instead of through cloud services. Microsoft quotes up to 1 petaflop of AI performance, though that's a manufacturer figure and we haven't seen it tested yet.

This is being pitched as a revolutionary laptop ecosystem, which draws on many huge players in creative tech to provide everything a creative needs. What do you think of the offer – and the price point?

items.title: US Embassy warns Americans about suspected plague case in Russia
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Russian article.

The U.S. Embassy in Russia is warning Americans about a suspected case of pneumonic plague and stressed that U.S. citizens should "refrain from travel" to Russia, and those already in the country should leave immediately.

"The U.S. Embassy is aware of media reports from the Irkutsk region regarding a suspected fatal case of pneumonic plague, as well as the associated quarantine measures and hospital closures in Irkutsk. We continue to closely monitor the situation," the embassy said in a statement Tuesday

The day before, the United States sent Russia an official request for information regarding a recent death of a lab worker. U.S. President Donald Trump told reporters at the White House that he had scheduled a phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin.

"We call on Russia to be transparent and to share more information with the world so that we can all respond accordingly," Secretary of State Marco Rubio said at a press conference in Iceland this week.

Twenty-eight-year-old lab worker Daria Shipilova died on October 2 in the intensive care unit of the Shelekhov district hospital in Irkutsk Region. According to local media, she broke a test tube containing the plague pathogen.

Irkutsk Governor Igor Kobzev said on Telegram on Monday that Shipilova's death was caused by pneumonia of unknown origin. According to the governor, no new cases of the disease have been recorded among other employees of the research institute.

Epidemiologist Dr. Michael Favorov, president of the Atlanta-based DiaPrep System Inc. advisory group, told VOA that Russia seemingly followed the protocols to contain the possible plague outbreak and that the risk to the U.S. is low.

“From the point of view of the United States, the chance of the spread of infection is zero. You can't really say that as epidemiologists call it close to zero because you never know what might happen,” said Favorov, who previously worked for the U.S. Centers for Disease Control.
CDC Director Erica Schwartz on Wednesday also said she believed any risk to the U.S. was low.

"What we're doing from a whole of government standpoint is we're making sure that we understand exactly what that threat is," Schwartz said at an event in Washington. "We are very confident that the threat to the United States is extremely low."
The WHO says it is contact with Russia over the recent death of the lab worker and is monitoring the situation.

“They informed WHO that an epidemiological investigation had been conducted, preventive and control measures implemented, and identified contacts placed under medical observation and tested,” WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said in a statement.

items.title: Iraq devalues dinar to ease economic pressure
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Kurdish article.

The Central Bank of Iraq announced that effective Wednesday it has changed the official exchange rate of the Iraqi dinar against the U.S. dollar, citing current economic and financial conditions and a recommendation from the country's Council of Ministers.

Under the new rates, the Central Bank will purchase U.S. dollars from the Ministry of Finance at 1,500 dinars per dollar and sell them to banks at 1,510 dinars. Banks will sell dollars to the public at 1,520 dinars.
Before the decision, the official selling rate to the public was 1,320 dinars per dollar. The increase to 1,520 represents a significant devaluation of the Iraqi currency.
The Central Bank said Iraq's foreign currency reserves remain sufficient to meet demand, including financing foreign trade, the use of bank cards abroad and providing dollars to travelers.

Mazhar Mohammed Salih, financial and economic adviser to the Iraqi prime minister, told VOA that the stability of the dinar depends largely on the availability of foreign currency and Iraq's ability to finance its foreign trade.

"Regional and international conditions, particularly conflicts and tensions in the region and their impact on oil transit through the Strait of Hormuz could affect oil revenues, the general budget and the flow of foreign currency," Salih said.

He said the government's current fiscal, tax, and customs measures are precautionary. Monetary policy will continue to manage the foreign currency market and provide dollars for foreign trade, while fiscal policy will seek to limit the effects of external economic shocks by managing government spending, revenues and taxes.

Addressing concerns about the impact of the weaker dinar on consumers, Salih said the Iraqi government would continue spending on food, medicine, fuel and basic services to reduce the impact of higher prices on citizens' purchasing power.

The decision has drawn opposition from members of the Iraqi parliament. Several lawmakers began collecting signatures seeking to reverse the measure, while parliament postponed its regular agenda on Wednesday to discuss the exchange rate.

Parliament later adjourned its session, and Speaker Mohammed al-Halbousi called on the governor of the Central Bank and the finance minister to appear before lawmakers early Thursday to explain the reasons for the decision and its expected economic and financial consequences.

The devaluation also triggered public concern and disruptions in some markets. Some shops, markets and currency exchange offices in Baghdad and several other provinces closed as the market exchange rate reportedly climbed to around 1,800 dinars per dollar.

The Central Bank, however, says adjusting the value of the dinar could provide longer-term benefits to the Iraqi economy by supporting domestic production and local industries, making Iraqi products more competitive, encouraging investment in non-oil sectors and creating new employment opportunities.

items.title: Secretary Bessent weighs in after Iran oil minister resigns
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Persian article.

U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has weighed in on the resignation of Iran’s oil minister earlier this week, and he suggested his replacement will have little work left, as a rigorous U.S. naval blockade halts Iran’s oil exports.
“Iran has a new oil minister. Considering Iran has not loaded a single barrel of crude onto a vessel since August 25th, what is the oil minister managing?” Bessent asked Tuesday in a post on X.
Hamid Bovard, the chief ‌executive of the Iran’s Oil Company was appointed after Mohsen Paknejad who held the post for over two years has resigned for “personal reasons.”

Bessent said the U.S. economic campaign against Iran is delivering results. He pointed to the free-fall of the value of the Iran's national currency, the rial, and the disruption in the transfer of crude oil over the past month. Iran’s currency was traded at 2.5 million rials against a U.S. dollar on Tuesday.

Bessent also cited statements made by high-ranking Iranian regime official acknowledging the deterioration of the country's economy as evident signs, including one of the regime’s senior security official, Mohsen Rezaei, the Secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, who had said the country was facing one of the most difficult periods in its history.
In a post on the social media platform X on Monday, Bessent wrote: “Economic outcast is delivering results."

“The Iranian regime allows its own people to suffer while it pours resources into terrorism,” he said. “Operation Economic Outcast will not stop until the Iranian regime understands that the Trump Administration will never allow the regime to fund terrorism and develop a nuclear weapon.”

Launched on August 24, 2026, Bessent said the aim of the economic pressure against Iran was to sever Tehran’s financial and economic connections and sources of revenue, while targeting networks that circumventing sanctions on Iran around the globe.
In addition, the U.S. Treasury Department has in recent weeks imposed new sanctions on Iran's aviation sector as well as its automotive, railway, steel, and manufacturing industries.
On October 1, the Department also sanctioned 10 individuals and entities in several countries for allegedly supplying weapons and parts to the Islamic Republic’s Ministry of Defense.

On the same day, the Treasury said it sanctioned A7 network, a Russian firm it alleged is used by the Iranian regime to evade sanctions. The Department also proposed measures that include establishing a rule that prohibits transmittals of funds involving A7 networks’ sub agents.

“Treasury is dismantling the financial infrastructure that allows Iran and other adversaries to evade sanctions, move illicit funds, and undermine the integrity of the global financial system,” said Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent.

Meanwhile, Mohsen Rezaei, a senior security official of the Islamic Republic, described Iran’s economic situation as one of the most difficult periods in the country’s history at a meeting of high-ranking regime officials on October 3, remarks that Secretary Bessent used as reference in his October 5th message.

Iran last month proposed a plan to reopen the strait, resume talks over its nuclear program, in return for the lifting of U.S. naval blockade, unfreezing of its assets and to be able to export its oil.
Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian told world leaders at the U.N General Assembly last month that that Tehran won’t yield to sanctions.
