items.title: WHO: Malnutrition is worsening in Afghanistan
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Pashto article.

Afghanistan faces a “serious and widespread” malnutrition problem, where more than 3.7 million children under the age of five face severe malnutrition, says a Kabul-based World Health Organization official.
“The number has increased this year to 3.7 million, and it is projected to increase even further in 2027,” said Ahmad Shakir Nasiry, national professional officer for nutrition for WHO in Kabul.
UNICEF reported last month that the malnutrition situation has worsened in Afghanistan, where about 1 million children, among the 3.7 million, are “with life-threatening severe acute malnutrition.”

The crisis “disproportionately affects the youngest and most vulnerable,” said Tajudeen Oyewale, UNICEF Representative in Afghanistan, in a statement, as four out of five children suffering from acute malnutrition are under the age of two.

Nasiri said that the malnutrition problem exists throughout the country, but conditions are particularly severe in the provinces of Helmand, Kandahar, Zabul, Paktika, Daikundi, Uruzgan, Kunduz, and Baghlan.
He said poverty and poor diets are the main causes of malnutrition.
“The most important causes are poverty and deprivation, poor diets, and particularly a lack of access to balanced, high-quality food,” Nasiri added.
In addition to economic problems and food insecurity, WHO stated that disease outbreaks, climate change, and access to health and nutrition services are compounding the situation.

Nasiri noted that malnutrition affects more than just children, with more than 1 million pregnant and breastfeeding women also facing malnutrition. “A malnourished mother gives birth to a vulnerable child, and the effects can extend to future generations,” he said.
Nasiri said measures should be taken to strengthen prevention alongside treatment so that children can be diagnosed and treated early.
“My most important recommendation is to preserve and strengthen Afghanistan’s health system, because it depends on international assistance,” said Nasiri.
He warned that delays in funding health programs, however, would increase both human and financial costs in the country in the future.

items.title: Why a mine blast in Demilitarized Zone fuels tensions between the Koreas
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Korean article.

The U.S.-led United Nations Command this week determined that North Korea violated the 1953 armistice agreement with South Korea, after landmine explosions injured three South Korean soldiers inside the Demilitarized Zone. Investigators found an operational North Korean mine south of the Military Demarcation Line, the dividing line established under the 1953 Korean War armistice.

South Korea’s military subsequently concluded that deliberately planted North Korean mines caused the September 21 explosions. It cleared the identified minefield on October 5 and said it would continue clearance operations unless North Korea removed the mines itself.

Pyongyang denies responsibility. In an October 6 statement carried by its state news agency, North Korea’s Foreign Ministry warned of a forceful response if South Korean troops crossed into territory Pyongyang considers its own.
The dispute combines an immediate safety threat with longstanding differences over how the boundary’s precise location is identified.
The explosions occurred on September 21 in the western DMZ near Paju, in an area controlled by South Korea’s 25th Infantry Division.
South Korea soldiers were opening a reconnaissance route to allow the United Nations Command to investigate an area suspected of containing North Korean mines.
The first explosion occurred as the soldiers withdrew. A second followed during efforts to rescue the wounded.
South Korea’s military said two soldiers sustained serious injuries, and one suffered minor injuries.
South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff announced its final findings on October 5, following a joint field investigation with United Nations Command conducted from September 26 to 29.
The military cited three main types of evidence – the location of the sites, the placement of the mines, and the remnants of the exploded mines.

GPS measurements placed both explosion sites and the recovered North Korean mine about 10 meters south of the Military Demarcation Line, according to the South Korean military’s account of the joint investigation.

Investigators found buried mines and assessed their spacing and the surrounding terrain. Lieutenant General Kwon Dae-won, the Joint Chiefs’ vice chairman, said the United Nations Command assessed that the recovered mine had been deliberately placed. South Korean investigators also concluded that the mines had not simply washed into the area.

Tests by South Korea’s National Forensic Service detected TNT on the wounded soldiers’ clothing and thermosetting resin in fragments recovered from clothing and during surgery. Further analysis found that the fragments matched the material used in previously recovered North Korean plastic antipersonnel mines.
The military said it received the final forensic results on October 2.
Why does the United Nations Command’s finding matter?

The United Nations Command oversees implementation of the 1953 armistice, which halted fighting in the Korean War. The agreement established a buffer zone extending two kilometers on either side of the Military Demarcation Line.
On September 30, the command announced that investigators had found an operational North Korean antipersonnel mine south of the line and determined that an armistice violation had occurred.
It said the violation would be addressed through established armistice mechanisms.

South Korea’s October 5 announcement separately identified North Korean mines as the cause of the explosions. The two findings should be distinguished: the command announced the discovery of a mine and an armistice violation, while South Korea presented its final assessment of what caused the injuries.
Many of the original markers identifying the Military Demarcation Line have deteriorated or disappeared.

South Korea’s military said only about 200 of the original 1,292 markers remain identifiable. Different maps and methods of connecting the surviving markers can produce discrepancies in the line’s precise location.
The military said it uses a reference based on a 2004 map from the U.S. National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency. The United Nations Command uses a reference developed through a 2016 mapping project.
South Korean officials have also said North Korea may use a different interpretation of the boundary.
South Korea’s Defense Ministry said on October 6 that a task force established earlier this year has been working to align the South Korean military’s and the command’s boundary references.
Kim Yo Jong, an official from North Korea's Workers’ Party, rejected responsibility in statements issued on September 30 and October 2.

She described the incident as a South Korean fabrication, threatened retaliation if South Korean forces fired on North Korean troops and dismissed a proposal for communication over identifying and measuring the boundary.
North Korea’s Foreign Ministry reiterated the denial on October 6, according to North Korea's state-run Korean Central News Agency.

It said Pyongyang would not concern itself with South Korea’s removal of mines that North Korea maintained were unrelated to it. But it warned of an immediate, forceful response if South Korean troops crossed into territory Pyongyang considers its own.
What has South Korea done, and what could happen next?
South Korea’s military said it cleared the identified minefield at 12:51 p.m. on October 5.
It said the operation was coordinated with the United Nations Command and conducted with precautions against further accidents or an unintended military clash.

Seoul has demanded an apology for the soldiers’ injuries and called on Pyongyang to remove mines installed in violation of the armistice. The military said it would continue clearance operations if North Korea did not remove them voluntarily.
On October 6, South Korea’s Defense Ministry said it was considering additional responses to press North Korea for an apology, without disclosing specific measures.
Any further clearance operations would take place amid competing accounts of the incident and differing interpretations of the boundary’s precise location.
South Korea’s military says it will coordinate with the United Nations Command on removing mines south of the line while taking steps to prevent an accidental clash.

items.title: Tropical Storm Isaias forecast to become first Atlantic hurricane of 2026
paragraphs: Satellite imagery shows thunderstorms clumping together to form Tropical Storm Isaias.
Tropical Storm Isaias has formed in the Gulf of Mexico and looks likely to strengthen into the first Atlantic hurricane of this year.
It is expected to reach hurricane strength by Thursday morning with forecasts suggesting it could then intensify to a category two storm.

It has the potential to bring damaging winds, torrential rain and a storm surge to parts of the US Gulf Coast with landfall expected on Friday or Saturday. Hurricane and Storm Surge Watches have been issued.
Isaias will bring an end to the lack of hurricanes that has led to a record-breakingly quiet Atlantic season so far with development suppressed by the growing El Niño pattern.

In its latest update, the US National Hurricane Center estimates that Tropical Storm Isaias is likely to reach hurricane strength by the start of Thursday. It will intensify further, reaching category 2 by Friday morning.
Parts of Mexico will feel the first impacts as the storm swirls out at sea, with 4in (100mm) of rain possible around the Bay of Campeche and the Yucatan Peninsula, accompanied by strong winds.
Isaias will then make landfall on the Gulf Coast - probably in Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama or Florida - late on Friday or early on Saturday.
Damaging winds, torrential rain and coastal flooding are the major risks from the developing hurricane
Between 3 and 6in (75-150mm) of rain could fall across the Gulf Coast, from south-east Louisiana to north-west Florida.
A few places could see up to 10in (250mm) with possible flash flooding, especially in urban areas, and the risk of isolated river flooding.
Dangerous winds are anticipated and a storm surge could inundate low-lying coastal areas.
The US National Weather Service has issued Hurricane and Storm Surge Watches along the Gulf Coast.
Florida Governor Ron DeSantis has declared a state of emergency across 25 counties over concerns about potential impacts.

As the storm moves further inland and loses contact with its warm water fuel source it will weaken but it is still expected to bring some potentially disruptive wet weather for large swathes of the south-east USA as far north as the Tennessee Valley and the Carolinas.
Forecasters in the US had predicted the 2026 hurricane season would be quieter than average - and so far this has come to pass.
Isaias is the ninth tropical storm of the Atlantic season, but will be the first to become a hurricane.
The developing strong El Niño in the Pacific Ocean is responsible. It leads to more wind shear over the Caribbean and Atlantic, which can tear storms apart before they have time to develop.
This lowers the odds of hurricane formation but does not make it impossible.
Isaias has managed to form in an area with limited wind shear and very high sea temperatures - currently 30 or 31C - giving it the fuel it needs to grow.

Forecasters expect it to encounter more wind shear as it moves northwards over the next few days which should limit its intensification somewhat - but exact forecasts are likely to shift over the coming days.

items.title: OpenAI’s release of mathematical findings draws concerns from experts
paragraphs: OpenAI has astounded mathematicians after releasing hundreds of new mathematical findings on Tuesday.

The company published over 370 mathematical results across a variety of topics such as algebra, theoretical computer science and mathematical logic, showcasing what some of its most advanced artificial intelligence models are capable of.
Last month, the company solved the Navier-Stokes equation, one of the world’s toughest mathematical problems with a $1m reward for anyone who cracked it.

The achievement prompted concerns from leaders in the field who say that frontier labs should not be testing the most advanced mathematical problems on proprietary AI models that are not accessible to the broader field of mathematicians. The Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, New Jersey, an independent group of mathematical experts, said that it does not endorse the practice.

“It is now the case that AI can output mathematical arguments in situations without the human who prompted it being able to understand the arguments, verify them, or take responsibility for them,” a statement from the organization read. “We believe that human understanding of mathematics remains of paramount importance. How, in this new era, can we work towards a new paradigm that includes human understanding of mathematics as part of responsible scholarly output?”
To address concerns from the mathematics community, OpenAI announced it would work with the Institute for Advanced Study in order to give “mathematicians a voice in how we move forward”.

The company did not indicate, however, that it would stop testing its AI models with these advanced problems. Experts in the field say they worry OpenAI is not doing the due diligence required to vet these results.

In an interview with the New York Times, Tristan Buckmaster, a New York University mathematician who was working on the Navier-Strokes problem, said mathematicians who were prompting AI models to solve equations could be providing information that helped the model get to the result.
“There’s likely to be a bunch of results where they take someone’s work and then take it to completion,” Buckmaster said.
The advisory board has also asked that AI labs grant “equitable access” to their AI models to the global mathematics community.

“The use of proprietary internal models by AI labs to do mathematical research risks creating a two-tier system where labs outrun the rest of the field, effectively alienating the mathematical community from its own discipline,” the group wrote.

items.title: Crush-worthy photography, camp sci-fi and a centenarian’s florals: five free exhibitions to see
paragraphs: If it’s a crime to have a crush on an elderly avant garde Japanese street photographer then lock me up and throw away the key, because I have some seriously strong feelings for Daidō Moriyama. His ultra-confrontational, high contrast, aggressive take on photography just gets me blushing, what can I say.

This little exhibition is Moriyama at his artiest and strangest. In the 1960s he discovered Warhol and became obsessed. The works here find him playing with repetition and silk screening, printing up ghostly, painterly, effervescent monochrome images of stacks of soft drinks, neon lit crosswalks and peep show adverts. This is the grim, gritty side of Japanese urbanity, but you can see American capitalism creeping in and taking hold, slowly suffocating the streets.

He repeats an image of lips like Warhol’s Marilyn Monroe, duplicates a photo of people walking down a street, their bodies becoming indistinguishable from the adverts hanging from the high rises around them. Then he snaps a woman lifting her skirt, another stomping down the road in thigh-high boots. It’s like Warhol without the pretence, and with added filth. Hamiltons Gallery, London, until 30 October
Jenkin van Zyl is hellbent on cementing their place as English art’s ultimate hyper-camp weirdo, and their new show at Somerset House Studios is a pretty persuasive argument.

The exhibition is centred on a speculative sci-fi movie about some bleak company where tourists can inhabit other people’s bodies. But when the central character, a starlet called Mercy, comes to end the lease on her body, the line between reality and fiction starts getting anxiously blurry. Who is the real Mercy, and who is the clone? Who controls your identity? Who has access to what makes you you?

Its grubby atmosphere is reinforced by an immersive installation that replicates the film set as you walk in, with broken automatons, flickering lights and piles of rubbish, all bathed in a pink glow. It’s an unsettling, uncomfortable, dirty, dystopian bit of art cinema – like an overblown, fetishistic take on Terry Gilliam’s Brazil. Van Zyl has a singular aesthetic, and this is pretty much as watchable as this kind of art film gets. It stays with you long after you’ve escaped its unnerving clutches.

The gallery handout wants to make out like this is about technological advancement and ideas of authorship. But like all good sci-fi, this feels more obviously allegorical than that. It’s about identity, the versions of ourselves that we present and preserve online, or in public, and how easy it is to lose your grip on the true you. Like a lot of artists these days who grew up with the internet and reality TV turning their brain into gloop, Van Zyl is trying to make sense of a post-reality world, a place where identity can be constructed, but never fully controlled. Somerset House, London, until 29 November

There’s nothing all that pleasant, or even particularly green, about the England of George Shaw’s paintings. There are no rolling hills or quiet pub afternoons here in this excellent show of small works by the 60-year-old artist. Instead, there are endless potholes, crumbling masonry, darkened alleys and damp, muddy, miserable, mid-winter landscapes. This is the England of council estates left to rot.

His landscapes – always based on his native Coventry – are devoid of life. There are no humans here, only the places they’re desperate to escape. Every sky is overcast, every tree barren, every path sodden with puddles. A union jack has been left crumpled on the pavement near an empty bottle of booze in one, endless knobs have been crudely graffitied on garage doors in another. There’s a painting of a single cloud blighting a blue sky, another of a robin lying dead on its side. Suburbia has leached into the countryside like a toxic spill.
They are gorgeously painted, especially the smaller works: sticky with enamel, glossy and horrifyingly alluring, like staring at a car crash.

But the car crash here is England itself. Sure, Shaw has been painting the same views of the same bit of Coventry for 30 years, but in that time the country has continued to erode. His whole career is a living portrait of England’s slow collapse. This time it doesn’t just feel like perpetual decline – it’s terminal. Anthony Wilkinson Gallery, London, until 7 November

The thing that’s so good about the main work in Tanoa Sasraku’s Turner prize installation – open now at Mima in Middlesbrough – is how perfectly it marries image with idea. Sasraku’s collection of corporate paperweights from oil companies acts as a horrifying symbol of the greed of that vile industry. Perfect.

Here at Vardaxoglou, Sasraku is showing works from another series, some of which are also on show at Mima, that don’t quite hit the same dopamine receptors. They’re all paper cut into the form of torsos, held together with clips. She places acetates of military camouflage on top of them and then pops them in a tanning bed, leaving behind the faintest impressions of the patterns.

They’re meant to evoke warfare, weapons crates and fruit boxes, all while alluding to Ken dolls, but they just look a bit like tea-stained gilets. The gap between image and idea, between the concept and its ability to communicate itself visually, is just a bit too wide. Vardaxoglou, London, until 31 October

items.title: World's largest penguin colony hit by 'alarming' decline in numbers
paragraphs: Chinstrap penguins get their name from a thin ring of feathers from ear to ear
Almost two-thirds of the population of chinstrap penguins have disappeared from a remote volcanic island near Antarctica, aerial surveys suggest.
Zavodovski Island was home to the largest penguin colony in the world, but researchers who carried out the surveys say it has now lost that accolade.
According to the study, there were 63% fewer occuplied nests of chinstrap penguins in 2025 than at the same time in 2011.
The research team say climate change is affecting the birds' food supply and survival, and the penguins may now be officially endangered.
Another species of penguin, the macaroni, also nests on the island and is thriving, which scientists believe is linked to their more varied diet.
The scientists used drones and trackers to study the penguin colony
Zavodovski is part of the South Sandwich Islands, a remote archipelago north of the Antarctic continent which is a UK overseas territory.

In 2011, it was hailed by the British Antarctic Survey (BAS) as home to the largest penguin colony in the world - with an estimated 600,000 chinstrap penguins and 90,000 macaroni penguins nesting on its bleak, rocky terrain.
BAS, which led this new research, says it is "one of the most extreme places in the world to undertake fieldwork".
A BAS team sailed for 15 days to reach the island and study its avian inhabitants, using drones, aerial photography and fitting tracking devices to 20 birds.
This research and satellite imagery suggested that - between 2011 and 2025 - the number of occupied chinstrap penguin nests declined by 63%.
Macaroni penguin populations increased as chinstrap penguins declined
The researchers say the "alarming" fall in the chinstrap population is all about the food supply and rising ocean temperatures brought about by climate change.
Prof Norman Ratcliffe, who led the research, explained that the chinstraps' "specialist diet" and preference for cooler waters appears to have left them vulnerable.
"With waters warming, the krill [that the chinstrap penguins eat] have moved southwards.
"Sea-ice cover to the south and a lack of suitable islands for nesting prevents chinstraps from following the food," he said.

The team examined other possible threats to the penguins' precarious existence on their remote island. Birds here nest in the shadow of an active volcano - Mount Curry, also aptly known as Mount Asphyxsia.
Sites downwind of the volcano have been given names including Stench Point, Noxious Bluff and Asphyxia Plain, because of the smell of fumes emitted from the crater.
Dr Ratcliffe told BBC News: "When you add all the penguin guano on top of that, and you really do have one of the smelliest places in the world.
Mount Curry's last major eruption was back in 2016, but the penguin declines that this study analysed have been steady and ongoing since 2011, suggesting that something else was happening.

Another concern was competition for the krill that chinstrap penguins rely on - possibly from migrating humpback whales. But, while the humpbacks eat huge quantities of krill, they also help boost krill production by fertilising marine plants that the krill feed on (with their huge quantities of whale poo).
Researchers say a more fundamental, climate-driven shift in ocean food supplies is to blame.
Two chinstrap penguins on Zavodovski Island

There is an unexpected element of this story that also adds to the picture of how - and why - this region is changing: While the chinstrap population has been declining, the number of macaroni penguins on the island has increased dramatically.
Macaroni penguins, scientists say, are more adaptable, because they have a broader, more flexible diet.

Tracking data from the study showed that the macaronis foraged in warmer waters to the northeast of the island, where scientists say they were were likely to be supplementing their diets with fish and other crustaceans.
Dr Ratcliffe said this shift was "biggest change in community composition ever observed at a single location in Antarctica".
"Our data shows that the cold-adapted Antarctic chinstrap species are no longer thriving beside their sub-Antarctic neighbours," he added.
"It is further evidence of how rapid warming in the Antarctic is impacting unique and sensitive ecosystems."
As for the title of world's largest penguin colony, scientists say that is now held by a site more than 5,000km away - on the other side of the Antarctic continent - Cape Adare in the Ross Sea.
The research is published in the journal Current Biology, external.
Zavodovski's penguins nest in the shadow of an active volcano

items.title: Robert Ryman review – can your brain handle a show that only has white paintings?
paragraphs: Writing about painting is a futile exercise at the best of times. This is especially the case when, as with Robert Ryman, the paintings in question are variations on the theme of white. If that sounds pretentious – or like a tired joke – then it might also be understood as a reaction against the dependence of so much art on language (which is also to say, bullshit). Because these bare-bones paintings – white paint, a flat surface, wall fixtures – are the “real thing” in the most literal way: they are not trying to tell you a story, they do not require you to be familiar with any abstruse theories. There is just you and the materials, how the paint lies, how it scatters the light. So the question is: how much do you like looking at paint?

Happily for me, given that it is a non-negotiable part of my job, I really like looking at paint. If you also like looking at paint, then there is much in this exhibition that will take your breath away. Take The Painting of the Mysterious Shadow from the mid-60s, after Ryman had left his job as a guard at MoMA, having given up on a career as a jazz musician, and settled into the project that would occupy the rest of his life. Six thick white stripes run horizontally across the canvas, as close to each other as can be managed by a steady hand without overlapping. The fabric is stretched over a deep wooden frame, meaning that its surface sits about three inches off the wall, and casts a thin shadow upon it. That’s your lot.

And it is a lot, if you are willing to go with it. Under this diffuse light, and against the warmer white of the walls, the surface of the painting comes to look grey-bluish. Because the eye adjusts the intensity of a colour by reference to those surrounding it, the previously imperceptible difference between those two shades of paint comes to seem dramatic. When I opened up my notebook to record this effect, I found that its pages, which had been white, were now a ghastly yellow-brown. This is exemplary of how Ryman’s intense focus on a narrow band of perception opens up worlds within it. And if you can sustain the same level of attention through the show, it will offer up revelations.

Because Ryman could do it all, within his tightly circumscribed field. His use of different white paints allows you to focus on how his handling of the material, by turns delicate and heavy handed, rough and precise, changes its effects. The gorgeous scuff of white cloud looks like it would lift the work titled Concert to the ceiling, were it not for the four screws fixing its fibreglass surface so conspicuously to the wall; an untitled 1958 work is slathered in a bilious yellow-white that, in combination with Ryman’s cartoonish signature, conjures a welcome energy. The numinous Surface Veil II stages the meeting of some lavender-tinted atmospherics with a cold front on a monumental scale. Most remarkable of all is the 13-part suite Standard, here installed as an immersive environment that stays just the right side of the forced transcendentalism that so dates the work of some of his peers.

These effects are made possible by the Barbican’s intelligent installation. Recognising that this is a demanding show even for true believers, benches direct viewers to the works most likely to open up under the pressure of their gaze. Refreshingly clear and intelligent texts are removed from the immaculate walls to a well-designed pamphlet. And yet, even as my eye adjusted to the point that I could identify (even revel in) the fractional discrepancies of white that animate these works, the law of diminishing returns began to take effect. And the question at the back of my mind returned to the front: does any of this matter? Is all of this just an exercise in academic connoisseurship?

In defences against that claim, Ryman’s work is vulnerable to what you might call the emperor’s new clothes inverted: namely, that if you present an art historian with a plain piece of white fabric, they will tell you that they have discovered the emperor beneath it. Ryman was not interested in justifying his paintings by grandiose theories, and neither am I. Instead, he chased after an indefinable “wellbeing and rightness” that might be understood as a harmonious arrangement of homogenous elements. Because Ryman’s unframed paintings bleed into the white walls, this rightness comes to be a function of the architectural environment. The gallery resembles heaven as imagined by a 1950s melodrama.

It might be that I am not ready for heaven. Because I came to feel trapped in this controlled space, so thoroughly insulated from the outside world. Neither the crises through which Ryman lived (as the literature notes) nor those of the present can penetrate it. His intense focus on a narrow band of colour might provide a momentary refuge from the stories that are crowding in on our lives. But there is no neutral colour, and no neutral space. In our historical moment, this show feels more like an escape from reality than a confrontation with it.
Robert Ryman: The Real Thing is at Barbican Art Gallery, London, from 8 October to 28 February

items.title: What the £350 Grand Theft Auto ‘collector’s box’ says about the escalating cost of gaming
paragraphs: As a parent (and partner) to a habitual collector, I do feel like an unwelcome portion of my life is occupied by an endless war against stuff. Surfaces in my home ceaselessly accumulate piles of random objects: a JoyCon wrist strap, a sticker sheet, an unidentifiable plastic piece of a toy or gizmo, an Xbox 360 controller with no batteries, cases for Switch cartridges lost down the side of the sofa … Stuff encroaches everywhere, especially in a gaming household. Much as I regret the imminent disappearance of physical games, I do not regret the extra space I have in my attic as a result of switching almost entirely to downloaded games over the last decade or so.

Speaking of the imminent disappearance of physical games: Rockstar recently announced a £350 ($400) “collector’s box” of Grand Theft Auto 6 goodies … that doesn’t include the game itself. Not even a download code. The Grand Theft Auto VI: The Goodtime State – Vice City Collection, to give it its full and unwieldy name, contains a hat, a bag, a pair of sunglasses, a figurine, a poster and more, including a mirror and a “swizzle spoon” that looks, unambigiously, like a cocaine spoon. The game retails at £70, so if you want something to play alongside all your stuff, you’re looking at an outlay of £420.

I’m not about to rag on this box of merch. People love this kind of stuff, and as a lifelong collector of Japanese gatcha and blind-box toys, I am in no position to judge how people spend their money. I have a few video game special editions that I cherish – the statue that came with my copy of The Last Guardian is still on my shelf – though I also have many more that are relegated to various cupboards. But it is unusual, however, for them to be this expensive. Usually with gaming special editions, we’re talking an extra £20-50 for a statue, or a steelbook, maybe a booklet and a keyring. 2009’s Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2’s “prestige edition” came with night vision goggles for $150. In 2015, Fallout 4’s $120 collector’s edition shipped with a plastic Pip Boy wrist unit (I had one; alas, it was flimsy and disappointing).

There have been some infamously expensive gaming special editions down the years, some of which were PR stunts (see Saints Row IV’s million-dollar pack, which included a Lamborghini and cosmetic surgery – nobody bought it). But in the 2020s high-priced video game merchandise has become more common, from a Balenciaga PlayStation tie-in line to £580 for Pokémon Lego.

What’s behind this is a troubling sense that video games as we once conceived of them – console games, played at home, perhaps on a nice 4K TV – have become a luxury item. People who can afford to spend up to £790 for a console and games are perhaps now people who can afford an extra £350 for a box of merch. Continual price-rises from Xbox and PlayStation suggest that video game companies do not seem particularly worried about pricing people out. Super-expensive merch and special editions like GTA 6’s form part of the same upward trend.

This stratification of the gaming world has been happening for years, ever since the first smartphones. The vast majority of the world’s players – about 80%, according to Newzoo – play for free, or at low cost, on mobile phones. The remaining 20% of players account for a disproportionate share of spending on the high-end gaming market on consoles and PC. With merch boxes like this, games companies are really going after that 20% for all they’ve got.

I’m saddened by the idea of gaming becoming even more of a luxury hobby. On the one hand, games in the broadest sense are more accessible than ever – you’re three taps away from playing Monopoly Go on a phone at any moment. But the kinds of games I grew up with and love to write about, games that feel like worlds rather than temporary diversions, are now increasingly locked behind a spending barrier. With the increasing scarcity of physical discs and cartridges, you can’t even reliably buy them second hand any more.
I guess there’s one advantage to the increasing cost of collector’s editions: the price has removed any lingering temptation to buy them. God knows I do not need more stuff.

Keith has been playing Silver Pines, a neo-noir detective drama with point-and-click adventure sensibilities. “As I played, I discovered countless references to 80s and 90s neo-noir culture – from Blue Velvet to Twin Peaks,” he writes in our review.

“It was a pleasure to explore every broken-down movie theatre, oily car garage and sweat-stinking interrogation room, collecting weird trinkets and working out how they’d all fit together – then exploring them again (and again) when the answers failed to show up. Silver Pines is a game to sit back and wallow in, like a private eye, kicking off his wingtip shoes and pulling that bottle of bourbon from the bottom drawer as rain trickles down the window and sodium street lights paint the walls a sickly shade of yellow.”
Available on: PC, PS5, Switch 2 Estimated playtime: 12 hours

Award-winning UK studio Ninja Theory has reportedly begun laying off staff. The creator of Hellblade was one of the developers affected by Microsoft’s programme of lay-offs and studio closures in July, and according to Xbox COO Matt Booty two agreements to keep the studio running have failed. It is a sad end to one of the UK’s most interesting development houses.

Meanwhile, Windows Central obtained the transcript to a recent in-house meeting held for Xbox staff by Xbox CEO Asha Sharma. In it, Sharma refers to the next generation Xbox platform currently known as Project Helix as “a family of devices” rather than a single console. “There is not one device that fits all,” she stated. “We will certainly have a great console first, but we also know that many players will be on the go.” Could the ROG Xbox Ally, launched in partnership with Asus last year, have just been a beta test for a fully fledged handheld Xbox?

The news site GamesIndustry.Biz has an interesting feature on Zach Cregger’s Resident Evil movie and how it has affected the Resident Evil games. Although the film led to a modest uptick in sales, the real value of movie and TV tie-ins, according to industry analysts, is that they keep those franchises in the minds of gamers so that subsequent titles benefit from the exposure. As game development cycles continue to widen, it looks like we can expect a lot more movies and TV shows to fill in the gaps.
From Super Bowl champ to master architect: Mike Tomlin’s sprawling Minecraft city is magnificent
Gears of War: E-Day – an alien invasion shouldn’t be this boring | ★★★☆☆
A question from my friend David via email:
“I keep hearing that game publishers are avoiding the whole of November because of GTA 6 – will there really be NO choice for those of us who don’t want to shoot stuff and run people over?”

Thankfully, it’s only the big western publishers who are staying clear of the GTA 6 launch window – lots of other developers are diving in regardless. Cozy strategy game Flame, Forest and Flood (try saying that three times) is launching on the same day as GTA, offering a delightful tactical alternative, set in a hex-based woodland idyl. Staying on a rural theme, the purposefully rage-inducing “precision platformer” Trees Hate You is a woodland hiking game, where you are attacked by nature. Alternatively, Football Manager 2027 is arriving on 10 November, so instead of leading a gang of drug dealers into a bloody turf war, you could lead Plymouth Argyle into the Premier League. I’m not sure which scenario is more challenging.
If you have a question for Question Block – or anything else to say about the newsletter – hit reply or email us at pushingbuttons@theguardian.com.

items.title: ‘My first photographs coincided with me falling in love’: why children have always adored taking pictures
paragraphs: What was the first photograph you took? Though most of us use cameraphones every day, few think about how the habit started or even why we choose the pictures we keep. Photography is one of the most popular hobbies in the world, typically picked up in childhood, but its impact – particularly pre-smartphone and digital imagery – has not been much studied. This lapse fascinates Annebella Pollen, professor of visual and material culture at the University of Brighton.

“My generation is used to being asked: ‘What was the first record you bought?’ Music is seen as a key part of identity formation, but what if something similar crystallises when we handle a camera?” she asks. “I certainly remember my first photos, because they coincided with me falling in love, as a 10-year-old, with a beautiful boy at school. I pursued him with my camera.”

Pollen’s question sent her down a rabbit hole into the fascinating history of a pastime that says a lot about how we see children and how they see themselves. As well as photographic museums which, understandably, have pretty limited archives of kids’ photography, she went through marketing campaigns, school records and photography books and magazines written for children. She also looked at social projects from the 1930s to the present day which gave cameras to children to help them develop personal skills and careers.
It’s a story that she tells in her new book Whippersnappers: How Children Became Photographers and in the exhibition Snap Happy! at The Photographers’ Gallery in London.

Of course, AI, apps and the ubiquity of cameraphones bring many new risks to photography, but Pollen’s historical research is a reminder of its benefits. As she says: “It can give children an accessible means of communication and autonomy; offering a space to try out tastes and identities in nonverbal and low-stakes ways. It lets you curate a complex, bewildering world into still scenes.”

Technological advances in the 1900s meant photography transformed from an expensive and laborious hobby for the wealthy to an accessible diversion for the masses. As equipment became portable and easier to use, cameras were marketed as so simple a child could use them. The idea really took off: receiving your first camera became a landmark childhood gift, like a first bike or watch, and there was a strong investment by schools in photography clubs.

While public schools may have had darkrooms and equipment from the late 19th century onwards, the Scouts offered a photographer badge from 1910 and by 1933 boys’ social clubs in east London were offering photography classes.

“Looking through school photography club archives,” says Pollen, “you see that long before smartphones children were sneaking cameras into class and taking clandestine photos of their teachers; I found examples going back to the 1950s. Similarly, kids have photographed their pets for more than 150 years – from eagles owned by Etonians to terrapins in 1960s tower blocks.”

Paul Carter, who ran a social outreach and community programme called Blackfriars Photography Project in 1970s London, brought together a diverse group of children and volunteers in his darkroom, but he still found that what kids really wanted to shoot was friends, family and pets. Even when he organised trips to the countryside, no one wanted to shoot the rural landscape.
Children may have remained steadfast in their photographic interests, but changing cultural attitudes were everywhere in Pollen’s research.

“In the earliest days, photography was a privilege; those who had access to expensive specialist equipment were those with time and money,” she says. “These children were expected to act as apprentice adults and their photographic views were not meant to communicate anything childish. By the mid-20th century, children’s photography was expected to be distinctive: a fresh perspective – a new youthful interpretation of the world. But now what they are deemed to be capable of has diminished in some ways, and there’s increasing fearfulness about their image-making practices. Some adults now view photographic production as risky. Children are increasingly perceived to be putting themselves in danger by making and sharing personal imagery.

“In the early 20th century, however, photography was considered healthy and engaging; it was promoted as outdoorsy and a form of productive leisure. Photography was described as unselfish rather than narcissistic.”

Pollen says that adults use their value system in a slightly arbitrary way when assessing children’s creativity. So child actors or musicians are applauded and the art world often reveres children’s drawing or painting as somehow unadulterated, but the same respect is rarely offered to photographers. Probably rightly so in the case of 18-year-old Brooklyn Beckham’s 2017 coffee-table book What I See. But there are surprisingly few really young British photographers who’ve enjoyed critical acclaim.

Jacques Henri Lartigue is a notable exception: his pictures of family taken during his childhood were described as “one of the most moving experiences of my life” by Richard Avedon. Elsewhere, American names such as Ryan McGinley, Petra Collins or Mike Brodie found fame for their teenage photographs, partly because they documented subcultures or showed unique pictures of worlds that adults couldn’t enter.

One of the most fascinating chapters of this history is the use of cameras and photography as a tool of social inclusion. Since the 1930s, cameras were bestowed on the needy as a form of betterment or as a potential career opportunity. All of these schemes were well-meaning and many had a positive effect on the kids, volunteers and photography teachers who took part. The 1990s brought a boom in projects that wanted to document how children saw the world, such as Kodak’s research and development report in children’s photography.

“These kinds of projects were affordable and low-risk for the organisers when disposable cameras became available,” says Pollen. “They’ve been utilised by artists and journalists, sociologists and charities. The claims made for them are sometimes very ambitious even if the platform they offer children is brief. Most were temporary moments of engagement, and the organisers moved on and the children grew up. Photography can be a powerful tool for communication, but it can’t change inequality.”

The Photographers’ Gallery show focuses on postwar children’s photography and the marketing push to bring a camera into every home during the 1950s. Clare Grafik, head of exhibitions at the gallery, hopes the show will reveal how children shape visual culture.

“[The exhibition] is an invaluable opportunity to think about young people’s relationship to photography, in a way that many people will relate to,” she says. “How young people have interacted with photography tells us a lot about changing societal norms and how children shape and are shaped by developments in technology and visual culture. It also helps us understand more about how the groundwork was laid for young people’s interaction with image-making in the digital age.”

Pollen’s fascination with photography is personal as well as academic. She became interested as a “broke single parent” who spent a lot of time at car-boot sales which often included old family photo albums. “Photos taken by children might seem a niche interest,” she admits, “but it is actually a mass practice. Everyone with a smartphone has a camera in their back pocket, and children’s smartphone usage is growing. The latest study shows that 99% of 15-year-olds own one and 25% of three and four-year-olds. These children grow up with photographic tools at their fingertips; they are making photos as soon as they are able to swipe. I see kids pointing their phones everywhere, all the time. Even before smartphones, most of the population has had access to a camera over the last 50 years. Everyone starts somewhere.”

items.title: Rainmakers: The drones used to seed clouds
paragraphs: On 23 August, Cooper Freeman had no idea clouds above his head were being filled with a silver compound in order to cause rainfall.
Neither did thousands of other residents in Homer, Alaska, who later discovered San Francisco start-up Rainmaker conducted an experiment in that region using cloud-seeding technology.
The company claims it produced 19 million US gallons of water in the sky in three hours.

This approach to weather modification, now more than 80-years-old, involves using planes and drones to disperse compounds such as silver iodide into clouds to form ice crystals. Those crystals eventually become large enough to fall as rain or snow, depending on the temperatures below.

Essentially, cloud seeding speeds up the natural process of water vapor condensing inside of clouds. Gravity then pulls those crystals to the ground. The technology, though, needs ideal climate environments, such as mountainous or cold regions such as Alaska.

Freeman, the Alaska director of the Center for Biological Diversity, isn't just concerned Homer residents weren't widely alerted to these experiments. He's sceptical about what was shot into the clouds, and questions how safe it was for both residents and their habitat.
"It doesn't appear that there was any downstream monitoring to verify that this silver iodide didn't impact the environment," he says.
Freeman adds, "Having a company come in to do this seeding isn't going to solve our water woes, and it feels like a distraction from solving the urgent issues related to water conservation."

Concerns are mounting about the challenges surrounding water security. United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres said in July "our world is using freshwater faster than it can be replenished, external", which echoes reports noting how the past five years have led to the driest period for global rivers, external in more than three decades.
Cloud-seeding technology may be a drop in the bucket, as it doesn't create rainstorms. For example, Rainmaker's 19 million gallons equates to around 0.01 inch of rain across 100 square miles.
Nevertheless, more than 50 countries, external are developing programmes to modify the weather and a surge of start-ups are developing systems to create rain.

As well developed and promising as this innovative field has become, these businesses continue to face thorny questions on safety and efficacy, leading to novel approaches with both finding the right material to spray into clouds and how they do it.

Augustus Doricko, the founder and CEO of Rainmaker, is quick to answer any questions on the consequences of how his company uses the silver iodide compound. It's clear he's been asked about chemical safety many times.

He says Rainmaker releases this form of silver at 20 grams per flight, distributed across thousands of square kilometres. "The resultant increase in concentration on the ground is in the parts per quadrillion, way below the threshold laid out by the FDA [Food and Drug Administration] on what is allowable."

Rainmaker's flights use drones to soar into clouds because without clouds, "we can't do anything," he says, pointing to one of the key limits of cloud-seeding processes. Cloud-seeding sessions have to wait for clouds to form to try to coax them into precipitation.

Their drones are outfitted with silver iodide flairs, and when lit the burning atomizes the water particles into a small enough size so they can stay suspended in the freezing cloud for hours, eventually turning into crystals and later rain.

Rainmaker operates in states such as Idaho, Utah, Colorado and areas of the Middle East such as Jordan. Doricko says, "Jordan residents often only have water for hours per week from their utility because of how scarce water is, and it's a privilege to try to help this storied region."

Cloud seeding's roots began in 1946 when researchers from the General Electric Research Laboratory used dry ice as the first seeding agent. A year later, silver iodide was found to be more effective than dry ice, which quickly turns into useless gas.
While seeding agents caused more rainfall, they didn't move the needle much. In fact, sobering statistics point to how patchy this technology can be in what it pours on the ground.
"With the right conditions, cloud seeding squeeze out about an extra five to 10% of precipitation," says Jon Meyer, an assistant state climatologist with the Utah Climate Center.

What was encouraging, though, for the cloud-seeding sector was a landmark 2017 study that found how silver iodide worked as expected, one of the first reports to observe cloud seeding in action using radar and precipitation gauges.

In the past several years, Meyer has been encouraged to see more companies such as Rainmaker bring innovation to an old industry. "Drones [such as Rainmaker's products] present this new avenue," says Meyer, "and they offer a more targeted nature to these clouds we hope will be responsive."

items.title: Jimmy McGovern claims young offender institution staff 'lazy'
paragraphs: McGovern said he recognised a need for "regimentation" in YOIs, but said keep-aparts - which he believed had got worse following lockdown measures imposed during the Covid-19 pandemic - allowed officers to avoid their duties.
"It allows officers to sit on their backsides all day and do nothing," he said.
"This happened before Covid, but Covid gave them the excuse to keep them banged up even more.
"After Covid, they didn't want to see the kids so it became worse."
When asked about the challenges faced by YOIs in regards to staffing and funding, McGovern dismissed these factors.
"I'm afraid they're lazy," he said. "I've met wonderful prison officers, but I've seen some lazy ones and the keep-apart system enables them to be lazy with an excuse for being lazy."
He said prison officers should be able to handle fights among the offenders.
"It is feral," he said. "They're young boys bursting with energy - cooped up. When they get out, they want to fight.
"But they are prison officers. They should be able to handle that."
He added: "These boys in these institutions are very, very difficult, so there has to be an element of regimentation - rules and regulations.
"I understand how tough it is, but that's your job."
POA chairman Mark Fairhurst said they shared some of the concerns raised by McGovern about violence in YOIs.
"I have the utmost respect for Jimmy's work," Fairhurst said. "He is right to highlight the serious problems within young offender institutions.
"YOIs are among the most violent prisons in the country. Prison officers routinely put themselves in harm's way to prevent serious injury and save lives.
"Many of my members have suffered life-changing injuries and been forced to leave the service following vicious assaults.
"These are not simply naughty schoolchildren. Keep-aparts are an essential safety measure in an environment where serious violence is a daily reality."
Fairhurst said staff at YOIs were "paying the price" of a lack of investment and staffing.
"It is also unfair to suggest staff are lazy," he said. "They are stretched to breaking point by chronic under-staffing and unmanageable workloads.
"Without serious investment in staffing, facilities and rehabilitation, we will continue to see violent and chaotic YOIs - and prison officers paying the price."
The Ministry of Justice said: "We do not recognise these claims about our hardworking prison staff.

"Their dedication helps ensure young offenders are punished as appropriate while being supported into rehabilitation, and we will deliver on our commitment to give children in prison more time outside their room."

items.title: How student went from YouTube to Bake Off
paragraphs: A student taking part in the new series of the Great British Bake Off says he taught himself to bake after "stumbling across a YouTube video".
When Mo Mahir, 22, from West Bromwich, was nine years old, he "found a video of a guy making a mug cake in a microwave", which he said ignited his passion for baking.

"I feel like as a Bengali, we don't really have a lot of cakes or baking in our cultural background," he said. "It started with me mixing a bunch of random stuff. My mum used to always be shouting at me saying 'stop, that's making a mess’."
As part of the Channel 4 series, Mahir, a student at Birmingham City University, has been competing against 12 other bakers.

"Growing up, I've always loved cakes and cookies and stuff and I've always wanted to eat them, but it's just that we never always got the, like, freshly baked stuff. So I kind of had to teach myself," he said.
"Nothing turned out right because I wasn't measuring anything, but it slowly just progressed from there."
On week one of the competition, Mahir landed star baker after he stunned TV judges Nigella Lawson and Paul Hollywood with his peanut and caramel chocolate stout cake.
On week two, viewers watched him bake a biscuit mosaic. His newfound TV fame means he has been spotted while out and about in Birmingham.
"It's been really positive, just like all the DMs [direct messages] I'm getting on Instagram is very supportive and kind.
"When I'm going to town to do a bit of shopping, I do get recognised and people are like rooting for me, and it's just nice to see and hear that."
Mahir's former teacher Sam Hayes, from George Salter Academy, previously said: "When I found out he would be going on, I knew he would do really well.
"I'll always remember being brought some of the delicious treats Mo had baked at home, a very welcome perk of having such a talented student.
"He always was an absolutely amazing baker while he was at school," he added.
Other contestants competing to win the series include a paediatric doctor, a competitive sprinter, a hairdresser and a drag artist.

items.title: Families of missing Yazidis in Syria search for hope
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Kurdish article.

Years after the territorial defeat of the Islamic State militant group, hundreds of Yazidis remain missing in Syria, an issue made more complicated by clashes earlier this year between the Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) and Syrian government forces, as well as the closure of the al-Hawl camp.

Before the recent instability affecting the SDF, the Women’s Protection Units (YPJ) and the Yazidi House Center, which advocates for Yazidi rights in Syria, had helped rescue more than 400 members of the Kurdish-speaking religious minority who were abducted by members of the Islamic State (IS). But more than 2,600 Yazidis remain missing, and search-and-rescue efforts have been halted since the beginning of 2026.

At the Yazidi House headquarters in the northeastern Syrian region of Rojava, cases of more than 900 Yazidi families remain open as relatives wait for information about their missing children and women.

The al-Hawl refugee camp, which once housed family members suspected of having ties to IS, was emptied in February this year. Dozens of missing Yazidis may have been transferred to other camps across Syria, according to reports.

The Yazidi House Center and Syria’s Ministry of Justice have held discussions about finding and releasing Yazidis currently in Syrian detention. Ismail Delf of the Yazidi House Center said the organization has information indicating that some missing Yazidis are believed to be in Syrian camps.

“We have confirmed the presence of dozens of missing Yazidis in certain camps. We cannot disclose the names of the camps because there are still extremist groups that could relocate them,” Delf told VOA. “In cooperation with the National Commission for the Missing, we possess solid information, and we are optimistic that further meetings will soon be held to initiate practical steps.”
Delf also said the organization has submitted requests for the return of all missing Yazidis and that government authorities have pledged to cooperate.

Human rights organizations say that following changes in territorial control in Syria, the central government now bears legal and moral responsibility for developing a clear plan to locate missing Yazidis and return them to their families.

“Today, since the Syrian government exercises control over the entire territory of Syria, mere promises are not enough,” said Abbas Musa, coordinator of the Missing Persons Platform (MPFP) at the Synergy Organization.
“Comprehensive plans and practical steps on the ground must be initiated to resolve the issue of missing persons and protect the rights of these victims,” Musa told VOA.

Amid concerns that evidence about the whereabouts of the missing could be lost, and as new channels for dialogue emerge, about 900 Yazidi families in Sinjar and Rojava continue to wait for concrete action to determine the fate of their missing loved ones and reunite with those who are still alive.

items.title: US cautions nations against supporting Taliban as Moscow hosts Afghanistan meeting
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Pashto article.
The United States cautioned countries against supporting the Taliban as the group took part in a consultative meeting on Afghanistan in Moscow.
A U.S. State Department spokesperson told VOA that the Taliban remains on the U.S. Specially Designated Global Terrorist list.
“We caution all countries against taking actions that could support terrorist groups, including the Taliban,” the State Department said in an email Saturday.
Russia invited a Taliban delegation led by Foreign Minister Amir Khan Muttaqi to the eighth annual meeting of the Moscow Format of Consultations on Afghanistan, which began Monday.
Representatives of Pakistan, Iran, China, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, India, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan attended the meeting, while Belarus and Egypt sent guest delegations.
In his opening remarks, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov praised the Taliban’s rule.
“Five years is a short time to overcome the consequences of many decades of occupation, yet your government’s achievements are evident, and we welcome them,” Lavrov said.
The Russian Foreign Ministry said Friday that Lavrov would meet separately with the Taliban’s foreign minister on the sidelines of the meeting to discuss “bilateral cooperation.”
Russia remains the only country to have officially recognized the Taliban since the group seized power in Afghanistan in 2021.
In July 2025, Moscow recognized the Taliban after removing the group from its list of banned organizations.
In March, U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz described the Taliban’s policies as causing widespread hardship and suffering in Afghanistan.

“The Taliban, through their policies, inflict constant and consistent hardship and suffering on the people of Afghanistan, limiting access to the very basic services and rights, perpetuating human rights abuses, including unconscionable and frankly disgusting restrictions on the exercise of women’s rights. These oppressive policies have led to humanitarian disaster and economic crisis,” he said.

items.title: Kurdistan Peshmerga minister praises US-led coalition support as troops leave Iraq
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Kurdish article.

The Kurdistan Regional Government’s minister of Peshmerga affairs praised the role of the U.S.-led coalition in supporting the Kurdistan Region and Iraq, saying the withdrawal of U.S. forces from Iraq was not unexpected but part of a previously agreed-upon plan.
Peshmerga Minister Shoresh Ismail made the comments in an exclusive television interview with Voice of America.

"Based on the agreement between the Kurdistan Regional Government’s Ministry of Peshmerga Affairs and the U.S. Department of War, a significant amount of money was provided directly to the Peshmerga forces over the past four years, and that support had an impact,” Ismail said.
He said the United States and its Western allies also provided weapons, ammunition and training to Peshmerga forces both inside and outside Iraq.
“I thank them for that,” Ismail said. “The Kurds will always remember the support they provided to the Kurdistan Region during this period, and we will speak of them with respect.”

During the international coalition’s campaign against the Islamic State group, also known as IS, the United States provided the Peshmerga with monthly financial assistance, as well as weapons, ammunition and training. It also supported the Peshmerga Ministry’s efforts to unify its forces.

Under a joint agreement reached with the Iraqi government in 2024, the United States withdrew its remaining forces participating in the mission against IS from Iraq on September 30, 2026. Their main base had been in Erbil.

A U.S. State Department spokesperson told VOA on September 29 that the move reflected “the increased capabilities of Iraq’s security forces, including the Kurdish Peshmerga,” and marked an important new chapter in U.S.-Iraq relations.
Several Kurdistan Region officials have previously expressed concerns about the threat posed by Iran-backed armed groups following the withdrawal of U.S. and coalition forces.

Ismail said Kurdish political leaders’ concerns about the withdrawal stem largely from instability and uncertainty across the region. He emphasized that the Kurdistan Region has no air defense system to protect against drone attacks and said such attacks have increased since the start of Operation Epic Fury on February 28.
“The concern of the Kurdish political leadership over the withdrawal of the international coalition and the United States is due to the deteriorating and unstable situation in the region,” he said.
Peshmerga Minister Ismail described the withdrawal of U.S. and coalition forces as a “difficult test” for Iraq.

“If Iraq and the Kurdistan Region deal properly with the constitution, the U.S. withdrawal will not pose a threat to the security of the Kurdistan Region,” he said. “But that does not mean there are no threats facing the region.”

items.title: From films to streaming prices - how the Warner Bros deal could affect you
paragraphs: Paramount and Warner Bros are coming together to form Skydance
ByFrancisco VelasquezBusiness reporterReporting fromNew York and Regan MorrisReporting fromCalifornia
It has been months in the making but Paramount Skydance has finally completed its $110bn (£82.8bn) merger with Warner Bros Discovery.
The deal welds two legacy Hollywood powerhouses, uniting franchises like Harry Potter and Game of Thrones, into an entertainment behemoth named Skydance.
Yet behind this milestone lies strict rules about what the combined business can and cannot do - from how many films it must produce a year to the editorial independence of its newsroom.
Here are four ways this could affect you and the movies, TV and news you watch.
HBO Max is the company behind Euphoria, a series starring Zendaya

Warner Bros owns HBO Max, home to The Sopranos, House of the Dragon and Euphoria among others. Meanwhile, Paramount Skydance has Paramount+, which streams the likes of Yellowstone, Parks and Recreation and NCIS.
Combining HBO Max and Paramount+ into a single platform or bundle will likely squeeze subscribers' wallets over time.
While existing subscribers to both might enjoy short-term savings, analysts expect overall prices to rise as the combined giant seeks profitability.
The merged company, Skydance, carries a massive $80bn in debt from the deal, even as executives target $6bn in annual cost savings.
Mike Proulx, research director at Forrester Research, said viewers will undoubtedly get access to a bigger catalog.
But he told the BBC: "There's no way that a combined Paramount+ and HBO Max streaming service won't end up costing more for those who subscribe to only one of the services."
As part of a settlement deal with US states who had objected to the merger, Paramount Skydance has agreed to release a set number of films every year for the next five years.
For the first two years, that's 30 movies annually, and for the remaining period it has to release 32 films each year.
That's 156 movies in total - and the majority have to be "wide releases," meaning they must to be shown in cinemas.
The merged studio must also release at least four independent films each year.
If Skydance misses its movie quota, it could be forced to sell its 49% stake in Miramax – the studio co-founded by disgraced Hollywood mogul Harvey Weinstein.
Breanne Gilliam, a corporate lawyer at Maddin Hauser, said the film commitment is meaningful, even if it comes with an expiration date.
"Once those obligations expire, the company will have far more flexibility," she said.
"Temporary rules cannot permanently fix a structural market shift".
Once the five-year deal ends, Skydance could follow rivals like Disney and Netflix by prioritizing streaming over cinema.
As Disney's $71bn buyout of 21st Century Fox in 2019 proved, mega-deals can lead to fewer films in cinemas.
Before the acquisition, 20th Century Fox routinely released 12 to 17 movies annually in theatres, but under Disney that slate scaled down to just three to six a year.
Members of the film and TV industry protested outside Paramount Studios in LA
For those working behind the scenes, the merger of two historic studios has been described as a "disaster" by those on the ground.
Actors and writers recently gathered at Paramount Studios in Los Angeles to oppose the deal, accusing regulators of failing to protect industry livelihoods.
Criminal Minds star Kirsten Vangsness told the BBC she was "heartbroken".
"It's people that make this city," she said. "It's people that make entertainment, it's the everyday creatives that this industry is built on - this is who it hurts."
A report by consultancy CVL Economics for LA County estimated the merger could eliminate roughly 4,500 direct film and TV jobs, while causing $1.26bn in lost wages over three years.
The blow could hit a region that has already lost roughly a third of its film and TV workforce, about 50,000 jobs, since 2022.
Syleecia Thompson, a business professor at National University, said that "it hits small businesses, vendors, caterers and local communities".
She warned that Hollywood may become less of a "single location" and more of a "dispersed network."
Although the settlement establishes a workforce fund to retrain displaced workers, lawyers note it does not block job cuts.
"Nothing in the settlement limits layoffs," attorney Gilliam added.
CNN White House correspondent Betsy Klein reports from outside the building
To address concerns over journalistic independence at CNN and CBS, the settlement creates a news editorial independence board that will be appointed directly by Paramount.
The $110bn deal brings two major US television news operations under a single corporate roof. Before the deal, Paramount owned CBS News, and Warner Bros. owned CNN.

Both networks have faced intense political pressure - CNN was one of a handful of news organisations banned from the White House by President Donald Trump - as well as leadership shifts amid broader industry consolidation.

Paramount chief executive David Ellison has asked CNN boss Mark Thompson - the former director general of the BBC - to remain at the helm after the takeover closes. CBS News's editor-in-chief Bari Weiss will remain in her role.
Yet as Paramount targets billions in cost cuts across the merged company, staff fear the consolidation will trigger significant job losses at CNN and CBS.
Beyond potential workforce reductions, media advocates and legal experts remain deeply skeptical about whether it can ensure newsroom freedom.
Seth Stern, chief of advocacy at Freedom of the Press Foundation, described the Paramount-appointed board as "worthless".
"The board creates the same First Amendment problems it claims to solve, the government meddling in news," Stern said.
Gilliam agrees paper promises mean little without real authority. "An oversight board only has as much power as the agreement gives it. Oversight without authority is just observation," she said.
